a noun, a verb, or a meaningful particle. For Sībawayh said at the beginning of his book:

“Speech consists of a noun, a verb, and a particle that conveys a meaning and is neither a noun nor a verb.”

He thus specified a particular sense of harf: a particle that conveys a meaning and is neither a noun nor a verb. Sībawayh’s contact with the language of the Arabs was still recent, and he knew that they called a noun or a verb a harf. He therefore qualified his statement by saying:

“They divided speech into a noun, a verb, and a particle that conveys a meaning and is neither a noun nor a verb.”

Sībawayh meant that speech is divided into these as a whole is divided into its parts, not as a universal is divided into its particulars. This resembles division as discussed by jurists: real estate and movable property are divided among heirs, with one group receiving a share distinct from that of another. Likewise, speech is composed of nouns, verbs, and meaningful particles, and is divided into these components. This division differs from dividing a genus into its species, as when one says, “Nouns are divided into inflected and indeclinable nouns.”

Al-Jazūlī and others subsequently objected to the grammarians on this point without understanding their words. They said:

“Whenever a genus is divided into its species or the individual members of those species, the name of what is divided must apply to those species and individuals; otherwise, they are not its subdivisions.”

They intended this as an objection to al-Zajjāj’s statement, “Speech consists of a noun, a verb, and a particle.” Yet what al-Zajjāj stated was precisely what Sībawayh and the other leading grammarians had stated. They meant the first, familiar kind of division: dividing existing things into their parts, as real estate and wealth are divided. They did not mean the division of universals—which do not exist as universals

Section

The term harf refers to meaningful particles, which constitute a category alongside nouns and verbs. Examples include prepositions, jussive particles, the two future particles, and particles resembling verbs, such as inna and its sister particles. These particles have well-known classifications in works on Arabic grammar. For example, grammarians classify them, with respect to inflection, into those specific to nouns and those specific to verbs. They say:

“A particle specific to either category, without being like a part of the word itself, governs inflection.”

Thus, prepositions and inna and its sister particles govern nouns, while subjunctive and jussive particles govern verbs. This contrasts with the definite article and the two future particles, sa- and sawfa, which do not govern inflection because they are like parts of the word itself.

They also say:

“By analogy, mā (‘not’) should not govern inflection, because it introduces both nominal and verbal sentences. The people of the Hijaz, however, made it govern inflection because of its resemblance to laysa (‘is not’).”

The Quran follows their usage in His words:

“This is no human being.”

“They are not their mothers.”

They also classify “particles” according to their meanings into interrogative particles, negative particles, particles of specification, and so forth. According to their structure, they classify them—as they do verbs and nouns—into one-, two-, three-, four-, and five-letter forms. Here, the term harf has been transferred from ordinary language into grammatical usage by restricting its meaning. In ordinary language, however, harf encompasses nouns, particles, and verbs. The alphabetic letter-names are also called hurūf, although they are nouns, as with the letters mentioned at the beginnings of surahs: what each name denotes is a letter forming part of a word.

Letters are also classified in another way, into guttural and labial letters. Those mentioned at the beginnings of surahs in the Quran constitute half the alphabet and include the nobler half of each class: half the guttural letters, the labial letters, the emphatic letters, the musmata (non-fluid) letters, and other classes of letters.

The original meaning of harf in the language is a boundary or edge, as in the expressions “the edges of a loaf” and “the edge of a mountain.” Al-Jawharī said:

The harf of anything is its extremity, edge, or boundary. Hence the expression “the harf of a mountain,” meaning its sharp summit, and the words of the Most High:

“And among people are those who worship Allah on an edge,”

through His words:

“and the Hereafter.”

Someone standing at the edge of something is not firmly established. Thus, whoever worships Allah in prosperity but not in adversity worships Him on an edge: at times he displays this worship, and at others he turns

back, like someone standing on the edge of a mountain. The letters of speech are thus called hurūf because they constitute its extremity, boundary, and endpoint: speech originates within the speaker and reaches its endpoint at the boundary and edge formed by his lips and tongue. Hence the Most High says:

“Have We not made for him two eyes,
and a tongue and two lips?”

The word harf can therefore carry any of these three meanings. Then, when speech is written in a codex, this too is called hurūf. Here, harf may refer to the particular shape—each nation has its own distinctive forms, constituting the script in which it writes its speech—or it may refer to the material, or to both together. These written letters correspond to the spoken letters, make them clear, and signify them; they are therefore given the same names, since a person writes spoken words with his pen. Hence the first revelation Allah sent down to His Prophet was:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created,”

through His words:

“what he did not know.”

Thus, in the very first revelation, He, glorified be He, made clear that He is the Creator and Guide, who created and proportioned, and who determined and guided. As Moses said:

“Our Lord is He who gave everything its form, then guided it.”

Creation encompasses all created things other than Him. He then singled out man, saying:

“He created man from a clinging clot.”

Then He mentioned that He taught, for guidance and instruction bring created beings to their perfection. Knowledge has “three levels”: knowledge in the heart, expression by the tongue, and writing

Concrete existence, however, is the existence of things in themselves, and Allah is the Creator of everything. Mental existence, which pertains to the heart, is the knowledge of those things held in the heart. The expression of that knowledge constitutes verbal existence, while writing it constitutes written existence, produced by the fingers. Teaching writing necessarily entails teaching verbal expression, which in turn entails imparting knowledge. Thus He said:

because teaching by the pen entails all three levels. He spoke of teaching in general, then specified, saying:

“He taught man what he did not know.”

People have disputed whether the existence of each thing is identical to its essence. This has been discussed at length elsewhere, where it was explained that the correct position is as follows: “existence” may mean what is established in external reality, while “essence” means what is conceived in the mind. Understood in this way, the existence of things established in external reality is not their essence as conceived in the mind. Yet Allah created what exists in external reality and knew the essences conceived in minds, as He explained in the first surah of the Quran that He revealed.

Both “existence” and “essence” may also refer to what is realized in external reality and to what is realized in the mind. If both terms mean what is realized in external reality, or what is conceived in the mind, then they are not two distinct things in external reality; rather, the one is the other. Part of attaining complete knowledge is to investigate what His Messenger intended by them, so as to affirm the meanings he affirmed and deny those he denied. We must believe everything he reported and obey him in everything he made obligatory and commanded. Then, when we understand these matters in detail, our knowledge and faith increase. As for expressions that occur neither in the Quran nor in the Sunnah, and whose affirmation or denial was not agreed upon by the early generations, no one is obliged to agree with anyone who denies or affirms them without first asking what he means. If he intends a meaning consistent with what the Messenger conveyed, it is accepted; if he intends a meaning contrary to what the Messenger conveyed, it is rejected.

When conveying these meanings, if the wording is confusing or ambiguous, other wording should be used, or its intended meaning clarified, so that the truth is made known in a manner consistent with revelation. Much disagreement among people arises from ambiguous, newly introduced expressions and unclear meanings. Thus, you may find two men quarrelling and becoming enemies over the unqualified affirmation or denial of certain expressions, yet if either were asked what he meant by his words, he would have no clear conception of it, let alone know the evidence for it. Even if he knew its evidence, it would not necessarily follow that someone who disagreed with him was mistaken; rather, his opponent’s position may contain a measure of truth. Each may be right in one respect, or the truth may lie in a third position.

translated_text:
In many books written on the “foundations of religious knowledge” and other subjects, you find the author presenting several positions on a “major question,” such as the Quran, seeing Allah, His attributes, the resurrection, the world’s coming into existence, and other matters. Yet the position conveyed by the Messenger and upheld by the early generations of the Muslim community is absent from those books. Indeed, their authors neither knew it nor were even aware of it. This is among the causes that deepen division and disagreement within the Muslim community—something the community has been forbidden to engage in, as Allah Most High says:

“Do not be like those who became divided and disagreed after clear proofs had come to them. Those will suffer a tremendous punishment, on the Day when some faces will turn white and others will turn black.”

Ibn ‘Abbās said: “The faces of the followers of the Sunnah and the united community will turn white, while the faces of the people of innovation and division will turn black.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects—you have nothing to do with them. Their affair rests only with Allah.”

And He says:

“Indeed, those who disagree over the Scripture are in profound discord.”

“The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) came out to his Companions while they were disputing about divine decree. One was saying, ‘Has Allah not said such-and-such?’ and another was saying, ‘Has Allah not said such-and-such?’ He said: ‘Is this what you were commanded to do? Is this what you were called to? Those before you perished only because of this: they set parts of Allah’s Book against one another. Look to what you have been commanded to do and do it, and avoid what you have been forbidden.’”

Among the things people have been commanded to do is to act upon the clear passages of the Quran and believe in its ambiguous passages.

Section (*)

Explaining that the magnificent Quran is the speech of Allah, the Almighty, the All-Knowing, and that none of it is the speech of anyone else—not Gabriel, Muhammad, or anyone besides them.

Allah Most High said:

The pronoun in His words, “Say: ‘He has brought it down,’” refers back to “what” in His words, “what He sends down.” What is meant is the Quran, as the context indicates. His words, “And Allah knows best

In the Quran, “sending down” may be qualified as being from Him, as with the sending down of the Quran. It may also be qualified as being from heaven, meaning from above; this encompasses rain descending from the clouds, angels descending from Allah’s presence, and other things. It may also occur without qualification, in which case it is not restricted to any particular kind of sending down. Indeed, it may encompass bringing something down from mountaintops, as in His words:

“And We sent down iron, in which there is great strength.”

It may also encompass a discharge from the backs of animals, as when a male animal discharges semen, and other such instances.

His words:

“The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth”

explain that Gabriel brought it down from Allah. For the Holy Spirit here is Gabriel, as demonstrated by His words:

“Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel—it is he who has brought it down upon your heart by Allah’s permission.”

He is also the Trustworthy Spirit, as in His words:

“Indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of all worlds.”

“The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down”

“Upon your heart, so that you may be one of the warners,”

“In a clear Arabic tongue.”

The word “Trustworthy” indicates that he is entrusted with what he has been sent to convey, neither adding anything to it nor taking anything away from it. A treacherous messenger, by contrast, may alter the message. As He says in describing him in another passage:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger,”

“Possessed of strength, held in honor with the Lord of the Throne,”

“Obeyed there and trustworthy.”

His words, “sent down from your Lord,” indicate several things. Among them is the falsity of the view of those who say that it is created speech which He created in a body

The early generations called anyone who denied the divine attributes, declared the Quran created, and denied that Allah would be seen in the Hereafter a Jahmī. For Jahm was the first to become known for the innovation of denying the divine names and attributes, and he carried this denial to extremes. What distinguishes him in this innovation is the extremity of his denial and his pioneering role in publicizing it widely and calling others to it, although al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham had preceded him in some of this.

Al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham was the first to introduce this into Islam. Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī therefore offered him as a sacrifice at Wāsit on the Day of Sacrifice, saying:

“O people, offer your sacrifices; may Allah accept them. I am offering al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham as a sacrifice, for he claimed that Allah did not take Abraham as a close friend and did not speak directly to Moses. Exalted is Allah, far above what al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham says!”

He then descended and slaughtered him.

Although the Muʿtazilah agree with Jahm on some of these matters, they disagree with him on others, such as divine decree, faith, and even some questions concerning the divine attributes. Nor do they carry denial to the extremes that he does.

Jahm says that Allah Most High does not speak, or that He speaks only figuratively. The Muʿtazilah, however, say that He speaks in a real sense, although their position amounts in substance to Jahm’s. Jahm also denies the divine names, as do the Bātiniyyah and those philosophers who agree with them. The majority of the Muʿtazilah, however, do not deny the divine names.

translated_text:
The point is that His words,

“Sent down from your Lord,”

make clear that it was sent down from Allah, not from any created being. Hence the early generations said, “From Him it originated,” meaning that He is the One who spoke it; it did not originate with anyone else, as those who hold it to be created claim.

Another implication of His words, “Sent down from your Lord,” is that they invalidate the view that it emanated into the soul of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, from the Active Intellect or some other source, as various groups among the philosophers and the Sabians maintain. This view is even greater in unbelief and misguidance than the preceding one.

Another implication is that this verse also invalidates the view that the Arabic Quran was not sent down from Allah but was instead created—either within Gabriel, within Muhammad, or within some other body. This is maintained by the Kullābiyyah and Ashʿariyyah who say that the Arabic Quran is not Allah’s speech; rather, His speech is only the meaning subsisting in His essence, and the Arabic Quran was created to signify that meaning.

On this account, it was either created in some physical body—air or something else—or Gabriel was inspired with it and expressed it as the Arabic Quran, or Muhammad was inspired with it and expressed it as the Arabic Quran, or Gabriel took it from the Preserved Tablet or elsewhere. These previously mentioned views are thus ramifications of this position, for this Arabic Quran must have had a speaker who first spoke it before it reached us.

translated_text:
This position agrees with that of the Mu'tazilah and others like them in affirming that the Arabic Quran is created, as is the Hebrew Torah, but differs from it in two respects.

First: The former say that what is created is Allah’s speech, whereas the latter say that it is not Allah’s speech, but is called His speech only figuratively. This is the position of their leading authorities and the majority of them. A group of their later scholars, however, said that the word “speech” applies to both in distinct senses. Yet this undermines their foundational argument denying that speech can subsist in anyone other than its speaker. Despite this, they do not say that what is created is literally Allah’s speech, as the Mu'tazilah do, although they say that it is His speech in a literal sense. Rather, they regard the Arabic Quran as the speech of someone other than Allah, and as speech in the literal sense. This is worse than the position of the Mu'tazilah and is, in reality, the position of the Jahmiyyah. In this respect, the position of the Mu'tazilah is closer to the truth, while that of the others is the position of the Jahmiyyah in its pure form. Nevertheless, the Mu'tazilah agree with them in substance and dispute with them only over wording.

Second: These people say that Allah has speech consisting of an eternal meaning subsisting in His essence, whereas those who hold His speech to be created say that no speech subsists in His essence. In this respect, the Kullābiyyah are outwardly better than those who hold His speech to be created. Most people, however, say that, upon examination, the proponents of this position have not truly affirmed any speech for Him apart from created speech. For they say that it is a single meaning that is at once command, prohibition, and statement: if it is expressed in Arabic

Then some of them said:

“Regarding the attributes, people either affirm them and hold them to be multiple, or deny them. Affirming them while holding them to be one and the same, however, contradicts the consensus.”

This is the approach of al-Qādī Abū Bakr, Abū al-Ma'ālī, and others. Others, such as Abū al-Hasan al-Āmidī, acknowledged that they had no answer to this objection.

“The point here” is that this verse demonstrates the falsity of this position, just as it demonstrates the falsity of others. His words,

“Say, ‘The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth,’”

entail that the Quran was sent down from his Lord. The name “Quran” denotes the Arabic Quran, both its wording and its meaning, as indicated by His words:

“So when you recite the Quran”.

One recites the Arabic Quran, not its meanings in isolation.

Furthermore, the object pronoun “it” in His words “has brought it down” refers back to “what” in His words:

“Allah knows best what He sends down.”

Thus, what Allah sent down is what the Holy Spirit brought down. If the Holy Spirit brought down the Arabic Quran, it necessarily follows that he brought it down from Allah. Hence, he cannot have brought any part of it down from a created entity, nor from himself.

Moreover, immediately after this verse, He said:

“We certainly know that they say, ‘It is only a human being who teaches him.’ The language of the one they refer to is foreign, whereas this is clear Arabic.”

They were saying that a human being taught him this Arabic Quran; they were not saying that a human being taught him only its meanings. This is indicated by His words:

“The language of the one they refer to is foreign, whereas this is clear Arabic.”

For Allah Most High refuted the disbelievers’ claim by pointing out that

translated_text:
the language of the man to whom they referred—by attributing this Quran to him and claiming that he was the one teaching Muhammad the Quran—was foreign, whereas the Quran is in clear Arabic. He expressed this meaning with the word “yulhidūn” (“they refer to”), because it conveys their turning away from the truth and towards the person to whom they attributed this Quran. The word “ilhād” denotes a wrongful turning away from one thing towards another. Had the disbelievers claimed that he taught him only its meanings, this would not have refuted their claim, for someone may learn something from a foreign speaker in that speaker’s language and then express it in his own words.

It is widely reported in Quranic commentary that some disbelievers used to say, “He learned it from a man in Mecca who spoke a foreign language.” It was said that this man was a client of Ibn al-Hadramī. Since the disbelievers claimed that a human being taught him what the Holy Spirit brought down, and Allah refuted this by pointing out that the man’s language was foreign whereas this is clear Arabic, it follows that the Holy Spirit brought down the clear Arabic wording, and that Muhammad did not compose the wording of the Quran but heard it from the Holy Spirit. Since the Holy Spirit brought it down from Allah, it follows that he heard it from Him and did not compose it himself. This is a declaration from Allah that the Quran, which is in clear Arabic, was heard by the Holy Spirit from Allah and brought down from Him.

A parallel to this verse is His saying, Most High:

“Thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy—devils from among mankind and jinn,”

through to His words:

“So leave them and what they fabricate.”

Likewise, His words:

“And it is He who has sent down to you the Book, explained in detail. And those to whom We have given

the Book know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth, so never be among the doubters.”

“The Book” is a designation for the Arabic Quran, as is necessarily known and agreed upon. The Kullābiyyah—or some of them—distinguish between Allah’s speech and Allah’s Book, saying: His speech is the meaning subsisting in His Essence, and it is uncreated, whereas His Book is the arranged and composed Arabic wording, and it is created. The term “Quran” sometimes refers to the former and sometimes to the latter.

Yet Allah Most High has called the very combination of wording and meaning “Quran,” “Book,” and “speech.” He, Most High, says:

“These are the verses of the Book and a clear Quran.”

And He says:

“Tā Sīn. These are the verses of the Quran and a clear Book.”

And He says:

“And when We directed towards you a company of jinn listening to the Quran,”

through to His words, Most High:

“They said, ‘O our people, we have heard a Book sent down after Moses, confirming what came before it.’”

He thus makes clear that what they heard was the Quran and that it was the Book.

And He says:

“Rather, it is a glorious Quran, in a Preserved Tablet.”

And He says:

“Indeed, it is a noble Quran, in a protected Book.”

And He says:

“Reciting purified pages, containing upright writings.”

And He says:

“By the Mount, and a Book inscribed on parchment unrolled.”

And He says:

“Even if We had sent down to you a book on paper, and they had touched it with their own hands.”

However, the word “Book” may refer to what is written, in which case it is the speech itself; or it may refer to the medium in which it is written, as in His words, Most High:

“Indeed, it is a noble Quran, in a protected Book.”

And He says:

“And on the Day of Resurrection We shall bring forth for him a book which he will find spread open.”

And the point here is that His words,

“It is He who has sent down to you the Book explained in detail,”

refer to the sending down of the Arabic Quran, whatever view is adopted. He has also declared:

“Those to whom We have given the Book know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth.”

He states this in appeal to their testimony, not to declare them mistaken. He says that they know this; He does not say that they suppose it or merely say it. Knowledge can only be true and correspond to what is known, unlike statements and suppositions, which may be true or false. Thus, it is established that the Arabic Quran was sent down from Allah—not from the air, the Tablet, any other physical body, Gabriel, Muhammad, or anyone else. Since the People of the Book know this, whoever in this community does not acknowledge it is, in this respect, inferior to those People of the Book who do acknowledge it.

This does not contradict what has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and others among the early generations in explaining His words,

“Indeed, We sent it down on the Night of Decree,”

namely, that He sent it down to Bayt al-ʿIzzah (the House of Honour) in the lowest heaven, then subsequently sent it down in separate instalments according to events. Nor does it contradict its having been written in the Preserved Tablet before being sent down, as He, Most High, says:

“Rather, it is a glorious Quran, in a Preserved Tablet.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Indeed, it is a noble Quran, in a protected Book, touched by none but the purified.”

And He, Most High, says:

“No indeed! It is a reminder—so whoever wills may take heed of it—in honoured pages, exalted and purified, in the hands of scribes, noble and righteous.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Indeed, it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and full of wisdom.”

For its being written in the Preserved Tablet and in purified pages in the hands of the angels does not preclude Gabriel having brought it down from Allah, whether Allah wrote it before sending Gabriel with it or afterward. If He sent it down in written form to Bayt al-ʿIzzah (the House of Honour), all at once on the Night of Decree, then He had written all of it before sending it down.

Allah, Most High, knows what has been, what will be, and what will not be—and how it would be if it were to occur. He, glorified is He, determined the destinies of all creatures and recorded His servants’ deeds before they performed them, as is explicitly established in the Book, the Sunnah, and the reports from the early generations. Then He commands the angels to record those deeds after they perform them. He thus compares the record made before the deeds occurred with the record made afterward, and there is no discrepancy between them. This is what Ibn ʿAbbās and others among the early generations said, and it is true. If He has recorded what He creates as distinct from Himself before creating it, how can it be considered implausible that He should write His speech, with which He sends His angels, before sending them with it?

The claim that Gabriel took the Quran from the Book and did not hear it from Allah is false for several reasons.

Among them is the following: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, wrote the Torah for Moses with His own hand. Thus, the Children of Israel took Allah’s speech from the Book in which He, glorified and exalted is He, had written it. If, then, Muhammad received it from Gabriel, and Gabriel from the Book,

then the Children of Israel would rank one degree higher than Muhammad. Likewise, whoever says that He conveyed the meanings to Gabriel and that Gabriel expressed them in Arabic speech necessarily implies that Gabriel received them by inspiration—a kind of inspiration granted even to individual believers.

As Allah, Most High, says:

“And when I inspired the disciples: ‘Believe in Me and in My Messenger.’”

And He says:

“We inspired the mother of Moses: ‘Suckle him.’”

He also revealed to the other prophets. Thus, this revelation received by individual prophets and believers would be superior to Muhammad’s receiving the Quran from Gabriel, since Gabriel, who taught it to Muhammad, would be on the same footing as any one of them.

For this reason, Ibn ʿArabī claimed that the Seal of the Saints is superior to the Seal of the Prophets, saying:

“Because he receives from the very source from which the angel who conveys revelation to the Messenger receives.”

He thus made his own reception and that of the angel who came to the Messenger derive from a single source, and claimed that his receiving from Allah was superior to the Messenger’s receiving the Quran. It is well known that this is among the gravest forms of disbelief, and that the view under discussion is of the same kind.

Furthermore, Allah, Most High, says:

“We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him, and We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes,”

up to His words:

“And Allah spoke to Moses directly.”

He thus favoured Moses, by speaking to him, over others to whom He gave revelation. This indicates several things: that Allah speaks to His servant with a kind of speech beyond the revelation that is distinguished from this particular form of speech; for

the terms “speaking” and “revelation” each have both a general and a specific sense. Thus, speaking is the general category subdivided in His words:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger.”

Speaking, when used without qualification, is a distinct category alongside revelation in its specific sense, not a subdivision of it. Likewise, the term “revelation” may have a general sense that includes speaking in its specific sense, as in His words to Moses:

“So listen to what is revealed.”

It may also denote a distinct category alongside speaking in its specific sense, as in Surah al-Shūrā. This invalidates the claim that speech is a single meaning subsisting in the divine essence, for on that account there would be no distinction between the speaking with which Moses was specially favoured and the revelation generally granted to individual servants.

Similar to this are His words in the other verse:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills.”

He distinguishes between imparting revelation, speaking from behind a veil, and sending a messenger who reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills. This indicates that speaking from behind a veil—as He spoke to Moses—is something distinct from imparting revelation.

Furthermore, His words:

“The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise,”

and His words:

“Hā Mīm.”

“The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Knowing,”

and His words:

“Hā Mīm.”

“A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful,”

and similar passages indicate that it is sent down from Allah, not from anyone else. Likewise, His words:

“Convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord,”

affirm that what has been sent down to him comes from his Lord, and that his role is to convey it, as he has been commanded.

Furthermore, they say that it is a single meaning. If Moses heard that meaning in its entirety, then he heard all of Allah’s speech; if he heard only part of it, then it has parts. Either possibility refutes their position, for they say that it is a single meaning admitting neither multiplicity nor division. If what Moses and the angels hear is that meaning in its entirety, then each of them would know all of Allah’s speech. His speech encompasses everything He communicates and commands. It would therefore follow that everyone to whom Allah has spoken, or to whom He has sent down any of His speech, knows everything Allah communicates and commands. This is self-evidently false. If, on the other hand, each of them hears only part of it, then His speech has parts, which contradicts their position.

Moreover, His words:

“And Allah spoke to Moses directly,”

and His words:

“When Moses came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him,”

and His words:

“We called to him from the right side of the Mount and brought him near for private conversation,”

and His words:

“When he came to it, he was called, ‘O Moses! Indeed, I am your Lord, so remove your sandals. You are in the sacred valley of Tuwā. I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed,’”

—and the verses that follow—provide evidence of speech that Moses heard. A bare meaning cannot be heard: this is self-evident, and anyone who says that it can be heard is obstinately denying the obvious. They also provide evidence that He called to him. A call can only be an audible sound. In the Arabic language, the word ‘calling’ cannot be understood as referring to anything without an audible sound, whether literally or figuratively.

Furthermore, the Most High says:

“When he came to it, he was called: ‘Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it. Glory be to Allah, Lord of all worlds!’”

And His words:

“When he came to it, he was called from

the right side of the valley, in the blessed place, from the tree: ‘O Moses! Indeed, I am Allah, Lord of all worlds.’” He also says:

“Has the story of Moses reached you, when his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwā?”

And He says:

“When he came to it, he was called: ‘O Moses! Indeed, I am your Lord.’”

This indicates that he was called at that moment and had not been called before it. The word “when” conveys a temporal meaning, as in His words:

Similar examples are His words:

He assigns the call a specific time, indicating that it occurs at that moment and not at other times. He makes that time the time of the call, which is heard only then. Similar examples are the words of the Most High:

“When your Lord said to the angels, ‘I am placing a successor on earth.’”

And His words:

“When We said to the angels, ‘Prostrate yourselves before Adam.’”

There are other such passages that assign particular statements of the Lord to a specific time. The Kullābiyyah and those followers of the four imams who agree with them say that He does not speak by His will and power.  بَلْ هِيَ صِفَاتٌ مُتَعَدِّدَةُ الْأَعْيَانِ لَكِنْ يَقُولُ: كُلُّ وَاحِدَةٍ وَاحِدَةُ الْعَيْنِ قَدِيمَةٌ قَبْلَ وُجُودِ مُقْتَضَيَاتِهَا كَمَا قَالُوا مِثْلَ ذَلِكَ فِي الْكَلَامِ وَاَللَّهُ تَعَالَى يَقُولُ: 
{ذَلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمُ اتَّبَعُوا مَا أَسْخَطَ اللَّهَ وَكَرِهُوا رِضْوَانَهُ}
 فَأَخْبَرَ أَنَّ أَفْعَالَهُمْ أَسْخَطَتْهُ قَالَ تَعَالَى: 
{فَلَمَّا آسَفُونَا انْتَقَمْنَا مِنْهُمْ}
 أَيْ أَغْضَبُونَا.
 وَقَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{ادْعُونِي أَسْتَجِبْ لَكُمْ}
 إلَى أَمْثَالِ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا يُبَيِّنُ أَنَّهُ سَخِطَ عَلَى الْكُفَّارِ لَمَّا كَفَرُوا وَرَضِيَ عَنْ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ لَمَّا آمَنُوا.
translated_text:
those who maintain that it is created is closer, it is because they say that Allah speaks by His will and power, which is the position of the early generations. The opposing group, however, holds that Allah has no power over any of His speech and that His speech is not subject to His will and choice. Rather, in their view, His speech is like His life. They say: “In our view, speech is an attribute of His essence, not an attribute of His action.” Those who maintain that it is created say that it is an attribute of His action, not of His essence. The position of the early generations is that it is both an attribute of His essence and an attribute of His action. Thus, each group agrees with the early generations in one respect but not in another.

Their disagreement concerning Allah’s speech resembles their disagreement concerning His actions, pleasure, anger, will, aversion, love, hatred, joy, wrath, and similar attributes. One group says that these are all created things, separate from Him, which amount to reward and punishment. The other group says that these are all individually eternal realities subsisting in His essence. Some of them then reduce all of these to one and the same will relating to all created things.

Others say: “Rather, they are distinct attributes.” Yet they maintain that each has a single, eternal reality, existing before the things it entails come into existence, just as they said concerning speech. Allah Most High says:

“That is because they followed what displeased Allah and hated His good pleasure.”

He thus states that their deeds displeased Him. He Most High says:

“So when they provoked Our anger, We took vengeance on them.”

That is, they angered Us. He Most High also says:

“Call upon Me; I will respond to you.”

These and similar passages make clear that He became displeased with the disbelievers when they disbelieved, and pleased with the believers when they believed.

translated_text:
Analogous to this is their disagreement concerning His actions, exalted is He, and questions of divine decree. The Muʿtazilah say that He acts for an intended wise purpose and out of a desire to show kindness to His servants, but they do not affirm any wisdom in His action whose end relates to Him Himself. The other group says that He does not act for any wisdom or purpose whatsoever. The former affirm wisdom, but not wisdom subsisting in Him; the latter affirm neither wisdom nor purpose as an attribute of His. Neither group affirms any wisdom or intended end that relates to Him Himself.

The same applies to “speech”: the former affirm speech that is His action but does not subsist in Him. The latter say that whatever does not subsist in Him cannot confer its corresponding attribute upon Him. Both groups deny that wisdom intended by Him can subsist in Him, just as both deny that speech and action that He wills can subsist in Him.

The former group’s position is closer to that of the early generations and the jurists, insofar as they affirm wisdom and benefit in His rulings and actions, and affirm speech that He utters by His power and will. The latter group’s position is closer to that of the early generations insofar as they affirm the attributes and say that He cannot be described merely on account of something created, separate from Him, that does not subsist in Him at all. Nor can any corresponding attribute be ascribed to Him on account of something that does not subsist in Him. Thus, He cannot be one who speaks by virtue of speech that does not subsist in Him, nor can He be wise, generous, and merciful by virtue of wisdom and mercy that do not subsist in Him—just as He cannot be knowing by virtue of knowledge that does not subsist in Him, or powerful by virtue of power that does not subsist in Him. Nor can He be loving, pleased, or angry by virtue of love, pleasure, and anger that do not subsist in Him.

Thus, both the Muʿtazilah and the Ashʿariyyah, concerning questions of Allah’s speech and Allah’s actions—indeed,

all His other attributes as well—agree with the early generations and the imams in one respect and disagree with them in another. Neither group’s position, to the exclusion of the other’s, represents that of the early generations. However, in questions of the attributes generally—indeed, in all questions of the attributes and divine decree—the Ashʿariyyah are closer to the position of the early generations and the imams than the Muʿtazilah.

If it is said:

“Allah Most High has said, ‘Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.’ This indicates that the messenger originated the Arabic speech.”

The reply is:

This is false, because Allah mentions this in two places in the Quran. In one, the messenger is Muhammad; in the other verse, the messenger is Gabriel.

Allah Most High says in Sūrat al-Hāqqah:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger. It is not the word of a poet—how little you believe! Nor is it the word of a soothsayer—how little you take heed! It is a revelation from the Lord of all worlds.”

The messenger here is Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. In Sūrat al-Takwīr, He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, possessed of power, held in honour with the Lord of the Throne, obeyed there and trustworthy.”

The messenger here is Gabriel. Had He attributed it to the messenger because he originated its letters, or originated any part of it, the two statements would have contradicted one another. For if one of them originated its letters, the other could not have originated them.

Furthermore, He said:

“The word of a noble messenger.”

He did not say, “The word of an angel,” or “of a prophet.” The term “messenger” necessarily implies someone who sent him. This therefore indicates that

the messenger conveys it from the One who sent him, not that he originated any part of it himself. This indicates that He attributed it to the messenger because he conveyed and delivered it, not because he originated or first uttered any part of it.

Furthermore, Allah has declared whoever regards it as the word of a human being a disbeliever, saying:

“Indeed, he thought and calculated. May he be destroyed—how he calculated! Again, may he be destroyed—how he calculated! Then he looked, then frowned and scowled, then turned away in arrogance and said, ‘This is nothing but magic handed down. This is nothing but the word of a human being.’”

Muhammad is a human being, so whoever says that it is Muhammad’s word has disbelieved. There is no difference between saying that it is the word of a human being, a jinn, or an angel. Whoever regards it as the word of any of these has disbelieved.

Yet Allah Most High has said:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger. It is not the word of a poet.”

Thus, He attributed it to the human messenger while declaring whoever says that it is the word of a human being a disbeliever. It is therefore clear that what is meant is that the messenger conveyed it from the One who sent him, not that it is speech originating from himself. It is the speech of Allah, who sent him, as Allah Most High says:

“If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of Allah.”

What the messenger conveyed is therefore Allah’s speech, not the messenger’s speech.

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would present himself to people at the seasonal gatherings and say:

“Is there a man who will take me to his people so that I may convey the speech of my Lord? Quraysh have prevented me from conveying the speech of my Lord.”

Reported by Abū Dāwūd and others. Speech belongs to the one who

first uttered it, not to the one who uttered it merely to convey and transmit it. Moses heard Allah’s speech from Allah without an intermediary, whereas the believers hear it from one another. Moses’ hearing was therefore unqualified, without an intermediary, whereas other people’s hearing is qualified by an intermediary.

As Allah Most High says:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills.”

He thus distinguished between speaking from behind a veil—as He spoke to Moses—and speaking through a messenger—as He spoke to the prophets by sending a messenger to them. People know that when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, spoke, he uttered the words, with their letters and meanings, in his own voice. Those who convey his words then convey them through their own movements and voices, as he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“May Allah brighten the face of a person who hears a hadith from us and conveys it as he heard it.”

The listener conveys his hadith as he heard it, but in his own voice, not the Messenger’s voice. The speech is the Messenger’s speech, which he uttered in his own voice; the transmitter conveys the Messenger’s speech, but in his own voice. If this is understood regarding someone who conveys the speech of a created being, it applies all the more to the speech of the Creator.

For this reason, Allah Most High says:

“If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of Allah.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Beautify the Quran with your voices.”

He thus identified the speech as the Creator’s speech, while identifying the voice in which the servant recites it as the reciter’s voice. The voices of the servants are not identical to the voice used in calling

His knowledge is not like the knowledge of created beings, nor is His power like theirs, His speech like their speech, His calling like their calling, or His voice like their voices.

Whoever says of the Quran that Muslims recite, “It is not Allah’s speech,” or, “It is someone else’s speech,” is a heretic and a misguided innovator.

Whoever says that the voices of the servants or the ink with which the Quran is written are eternal and without beginning is likewise a heretic and a misguided innovator. Rather, this Quran is Allah’s speech, recorded in written copies. It is Allah’s speech conveyed from Him and heard from the reciters, not heard directly from Him.

A person sees the sun, the moon, and the stars directly, and also sees them in water or a mirror. The latter is seeing through an intermediary, whereas the former is unqualified, direct seeing. Likewise, speech is heard directly from the one who utters it, and indirectly from the one who conveys it on his behalf. In both cases, what one seeks to hear is the speaker’s speech, just as in both cases of seeing, what one seeks to see is the object itself.

Whoever understands how these two situations coincide and differ, and what they share and do not share, will be rid of the confusion that afflicts many people concerning this matter. These are subtle points that have been discussed at length elsewhere.

Section

If it is asked, “What is the source of this dispute, confusion, division, and disagreement?” the answer is:

Its source is the speculative theology that the early Muslim generations condemned and criticized: ambiguous discourse containing both truth and falsehood. Some of it accords with reason and revelation, while some contradicts them. One group adopts negation, thereby denying both truth and falsehood, while another adopts affirmation, thereby affirming both truth and falsehood. In sum, this is discourse contrary to the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early Muslim generations. Any discourse that contradicts these is false, and nothing contradicts them except discourse that also contradicts reason and revelation.

This arose because, when they debated the world’s having a beginning and the existence of the Maker, the Jahmiyyah, the Muʿtazilah, and those groups of speculative theologians who agreed with them argued that whatever is never free of events that come into being must itself have come into being.

Those who used this argument to establish that bodies have a beginning said:

Bodies are never free of events that come into being, and whatever is never free of such events must itself have come into being. They then adopted different approaches to establishing the first premise. Sometimes they establish it by arguing that bodies are never free of motion or rest, both of which come into being. translated_text:
Those who say that rest is a positive reality maintain that, when motion is absent from a body that is never without either motion or rest, a positively existing state of rest inheres in it. This is the position of those who argue from the alternation of motion and rest that whatever possesses these attributes must have come into being. For those who say that rest is an absence, however, the absence of motion from a subject does not entail the presence of a positively existing state of rest.

Thus, those who hold that motion or originated events can inhere in something after previously not inhering in it, while also holding that a succession of originated events is impossible—as is the position of the Karrāmiyyah and others—say that when motion inheres in it, this does not bring a positively existing state of rest to an end. Rather, in their view, this is analogous to their assertion, shared by the Muʿtazilah, the Ashʿariyyah, and others, that He acts after previously not acting. They do not say that the absence of action is a positive reality. They regard motion in the same way.

Many speculative theologians used to say, “Whatever is never free of originated events must itself have come into being,” or, “Whatever does not precede originated events must itself have come into being,” considering this a self-evident premise. For whatever does not precede something that comes into being must either coincide with it or come after it; whatever coincides with something that comes into being must itself have come into being, as must whatever comes after it.

This statement, however, is ambiguous. If it means that whatever is never free of a particular originated event, or does not precede a particular originated event, must itself have come into being, then it is undoubtedly true and undisputed. The same applies if “what comes into being” means the totality of what has a beginning, or what exists after nonexistence, or something similar. But if “originated events” means things that occur one after another without any first event, and it is then said that whatever is never free of them, or has never been free of them, must itself have come into being, this is neither self-evident nor clear.

" ثَلَاثَةِ أَقْوَالٍ "

 فَقِيلَ:
 مَا لَا يَخْلُو عَنْ الْحَوَادِثِ فَهُوَ حَادِثٌ وَبِامْتِنَاعِ حَوَادِثَ لَا أَوَّلَ لَهَا مُطْلَقًا وَهَذَا قَوْلُ الْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَمَنْ اتَّبَعَهُمْ مِنْ الكَرَّامِيَة وَالْأَشْعَرِيَّةِ وَمَنْ دَخَلَ مَعَهُمْ مِنْ الْفُقَهَاءِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ.
 وَقِيلَ:
 بَلْ يَجُوزُ دَوَامُ الْحَوَادِثِ مُطْلَقًا وَلَيْسَ كُلُّ مَا قَارَنَ حَادِثًا بَعْدَ حَادِثٍ لَا إلَى أَوَّلَ يَجِبُ أَنْ يَكُونَ حَادِثًا؛ بَلْ يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَكُونَ قَدِيمًا سَوَاءٌ كَانَ وَاجِبًا بِنَفْسِهِ أَوْ بِغَيْرِهِ وَرُبَّمَا عُبِّرَ عَنْهُ بِالْعِلَّةِ وَالْمَعْلُولِ وَالْفَاعِلِ وَالْمَفْعُولِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ وَهَذَا قَوْلُ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ الْقَائِلِينَ بِقِدَمِ الْعَالَمِ وَالْأَفْلَاكِ كَأَرِسْطُو وَأَتْبَاعِهِ مِثْلِ ثامسطيوس وَالْإِسْكَنْدَرِ الأفريدوسي وبرقلس وَالْفَارَابِيّ وَابْنِ سِينَا وَأَمْثَالِهِمْ. وَأَمَّا جُمْهُورُ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ الْمُتَقَدِّمِينَ عَلَى أَرِسْطُو فَلَمْ يَكُونُوا يَقُولُونَ
translated_text:
Rather, this issue has bewildered many minds and occasioned much dispute and contention. Hence, those who argue that whatever is never free of originated events must itself have come into being recognize that this argument is incomplete unless they establish the impossibility of a beginningless succession of originated events. They have offered various arguments for this, which we have discussed elsewhere. There are “three views” on this principle.

One view holds that whatever is never free of originated events must itself have come into being, and that a beginningless succession of originated events is impossible without qualification. This is the position of the Muʿtazilah and those who followed them among the Karrāmiyyah, the Ashʿariyyah, and the jurists and others who joined them.

Another view holds that a perpetual succession of originated events is possible without qualification. Not everything that coexists with one originated event after another, in a beginningless succession, must itself have come into being. Rather, it may be eternal, whether its existence is necessary in itself or through another. This is sometimes expressed in terms of cause and effect, agent and product, and the like. This is the position of the philosophers who affirm the eternity of the world and the celestial spheres, such as Aristotle and his followers, including Themistius, Alexander of Aphrodisias, Proclus, al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, and others like them. As for the majority of philosophers who preceded Aristotle, they did not hold

translated_text:
that the celestial spheres were eternal. Philosophers in both groups disagree over whether attributes and originated events subsist in the Necessary Existent, holding two well-known positions. Many leading ancient philosophers affirmed this, as did some later philosophers, such as Abū al-Barakāt, the author of al-Muʿtabar, and others. I have set out their views at length elsewhere.

Another view holds:

Rather, if that which necessarily entails originated events is contingent in itself—and it is this that is termed a product, an effect, something subject to a Lord, or similar expressions—it must have come into being. If, however, its existence is necessary in itself, it cannot have come into being. This is the position of the leading authorities of the religious communities and the foremost philosophers, and it is the position of the great majority of the people of hadith.

The proponent of this view says: Whatever is never free of originated events and is contingent in itself must have come into being. Or: Whatever is never free of originated events and is an effect, a product, something created or fashioned, must have come into being. For if it is a product that necessarily entails originated events, it cannot be eternal. An eternal effect could be eternal only if it had a cause that was itself eternal and necessarily entailed its effect, such that the effect existed with it from eternity, without coming after it. This, however, is impossible. Being a product is incompatible with being eternal. Indeed, being eternal is incompatible with being contingent: according to the great majority of rational thinkers, both earlier and later, only what has been brought into being can be contingent. This is the position of all the ancient philosophers, such as Aristotle and his followers. Only some later philosophers, such as Ibn Sīnā and his followers, affirmed an eternal contingent being; they differed in

" الْفَلْسَفَةُ "

translated_text:
this from all the ancient philosophers, just as they differed from the great majority of rational thinkers of every other school. Consequently, they contradicted themselves concerning the properties of contingent beings and faced questions they could not answer, as I have explained in my refutation of al-Arba'īn (The Forty) and elsewhere.

The claim that an effect may be simultaneous with its cause is intelligible only when that cause is a condition, not an agent. They say, for example: “I moved my hand, and the ring moved.” The movement of the hand is a condition for the movement of the ring, and a condition and that which depends upon it may necessarily accompany one another. The hand’s movement, however, is not an agent that brings the ring’s movement into being. The same applies to rays in relation to fire and the sun, and similar examples.

As for an agent, its product cannot conceivably be simultaneous with it, whether it acts voluntarily or is supposed to act without volition. Whether it is called an agent by essence, by nature, or however else it may be conceived, its product cannot conceivably be simultaneous with it, as the great majority of rational thinkers, earlier and later, have acknowledged. Aristotle and his followers did not say that the celestial sphere was a product of the Lord, nor that it was the effect of an efficient cause that brought its very being into existence. Rather, they claimed that it was eternal and necessary in itself, and that it had a final cause which it sought to resemble, as in the case of the movement of a beloved who must be emulated. In their view, the celestial sphere moves in order to resemble that cause. Hence they said:

“Philosophy is to resemble God as far as one is able.”

Thus, since this proposition is firmly rooted in the natural disposition of rational people, and merely knowing or being told that the heavens are created, fashioned, or produced entails knowing that they came into existence, it does not occur to anyone of sound natural disposition that they could be produced by an agent who made them while also being eternal, having always coexisted with that agent. Hence, only this small band of philosophers has made such a claim.

Furthermore, whatever necessarily entails temporal events cannot have as its agent a cause that necessitates by its very essence and entails its effect from eternity. For events occurring successively, one after another, do not exist in their entirety from eternity, nor is any individual event eternal. Rather, what is eternal is their continuing succession, one after another. A cause that necessitates by its very essence and entails its effect from eternity cannot have an effect that comes about successively, whether it proceeds from that cause through an intermediary or without one. For whatever occurs one after another arises successively, and therefore cannot be an effect coexisting with its cause from eternity.

This differs from saying that what coexists with it is the cause that necessitates by its very essence and acts successively. On this supposition, it would not, from eternity, be a cause necessitating by its very essence, nor a prior, complete cause of anything in the world. Thus, no created thing would coexist with it from eternity. Rather, the agent would produce its effects successively, and each effect would come into existence when the agent’s agency is complete.

since the effect of a complete cause, which entails all the conditions of causation, cannot lag behind it; if it did, the cause would not be complete. Thus, the existence of the effect necessarily entails the existence of its complete cause, and the existence of the complete cause necessarily entails the existence of its effect. Hence, there is no complete cause from eternity, and nothing among Allah’s creatures is eternal alongside Him, sharing His eternity. Past eternity is neither a fixed boundary nor a particular moment. Rather, whatever ultimate limit the mind may conceive, past eternity lies before it, just as it lies before whatever else the mind has conceived. Past eternity has no beginning, just as future eternity has no end.

An authentic hadith relates that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say:

“You are the First, and nothing is before You; You are the Last, and nothing is after You.”

If it were said that He is the complete cause of anything from eternity, it would follow that this thing has always coexisted with Him. That, however, is incompatible with its being something He has produced. Such a statement is valid only regarding an attribute inseparable from the one possessing it. For if one says, “The essence fully necessitates the attribute,” this means that the essence necessarily entails the attribute—not that the essence originates it. Once the meaning of an originator is understood, clear reason rules out its originating something that has always coexisted with it, whether it is called an efficient cause, a creator, or something else.

It would also be impossible for any temporal event to occur within the effect, because no temporal event comes into existence unless its complete cause exists at the time it comes into existence. Although the cause itself may have existed beforehand, all the conditions of causation must be fully present when the effect comes into existence

All of this is impossible. It is therefore impossible for Him to cause any temporal event from eternity, or to cause from eternity anything that necessarily entails temporal events, for something cannot exist without what it necessarily entails. Thus, anything produced that necessarily entails temporal events cannot be eternal.

If it is said, “His essence necessitates the second temporal event on condition that the first has ceased,” the reply is:

“He does not, then, perpetually necessitate any single thing, so none of the things He produces can be eternal alongside Him.”

A further reply is:

“This can only be so if His essence has successive states that account for the differences between the things He produces. But if it is assumed that no successive states subsist in His essence, and that its state when a temporal event occurs is the same as before it, then His producing successive temporal events external to Himself is even more impossible than His producing a particular temporal event. If they regard the latter as impossible, the former is all the more so.”

Whenever successive states subsist in the essence, every argument they advance for the eternity of anything in the world is invalidated. The eternity of anything in the world is also impossible if whatever is produced must have an agent, and what is produced by a temporally occurring act can only be temporal. This is discussed at length elsewhere.

translated_text:
Section

With the principle underlying people’s disagreement over the question of Allah’s speech now established, those who held without qualification that whatever does not precede temporal events is itself temporal disagreed over Allah’s speech.

Many of them said: “Speech occurs only through the speaker’s will and power, and is therefore temporal, like other temporal events.” Then one group said: “Temporal events do not subsist in the Lord, so speech must be created in something other than Him.” Thus they made His speech one created thing among others, drawing no distinction between “He spoke” and “He acted.”

Yet it is known that created things are not attributes of the Creator. He is not characterized by the colours, sounds, smells, movement, knowledge, power, hearing, or sight that He creates in others. How, then, could He be characterized by speech that He creates in others? If that were possible, whatever He creates by causing inanimate objects to speak would be His speech. Anyone who knows that He creates His servants’ speech and actions would then be obliged to say that every utterance in existence is His speech, as one of the Ittihādiyya said:

“Every utterance in existence is His speech;
Prose or verse—it is all the same to us.”

This is the position of the Jahmiyya, the Najjāriyya, the Dirāriyya, and others, for these groups

Many of those who hold without qualification that a beginningless succession of temporal events is impossible said: “Speech is inseparable from the Lord’s essence, just as life is. It does not depend on His will and power; rather, it is eternal, just as life is eternal. For if we said that it occurs by His power and will, it would necessarily be temporally originated. It would then have to be either created or subsist in the Lord’s essence. The latter would entail temporal events subsisting in Him, which would entail an infinite regress of temporal events, because whatever is capable of receiving something is never without either it or its opposite.”

They said: “An infinite regress of temporal events is impossible”—for the argument here proceeds from this premise.

Then, having affirmed the eternity of speech itself, they disagreed about it. One group said:

original_text:
الْقَدِيمُ لَا يَكُونُ حُرُوفًا وَلَا أَصْوَاتًا؛ لِأَنَّ الصَّوْتَ يَسْتَحِيلُ بَقَاؤُهُ كَمَا يَسْتَحِيلُ بَقَاءُ الْحَرَكَةِ وَمَا امْتَنَعَ بَقَاؤُهُ امْتَنَعَ قِدَمُ عَيْنِهِ بِطَرِيقِ الْأَوْلَى وَالْأَحْرَى فَيَمْتَنِعُ قِدَمُ شَيْءٍ مِنْ الْأَصْوَاتِ الْمُعَيَّنَةِ كَمَا يَمْتَنِعُ قِدَمُ شَيْءٍ مِنْ الْحَرَكَاتِ الْمُعَيَّنَةِ. لِأَنَّ تِلْكَ لَا تَكُونُ كَلَامًا إلَّا إذَا كَانَتْ مُتَعَاقِبَةً وَالْقَدِيمُ لَا يَكُونُ مَسْبُوقًا بِغَيْرِهِ فَلَوْ كَانَتْ الْمِيمُ مِنْ (بِسْمِ اللَّهِ قَدِيمَةً مَعَ كَوْنِهَا مَسْبُوقَةً بِالسِّينِ وَالْبَاءِ لَكَانَ الْقَدِيمُ مَسْبُوقًا بِغَيْرِهِ وَهَذَا مُمْتَنِعٌ فَيَلْزَمُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الْقَدِيمُ هُوَ الْمَعْنَى فَقَطْ وَلَا يَجُوزُ تَعَدُّدُهُ؛ لِأَنَّهُ لَوْ تَعَدَّدَ لَكَانَ اخْتِصَاصُهُ بِقَدْرِ دُونَ قَدْرٍ تَرْجِيحًا بِلَا مُرَجِّحٍ وَإِنْ كَانَ لَا يَتَنَاهَى لَزِمَ وُجُودُ أَعْدَادٍ لَا نِهَايَةَ لَهَا فِي آنٍ وَاحِدٍ.
 قَالُوا:
 وَهَذَا مُمْتَنِعٌ فَيَلْزَمُ أَنْ يَكُونَ مَعْنًى وَاحِدًا هُوَ الْأَمْرُ وَالْخَبَرُ وَهُوَ مَعْنَى التَّوْرَاةِ وَالْإِنْجِيلِ وَالزَّبُورِ وَالْقُرْآنِ وَهَذَا أَصْلُ قَوْلِ الْكُلَّابِيَة وَالْأَشْعَرِيَّةِ.
 وَقَالَتْ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ وَالْحَدِيثِ وَالْفُقَهَاءِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ:
 بَلْ هُوَ حُرُوفٌ قَدِيمَةُ الْأَعْيَانِ لَمْ تَزَلْ وَلَا تَزَالُ وَهِيَ مُتَرَتِّبَةٌ فِي ذَاتِهَا لَا فِي وُجُودِهَا كَالْحُرُوفِ الْمَوْجُودَةِ فِي الْمُصْحَفِ وَلَيْسَ بِأَصْوَاتِ قَدِيمَةٍ.
 وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ قَالَ:
 بَلْ هُوَ أَيْضًا أَصْوَاتٌ قَدِيمَةٌ وَلَمْ يُفَرِّقْ هَؤُلَاءِ بَيْنَ الْحُرُوفِ الْمَنْطُوقَةِ الَّتِي لَا تُوجَدُ إلَّا مُتَعَاقِبَةً وَبَيْنَ الْحُرُوفِ الْمَكْتُوبَةِ الَّتِي تُوجَدُ فِي آنٍ وَاحِدٍ كَمَا يُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ الْأَصْوَاتِ وَالْمِدَادِ. فَإِنَّ الْأَصْوَاتَ لَا تَبْقَى بِخِلَافِ الْمِدَادِ فَإِنَّهُ جِسْمٌ يَبْقَى وَإِذَا كَانَ الصَّوْتُ لَا يَبْقَى امْتَنَعَ
translated_text:
“What is eternal cannot consist of letters or sounds, because sound cannot persist, just as motion cannot persist. Whatever cannot persist is all the more incapable of being eternal in its individual instance. Thus, no particular sound can be eternal, just as no particular movement can be eternal. For these constitute speech only when they occur in succession, whereas what is eternal cannot be preceded by anything else. If the mīm in bism Allāh (‘In the name of Allah’) were eternal despite being preceded by the sīn and the bā’, then something eternal would be preceded by something else, which is impossible. It follows that only the meaning can be eternal. Nor can there be a plurality of such meanings, for restricting them to one number rather than another would amount to preferring one possibility without a determining factor. If, however, they were infinite, this would entail an infinite multitude existing at a single instant.”

They said: “This is impossible. It therefore follows that there is a single meaning which is both command and statement, and which is the meaning of the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Quran.” This is the basis of the position of the Kullābiyya and the Ashʿariyya.

A group of theologians, hadith scholars, jurists, and others said: “Rather, it consists of letters whose individual instances are eternal: they have always existed and will always exist. Their order is intrinsic, not an order of coming into existence, like the letters found in a written copy of the Quran. It does not consist of eternal sounds.”

Some of them said: “Rather, it also consists of eternal sounds.” These did not distinguish between spoken letters, which can exist only in succession, and written letters, which exist at a single instant, as one distinguishes between sounds and ink. Sounds do not persist, whereas ink is a body that does persist. If a sound cannot persist, it is impossible

أَنْ يَكُونَ الصَّوْتُ الْمُعَيَّنُ قَدِيمًا؛
 لِأَنَّ مَا وَجَبَ قِدَمُهُ لَزِمَ بَقَاؤُهُ وَامْتَنَعَ عَدَمُهُ وَالْحُرُوفُ الْمَكْتُوبَةُ قَدْ يُرَادُ بِهَا نَفْسُ الشَّكْلِ الْقَائِمِ بِالْمِدَادِ أَوْ مَا يُقَدَّرُ بِقَدَرِ الْمِدَادِ:

{وَمِنَ النَّاسِ مَنْ يَعْبُدُ اللَّهَ عَلَى حَرْفٍ}
 وَقَدْ يُرَادُ بِالْحُرُوفِ الْحُرُوفُ الْخَيَالِيَّةُ الْبَاطِنَةُ وَهِيَ مَا يَتَشَكَّلُ فِي بَاطِنِ الْإِنْسَانِ مِنْ الْكَلَامِ الْمُؤَلَّفِ الْمَنْظُومِ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَتَكَلَّمَ بِهِ. وَقَدْ تَنَازَعَ النَّاسُ هَلْ يُمْكِنُ وُجُودُ حُرُوفٍ بِدُونِ أَصْوَاتٍ فِي الْحَيِّ النَّاطِقِ؟ عَلَى قَوْلَيْنِ لَهُمْ وَعَلَى هَذَا تَنَازَعْت هَذِهِ الطَّائِفَةُ الْقَائِلَةُ بِقِدَمِ أَعْيَانِ الْحُرُوفِ هَلْ تَكُونُ قَدِيمَةً بِدُونِ أَصْوَاتٍ قَدِيمَةٍ أَمْ لَا بُدّ مِنْ أَصْوَاتٍ قَدِيمَةٍ لَمْ تَزَلْ وَلَا تَزَالُ؟ ثُمَّ الْقَائِلُونَ بِقَدَمِ الْأَصْوَاتِ الْمُعَيَّنَةِ تَنَازَعُوا فِي الْمَسْمُوعِ مِنْ الْقَارِئِ. هَلْ يُسْمَعُ مِنْهُ الصَّوْتُ الْقَدِيمُ؟
 فَقِيلَ:
 الْمَسْمُوعُ هُوَ الصَّوْتُ الْقَدِيمُ وَقِيلَ بَلْ الْمَسْمُوعُ هُوَ صَوْتَانِ أَحَدُهُمَا الْقَدِيمُ وَالْآخَرُ الْمُحْدَثُ فَمَا لَا بُدَّ مِنْهُ فِي وُجُودِ الْقُرْآنِ فَهُوَ الْقَدِيمُ وَمَا زَادَ عَلَى ذَلِكَ فَهُوَ الْمُحْدَثُ.
translated_text:
for a particular sound to be eternal; for whatever is necessarily eternal must persist and cannot cease to exist.

By written letters, one may mean the actual shape formed in ink, or a corresponding form of the same dimensions, such as a shape fashioned in stone or paper. Removing some of its parts demonstrates that it had a beginning. Alternatively, “letters” may mean the ink itself.

As for spoken letters, these may likewise mean the segmented sounds combined together, or they may mean the boundaries and extremities of sounds, just as the word harf, when applied to a physical body, means its edge or extremity. Thus, one speaks of the edge of a loaf, the edge of a mountain, and the like. This is also its meaning in the words of Allah Most High:

“Among people are those who worship Allah on an edge.”

“Letters” may also mean the inwardly imagined letters: the composed, ordered speech that takes shape within a person before he utters it. People have differed over whether letters can exist without sounds in a living being capable of speech, holding two views on the matter. Accordingly, this group, which maintains that individual letters are eternal, differed over whether they can be eternal without eternal sounds, or whether there must necessarily be eternal sounds that have always existed and will always exist.

Those who maintain that particular sounds are eternal then differed over what is heard from the reciter: is the eternal sound heard from him? Some said: “What is heard is the eternal sound.” Others said: “Rather, what is heard consists of two sounds, one eternal and the other originated. Whatever is indispensable to the Quran’s existence is eternal, while whatever is additional to that is originated.”

وَتَنَازَعُوا فِي 
" الْقُرْآنِ "
 هَلْ يُقَالُ إنَّهُ حَالٌّ فِي الْمُصْحَفِ وَالصُّدُورِ أَمْ لَا يُقَالُ ذَلِكَ؟ عَلَى قَوْلَيْنِ.

 هُوَ ظَاهِرٌ فِي الْمُحْدَثِ لَيْسَ بِحَالِّ فِيهِ.
 وَقِيلَ:
 بَلْ الْقُرْآنُ حَالٌّ فِي الصُّدُورِ وَالْمَصَاحِفِ فَهَؤُلَاءِ الخلقية والحادثية والاتحادية والاقترانية أَصْلُ قَوْلِهِمْ أَنَّ مَا لَا يَسْبِقُ الْحَوَادِثَ فَهُوَ حَادِثٌ مُطْلَقًا. وَمَنْ قَالَ بِهَذَا الْأَصْلِ فَإِنَّهُ يَلْزَمُهُ بَعْضُ هَذِهِ الْأَقْوَالِ أَوْ مَا يُشْبِهُ ذَلِكَ فَإِنَّ مِنْ النَّاسِ مَنْ يَجْعَلُهُ حَادِثًا يُرِيدُ أَنَّهُ كَائِنٌ بَعْدَ أَنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ وَيَجْعَلُ الْحَادِثَاتِ إرَادَاتٍ وَتَصَوُّرَاتٍ لَا حُرُوفًا وَأَصْوَاتًا. وَالدَّارِبِيَّ وَغَيْرُهُ يَمِيلُونَ إلَى هَذَا الْقَوْلِ؛ فَإِنَّهُ إمَّا أَنْ يَجْعَلَ كَلَامَ اللَّهِ حَادِثًا أَوْ قَدِيمًا وَإِذَا كَانَ حَادِثًا فَإِمَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ حَادِثًا فِي غَيْرِهِ وَإِمَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ حَادِثًا فِي ذَاتِهِ وَإِذَا كَانَ قَدِيمًا فَإِمَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ الْقَدِيمُ الْمَعْنَى فَقَطْ أَوْ اللَّفْظَ فَقَطْ أَوْ كِلَاهُمَا فَإِذَا كَانَ الْقَدِيمُ هُوَ الْمَعْنَى فَقَطْ لَزِمَ أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ الْكَلَامُ الْمَقْرُوءُ كَلَامَ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى ثُمَّ الْكَلَامُ فِي ذَلِكَ الْمَعْنَى قَدْ عُرِفَ. وَأَمَّا قِدَمُ اللَّفْظِ فَقَطْ فَهَذَا لَمْ يَقُلْ بِهِ أَحَدٌ؛ لَكِنْ مِنْ النَّاسِ مَنْ يَقُولُ إنَّ الْكَلَامَ الْقَدِيمَ هُوَ اللَّفْظُ. وَأَمَّا مَعْنَاهُ فَلَيْسَ هُوَ دَاخِلًا فِي مُسَمَّى الْكَلَامِ بَلْ هُوَ الْعِلْمُ وَالْإِرَادَةُ وَهُمَا قَدِيمَانِ لَكِنْ لَيْسَ ذَلِكَ دَاخِلًا فِي مُسَمَّى الْكَلَامِ فَهَذَا يَقُولُ الْكَلَامُ الْقَدِيمُ هُوَ اللَّفْظُ
translated_text:
It was also said: “Rather, the eternal sound is distinct from what is heard from the servant.”

They also differed over whether the Quran may be said to inhere in the written copy and in people’s hearts, holding two views. Some said: “It is manifest in what is originated, but does not inhere in it.” Others said: “Rather, the Quran inheres in people’s hearts and in written copies.”

These groups—the Khalqiyya, Hādithiyya, Ittihādiyya, and Iqtirāniyya—base their positions on the principle that whatever does not precede originated things is itself originated, without qualification. Anyone who adopts this principle is necessarily committed to some of these positions or something similar. Some people regard it as originated, meaning that it comes into existence after not existing, and hold that what originates consists of volitions and conceptions, not letters and sounds. Al-Dāribī and others incline towards this position.

For one must regard Allah’s speech as either originated or eternal. If it is originated, it must originate either in something other than Him or in His own essence. If it is eternal, then either its meaning alone is eternal, its wording alone is eternal, or both are eternal. If its meaning alone is eternal, it necessarily follows that the speech recited is not the speech of Allah Most High. The discussion concerning that meaning has already been set out.

As for the wording alone being eternal, no one has held this view. Some people, however, say that eternal speech is the wording, while its meaning is not included in what is designated as speech. Rather, its meaning is knowledge and will, both of which are eternal, but neither is included in what is designated as speech. Thus, such a person says that eternal speech is the wording

As for “the second group,” who held, without qualification, that originated events may have no beginning, and that what is eternal and necessary in itself may undergo successive originated events without qualification, even if it is contingent rather than necessary in itself—these are the proponents of the eternity of the world. They hold that the celestial spheres are eternal and that they have always been, and will always remain, effects of an eternal, beginningless cause. Those among them who affiliate themselves with religious traditions, such as Ibn Sīnā and others, maintain that the spheres emanate from that which is necessary in itself and which, by its very essence, necessitates their existence.

Aristotle and his followers, however, maintained that the spheres have a final cause, which they seek to resemble through their motion, just as the beloved moves the lover. They did not affirm an originator that necessitates their existence, nor a self-subsisting cause that necessitates it. Nor did they say that the celestial sphere is contingent in itself and necessary through another. Rather, according to them, the celestial sphere is necessary in itself. Yet they also maintained that it has a final cause, which it seeks to resemble through its motion, and without which it cannot subsist. Thus, they made what is necessary in itself and has no agent dependent upon a final cause separate from it. This is the true substance of the position of Aristotle and his followers.

For this reason, they did not affirm that the First knows anything other than itself, since, according to them, the First did not originate the celestial sphere. For an originator must know what it brings into being, as Allah says:

“Does He who created not know, when He is the Most Subtle, the All-Aware?”

If they say that motion occurs through its mediation—that is, through the mediation of the celestial sphere’s motion—they may be told: The very issue under discussion is the origination of celestial motion. Motion that comes into being successively cannot be brought about by a complete, eternal cause that necessarily entails its effect, for this would combine two contradictories. To maintain that an effect coexists with its cause from eternity and exists alongside it contradicts the claim that the effect, or any part of it, does not exist from eternity. Indeed, what brings about this motion cannot be a simple essence in which no attributes or states subsist that entail the occurrence of successive, differing events. Nor can it be an essence endowed with attributes but in which no states subsist that necessitate the occurrence of the events mentioned. For the renewal and multiplicity found in effects cannot proceed from a single cause that is simple in every respect. Thus, the true substance of their position is that events in the higher and lower realms have no originator.

These thinkers say that Allah’s speech is what emanates upon purified souls, just as Allah’s angels, according to them, are the luminous forms that take shape within those souls. Thus, they affirm no speech of His beyond what exists in human souls, nor any angels beyond what exists in their souls, apart from “the ten intellects” and “the nine celestial souls,” although most of them say that they are accidents. translated_text:
of an intellectual nature—namely intellects, souls, matter, and forms—exist only in minds, not in external reality.

As for the “third group,” who distinguished between the necessarily existent and the contingently existent, between the Creator and the created, and between the Self-Sufficient, who needs no other, and the dependent, whose existence is sustained only by the Self-Sufficient, they said: Every contingent being accompanied by originated events is itself originated, coming into existence after not having existed; it is created, made, and subject to its Lord. Nothing dependent, contingent, and subject to a Lord can be beginningless, let alone be accompanied by events that have no beginning. Hence the motions of the celestial sphere are evidence that it originated, as previously indicated.

As for “the Lord, exalted is He,” if it is said that He has always spoken whenever He wills, or has always done whatever He wills, there is nothing impossible about His perpetually speaking by His will and power, or His perpetually acting by His will and power. Rather, this is necessary, because speech is an attribute of perfection involving no deficiency. The Lord is therefore more entitled to possess the attribute of speech than anyone else who possesses it. For every perfection involving no deficiency that belongs to a created being is more fittingly attributed to the Creator: the eternal, necessarily existent Creator is more entitled to absolute perfection than the originated, contingent creature. Moreover, every perfection possessed by a created being comes only from the Creator.

Any perfection that He can possess must necessarily belong to Him. For if it did not necessarily belong to Him, it would either be impossible—which is absurd, since it contradicts the premise—or contingent, in which case His possessing it would depend on another, and the Lord
