Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Concerning the words of Allah Most High:

“If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of Allah.”

Here He calls it the speech of Allah, while elsewhere He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.”

What does this mean? A group of those who maintain that the Quran is an expression of Allah’s speech claim that this supports their position. They then say:

“You believe that Moses—may Allah’s blessings be upon him—truly heard the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, directly from Allah, without any intermediary. Yet you say that what you hear is truly Allah’s speech, although you hear it through intermediaries in different voices. What is the difference between the two?

“You also say that the Quran is an attribute of Allah Most High and that His attributes are without beginning. If you say that this is the very speech of Allah Most High, then you have affirmed divine indwelling, yet you declare those who profess divine indwelling and union to be disbelievers. If you say otherwise, you have adopted our position.”

We ask you for an answer to this upon which we may rely, if Allah Most High wills.

He replied:

All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds. This verse is true, as Allah has stated, and it is not the case that

either verse contradicts the other in any way. Nor does either provide evidence for a false position, even though some people may cite either verse in support of one. For His words:

“If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of Allah”

indicate that he hears Allah’s speech from the reciter who conveys it, and that what Muslims recite is Allah’s speech. Similarly, the hadith of Jābir in the Sunan collections states:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to present himself to the people at the gathering, saying: ‘Is there no man who will take me to his people so that I may convey the speech of my Lord? For Quraysh have prevented me from conveying the speech of my Lord.’”

The report concerning Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, relates that when he went out to the polytheists and recited to them:

“Alif Lām Mīm. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land. But after their defeat they will be victorious,”

they asked him, “Is this your speech or your companion’s?”

He replied, “It is neither my speech nor my companion’s; rather, it is Allah’s speech.”

Allah Most High has also said:

“Leave Me with the one I created alone, and granted abundant wealth, and sons at his side, and made life easy for him. Yet he desires that I give him more. No! He has stubbornly opposed Our signs. I will burden him with an arduous ascent. Indeed, he thought and calculated. May he be destroyed—how he calculated! Again, may he be destroyed—how he calculated! Then he looked; then he frowned and scowled; then he turned away in arrogance and said, ‘This is nothing but magic handed down. This is nothing but the word of a human being.’”

Thus, whoever says that this Quran is the word of a human being makes a statement resembling that of the man created alone, whom Allah cast into Saqar. It is common knowledge among rational people that someone who conveys another’s speech—like one who conveys the words of

the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Actions are judged by intentions, and each person will have only what he intended”—when people hear this from the one conveying it, they say: “This is a hadith of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; these are the words of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.” If the one conveying it were to say, “These are my words and my speech,” people would declare him a liar, knowing that speech belongs to the one who first uttered and originated it, not to someone who merely transmits it as a narrator and conveyor. If this is understood when conveying the speech of a created being, how can it not be understood when conveying the speech of the Creator, whose speech has an even greater right not to be attributed to anyone other than the Creator, exalted and sublime is He?

The Most High has stated that it was sent down from Him, saying:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth.”

He also says:

“Hā Mīm. A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.”

“Hā Mīm. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

Gabriel, Allah’s messenger from among the angels, brought it to Allah’s Messenger from among mankind, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind, and both convey it, as He says:

“O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord.”

He also says:

“Except a messenger whom He has chosen; then He appoints guards before him and behind him, so that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord.”

Nevertheless, it is Allah’s speech. Neither Gabriel nor Muhammad has any role in it beyond conveying and delivering it. Likewise, those who teach it in our time and those who recite it, whether during prayer or outside prayer, do no more than that: they have originated none of its letters or meanings. Allah Most High says:

“When you recite the Quran, seek refuge with Allah from

Satan, the accursed,” up to His words:

“When We substitute one verse for another—and Allah knows best what He sends down—they say, ‘You are only a fabricator.’ Rather, most of them do not know.”

“Say: ‘The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth, to strengthen those who believe, and as guidance and glad tidings for the Muslims.’”

“We certainly know that they say, ‘It is only a human being who teaches him.’ The language of the one they refer to is foreign, while this is clear Arabic speech.”

Some of the polytheists claimed that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had learned it from one of the non-Arabs in Mecca—either a slave of Ibn al-Hadramī or someone else—as the Quran commentators have mentioned. Thus, the Most High said:

“The language of the one to whom they refer”—that is, the one to whom they attribute the teaching—is a language that is “foreign, while this is clear Arabic speech.”

How, then, could a non-Arab have taught him this when this speech is Arabic? Allah has also stated that the Holy Spirit brought it down from your Lord in truth. This makes clear that the Prophet did not originate the letters and composition of this Arabic Quran, which he learned from another. For, had he done so, it would have been possible for him to have received its meanings from the non-Arab and composed its wording himself. The statement that the Holy Spirit brought down from your Lord in truth what he learned from another demonstrates that the entire Quran was sent down from the Lord, glorified and exalted is He. He did not send down its meanings without its letters.

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills.”

Whoever says, “Allah has spoken to us through the Quran just as He spoke to Moses son of ʿImrān,” or, “We hear His speech just as Moses son of ʿImrān heard it,” is among the most ignorant and misguided of people.

If someone were to say, “We hear the Prophet’s speech—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—just as his Companions heard it from him,” his error would be obvious. What, then, of someone who says, “I hear Allah’s speech directly from Him just as Moses heard it”? Even if Allah spoke directly to Moses with a voice that Moses heard, the voices of created beings are not the Creator’s voice.

The same applies to His calling His servants with a voice heard by those far away just as it is heard by those nearby; His speaking revelation so that the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth hear His voice like the sound of a chain being dragged across smooth rock; and similar matters related in the scriptural texts and transmitted reports. None of these indicates that a creature’s attribute is the Creator’s attribute, or even that it resembles it. Rather, they indicate the distinction between the Creator’s attributes and those of created beings.

Thus, His speech is not like a creature’s speech; its meaning is not like the meaning of a creature’s speech; its letters are not like the letters of a creature’s speech; and His voice is not like a creature’s voice. Likewise, His knowledge is not like a creature’s knowledge, His power is not like a creature’s power, His hearing is not like a creature’s hearing, and His sight is not like a creature’s sight. For there is nothing like Allah, whether in His essence, His attributes, or His actions.

Since the distinction between hearing speech directly from its original speaker and hearing it from someone conveying it on his behalf is firmly rooted in the innate nature of all creatures, this distinction in hearing Allah’s speech from those who convey it on His behalf is too obvious to require lengthy explanation. The leading scholars of the Sunnah—such as Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhārī, the compiler of the Sahīh, in his book on the creation of acts, and others—have explained the distinction between Allah’s voice heard directly from Him and the voices of His servants reciting the Quran or speaking otherwise. No scholar endowed with sound reason and religious commitment disputes this distinction.

These two foolish innovations sparked turmoil and intensified animosity, although the adherents of both positions may explain them in ways that confuse many people. For example, someone who maintained that the sound heard from a person, or part of it, is eternal explained this by saying that the eternal had manifested in what was brought into being, without dwelling within it.

As for “human actions,” I have seen a later writer claim that they are eternal, both good and evil. He explained this by saying that divine legislation is eternal and divine decree is eternal, and that these actions are governed by that legislation and decree. He did not distinguish between divine legislation, which is Allah’s speech, and what it governs, namely what is commanded or forbidden. Nor did he distinguish between divine decree, which is Allah’s knowledge and speech, and the things decreed, which are His creations.

All rational people know as a self-evident truth that commands and statements are two kinds of speech, in both its wording and its meaning. Commands and statements are not attributes of a single subject. Whoever makes commands, prohibitions, and statements attributes of speech rather than kinds of speech contradicts what reason knows necessarily.

In this respect, these people are like someone who claims that existence is one, failing to distinguish between unity in kind and identity as a single entity. For the division of “what exists” into the eternal and the originated, the necessary and the contingent, the Creator and the created, and what subsists by itself and what subsists in another is like the division of “speech” into commands and statements, or into non-declarative and declarative speech, or into commands, prohibitions, and statements. Whoever says that speech is a single meaning that is both command and statement is like someone who says that existence is one and is both the Creator and the created, or both the necessary and the contingent. this position amounts to denying His speech and His speaking. This is the true substance of Pharaoh’s position, for he denied the Creator and His speaking to Moses. Thus, the most thoroughgoing exponent of these views ultimately came to venerate Pharaoh, ally himself with him, and affirm his declaration:

“I am your lord, the Most High.”

Indeed, he went so far as to exalt him above Moses and belittle Allah’s speaking to Moses, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

(Further, one may ask: What do you say about someone’s speech when another person transmits it—as the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the Companions, scholars, poets, and others are transmitted and heard from narrators or those conveying them? Is what is heard from the transmitter, in the transmitter’s voice, the speech of the transmitter or of the person whose words he conveys?

If he says that it is the transmitter’s speech, it necessarily follows that the Quran is the speech of everyone from whom it is heard. The Quran as heard would therefore be the speech of a million reciters, not the speech of Allah Most High. Likewise, the words, “Actions are judged only by intentions,” and similar statements would be the speech of everyone who narrates them, not the speech of the Messenger. In that case, no distinction would be conferred upon the Quran by the statement:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.”

For, according to these people, it is the word of every hypocrite who recites it. Both believers and hypocrites recite the Quran, as is related in the two Sahih collections from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“The believer who recites the Quran is like a citron: its taste is pleasant and its fragrance is pleasant. The believer who does not recite the Quran is like a date: its taste is pleasant, but it has no fragrance. The hypocrite who recites the Quran is like sweet basil: its fragrance is pleasant, but its taste is bitter. And the hypocrite who does not recite the Quran

is like a bitter gourd: its taste is bitter, and it has no fragrance.” On this account, the Quran would not be the word of one human being, but the word of a million human beings and more. The falsity of this is clear both to reason and to religion.

If, however, he says, “It is the speech of the one whose words are conveyed,” then it is established that the Quran is not the speech of the messenger who conveys it, but the speech of Allah. Yet because the angelic messenger might be alleged to be a devil, Allah made clear that it is conveyed by a noble angel, not by an accursed devil. Hence He said:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, endowed with power, held in honour by the Lord of the Throne,”

up to His words:

“And it is not the word of an accursed devil.”

In this passage, He also made clear that the human Messenger whose company we have shared, and from whom we have heard it, is not mad, nor is he to be suspected concerning the unseen. He called him “the companion” because this expresses the blessing bestowed upon us through him: we could not bear to receive revelation except from someone whose company we shared and who was of our own kind. As Allah Most High said:

“There has certainly come to you a messenger from among yourselves.”

And He said:

“Had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and would have left them as confused as they are now.”

Likewise, He said in the other passage:

“By the star when it descends! Your companion has neither strayed nor erred.”

He made clear that both the messenger from among ourselves and the angelic messenger are conveyors. This establishes that it is the speech of Allah.

Since the human Messenger was alleged to be mad or a fabricator, Allah declared him free of both accusations. Likewise, in the other surah, He said:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger. It is not the word of a poet—how little you believe! Nor is it the word of a soothsayer—little

do you reflect! It is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.”

This further shows that He attributed it to the messenger because he conveyed and delivered it, not because he originated and composed it. For He said:

“Indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds. The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down.”

Thus He combined His statement, “Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger,” with His statement, “Indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.” Both pronouns refer to the same thing. Had the messenger originated and composed it, it would not have been a revelation from the Lord of the worlds; rather, it would have been a revelation from the messenger.

As for anyone who takes the pronoun here to refer to something other than the referent of the other pronoun—even though nothing in the wording requires different referents—or who says that this is an expression of Allah’s speech, tell him:

Is what you recite an expression of the expression which, according to your claim, the angelic or human messenger originated? Or is it that very expression itself? If you make this an expression of that expression, then Gabriel’s or the Messenger’s expression could likewise be an expression of Allah’s expression. In that case, the dispute remains merely verbal. For once he says that Muhammad heard all of it from Gabriel, that Gabriel heard all of it from Allah, and that the Muslims heard all of it from the Messenger, he has spoken the truth. After this, his use of the term “expression” is intended to distinguish between the act of conveying and the one whose speech is conveyed, as we shall explain.

But if you say that this is not an expression of that expression, but that very expression itself, then you have made what is heard from the conveyor identical to what is heard from the original speaker

translated_text:
, since you have made this expression identical to Gabriel’s own expression. This, then, invalidates the very basis of your position.

Know that the doctrine of “expression” originated with Abū Muhammad ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd ibn Kullāb. He was the first in Islam to say: “The meaning of the Quran is Allah’s speech, but its letters are not Allah’s speech.” He thus adopted half the position of the Muʿtazilah and half the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah. He had affirmed Allah’s attributes, opposing the Muʿtazilah on this matter. He also affirmed that Allah is above the Throne and distinct from created beings, establishing this more thoroughly than his later followers did.

People had already debated whether conveying another’s speech should be called a reproduction of it. Most of the Muʿtazilah said that it was a reproduction of it. Ibn Kullāb therefore said: “The Arabic Quran is a reproduction of Allah’s speech; it is not Allah’s speech.”

Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī came after him and followed his approach in affirming most of the attributes, and likewise on the question of the Quran. However, he took issue with his description of it as a reproduction, saying: “A reproduction must resemble what it reproduces. This therefore accords with the position of the Muʿtazilah. What accords with our position is to say that it is an expression of Allah’s speech, because the speech is not of the same kind as the expression.”

Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah objected to several aspects of their position.

translated_text:
The first was their assertion: “The meaning is Allah’s speech, but the Arabic Quran is not Allah’s speech.” The Muʿtazilah used to say: “It is Allah’s speech, and it is created.” These others, however, said: “It is created, and it is not Allah’s speech.” For one of the principles of Ahl al-Sunnah is that when an attribute subsists in a subject, the corresponding description applies to that subject. Thus, when speech subsists in a subject, that subject is the one speaking it, just as a subject in which knowledge and power subsist is knowing and powerful. The same applies to “motion.”

This was among the arguments they used against the Muʿtazilah and other Jahmiyyah concerning their assertion: “Allah’s speech is created; He created it in certain bodies.” They replied to them: “If that were so, the speech would belong to the body in which He created it. The tree would then have been the one saying:

‘Indeed, I am Allah, Lord of the worlds.’”

The leading scholars of the Kullābiyyah therefore said: “If the Arabic Quran is created, it cannot be Allah’s speech.” A group of their later followers said: “Rather, we say that ‘speech’ is a term shared by both abstract meaning and ordered letters.” The critical scholars replied: “This undermines the very basis of your argument against the Muʿtazilah. For if you concede that what is truly Allah’s speech cannot subsist in Him, but only in another, the Muʿtazilah can then say that His speech is nothing other than what He creates in another.”

(Second was their assertion: “That meaning is command, prohibition, and statement, and it is the meaning of the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran.” Most people of reason said: “The falsity of what they have said is self-evident to reason.”

translated_text:
Third was their assertion that the meanings and wording brought down by Gabriel, and the meanings and wording conveyed by Muhammad to his community, are not Allah’s speech.

The “question of the Quran” has two aspects: first, Allah’s speaking it, which is the more important of the two; and second, its being sent down to His creation. Discussing the latter is straightforward once the former has been established.

We have discussed this at length in several places, explaining the views of all the peoples of the earth on these questions, the confusion that has arisen concerning them, the grounds for each group’s position, and the meaning of the early generations’ statement:

“The Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated.”

We explained that they intended thereby to refute those who say that no speech subsists in Allah’s essence. This is why the leading scholars said: “Allah’s speech is from Allah; it is not separate from Him.” We also discussed the disagreement among those who affiliate themselves with the Sunnah over whether His speech is connected to His will and power, and the statement of some leading scholars of the Sunnah: “Allah has always been One who speaks whenever He wills.”

When the early generations said, “From Him it originated,” they did not mean that it departed from His essence and came to subsist in another. A created being’s speech—indeed, all its attributes—does not leave it and pass into another. How, then, could Allah’s speech or any other attribute of His depart from His essence? Rather, they said, “From Him it originated,” meaning that He is the One who spoke it. This was a rebuttal of the Muʿtazilah, the Jahmiyyah, and others who said that it originated from the created being in whom it was created.

Their statement, “To Him it will return,” means that it will be taken away by night, leaving not a single letter of it in the written copies of the Quran, nor a single verse of it in people’s hearts.

translated_text:
Our purpose here, however, is to answer the questioner’s questions.

Section

As for the statement:

“You believe that Moses truly heard Allah’s speech directly from Him, without an intermediary. Yet you say that what you hear is truly Allah’s speech, although you hear it through intermediaries speaking in different voices. What, then, is the difference between the two?”

The answer is: the difference between the two is greater than the distance from the foot to the crown of the head. Every rational person distinguishes between hearing the Prophet’s speech directly from him, without an intermediary—as the Companions heard him—and hearing it through those who conveyed it from him, such as Abū Hurayrah, Abū Saʿīd, Ibn ʿUmar, and Ibn ʿAbbās. Yet each listener has truly heard the Prophet’s speech, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Likewise, someone who hears the poetry of Hassān ibn Thābit, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāhah, or another poet directly from its author, and someone who hears it from those who transmit it from him, knows the difference between the two. In both cases, it is Hassān’s poetry, not anyone else’s. When a person learns another’s poetry, he knows that the poet originated its meanings and arranged its letters using the articulated sounds of his own voice, even though the transmitter recites it using his own movements and vocal sounds.

If, then, this distinction is intelligible in the speech of created beings—between hearing speech directly from its original speaker and hearing it through someone who transmits or conveys it from him—how could it not be intelligible when hearing Allah’s speech? It has already been explained that anyone who thinks that what is heard from the reciters is the Lord’s voice has more need of the discipline given to the insane than of discourse addressed to rational people. Likewise, anyone who imagines that the voice is eternal, or that the ink is eternal, holds a view that no person of sound perception would express.

Rather, what lies between the two covers of the Quran is Allah’s speech. It is Allah’s speech, not anyone else’s, that is recorded in the Muslims’ copies of the Quran. Whoever says that what is in the written Quran is not Allah’s speech but someone else’s is a heretic and a renegade. Whoever claims that Allah’s speech has departed from His essence and passed into something else when written in copies of the Quran, or that the ink is eternal and without beginning, is likewise a heretic and a renegade. Even the speech of created beings is written on paper without departing from their persons. How, then, could something similar not be intelligible concerning the speech of Allah Most High?

“Confusion” in matters like this arises because some people do not distinguish between unqualified and qualified statements. For example, a person says, “I saw the sun, the moon, and the crescent,” when he has seen them without an intermediary. “This is unqualified seeing.” He may also see them in water or a mirror; this is “qualified seeing.” Thus, when he simply says, “I saw it,” or “I did not see it,” his statement is understood according to the unqualified meaning of the expression. But if he says, “I did indeed see the sun in water and in a mirror,” this is a correct statement with that qualification. The meaning of an expression varies

translated_text:
according to whether it is unqualified or qualified. When something that changes the meaning is joined to a statement—such as a condition, an exception, or another qualification attached to it, as in His words:

“A thousand years less fifty”—

the expression as a whole literally denotes nine hundred and fifty years, according to the vast majority of people. Whoever calls this figurative usage is mistaken, for the expression as a whole has not been used outside its proper sense. The conventionally established verbal indicators accompanying an expression form an integral part of the statement. With these indicators, the statement does not admit two meanings, nor can the meaning they jointly convey validly be negated. This differs from using the word “lion” for a courageous man.

Nevertheless, whether one calls an expression literal or figurative is a merely verbal dispute. This is the basis on which some have denied figurative usage in language or in the Quran. None of the early generations or the imams spoke in these terms. The term majāz is not known to occur in the words of any of the imams except Imam Ahmad, who wrote in his Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah: “This is an instance of majāz in the Quran.” The first to use this term at all was Abū ‘Ubaydah Ma‘mar ibn al-Muthannā, in his book Majāz al-Qur’ān (Modes of Expression in the Quran).

Among the earlier scholars, however, this meant what was permissible and acceptable in the language. They thus derived it from jawāz in the sense of permissibility, just as jurists speak of binding and nonbinding contracts. Many later scholars instead derived it from jawāz in the sense of crossing over: passing from a literal meaning to a figurative one. There is, moreover, no doubt that figurative usage may become so widespread and familiar that it becomes literal usage.

translated_text:
The point is that when someone says, “I saw the sun, the moon, the crescent, or something else in water or a mirror,” all rational people agree that this seeing differs from seeing the same thing directly, without an intermediary. If someone says, “He did not see the thing itself; rather, he saw its likeness, its image, reflected rays, or the like,” this does not invalidate what people know and say: that he saw it in water or a mirror. Such seeing in water or a mirror is literal, though qualified.

Likewise, the Prophet’s statement, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Whoever sees me in a dream has truly seen me, for Satan cannot take my form.”

It is just as he said, peace and blessings be upon him: the person has truly seen him in a dream. Whoever denies that he has truly seen him in a dream is mistaken. Whoever says that seeing him directly while awake is the same as seeing him through an intermediary, under the qualification of sleep, is also mistaken. Hence the dream-vision admits of interpretation and explanation, unlike the waking vision.

Similarly, whatever words a person hears from him in a dream constitute hearing him in a dream; this is not the same as hearing him while awake. A dreamer may see people who speak to him, while those people are entirely unaware of it. He has only seen their likenesses. Nevertheless, it is said that he truly saw them in a dream. This qualification excludes dreams arising from one’s own thoughts. For “dreams are of three kinds”: a dream conveying glad tidings from Allah; a dream through which Satan causes distress; and a dream arising from what a person thinks about while awake and then sees in sleep. This classification is established in an authentic report from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him,

Just as seeing may be unqualified or qualified by the intermediary of a mirror, water, or something else—so that what is seen varies with the mirror: if it is large and round, one sees accordingly, and if it is small or elongated, one sees accordingly—so too, in “hearing,” a distinction is drawn between someone who hears another person’s speech directly from him and someone who hears it through an intermediary conveying it. In both cases, the aim is to hear his speech, just as, in both cases mentioned earlier, the aim is to see the Prophet himself. When an intermediary is involved, however, the experience varies according to that intermediary. Thus, what is heard varies with the voices of those conveying it, just as what is seen varies with the mirrors.

Allah Most High says:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills.”

He thus made “speaking of three kinds”: revelation alone; speaking from behind a veil, as He spoke to Moses, peace be upon him; and speaking through the sending of a messenger, as He spoke to the messengers by sending angels, and as Allah informed us about the hypocrites by sending Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.

Muslims agree that Allah has commanded them to do what He commands them in the Quran, forbidden them what He forbids them in the Quran, and informed them of what He tells them in the Quran. His commanding, forbidding, and informing are through the Messenger. This is thus speaking qualified by the sending of a messenger, and our hearing His speech is qualified by hearing it from the one conveying it, not from Him. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, narrates from his Lord, reports from his Lord, and recounts from his Lord. He thus relates the speech that his Lord spoke, narrating and recounting it from Him.

If someone who says that the Quran is a “recounting” meant that Muhammad recounted it from Allah—just as one says that he conveyed it from Allah and relayed it from Allah—he would have intended a sound meaning. But what they intend is the meaning conveyed by saying, “So-and-so imitates so-and-so,” meaning that he does as the other does: namely, that he utters speech like Allah’s speech. This is false. Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce its like, even if they helped one another.’”

The crux of the matter is that what counts is the intended reality, not the means sought for the sake of something else. Thus, if someone wishes to see a face, for example, and sees it in a mirror, his purpose is fulfilled, and he says, “I saw the face,” even though this occurred through the reflection of light rays in the mirror. Likewise, someone may wish to hear the words spoken by another person, who composed their wording and intended their meanings. If he hears them from that person or from someone else, his purpose is fulfilled, even though hearing them from someone else involves the intermediary of that person’s voice, which varies from speaker to speaker.

Hearts are directed only toward what is intended, not toward that through which it becomes manifest. This is likewise the case with “the name and the one named.” When someone says, “Zayd came and Amr went,” his sole intention is to report that “the one named” has come

Anyone who supposes that what is described as coming and arriving is the word “Zayd” or “Amr” is mistaken. Likewise, when someone says, “This is Allah’s speech, and Allah’s speech is uncreated,” what is intended is the speech itself, considered in itself, even though it becomes manifest and is heard only through the reciter’s movements and voice. Anyone who supposes that the reference is to the reciter’s voice and movements is mistaken.

Thus, when Abū Tālib al-Makkī recited before Imam Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him,

“Say, ‘He is Allah, the One,’”

and asked him, “Is this Allah’s speech, and is it created?” he answered that it was Allah’s speech and was uncreated. Abū Tālib then mistakenly reported that Ahmad had said, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” Ahmad summoned him and, angered with him, asked, “Did I tell you, ‘My utterance of the Quran is uncreated’?”

He replied, “No, but I recited before you, ‘Say, He is Allah, the One,’ and said to you, ‘This is uncreated,’ and you said, ‘Yes.’”

Ahmad said, “Then why do you attribute to me something I did not say? Do not say this, for no scholar has said it.”

This account is well known. It was related by ‘Abd Allāh, Sālih, Hanbal, al-Marwazī and Fawrān, and al-Khallāl presented it at length in his Book of the Sunnah. Al-Marwazī also wrote a work on the question of utterance, in which he recorded the statements of the leading scholars.

But saying “my utterance” treats the intermediaries themselves as uncreated, which is false. Likewise, if someone sees a face in a mirror and says, “May Allah honour this face and grant it life,” or “May He make it ugly,” his supplication concerns the actual face that he sees through the mirror, not the light reflected in it. Similarly, if he sees the moon reflected in water and says, “It has become full,” or “It has not become full,” he means the moon in the sky, not its reflection. Likewise, if someone hears another person mentioning a man and says, “This is a righteous man,” or “a wicked man,” it is understood that he is referring to the person designated by the name, not the actual sound heard from the speaker. If he were to say, “This sound,” or “My voice when mentioning so-and-so, is righteous or wicked,” the meaning would be corrupted.

One person used to say, “My utterance of the Quran is created.” He then dreamed that someone was beating him while he was wearing a fur coat. Similarly, if you hear someone mentioning a man and say, “I love this man,” or “I hate this man,” your words refer to the person intended by the name, not to the voice of the one mentioning him.

Section

As for the objection:

“You say that the Quran is an attribute of Allah and that Allah’s attributes are uncreated. If you say that this is Allah’s very speech, then you have affirmed indwelling, yet you declare those who profess indwelling and union to be unbelievers. If you say otherwise, you have adopted our position.”

Anyone who understands what we have pointed out will find it easy to answer this objection and others like it. The misconception arises because the statement “This is Allah’s speech” is taken to mean that the same judgments apply to it whether His speech is heard directly from Him or conveyed on His behalf. This is where various groups diverge.

One group said: “This is Allah’s speech, and this consists of created letters and sounds; therefore, Allah’s speech is created.”

Another group said: “This is created, whereas Allah’s speech is not created; therefore, this is not Allah’s speech.”

Another group said: “This is Allah’s speech, and Allah’s speech is not created. This is also our utterance and our recitation; therefore, our utterance and our recitation are uncreated.”

translated_text:
The misguidance of all these groups stems from their failure to distinguish what the word “this” refers to.

When you hear speech from its original speaker, you say: “This speech is truthful, true, and correct; it is the speech of a wise person.” Likewise, when you hear it from someone conveying it, you say: “This speech is truthful, true, and correct; it is the speech of a wise person.” What is referred to in both cases is one and the same.

You also say: “This is a beautiful voice, and these words come from the depths of the heart.” Then, when you hear it from the person conveying it, you say: “This is a beautiful voice,” or, “These words come from the depths of the heart.” Here, however, what is referred to in one case is not what is referred to in the other. Rather, in the first case the reference is to the original speaker’s own voice and heart, and in the second to the transmitter’s own voice and heart.

Similarly, when speech is written on two pages, as in two copies of the Quran, you say of each: “This is a noble Quran; this is a glorious Book; this is Allah’s speech.” What is referred to is one and the same. Then you say: “This is beautiful handwriting,” “This is naskh or thuluth script,” or, “This writing is red or yellow.” Here, what is referred to is what distinguishes each copy of the Quran from the other.

When a person distinguishes what “this” refers to in each instance, what is common and what is distinct become clear. He understands that when someone says, “This Quran is Allah’s speech, and Allah’s speech is uncreated,” the reference is to the speech itself, considered apart from the servants’ movements and voices through which it has reached us.

As for someone who says, “This is created,” referring solely to the servant’s voice and movement, this gives him no proof that the Quran itself—its letters and meanings, which this reciter learned from someone else and conveyed through his movement and voice—is created. Whoever believes that has erred and gone astray.

Such a person should be told:

This speech to which you have referred existed before this reciter was created. Suppose, then, that the reciter himself had never been created, and neither his actions nor his sounds had ever existed. How does it follow that the speech itself, which existed before him, should be nonexistent when he is nonexistent and come into being when he comes into being?

If, in calling it created, he is referring to this reciter’s own actions and sounds, then the Quran has no need of this reciter and existed before him. Thus, this reciter’s nonexistence does not entail its nonexistence. But if he is referring to the speech that people learn from one another, then this is the speech sent down from Allah, which Gabriel brought to Muhammad and Muhammad conveyed to his nation. It is Allah’s speech, which He Himself spoke. It cannot, therefore, be created. For if it were created, it would be the speech of that in which it was created, not Allah’s speech.

Moreover, if speech became His speech merely because He—glory be to Him—created it, then whatever He caused any speaker to utter would be His speech: the glorification uttered by mountains and pebbles, the testimony borne by skins—indeed, all speech in existence. This is the position of those who advocate divine indwelling, who say:

“All speech in existence is His speech;
To us, its prose and verse are alike.”

Whoever says that the Quran is created faces one of two alternatives: either he makes all speech in existence Allah’s speech, or he holds that Allah does not speak anything at all. The same applies when someone says, “This is Allah’s own speech, His very speech,” or, “What is in this written copy of the Quran is Allah’s very speech, His own speech,” and similar expressions. When used without qualification, Muslims naturally understand these expressions to mean that it is His speech, not anyone else’s, and that nothing has been added to it or omitted from it. For someone who transmits another person’s words and writes them in a document may add to them or omit something, as people commonly do in much correspondence involving kings and others.

Thus, when a letter from the ruler arrives and someone says, “What it contains is the ruler’s very own speech, without addition or omission,” this means that the scribe has neither added anything to it nor omitted anything from it.

Likewise, when someone quotes an imam’s discussion of a particular question from one of his works, it may be said, “These are the very words of so-and-so,” meaning that the person quoting them has neither added nor omitted anything. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“May Allah brighten the face of a person who hears a hadith from us and conveys it just as he heard it.”

By “conveys it just as he heard it,” he did not mean conveying it with the very movements and sounds through which he heard it. Rather, he meant relating the hadith accurately, neither adding anything to it nor omitting anything from it. In this way, he conveys it just as he heard it. The person listening to the transmitter thus hears it just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said it, and has thereby heard the speech of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, just as he spoke it. This is what people mean when they say, “This is his very speech,” and, “This is his own speech.”

translated_text:
They do not mean that this is his actual voice and movements. No rational person says this, nor would it initially occur to any rational person. Yet following conjecture and personal desires drives those who do so into “Qarmatianism” in matters of revelation and “sophistry” in matters of reason. Were people left with their natural disposition, it would remain sound and intact.

When people encounter sound speech—whether someone has spoken it and it has been heard from him and transmitted, or he has written it in a book—no rational person says that the very meanings within the speaker’s heart and the words uttered by his tongue have left him and passed to the listener and the person conveying his speech, or that they have left him and come to reside in the paper. Nor does anyone say that the very meanings and words that subsist in him are the ink on the paper. Nor does anyone even say that his actual utterances, which are his sounds, are the sounds made by the person conveying his speech.

All of this is clear: no rational person makes such claims about a created being’s speech when it is heard and conveyed or written in a book. How, then, could this be said of Allah’s speech, which has been heard from Him and conveyed from Him, or which He, glory be to Him, has written—as He wrote the Torah for Moses and wrote the Quran in the Preserved Tablet, and as Muslims have written it in their copies of the Quran?

And if someone hears a created being’s speech and conveys its wording and meaning—even the poetry of a created being, as the poetry of Hassān, Ibn Rawāhah, Labīd, and other such poets is conveyed—and people say, “These are Hassān’s very verses; this is Hassān’s own poetry,” and, “These are Labīd’s very verses,” as in his words:

translated_text:
“Indeed, everything apart from Allah is vain.”

Yet every rational person knows that those who transmit and recite poetry have not stripped the poets of their very attributes so that these have come to reside in them. Nor have the actual attributes and actions that subsisted in those poets, such as their voices and movements, come to reside in the transmitters and reciters. How, then, could anyone imagine that the Creator’s attributes—His speech or His other attributes—have departed from His essence and come to reside in His creatures, or that a creature’s own attributes and actions, such as its movements and sounds, are the Creator’s attributes residing within it? They do not say anything of this kind even about created beings.

Rather, they compare knowledge to the light of a lamp: the learner draws from it without diminishing what the scholar possesses, just as someone takes light from a lamp and Allah brings light into being for him. As it is said, “Air turns into fire when a wick is brought near a lamp, without the fire in the lamp itself changing.” Likewise, someone who teaches Quran recitation or imparts knowledge loses nothing of what he possesses; rather, the learner comes to possess the like of what the teacher possesses.

Hence people say, “So-and-so transmits so-and-so’s knowledge and conveys his words.” They also say, “The knowledge that so-and-so possessed has passed to so-and-so,” and similar expressions. Likewise, one says, “I transcribed what is in the book,” “I copied what is in the book,” or, “I transcribed the book,” or, “I copied it.” They do not mean that the actual letters in the first book have ceased to exist there and come to reside in the second. Rather, since the purpose of copying and transcribing books is of the same kind as conveying knowledge and speech, and this is achieved by placing in the second

the like of what is in the first, what the first was intended to convey is thus transmitted and copied, even though the first remains unchanged. This differs from moving physical bodies and their accompanying properties: when these are moved from one place to another, they cease to be in the first place. For things have an existence in themselves—their concrete existence—and they are also present in knowledge, then in words corresponding to that knowledge, and then in writing.

This is what is meant by the saying: “Existence in external reality, existence in minds, existence in speech, and existence through the fingers”—that is, concrete, cognitive, verbal, and written existence. Hence Allah began His Book with His words, Exalted is He:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created—
created man from a clinging clot.
Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous,
who taught by the pen,
taught man what he did not know.”

He mentioned creation in general and in particular, then teaching in general and in particular. Writing corresponds to words, words correspond to knowledge, and knowledge corresponds to what is known.

It is here that some have gone astray, imagining that the Quran is present in a written copy in the same way that concrete entities are represented on paper. They therefore supposed that His words:

“Indeed, it is a noble Quran,
in a well-protected Book”

are like His words:

“Whom they find written of in the Torah and the Gospel that are with them.”

They thus equated recording the Quran—which is Allah’s speech—in written copies with recording the Messenger in written copies. This is an error: recording the Quran is like recording the Messenger’s name; both are speech. As for recording the Messenger’s name, this is like recording deeds, or like recording the Quran in

translated_text:
the scriptures of earlier peoples. Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“Everything they did is in the written records.”

And He, Exalted is He, says:

“Indeed, it is in the scriptures of earlier peoples.”

Deeds being recorded in the written records, and the Quran being recorded in the scriptures of earlier peoples, are like the Messenger being found written of in the Torah and the Gospel that are with them. For this reason, He, Glorified is He, qualified this with the word zubur (“written records”). Books are zubur: one says zabartu al-kitāb (“I wrote the book”), and zabūr means mazbūr, that is, “written.” The Quran itself is not with the Children of Israel; rather, mention of it is, just as Muhammad himself is not with them, but mention of him is. Thus, the Messenger being recorded in their books is like the Quran being recorded in their books. This differs from the Quran being recorded in the Preserved Tablet and in written copies, for it is the Quran itself that is recorded in these. Whoever equates the two is plainly astray. This has been discussed at length in its proper place.

(The point here is that when existing things themselves and their attributes move from one place to another, they come to reside in that second place. Knowledge of them and accounts of them, however, are received by a second person from the first while remaining with the first, although what the second possesses is a counterpart and likeness of what the first possesses. Yet because the object of both instances of knowledge is one and the same in itself, the oneness of that object entails the oneness of what corresponds to it and points to it. People have no interest in the multiplicity of what corresponds to it, as is the case with a name and the one named.

For even if several people mention a person’s name, and several people call him by it, people still say that it is one name for one person. Thus, when the caller to prayer says:

and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,” and this caller to prayer says it, and that caller to prayer says it, and someone other than a caller to prayer says it, people say that what is written here is the name of Allah and the name of His Messenger, just as those named are Allah and His Messenger.

Likewise, when someone says:

“Read in the name of your Lord,”

and says:

“Board it in the name of Allah,”

and says:

“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High,”

and says:

“In the name of Allah,”

in all these cases, what is mentioned is Allah’s name, even though the mentions and those who make them are many. Thus, a single report from a single informant concerning what he reports, and a single command from a single commander concerning the prescribed action, are like a single name designating its bearer. The case of a compound expression is analogous to that of a single word. It is one with respect to its reality and to the identity of what is intended, even though those who mention that name and report are many, and their movements, voices, and other attributes are many.

As for someone saying, “If you say that this is Allah’s very speech, then you have affirmed indwelling, whereas you declare the adherents of indwelling and union to be unbelievers,” this is an invalid analogy.

It is like a man claiming that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, dwells in his very person within the body of someone reading his hadith. People reject his claim and say that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, does not dwell within anyone else’s body. He then says: “You say that the hadith narrator reads his words, and that what he reads is the speech of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. By saying this, you have affirmed indwelling.” It is well known that this is utterly unsound.

translated_text:
People agree that one may say without qualification, “Zayd’s speech is in this book,” and “What we have heard is Zayd’s speech.” Yet no rational person would consider it permissible to say that Zayd himself is in this speaker or in these sheets of paper.

The revealed texts explicitly state that the Quran is in people’s breasts, as in the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Keep the Quran fresh in your memory, for it escapes from men’s breasts more readily than livestock escape their tethers.”

And his words:

“A breast containing nothing of the Quran is like a ruined house.”

There are other such texts. No rational person regards this as equivalent to saying that Allah is within our breasts and bodies. Thus, when a man called al-Sūrī introduced the claim that anyone who says, “The Quran is in our breasts,” has professed the Christians’ doctrine, Ahmad was told, “A fourth Jahmī sect has appeared”—meaning the Khalqiyyah, the Lafziyyah, the Wāqifah, and this fourth group. He vehemently denounced this and said, “This is worse than the Jahmiyyah.”

It is indeed as he said. None of the Jahmiyyah denies that one may say, “The Quran is in people’s breasts.” Only someone utterly astray and ignorant would liken this to the Christians’ doctrine of indwelling. For the Christians say, “The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God,” and that the Word, which is the divine nature, clothed itself in human nature. In their view, he is a god who creates and provides.

Hence they said, “Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary,” and they say, “The Messiah is the son of Allah.” This is why their position is contradictory: if what clothed itself in the Messiah was the God encompassing the persons of the Trinity, then it was the Father himself; but if it was one attribute among

His attributes, then an attribute neither creates nor provides, nor is it a god, whereas the Messiah, in their view, is a god. Had the Christians said that Allah’s speech was in the Messiah’s breast just as it is in the breasts of the other prophets and believers, there would have been nothing objectionable in their statement.

Those commonly known as proponents of indwelling are those who maintain that Allah dwells within human beings, as do the Christians, the extremists among the Rāfidah, and the extremist followers of religious masters; or those who maintain that He dwells within everything, as the Jahmiyyah claim that He Himself is in every place. Yet He—glorified be He—has nothing of His essence within His creatures, nor anything of His creatures within His essence. The same applies to anyone who maintains that He is united with the Messiah or anyone else, that He is united with all created things, that His existence is the very existence of created things, or anything similar.

As for saying, “Allah’s speech is in the hearts of His prophets and His believing servants; the messengers conveyed Allah’s speech, and what they conveyed is Allah’s speech; and the speech is in the written sheet,” and similar statements, this is not called indwelling. Whoever calls it indwelling does not, by giving it that name, negate the realities involved.

It has already been explained that this does not entail an attribute’s separating from a created being and passing to another. How much less could this apply to an attribute of the Creator, blessed and exalted be He! However, because this bears an apparent resemblance to indwelling, people have disagreed over whether to affirm or deny the term “indwelling” in this context. May one say, “Allah’s speech dwells within the codex,” or “dwells within people’s breasts”? And may one say, “People’s written speech dwells within the codex,” or “dwells within the hearts of those who have memorized it,” and the like? One group denied indwelling, such as Judge

He, glorified be He, thus states that it is sent down from Allah. He has not described anything as being sent down from Allah except His speech, in contrast to the descent of the angels, rain, iron, and other things. Hence the well-known position of the early generations was that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated: from Him it originated, and to Him it returns. Those who say that it is created maintain that it was created in one of the created entities that exist in their own right. It would therefore have descended and originated from that created entity, not from Allah. Allah Most High’s statement that it is sent down from Allah is incompatible with its having descended from other than Allah. For this reason, Imam Ahmad explained the phrase “From Him it originated” as meaning that He is the One who spoke it. Ahmad also said: “Allah’s speech is from Allah; it is not separate from Him.”

Furthermore, if it were created in something other than Him, it would not be His speech; rather, it would be the speech of the created entity in which it was created. The same applies to all the other attributes with which He has described Himself—will, love, volition, pleasure, anger, abhorrence, and so forth. Had these been created in something other than Him, the Lord Most High would not be characterized by them; rather, they would be attributes of the subject in which they subsisted. For when a quality subsists in a subject, it is an attribute of that subject, not of another. It is therefore impossible for a created being or the Creator to be characterized by an existing attribute that subsists in another, for this is known innately. Thus, regarding the intransitive acts with which He has described Himself, it is impossible for a subject to be characterized by something that does not subsist in it. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Nor did the early generations say that the Prophet heard it from Allah Most High, as some later scholars claim. Allah Most High says:

“Allah has certainly bestowed a favour upon the believers by sending among them a Messenger from their own midst, reciting His verses to them.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn Masʿūd is reported to have said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to me, ‘Recite the Quran to me.’ I said, ‘Shall I recite it to you when it was revealed to you?’ He replied, ‘I like to hear it from someone else.’ So I recited Surah al-Nisā’ to him until I reached this verse: ‘How will it be when We bring a witness from every nation and bring you as a witness against these?’ He said, ‘That is enough.’ I looked, and his eyes were streaming with tears.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, heard it from Gabriel, who brought it down to him. Gabriel heard it from Allah Most High, as Ahmad and other imams explicitly stated. Allah Most High says:

“Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel—it is he who brought it down upon your heart by Allah’s permission.”

And Allah Most High says:

“The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down”
“upon your heart, so that you might be one of the warners,”
“in a clear Arabic tongue.”

Allah Most High also says:

“When We replace one verse with another—and Allah knows best what He sends down—they say, ‘You are only a fabricator.’ Rather, most of them do not know.”
“Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth.”

Thus He, glorified be He, states that the Holy Spirit—who is the Trustworthy Spirit, Gabriel—brought it down from Allah in truth. None of the early generations said that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, heard it from Allah. Only some later scholars said this.

Allah Most High’s words:

“It is for Us to gather it and recite it.
So when We have recited it, follow its recitation.
Then it is for Us to explain it.”

are like His words:

“We recount to you in truth some of the story of Moses and Pharaoh,”

and His words:

“We relate to you the best of stories through Our revelation of this Quran to you,”

and similar passages concerning what the Lord does through His angels. The word “We” is used for one who commands obedience and has helpers who obey him. The Lord Most High created the angels and all other beings; the angels obey Him far more fully than a created being obeys his helpers. Thus He, glorified be He, has a greater right than anyone else to such expressions as “We,” “We did,” and the like.

In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn ʿAbbās said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, experienced great hardship when receiving revelation and would move his lips.”

Ibn ʿAbbās said: “I shall move them for you as the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to move them.”

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: “I shall move them as I saw Ibn ʿAbbās move them.” He then moved his lips.

Then Allah revealed:

“Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it.
It is for Us to gather it and recite it.”

He explained: “To gather it in your heart for you, so that you may recite it.”

“So when We have recited it, follow its recitation.”

“When Our messenger recites it”—or, in another wording, “when Gabriel recites it”—“listen to him and remain silent.”

“Then it is for Us to explain it.”

“That is, We shall recite it.”

After that, whenever Gabriel came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he would listen. Once Gabriel had departed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would recite it just as Gabriel had recited it.

Allah Most High has explained the ways in which He speaks to His servants in His words:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills.”

He, glorified be He, thus explained that He sometimes speaks by revelation, sometimes from behind a veil—as He spoke to Moses—and sometimes by sending a messenger who reveals, by Allah’s permission, whatever He wills. Allah Most High also says:

“Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind.”

When Allah Most High sends a messenger, this is one of the ways in which He speaks to His servants, reciting His message to them and informing them through it. Thus Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘Make no excuses; we will never believe you. Allah has already informed us of some of your affairs.’”

He informed them only through the Messenger, and the Messenger conveys His message, as Allah Most High says:

“O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord.”

And Allah Most High says:

“So that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord.”

And Allah Most High says:

“The Messenger’s duty is only to convey the message clearly.”

The Messenger commanded his community to convey his teachings on his behalf. In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr relates that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Convey from me, even if only one verse. Relate reports from the Children of Israel; there is no harm in doing so. Whoever deliberately attributes a lie to me, let him take his seat in the Fire.”

When addressing the Muslims, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Let those present convey this to those absent, for someone to whom it is conveyed may understand it better than one who heard it directly.”

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“May Allah brighten the face of a person who hears a hadith from us and conveys it to someone who has not heard it. For many a transmitter lacks understanding, and many a bearer of knowledge conveys it to someone who understands it better than he does.”

translated_text:
In the Sunan collections, Jābir reported:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would present himself to people during the pilgrimage season, saying, ‘Is there no man who will take me to his people so that I may convey the speech of my Lord? For Quraysh have prevented me from conveying the speech of my Lord.’”

Just as none of the early generations said that it was created, none of them said that it was eternal. Neither the Companions, nor those who followed them in righteousness, nor those after them—whether the four imams or anyone else—made either statement. Rather, mass-transmitted reports establish that they used to say, “The Quran is the speech of Allah.” When people appeared who said that it was created, they responded by saying, “It is uncreated.”

By this, they did not mean that it was fabricated, as some people have supposed. No Muslim ever said that it was fabricated; rather, this is manifest disbelief, as every Muslim knows. They only said that it was something created, which Allah created in something other than Himself. The early generations rejected this statement, as mass-transmitted reports from them establish, and they wrote numerous works on the subject. They said, “From Him it originated, and to Him it will return.”

The first people known to have said that it was created were al-Ja‘d ibn Dirham and his associate al-Jahm ibn Safwān. The first person known to have said that it was eternal was ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb. Those who shared this latter position subsequently differed among themselves.

Some of them held that speech is a single meaning subsisting in the Lord’s essence; that the meaning of the entire Quran, the Torah, the Gospel, and all the other books of Allah, as well as His speech, is that one meaning, which neither admits of multiplicity nor can be divided; and that Allah did not speak the Arabic Quran

translated_text:
but that it is created, something He created in something other than Himself.

The majority of rational thinkers said: This position is self-evidently false. Sound reason plainly establishes that the meaning of the “Verse of the Throne” is not the meaning of the “Verse of Debt,” nor is the meaning of “Say, ‘He is Allah, the One’” the meaning of “May the hands of Abū Lahab perish, and may he perish!” What, then, of the meanings of all Allah’s speech in the revealed scriptures, His address to His angels, His calling His servants to account on the Day of Resurrection, and His other speech?

Others held that it consists of letters, or letters and sounds, eternal and beginningless, inseparable from His essence, which He has always possessed as attributes and always will.

Both groups say that Allah Most High does not speak by His will and power, and that He has always been and will always be saying, “O Noah! O Abraham! O you wrapped in garments! O you cloaked!” I have explained their positions at length elsewhere.

None of the early generations held either position. Nor did any of them say that this Quran is an expression of Allah’s speech or a reproduction of it. None of them said, “My utterance of the Quran is eternal or uncreated,” let alone, “My voice in reciting it is eternal or uncreated.” Rather, they affirmed what the Book and the Sunnah indicate: this Quran is the speech of Allah; people recite it with their own voices and write it with their own ink; what is between the two covers is the speech of Allah; and the speech of Allah is uncreated.

In the two Sahīh collections, it is reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Do not travel

with the Quran to enemy territory.” Allah Most High says:

“Rather, it is a glorious Quran,
in a Preserved Tablet.”

The ink with which the Quran is written is created, and the voice with which it is recited is the servant’s voice. The servant, his voice, his movements, and all his other attributes are created. Thus, the Quran that Muslims recite is the speech of the Creator, while the voice with which the servant recites it is the reciter’s voice. As Allah Most High says:

“If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of Allah, then convey him to his place of safety.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Beautify the Quran with your voices.”

He thus made clear that the voices with which the Quran is recited are our voices, while the Quran is Allah’s speech. Hence Ahmad ibn Hanbal and other leading scholars of the Sunnah said that a person beautifies it with his voice, as Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Had I known that you were listening, I would have made my recitation truly beautiful for you.”

Thus, the statement of Ahmad and other leading scholars of the Sunnah—that the voice is the servant’s voice—accords with the Book and the Sunnah. Allah Most High says:

“Be moderate in your pace and lower your voice.”

And He says:

“O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet.”

And He says:

“Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of Allah’s Messenger are those whose hearts Allah has tested for piety.”

And He says:

“Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought its like as a replenishment.”

He, glorified be He, thus distinguished between the ink with which His words are written and His words themselves. Thus the sea and any other ink with which the words are written

is created, whereas Allah’s words are uncreated. Allah Most High says:

“Even if all the trees on earth were pens, and the sea, replenished by seven more seas, were ink, Allah’s words would not be exhausted.”

Thus, if the seas were imagined as ink, they would be exhausted, but Allah’s words would never be exhausted. Hence the leading scholars of the Sunnah said that Allah has always spoken however He wills and whatever He wills, as conveyed in reports from Ibn al-Mubārak, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others.

Moreover, He, glorified be He, has described Himself as calling out in more than ten passages. Allah Most High says:

“When they tasted the tree, their nakedness became apparent to them, and they began covering themselves with leaves from Paradise. Their Lord called to them: ‘Did I not forbid you that tree and tell you that Satan is a clear enemy to you?’”

Allah Most High also says:

“On the Day He calls to them and says: ‘Where are those you claimed to be My partners?’”

“On the Day He calls to them and says: ‘How did you respond to the messengers?’”

He, glorified be He, mentions His calling to Moses, peace be upon him, in Surah Tā-Hā, Surah Maryam, the three Tā-Sīn surahs, and Surah al-Nāziʿāt. He states that He called to him at a particular time. Allah Most High says:

“When he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed place, from the tree: ‘O Moses, indeed I am Allah, Lord of all worlds.’”

Allah Most High says:

“Has the story of Moses reached you?”

“When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwā.”

Allah Most High also says:

“You were not beside the Mount when We called.”

Reports have been abundantly transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the Companions, the Successors, and the leading scholars of the Sunnah after them, affirming that He, glorified be He, calls with a voice: He called to Moses

and will call to His servants on the Day of Resurrection with a voice, and He speaks revelation with a voice. It has not been transmitted from anyone among the early generations that he said Allah speaks without a voice or without letters, or that he denied that Allah speaks with a voice or with letters. Likewise, none of them said that the voice Moses heard was beginningless, or that this call was beginningless. Nor did any of them say that the voices heard from reciters are the voice with which Allah spoke. Rather, reports from them are abundant distinguishing between the voice with which Allah speaks and the voices of His servants.

The leading scholars of the Sunnah regarded those who denied that He speaks with a voice as belonging to the Jahmiyyah. Thus, when Imam Ahmad was asked about someone who said that Allah does not speak with a voice, he replied: “These are Jahmīs; their entire position revolves around denying the divine attributes.” He then mentioned some of the reports stating that He, glorified be He, speaks with a voice. Those who compiled works on the Sunnah . . . (1) included a selection of these reports. Al-Bukhārī likewise devoted a chapter in his Sahīh to this subject, using as its heading the words of Allah Most High:

“Until, when fear is lifted from their hearts.”

In The Creation of Deeds, al-Bukhārī cited numerous reports clarifying the distinction between the two voices. Al-Bukhārī’s ordeal involving his associates, Muhammad ibn Yahyā al-Dhuhlī and others, occurred years after Ahmad’s death. Ahmad spoke of al-Bukhārī only with praise. Whoever reports that Ahmad spoke ill of al-Bukhārī has fabricated a lie against him.

translated_text:
Shaykh Abū al-Hasan Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Malik al-Karajī recorded in his book, Al-Fusūl fī al-Usūl (Chapters on the Foundations), that he heard Imam Abū Mansūr Muhammad ibn Ahmad say:

“I heard Abū Hāmid al-Isfarāyīnī say: ‘My position, and that of al-Shāfiʿī and the jurists of the various lands, is that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated. Whoever says that it is created is a disbeliever. Gabriel conveyed the Quran, having heard it from Allah; the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, heard it from Gabriel; and the Companions heard it from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It is what we recite with our tongues, what lies between the two covers, and what is in our hearts—heard, written, and memorized. Every letter of it, such as bā and tā, is Allah’s speech, uncreated. Whoever says that it is created is a disbeliever; upon him be the curses of Allah and all mankind.’”

A group of hadith scholars and those who affiliated themselves with the Sunnah disputed whether uttering the Quran could be described as created. When discussion of this arose, the leading scholars of the Sunnah, such as Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others, rejected both statements: “My utterance of the Quran is created” and “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” They said: “Whoever says it is created is a Jahmī, and whoever says it is uncreated is an innovator.”

As for a person’s voice, they did not dispute that it is created. Someone who conveys another person’s speech in the original speaker’s wording merely conveys it to someone else—as when one says, “He narrated the hadith in its original wording.” He conveys it in his own voice, not in the voice of the original speaker.

“Utterance” (lafz) is originally the verbal noun of lafaza, yalfizu, lafzan (“to utter”); likewise, “recitation”

and “reading” are both verbal nouns. However, these terms have come to be commonly used for the speech itself that is uttered, read, and recited. This is what they mean by “utterance” when they use the term without qualification. Thus, saying “My utterance of the Quran is created,” or “Uttering the Quran is created,” suggests that this Quran which one reads and utters is created. Saying “My utterance is uncreated” suggests that something attributed to oneself is uncreated. Yet one’s voice and movements are created, whereas Allah’s speech, which one recites, is uncreated.

“Recitation” may refer to the speech itself that is recited, to the servant’s own movements, or to both together. If it refers to the speech itself that is recited, then the recitation is what is recited. If it refers to the servant’s movements, then the recitation is not what is recited. If it refers to both together, it encompasses both the act and the speech; it cannot then be said without qualification either that it is what is recited or that it is something other than it.

None of the early generations meant by “recitation” merely the servants’ act of reading, and by “what is recited” merely a single meaning subsisting in the essence of the Creator, Most High. Rather, their position was that the Quran is Allah’s speech: Allah spoke it, both its letters and its meanings. Nothing in it is the speech of anyone else—not Gabriel, Muhammad, or anyone besides them. Indeed, Allah has declared whoever calls it human speech a disbeliever, even though He, glorified be He, has attributed it at times to a human messenger and at times to an angelic messenger. The Most High said:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.
It is not the word of a poet—little do you believe!
Nor is it the word of a soothsayer—little do you take heed!
It is a revelation from the Lord of all worlds.”

The messenger here is Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. And the Most High said:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger,
endowed with strength, held in honour with the Lord of the Throne,
obeyed there and trustworthy.
Your companion is not mad.
He certainly saw him on the clear horizon.
He does not withhold knowledge of the unseen.
Nor is it the word of an accursed devil.
So where are you going?
It is nothing but a reminder to all worlds.”

The messenger here is Gabriel. He, glorified be He, attributed it to each of them using the designation “messenger,” because this indicates that he conveys it on behalf of another and acts as a messenger in conveying it, without originating any part of it himself. Had he originated any part of it, he would not have been a messenger with respect to that part, but would instead have composed it himself. He, glorified be He, attributes it sometimes to an angelic messenger and sometimes to a human messenger. If this attribution meant that the messenger had composed its letters, the two statements would contradict one another, since its composition by one would contradict its composition by the other.

Allah Most High has declared whoever says, “It is human speech,” a disbeliever. Thus, whoever says that the Quran, or any part of it, is the speech of a human being or an angel has spoken falsely. Whoever says that it is the word of a human or angelic messenger who conveyed it from the One who sent him, rather than speech he composed himself, has spoken the truth.

None of the early generations said that Gabriel originated its wording, or that Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did so; nor did they say that Allah Most High created it in the air or in any other created thing, or that Gabriel took it from the Preserved Tablet. Rather, these are views held by some later scholars. Elsewhere, the disputes of the innovators who differed concerning the Book have been discussed at length, the falsity of their views has been demonstrated, and it has been explained that the sound position is that of
