‘The basin filled and said, “Enough for me.”’ And ‘it said’ (1): ‘the expansion of his belly,’ and the like.”

When the early generations understood the true nature of this view, and that it resembled the doctrine of the philosophizing deniers of the divine attributes—who say that Allah Most High did not speak, but that the messengers attributed speech to Him only by way of what circumstances imply—they declared them disbelievers and exposed their error. Among the arguments they put to them was this:

A herald speaking on behalf of another—such as a ruler’s herald—says, “The ruler has commanded such-and-such,” or, “His decree has been issued concerning such-and-such.” He does not say, “I command you to do this and forbid you to do that.” Yet Allah Most High says when speaking to Moses:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.”

And when He descends during the remaining third of the night, He, Most High, says:

“Who is calling upon Me, that I may answer him? Who is asking Me, that I may give him? Who is seeking My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?”

When the speaker is an angel, however, he speaks as described in the hadith in the two Sahīh collections:

“When Allah loves a servant, He calls out in heaven, ‘O Gabriel, I love so-and-so, so love him.’ Gabriel then loves him and calls out in heaven, ‘Allah loves so-and-so, so love him.’ The inhabitants of heaven then love him, and acceptance is granted to him on earth.”

Thus, when Gabriel calls out on behalf of Allah Most High, he says:

“Allah loves so-and-so, so love him.”

But when the Lord calls out, He says:

“Who is calling upon Me, that I may answer him? Who is asking Me, that I may give him? Who is seeking My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?”

The compiler noted in the margin after qālat (“she said”): “Thus in the original.” I do not know what he found objectionable—may Allah have mercy on him—whether the word qālat or the phrase ittisāʿ batnihi (“the expansion of his belly”). It appears to be a proverb or something similar. In both aforementioned passages in al-Fatāwā, the wording is ittisāʿ, with a tāʾ, whereas al-Darʾ has insāʿ, with a nūn. The latter seems more likely, for the Arabs say insāʿa al-māʾ when water flows over the surface of the ground, and insāʿa al-jāmid when a solid substance melts. Perhaps, therefore, what is meant is looseness of the bowels. Allah knows best.

If it is objected, “But it has been reported that He commands a herald to call out,” the reply is: This is not found in the Sahīh. If it is authentic, the two reports can be reconciled: He Himself calls out and also commands a herald to call out. However, this report cannot be used to contradict the authentic, widely transmitted report whose authenticity hadith scholars have unanimously affirmed and which they have accepted, especially since it explicitly states that Allah Most High Himself says:

“Who is calling upon Me, that I may answer him? Who is asking Me, that I may give him? Who is seeking My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?”

Likewise, Jahm denied the names of Allah Most High. He would not call Him a thing, living, or anything else except metaphorically. He said, “Calling Him by a name also applied to a created being would amount to likening Him to creation.” Jahm was also a determinist, saying that the servant does nothing. Thus, it is reported that he called Allah Powerful, since, in his view, the servant has no power.

Then the Mu‘tazilah, who followed ‘Amr ibn ‘Ubayd’s position on divine decree and the threat of punishment, adopted Jahm’s doctrine. They affirmed the names of Allah Most High but did not affirm His attributes. They said, “We say that Allah truly speaks.” They sometimes even cite the Muslims’ consensus that Allah truly speaks, lest the view that He does not speak be attributed to them. Yet, in their view, His being a speaker—glory be to Him—means that He created speech in something other than Himself. Thus, their doctrine and that of the Jahmiyyah are identical in substance. The former, however, say that He truly speaks, whereas the latter deny that He truly speaks. The true import of both groups’ position is that He is not

Many of the Mu‘tazilah who followed Abū Hanīfah in jurisprudence agreed with them on this. Among the other imams of the Muslims, none espouses the Mu‘tazilah’s positions on denying the attributes, divine decree, the intermediate position between the two positions, or carrying out the threat of punishment.

The Mu‘tazilah and the Kullābiyyah then disputed the true meaning of “speaker.” The Mu‘tazilah said: A speaker is one who produces speech, even if he brings it into being in another. This allowed them to say that Allah creates speech in another and is its speaker.

The Kullābiyyah said: A speaker is one in whom speech subsists, even if he does not speak by his will and power and performs no act at all. Rather, they regarded a speaker as analogous to a living being in whom life subsists, even if his life is not by his will or power and does not result from any act of his.

As for the early generations, their followers, and the majority of rational people, a speaker, as they understand the term, is one in whom speech subsists and who speaks by his will and power. A speaker in whom speech does not subsist is inconceivable, as is a speaker who speaks without his will and power. Thus, each of these two groups of innovators adopted only part of what characterizes a speaker: the Mu‘tazilah held that he produces speech, while the Kullābiyyah held that he is the subject in whom speech subsists. In his book Khalq Af‘āl al-‘Ibād (The Creation of the Acts of the Servants), al-Bukhārī reported the scholars’ consensus on this.

Those who held that an act does not subsist in its agent, yet also held that Allah is the agent of the servants’ acts—as did Abū al-Hasan and others—that the servant performs no act, and that everything the servant creates is an act of His, ascribe to Him attributes of action that are separate from Him. They divide His attributes into attributes of essence and attributes of action, although, in their view, these actions are the effects produced separately from Him. Their position therefore entails that He be characterized by the injustice and evil deeds He creates, despite their assertion that He is not characterized by the speech and other things He creates. This was a contradiction on their part, which the Mu‘tazilah exploited against them.

When they affirmed a principle of Ahl al-Sunnah—that when a quality subsists in a subject, a name is derived from it for that subject and not for another, as with the name “speaker”—the Mu‘tazilah challenged them with the names “Creator” and “Just.” They offered no sound answer to this objection. The principle upheld by the early generations and the imams, however, is consistent throughout.

Among the proofs they cited that the Quran is uncreated was the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, invoked by Imam Ahmad and others:

The seeker thereby recognizes the unsoundness of those positions, and this prompts him to seek the truth. You will find that the truth invariably accords with what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought, and that what the Messenger brought invariably accords with sound reason. The seeker thus becomes one who has a heart, or listens with full attentiveness—one who has a heart with which to understand and an ear with which to hear—unlike those who said:

Alongside the Kullābiyyah and their like, other groups emerged among scholars of jurisprudence, hadith, and speculative theology, including Karrāmiyyah and non-Karrāmiyyah. They said that He, glorified be He, speaks by His will and power, with speech that subsists in His essence, and that He speaks with letters and sounds by His will and power. In this way, they sought to escape the two innovations of the Muʿtazilah and the Kullābiyyah. Yet they said that it had not been possible for Him to speak in pre-eternity; rather, speech became possible for Him after having been impossible for Him, without any cause arising that necessitated its becoming possible or His becoming able to speak.

Many scholars of speculative theology, jurisprudence, and hadith agreed with the Karrāmiyyah on this position. However, no such view has been transmitted from any of the four imams or comparable imams of the Muslims. In this, they shared the position of the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah, for all these groups say that speech had not been possible for Him in pre-eternity, but then became possible for Him after having been impossible for Him, without any cause arising that necessitated its becoming possible.

The Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah, however, say that He created speech in something other than Himself, without any speech subsisting in Him. For if speech subsisted in Him by His will and power, temporal occurrences would subsist in Him. They say that temporal occurrences do not subsist in Him.

The Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah explain that temporal occurrences fall within the category of attributes that they call accidents. In their view, no attributes subsist in Him. They argue that attributes are accidents, and an accident can subsist only in a body, whereas He is not a body. This is because a body is never free of temporal occurrences, and whatever is never free of temporal occurrences is itself originated in time.

{وَإِذَا رَأَيْتَهُمْ تُعْجِبُكَ أَجْسَامُهُمْ وَإِنْ يَقُولُوا تَسْمَعْ لِقَوْلِهِمْ}

" الْجِسْمِ "
 تَارَةً الْمِقْدَارَ وَقَدْ يُسَمُّونَهُ الْجِسْمَ التَّعْلِيمِيَّ وَتَارَةً يُرِيدُونَ بِهِ الشَّيْءَ الْمُقَدَّرَ وَهُوَ الْجِسْمِيُّ الطَّبِيعِيُّ وَالْمِقْدَارُ الْمُجَرَّدُ عَنْ الْمُقَدَّرِ كَالْعَدَدِ الْمُجَرَّدِ عَنْ الْمَعْدُودِ وَذَلِكَ لَا يُوجَدُ إلَّا
translated_text:
The Kullābiyyah, however, said: Attributes do subsist in Him, but temporal occurrences do not. We do not call attributes accidents, because, in our view, an accident does not persist for two successive moments, whereas Allah’s attributes endure.

They also said: If temporal occurrences subsisted in Him, He would never be free of them, because whatever is receptive to something cannot be devoid of both that thing and its opposite. Whatever is never free of temporal occurrences is itself originated in time.

The majority who opposed both groups replied: As for their assertion that attributes do not subsist in Him because they are accidents, that an accident can subsist only in a body, and that He is not a body: calling whatever subsists in something else an “accident” is a newly introduced convention. Likewise, calling anything that can be pointed to a “body” is also a newly introduced convention. In Arabic, jism means the body—the badan or jasad—as several authorities on the language have stated, including al-Asmaʿī and Abū ʿAmr. Thus, the word jism is similar in meaning to jasad, referring to that which is thick and dense. The Arabs say, “This is jasīm (bulky),” and “This is ajsam (bulkier) than that,” meaning thicker than it. Allah Most High says:

“And has increased him abundantly in knowledge and stature.”

And He Most High says:

“When you see them, their bodies impress you, and when they speak, you listen to their words.”

The word “body” may denote thickness and density themselves, or it may denote that which is thick and dense. Similarly, speculative thinkers sometimes use “body” to mean magnitude, which they may call the “mathematical body.” At other times, they mean the thing possessing magnitude, which is the natural body. Magnitude abstracted from that which possesses it is like number abstracted from that which is counted, and this exists only

They said: If this is the meaning of “body” in Arabic, then it is narrower than “that which can be pointed to.” For the Arabs do not call the spirit, which subsists in its own right, a body. Rather, they say, “His spirit has left his body,” and, “He is body and spirit.” They do not call the spirit a body, nor do they call the breath that leaves a person a body. The speculative theologians, however, adopted the convention of calling everything that can be pointed to a “body,” just as they adopted the convention of calling everything that subsists in its own right a “substance.” They then disagreed over whether everything that can be pointed to is composed of indivisible atoms, or of matter and form, or of neither. These three positions have been discussed at length elsewhere. Hence many of them would say: In our terminology, a body is that which subsists in its own right, or that which exists—not that which is composite.

The scholars who adhere to the Sunnah said: When the Jahmiyyah and other deniers of the attributes say that attributes can subsist only in a body, and that Allah Most High is not a body, they are answered: If by “body” you mean something composed of indivisible atoms, or something composed of matter and form, we do not concede your “first premise,” namely, your assertion that attributes can subsist only in something of that kind. Anyone who takes realities known through revelation and reason and gives them repellent names to turn people away from them is told: The dispute concerns meanings, not words—even if those words conform to the language. How, then, when they are your own inventions? Clearly, realities established by revelation and reason cannot be dismissed by such groundless verbal disputes.

As for calling the attributes “accidents,” this is a terminological convention adopted by those speculative theologians who use it, not the customary usage of Arabic speakers or of other scholars. Realities known through revelation and reason are unaffected by differences in terminology; rather, these are merely verbal disputes. In such disputes, the soundest usage is that which accords with the language of the Quran, the Messenger, and the early generations. The Muslims agree that expressions used by the Messenger and the Companions may be used. As for expressions they did not use, there is disagreement and a need for distinctions that are beyond the scope of this discussion.

As for the Kullābiyyah’s claim, “Whatever admits temporal occurrences is never free of them, and whatever is never free of temporal occurrences has itself come into being,” the majority of rational thinkers have disputed both premises. Even their own later followers disputed them on this point and acknowledged the invalidity of the rational arguments their predecessors advanced to deny that temporal occurrences subsist in Him. Later leading scholars among the Ashʿariyyah, the Shiʿah, the Muʿtazilah, and others acknowledged this, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

 فَقَالُوا:
 الْقُرْآنُ قَدِيمٌ وَهُوَ حُرُوفٌ وَأَصْوَاتٌ قَدِيمَةٌ أَزَلِيَّةٌ لَازِمَةٌ لِنَفْسِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى أَزَلًا وَأَبَدًا. وَاحْتَجُّوا عَلَى أَنَّهُ قَدِيمٌ بِحُجَجِ الْكُلَّابِيَة وَعَلَى أَنَّهُ حُرُوفٌ وَأَصْوَاتٌ بِحُجَجِ الْمُعْتَزِلَةِ.
 فَلَمَّا قِيلَ لَهُمْ:
 الْحُرُوفُ مَسْبُوقَةٌ بَعْضُهَا بِبَعْضِ فَالْبَاءُ قَبْلَ السِّينِ وَالسِّينُ قَبْلَ الْمِيمِ وَالْقَدِيمُ لَا يُسْبَقُ بِغَيْرِهِ وَالصَّوْتُ لَا يُتَصَوَّرُ بَقَاؤُهُ فَضْلًا عَنْ قِدَمِهِ قَالُوا: الْكَلَامُ لَهُ وُجُودٌ وَمَاهِيَّةٌ كَقَوْلِ مَنْ فَرَّقَ بَيْنَ الْوُجُودِ وَالْمَاهِيَّةِ مِنْ الْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ.

 وَالْكَلَامُ لَهُ تَرْتِيبٌ فِي وُجُودِهِ وَتَرْتِيبٌ مَاهِيَّةٌ الْبَاءُ لِلسِّينِ بِالزَّمَانِ هِيَ فِي وُجُودِهِ وَهِيَ مُقَارِنَةٌ لَهَا فِي مَاهِيَّتِهَا لَمْ تَتَقَدَّمْ عَلَيْهَا بِالزَّمَانِ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ مُتَقَدِّمَةً بِالْمَرْتَبَةِ كَتَقَدُّمِ بَعْضِ الْحُرُوفِ الْمَكْتُوبَةِ عَلَى بَعْضٍ. فَإِنَّ الْكَاتِبَ قَدْ يُكْتَبُ آخِرُ الْمُصْحَفِ قَبْلَ أَوَّلِهِ وَمَعَ هَذَا فَإِذَا كَتَبَهُ كَانَ أَوَّلُهُ مُتَقَدِّمًا بِالْمَرْتَبَةِ عَلَى آخِرِهِ. فَقَالَ لَهُمْ جُمْهُورُ الْعُقَلَاءِ هَذَا مِمَّا يُعْلَمُ فَسَادُهُ بِالِاضْطِرَارِ؛ فَإِنَّ الصَّوْتَ لَا يُتَصَوَّرُ بَقَاؤُهُ وَدَعْوَى وُجُودِ مَاهِيَّةِ غَيْرِ الْمَوْجُودِ فِي الْخَارِجِ دَعْوَى
translated_text:
Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal—and this became widespread among some later adherents of Ahmad ibn Hanbal—and they combined the positions of the Muʿtazilah and the Kullābiyyah. They agreed with the latter that it is eternal, and with the former that it consists of letters and sounds. They introduced an innovated doctrine—as others had done—saying:

The Quran is eternal, consisting of eternal, beginningless letters and sounds, inseparable from Allah Himself, exalted is He, throughout eternity, past and future. They supported its eternity with the arguments of the Kullābiyyah, and its consisting of letters and sounds with the arguments of the Muʿtazilah.

When they were told that some letters are preceded by others—bā precedes sīn, and sīn precedes mīm—whereas what is eternal cannot be preceded by anything else, and that sound cannot conceivably persist, let alone be eternal, they replied: Speech has both existence and essence. This resembles the position of those among the Muʿtazilah and others who distinguish between existence and essence.

They said: Speech has an order in its existence and an order in its essence. The temporal [precedence] of bā over sīn pertains to its existence, whereas in its essence bā coexists with sīn, without preceding it in time, although it precedes it in position. This is like some written letters preceding others: a scribe may write the end of the Quranic codex before its beginning, yet once he has written it, its beginning precedes its end in position.

The majority of rational thinkers replied to them: This is something whose invalidity is self-evident, for sound cannot conceivably persist, and the claim that an essence exists apart from what exists in external reality is a claim

that is invalid, as has been explained at length elsewhere. The arrangement in the Quranic codex is an arrangement of letters written in ink. Ink is corporeal, so its arrangement resembles that of the parts of a house or a human being: the first part exists alongside the second. Sound is different: its second part does not exist until the first has ceased to exist, just as with motion. Drawing an analogy between the two is therefore invalid.

Some of these people use the term “eternal” without understanding its meaning. Others say that by “eternal” they mean that it originated from Allah and is uncreated. This meaning is correct. However, those who disputed whether it is eternal did not intend this meaning. Anyone who tells them that it is eternal, intending this meaning, intends something correct, but is ignorant of what people mean, misleads those he addresses with these words, and introduces innovations into both religious law and language.

Many of these people then say that the eternal letters and sounds are neither the sounds heard from reciters nor the ink in the Quranic codex. Others say, rather, that the sounds heard from reciters are the eternal sound. Still others say that two things are heard from the reciter: the eternal sound, which is indispensable to the existence of speech, and the newly produced sound, which is whatever exceeds that.

These people say that the ink in the Quranic codex is created, but that the eternal letters are not the ink; rather, they are the shapes and dimensions made visible by the ink. These may also be engraved in stone or cut into paper. Some of them forbid saying of the ink that it is eternal or

Shaykh al-Islām, the mufti of mankind, Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah, was asked about people who say:

“The speech of human beings and others is eternal—whether true or false, obscene or otherwise, verse or prose—and there is no difference between Allah’s speech and theirs in respect of eternity, except with regard to reward.”

Some of them—indeed, most of them—also say that the sounds made by donkeys and dogs are likewise eternal. When what was transmitted from Imam Ahmad in refutation of their position was read to them, they reinterpreted it, saying that Ahmad had said this only out of fear of people. Are these people correct or mistaken? Must the ruler—may Allah Most High grant him success—restrain them from this or not? Do they become disbelievers by persisting in it or not? And is what was transmitted from Ahmad true, as they claim, or not?

He replied—may Allah be pleased with him:

All praise is due to Allah. Rather, these people are mistaken in this, committing an error that is forbidden by the consensus of the Muslims. They have uttered an abominable statement and a falsehood—indeed, disbelief and absurdity. Nor would any sane person who understands what he is saying profess it. However, those who have professed it have fallen prey to a misconception, which we shall explain, if Allah Most High wills.

When a statement’s falsity is self-evident to reason, there is no need to appeal to anything transmitted from an imam, except to demonstrate that its rejection and denunciation have been transmitted from the imams, and that whoever professes it opposes the Muslim community and introduces an innovation into religion. This also dispels the misconception of anyone who imagines that their position necessarily follows from a statement of one of the early generations, making him aware that they oppose the positions of the revered imams who are followed as exemplars. It also makes clear that the opposite of their statement is expressly affirmed by the imams followed in the Sunnah, and that this is not a matter on which they remained silent, neither affirming nor denying it.

There is no doubt that Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and the imams before and after him, expressly stated, without qualification, that human speech is created. Indeed, Ahmad and many other imams expressly affirmed this regarding “the acts of Allah’s servants” generally and “human speech” specifically. They did not refrain from making this unqualified statement because of the misconception that befell these dissenting innovators. He replied: ‘This is disbelief.’”’”

These reports and others like them were relied upon by those renowned for their adherence to the Sunnah, such as al-Marwadhī, al-Khallāl and others. Likewise, Imam Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Battah relies on these reports and similar ones in his book al-Ibānah al-Kabīr (The Greater Exposition).

I say: Hammād ibn Zayd was one of the eminent imams of the Sunnah, belonging to the same generation and holding a comparable standing as Mālik, al-Thawrī, al-Awzā‘ī, Hammād ibn Salamah and al-Layth ibn Sa‘d. Indeed, the scholars of the Sunnah considered him more firmly grounded in the Sunnah than al-Thawrī, although al-Thawrī surpassed him in knowledge and asceticism. Hadith scholars considered him more proficient in retaining hadith than Hammād ibn Salamah, although the latter was better known for asceticism and more active in calling people to the Sunnah. He was the leading imam of Basra at a time when Basra was the gathering place of Islamic learning. No one said that they were eternal. However, the “Qadariyyah” among the Mu‘tazilah and others believed that Allah did not create the voluntary acts of angels, jinn and humans—whether acts of obedience or disobedience—or the acts resulting from them.

They argued that, had He created them, this would necessarily mean that the servant was compelled to act, and that religious accountability, promise and warning, reward and punishment would all be nullified. They also argued that the servant knows with self-evident certainty that he himself brings his acts into being. They supported this with reasoned arguments.

When they introduced this “doctrine,” the imams of the Sunnah denounced it, just as the Companions—may Allah be pleased with them—had denounced the beginnings of this innovation when the Qadariyyah emerged towards the end of the Companions’ era. Ibn ‘Umar, Ibn ‘Abbās, Wāthilah ibn al-Asqa‘ and other Companions refuted them. The imams explained that anyone who holds that something which has come into existence, such as the servants’ acts or anything else, was not created by Allah is like someone who denies that Allah created other things that have come into existence, such as the heavens and the earth.

For Allah is the Lord of all worlds, the Sovereign of all dominion and the Creator of all things. Nothing in all the worlds lies outside His lordship, nothing in all dominion lies outside His sovereignty, and nothing that has come into existence lies outside His creation. Allah Most High says:

“Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the Guardian over all things.”

“To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Or have they assigned to Allah partners who created as He created, so that it became difficult to distinguish

one creation from the other? Say, ‘Allah is the Creator of all things.’” And Allah Most High says:

“The Originator of the heavens and the earth! How could He have a child when He has no consort? He created all things, and He has knowledge of all things.”

“That is Allah, your Lord; there is no deity but Him, the Creator of all things. So worship Him, and He is the Guardian over all things.”

“No vision can encompass Him, but He encompasses all vision.”

And Allah Most High says:

“That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things; there is no deity but Him. How then are you turned away?”

And Allah Most High says:

“To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He has taken no child and has no partner in His dominion. He created all things and determined them with precise determination.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, We have created all things according to a decree.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not then take heed?”

“If you tried to count Allah’s blessings, you could never enumerate them. Indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

“Allah knows what you conceal and what you reveal.”

“Those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, while they themselves are created.”

“They are dead, not alive, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.”

Thus, the adherents of the Sunnah and the united community—the people of hadith—were the ones who followed Allah’s Book and believed in what these texts entail. They held that Allah is the Creator, Lord, Owner, Sovereign and Guardian of everything that comes into existence: all entities and attributes, all direct acts and acts resulting from them, and every movement, whether natural, voluntary or forced. They also held that He, glorified be He, has power over all things and knows all things. They therefore believed in His all-encompassing knowledge, His perfect power, His all-embracing will and His complete lordship. For this reason,

Ibn 'Abbās said:

“Belief in divine decree is what holds belief in Allah’s oneness together. Whoever affirms Allah’s oneness and believes in divine decree has perfected his belief in His oneness; whoever affirms Allah’s oneness but denies divine decree has nullified his belief in His oneness through that denial.”

As for Allah’s attributes, they are included in what His explicit names and the pronouns referring to Him denote. When you say, “I worshipped Allah,” “I called upon Allah,” or “You alone we worship,” nothing of His attributes—His knowledge, mercy, speech or any other attribute—is excluded from this designation. For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever wishes to swear an oath, let him swear by Allah or remain silent.”

He also said:

“Whoever swears by other than Allah has committed shirk.”

Yet it is authentically established that he swore “by Allah’s might” and used the oath “By Allah’s life.” It is therefore clear that this is not swearing by other than Allah.

They thus gave these explicit verses their due by accepting the universal scope they expressly affirm: that Allah is the Creator of all things. For it is known that Allah Himself is not included among created things, and that His attributes are not excluded from what His name denotes.

As for the Mu'tazilah, who combined Jahmī and Qadarī doctrines, they excluded from these verses’ scope things unquestionably encompassed by the expression: the actions of angels, jinn, human beings and animals, whether acts of obedience or otherwise. Nor did they consider that the scope of His words, “all things,” depends on the surrounding statement, for a term’s scope varies according to its qualifications.

Thus, His saying, “He has knowledge of all things,” includes Himself, since He can be known. His saying, “He has power over all things,” includes everything that can be subject to power, encompassing everything whose existence is intrinsically possible. It may also be said that this includes everything called a “thing” in the sense of “something willed,” for shay’ (“thing”) was originally a verbal noun bearing the meaning of mashī’ (“something willed”). Thus, He has power over everything that can be willed. Alternatively, you may say: He has power over everything that can be subject to power. What is intrinsically impossible is not a thing, as all rational people agree.

Regarding His saying, “Allah is the Creator of all things,” it is known that the Creator is not the creation and is not included within the term’s scope here. Rather, it encompasses every created thing—that is, everything that has come into existence.

People did not dispute that human speech which Allah Most High has not revealed is brought into being and created. There was, however, disagreement concerning the “letters of the alphabet” and the “names of created things.” It was this disagreement that led these ignorant people into the absurdities they embraced, as we shall explain, Allah Most High willing. This response does not permit a detailed exposition of the “question of utterance,” but we shall address it briefly, saying:

Allah Most High sent His messengers, revealed His Books to them, and commanded them to convey to people the revelation and speech He had sent down to them. Some people believed in Allah and His messengers, accepted as true what they brought from Allah, and obeyed their commands. These are the believers in every age and era, and they are the people of Paradise and felicity. As Allah Most High says:

“Race toward forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden as wide as heaven and earth, prepared for those who believe in Allah and His messengers.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, those who believed, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians—whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteous deeds—will have their reward with their Lord. No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.”

Others disbelieved in the messengers and declared them liars, such as the nations whose accounts Allah has related to us: the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Lot, the dwellers of the Thicket, and Pharaoh

and the Arab polytheists, as well as all those who do not believe in messengership itself—among the Indians, the Brahmins and others, the Turks, the black peoples, and other unlettered nations who have no scripture—whether they declare the messengers liars or turn away from following them. For disbelief is the absence of faith in Allah and His messengers, whether accompanied by outright denial or, instead, by doubt and uncertainty, or by turning away from all of this out of envy, arrogance, or obedience to desires that divert one from following the divine message. Nevertheless, the disbeliever who declares the messengers liars is more extreme in disbelief, as is one who repudiates and rejects them out of envy despite being certain of their truthfulness. All the Meccan surahs address these people.

This is why He, glorified be He, says:

“The people of Noah denied the messengers.”

For they denied all the messengers and did not believe in messengership itself. Allah Most High said when He sent their father Adam down:

“He said, ‘Go down from it, both of you, all together, as enemies to one another. Then if guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer misery.

But whoever turns away from My remembrance will have a life of hardship, and We will raise him blind on the Day of Resurrection.’

He will say, ‘My Lord, why have You raised me blind when I used to see?’

He will say, ‘Just as Our signs came to you and you neglected them, so today you will be neglected.’

Thus do We recompense whoever transgresses and does not believe in the signs of his Lord. And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting.”

He thus declares that when guidance comes to them from Him—the Reminder He revealed to His messengers—whoever follows it is rightly guided and attains happiness in this world and the Hereafter, while whoever turns away from it suffers misery and becomes blind.

And for this reason, He says near the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqarah, describing the believers:

“They are upon guidance from their Lord, and it is they who will succeed.”

Similarly, He says here:

“Will neither go astray nor suffer misery.”

For guidance is the opposite of misguidance, and success is the opposite of misery. Allah Most High also says:

“O children of Adam, if messengers from among you come to you, relating My signs to you, then whoever fears Allah and reforms—no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.

But those who deny Our signs and disdain them—those are the inhabitants of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.”

Some people believe in part of what the messengers brought and disbelieve in another part, as do those who believe in some messengers but not others. Such are the Jews and Christians, who believe in Moses, or in Moses and the Messiah together, but not in Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Thus, in the Quran, Allah addresses both the unlettered peoples who have not followed any messenger and the People of the Book who affirm some of the messengers, as in His saying:

“And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered, ‘Have you submitted yourselves to Allah?’”

And His saying:

“Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not to desist.”

Likewise, some believe in certain aspects of messengership and disbelieve in others. These include the Sabian philosophers and others like them, who may acknowledge messengership in principle but regard the messenger as a just king who has established a code of law for his people. Or they say that the message is for the common people, not the elite; or that it concerns practical matters, not matters of knowledge; or that it concerns matters common to all people, not the distinctive qualities of those who have attained perfection,

and they acknowledge Muhammad’s messengership in general, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and hold him in esteem. They say:

“The philosophers of the world agree that no religious code greater than his has ever come to earth.”

Yet despite this, they disbelieve in some of what he brought. For example, they consider it permissible to follow religions other than his, such as Judaism and Christianity. They may also permit polytheism for the common people or the elite, such as invoking the celestial bodies, worshipping them, and prostrating before them. Inwardly, they may deny some of what he conveyed, claiming that what he taught concerning belief in Allah and the Last Day consists merely of parables intended to help the common people understand matters that must not be disclosed or have their true nature explained. This is because they consider it permissible for him to lie for what they claim is the benefit of the common people.

They may also claim that true knowledge of Allah is acquired from sources other than what the Messenger brought, and that some people know Allah better than he does or are superior to him, along with other such assertions. People of this kind have always existed, especially among the esoteric Qarmatians—the Ismāʿīlīs, the Nusayrīs, and the Ubaydid rulers who claimed the caliphate—and among the Khurramites, the Mazdakites, and similar sects.

Their elite are more extreme in disbelief than the Jews and Christians, and than the extremists who claim divinity or prophethood for ʿAlī or other human beings like him. They are hypocrites and heretics; yet among many of their followers

are those who think themselves believers in the Scriptures and the messengers because these people have misled them about the foundations of their doctrine, or because they agree with some of them in their views but not with others. Most of these people incline toward the Rāfidah. Some affiliate themselves with Sufism, others with speculative theology, and others join the jurists in their schools of law.

People of this kind abound under ignorant regimes far removed from knowledge of Islam and adherence to it. They were numerous under the rule of the Daylamites, the Ubaydids, and others like them. Likewise, they abound under the rule of ignorant Turks and other such people who believe in the message in general without knowing the details of what the Messenger brought. For the ignorant among the Turks and others resemble this type more than any other. These people do not regard following the Messenger as obligatory for everyone on earth. They may, however, consider following him better than following anyone else, and so follow him as a recommended practice; or they may follow only some of what he brought, or not follow him at all. Even so, they acknowledge him and his followers.

One who believes in part of the message but not the rest is also a disbeliever, as Allah Most High says:

“Those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and seek to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers, saying, ‘We believe in some and disbelieve in others,’ and seek to take a path in between.”

“They are truly the disbelievers, and We have prepared a humiliating punishment for the disbelievers.”

“But those who believe in Allah and His messengers and make no distinction between any of them—to them He will give their rewards. And Allah is Ever-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

Allah Most High also says, addressing the People of the Book:

“Yet here you are, killing one another and expelling a group of your own people from their homes, joining forces against them in sin and aggression; yet if they come to you as captives, you ransom them

although their expulsion was forbidden to you. Do you then believe in part of the Scripture and disbelieve in the rest? What recompense can there be for those among you who do this except disgrace in this worldly life? On the Day of Resurrection, they will be returned to the severest punishment. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Have you not seen those who claim to believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you? They wish to seek judgment from false deities, although they were commanded to reject them. Satan wishes to lead them far astray.”

“When they are told, ‘Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger,’ you see the hypocrites turn away from you in outright aversion.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Have you not seen those who were given a share of the Scripture? They believe in idols and false deities, and say of the disbelievers, ‘These are more rightly guided than the believers.’”

“Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed, and whoever Allah curses, you will find no helper for him.”

Thus, He condemned those who were given a share of the Scripture because they believed in what lay outside the message and preferred those outside the message to those who believed in it. Likewise, some people prefer the Sabian philosophers and regimes of ignorance—the ignorance of the Turks, Daylamites, Arabs, Persians, and others—to those who believe in Allah, His Book, and His Messenger.

He likewise condemned those who claim to believe in all the Scriptures, yet abandon recourse to the Book and the Sunnah for judgment and instead seek judgment from certain false deities venerated besides Allah. Islam, including rulers of the Turks and others. When they are told, “Come to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger,” they turn away in outright aversion. When calamity afflicts their minds, religion, and worldly affairs through specious doubts and desires, or strikes their persons and property as punishment for their hypocrisy, they say that they only intended to do good by establishing knowledge through inward experience and to reconcile “scriptural proofs” with “rational certainties”—which are, in reality, conjectures and specious doubts—or “experiential certainties”—which are, in reality, delusions and fantasies.

“Those are the ones whose hearts Allah knows. So turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them in words that reach their hearts.”

Up to His words:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in their disputes, then find within themselves no unease over your judgment and submit wholeheartedly.”

Allah Most High also says:

“They say, ‘We believe in Allah and in the Messenger, and we obey.’ Then a group of them turns away after that. Such people are not believers.”

“When they are called to Allah and His Messenger so that he may judge between them, a group of them turns away.”

Up to His words:

“The only response of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger so that he may judge between them, is to say, ‘We hear and we obey.’”

And the rest of the verse. Allah Most High also says:

“When they are told, ‘Believe in what Allah has revealed,’ they say, ‘We believe in what was revealed to us,’ yet they disbelieve in what came after it, although it is the truth, confirming what they have.”

Allah, glorified is He, has condemned those who divide and disagree over the Scripture, each believing in some of it but not the rest. As Allah Most High says:

“Mankind was one community. Then Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Scripture in truth to judge

between people concerning their differences. None differed over it except those who had been given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of mutual animosity. Then Allah, by His permission, guided those who believed to the truth over which they had differed. And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects—you have nothing to do with them.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together, and do not become divided.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Do not be like those who became divided and differed after clear proofs had come to them. Those will have a tremendous punishment.”

“On the Day when some faces will turn white and others will turn black.”

Ibn Abbās said: The faces of those who adhere to the Sunnah and the united community will turn white, while the faces of those who follow religious innovation and division will turn black.

Allah Most High also says:

“So devote yourself to the religion, inclining to truth. Adhere to the natural disposition upon which Allah created mankind. There is no changing Allah’s creation. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.”

“Turn to Him in repentance, fear Him, establish prayer, and do not be among those who associate partners with Him.”

“Those who divided their religion and became sects, each faction rejoicing in what it has.”

Allah Most High also says:

“He has ordained for you the religion He enjoined upon Noah, that which We have revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: ‘Uphold the religion and do not become divided over it.’ What you call the polytheists to is burdensome to them. Allah chooses for Himself whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns to Him.”

“They became divided only after knowledge had come to them, out of mutual animosity. Had it not been for a prior decree from your Lord granting respite until an appointed term, judgment would have been passed between them. Indeed, those who inherited the Scripture after them are in troubling doubt about it.”

“So call to this, and remain steadfast as you have been commanded. Do not follow their desires, and say, ‘I believe in every Scripture Allah has sent down

, and I have been commanded to judge justly between you. Allah is our Lord and your Lord.’”

Thus Allah commanded His Prophet to believe in all the revealed Scriptures and to deal justly with all people, giving everyone their due and restraining every wrongdoer from wrongdoing. For what he brought embodies fairness and justice in all religious and worldly affairs. This is the purpose of sending the messengers and revealing the Scriptures, as Allah Most High says:

“We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance, so that people may uphold justice.”

Allah Most High also says:

“The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, as do the believers. All believe in Allah, His angels, His Scriptures, and His messengers, saying, ‘We make no distinction between any of His messengers.’ And they say, ‘We hear and obey. Grant us Your forgiveness, our Lord; to You is the final return.’”

And so on to the end of the surah. It is established in an authentic report that “the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was given these two verses from a treasure beneath the Throne, and whenever he recited any part of them, he was granted what he sought.” It is also established in an authentic report that “whoever recites them in a night, they will suffice him.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Say, ‘We believe in Allah and what has been sent down to us, and what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, and what was given to Moses and Jesus, and what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we submit.’”

“If they believe as you believe, then they are rightly guided. But if they turn away, they are merely in opposition. Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.”

Section

Among the nations were disbelievers and hypocrites who rejected some of the message but not all of it, whether in respect of its extent or its character, just as there were disbelievers and hypocrites who rejected the message altogether. Among those who rejected the message altogether were some who claimed that the Messenger was a poet, a sorcerer, a soothsayer, someone taught by others, a madman, or a fabricator. Such was al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, “the Peerless,” the chief, philosopher, and sage of Quraysh, who is mentioned in the words of Allah Most High:

“Leave Me with the one I created alone, and to whom I granted abundant wealth and sons by his side, and for whom I made ample provision. Yet he desires that I give him more. No! He has stubbornly opposed Our signs. I shall burden him with an arduous ascent. He thought and calculated. May he be destroyed—how he calculated! Again, may he be destroyed—how he calculated! Then he looked; then he frowned and scowled; then he turned away in arrogance and said, ‘This is nothing but magic passed down; this is nothing but the word of a human being.’”

He acted as a philosopher opposed to the messengers acts: first he thought—that is, he sought to proceed from conceiving the two terms of a proposition to the premises that necessitate assent, in order to discover the middle term. For number abstracted from the things numbered, and magnitude abstracted from bodies, exist only in the mind. But how can its premises be sound when most of those used in metaphysics are mere claims whose universality is asserted, and whose propositions are taken as conceded without proof? Whenever a syllogism lacks a proposition known to be universal, it does not establish the desired conclusion. They confuse unquantified propositions, which have the force of particular propositions, with universally applicable, conceded propositions; alternatively, they assert their universality through some form of analogical reasoning.

It is well known that every syllogism must contain a “universal proposition.” Yet most of the “universal propositions” they use to establish their metaphysical conclusions are not known to be universally applicable. Their universality is supposedly established only through analogical reasoning, which may be among the most unsound forms of reasoning, entailing the likening of Allah to His creation. Thus they say, “From one, only one proceeds.” Yet they have nothing to support this except likening the Creator of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of all worlds, to natural properties, such as those of water and fire.

Moreover, the “one” they posit in metaphysics—and likewise in logic, where they treat the proposition concerning species as composed of it, namely “genus” and “differentia”—has no reality and exists only in minds, not in external particulars. The “rational inference” they employ as proof must contain a universal proposition. Inference is of two kinds: “syllogistic reasoning” and “analogical reasoning.” People disagree about what the term “inference” denotes. For if someone says, “The disputed fermented drink is forbidden because it is intoxicating, and is therefore forbidden by analogy with grape wine,” he must establish that intoxication is the basis of prohibition. In analogical reasoning, this is called the “basis,” the “effective cause,” the “indicator,” the “common factor,” the “posit,” and similar terms.

For the analogy to be valid, he must provide evidence that intoxication is the basis of prohibition, such that wherever intoxication is present, prohibition follows. If he formulates the argument syllogistically—“This fermented drink is intoxicating, and everything intoxicating is forbidden”—then intoxication is the repeated middle term in this formulation, just as it is the effective cause in analogical reasoning. In this syllogism, he must establish the universal major premise: “Everything intoxicating is forbidden.” Whatever establishes this proposition in the syllogistic formulation also establishes intoxication as the basis of prohibition in the analogical formulation. There is no difference between them.

In matters concerning Allah, both forms of reasoning may be used only as a fortiori arguments. This is the “method” employed by the Quran and followed by the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars. For nothing that exists is comparable to Allah—glorified is He—in “analogical reasoning,” nor can He be included in “syllogistic reasoning” whose individual instances are on an equal footing. Rather, whatever perfection is established for others, involving no deficiency whatsoever, He is all the more entitled to possess; and whatever imperfections others are declared free of, He is all the more entitled to be declared free of. As the Most High says:

“To those who do not believe in the Hereafter belong evil attributes, while to Allah belong the highest attributes.”

And the Most High says:

“He presents to you an example from yourselves: do you have, among those whom your right hands possess, any partners in what We have provided for you, so that you share equally in it, fearing them as you fear one another?”

We have discussed this at length elsewhere and explained that, in most matters, what is learned through “syllogistic reasoning” may be learned without it. Thus, the judgments concerning the particulars included in the syllogism can be known without knowing the judgment expressed by the universal proposition. For example, it is said: “The whole is greater than the part,” and “Two contraries cannot coexist.” Yet, for any particular whole and any particular pair of contraries, once it is known that one thing is part of another and that one thing is contrary to another, it is known that the whole is greater than its part and that the two contraries cannot coexist

We have explained that the proofs pointing to the Maker are signs that, in themselves, point to His holy Self. We have also explained the difference between the indicative force of signs and that of syllogistic reasoning: these proofs are more perfect and beneficial, while the syllogistic method is subordinate to them and inferior in benefit and perfection. The Quran employs both approaches. For knowledge of divine matters, prophethood, and other subjects, the former approach is more perfect and complete.

Yet these people claim that no truth accessible to our innate nature can be attained except through syllogistic reasoning, which necessarily requires a universal proposition. A universal proposition, however, yields only a universal concept apprehended by the intellect; it does not yield knowledge of any particular thing. Everything that exists is particular. How, then, can any rational person nevertheless claim that knowledge can be attained only by this method?

On what basis, then, do they claim that no knowledge can be attained except through them? And on what basis do they claim that there are no grounds for certainty beyond those a claimant possesses: familiar outward and inward intuitions, familiar self-evident truths, mass-transmitted reports, and familiar empirical findings?

Familiar intuitions, inward and outward perception, experience, and the like yield, by themselves, knowledge only of a specific particular, which is unsuitable as a premise in a syllogism. Its universal application, however, is known either through analogical reasoning or through non-inferential knowledge that Allah creates directly in the heart. If He creates non-inferential knowledge universally applicable to a set of particulars, then creating knowledge of some of those particulars is easy. Rarely does their method yield knowledge of a conclusion without that conclusion also being knowable through the same means by which the premises were known, or through an easier means. Their syllogisms thus add nothing but prolixity, intimidation, and misguidance.

Elsewhere, we have discussed “Greek logic” at length, explaining what is true and false, beneficial and harmful in it. To deny that knowledge can be attained except through such syllogisms, and that syllogisms can yield certainty except through these premises, is to speak without knowledge and to reject what one has not fully grasped. Rather, it is known that every perfection established for a created being—which involves no deficiency whatsoever—belongs more fittingly to the Creator, and every deficiency that must be denied of a created being must all the more be denied of the Creator. Such “rational arguments” belong to the kind of comparisons set forth in the Quran, and to Allah belongs the highest description. We have discussed this at length elsewhere.

Since those who disbelieved in the revealed message held the views described above, some who disbelieved in part of it came to share certain aspects of those views.

Thus, the Jahmiyyah denied that Allah speaks, says anything, loves, or hates, and denied all His other attributes conveyed by the messengers. They thereby denied part of the very reality of the revealed message, which is Allah’s speech, and denied some of the attributes of Allah conveyed in that message.

The first to proclaim this within Islam—although it had existed among other nations before Islam—was al-Ja'd ibn Dirham, the teacher of al-Jahm ibn Safwān. He was reportedly from Harrān, whose people included leading philosophers. From them Abū Nasr al-Fārābī learned much of the philosophy he acquired, according to what 'Abd al-Latīf ibn Yūsuf al-Baghdādī related.

Khālid ibn 'Abd Allāh al-Qasrī then slaughtered al-Ja'd as a sacrifice at Wāsit, in the days of scholars among the Successors and other Muslim scholars. Among those still living from the Successors at that time were al-Hasan al-Basrī and others, who praised him for what he had done and expressed their gratitude. They based this on the principle of the innovators among the Sabians who deny some of what the messengers brought and describe the Lord only through negative or relational attributes, or attributes combining the two. In this negation of the divine attributes, they in fact agree with Pharaoh, the leader of the disbelievers, who denied the Maker altogether; for denying His attributes necessarily entails denying His very essence.

Thus they agreed with Pharaoh in rejecting Moses’ statement that his Lord is above the heavens. Pharaoh said:

“O Haman, build me a tower so that I may reach the ways—”

“The ways into the heavens—and look upon the God of Moses, though I certainly think he is a liar.”

This contrasts with Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who confirmed Moses when he was taken up to his Lord. He reported that he found Moses there and went back and forth between his Lord and Moses. Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus affirmed Moses’ statement that his Lord is above the heavens, whereas Pharaoh denied it. People are either followers of Muhammad and Moses or followers of Pharaoh: Pharaoh denied Moses’ statement that Allah is above and that Allah had spoken to him, just as he denied the existence of the Maker, while Muhammad affirmed Moses in all of this.

These pure Sabians among the philosophers say that Allah does not truly have speech. Rather, according to those among them who outwardly profess belief in the messengers, His speech is what emanates into the souls of the prophets: it is something brought into being within their souls, without

For this reason, Imam Ahmad and the other imams understood their intent: their aim was to deny the divine attributes, and they were zindīqs (heretics)—a zindīq being a hypocrite. Thus, you find the imams describing them as heretics in their writings. Imam Ahmad, for example, wrote Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah, and al-Bukhārī entitled the final book of his Sahīh “The Book of Divine Oneness and the Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah.” ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak used to say, “We can indeed recount the statements of the Jews and Christians, but we cannot bring ourselves to recount the statements of the Jahmiyyah.”

The pure Sabians—who professed faith outwardly and inwardly believed in only part of the Scripture—say that “Allah’s speech” is a name for what emanates into the prophet’s heart from the “Active Intellect” or something else, and that “Allah’s angels” is a name for the luminous forms that take shape within his soul. They may say that Gabriel is the “Active Intellect,” or that he is one of the imaginary forms appearing within the prophet’s soul, like those a sleeper sees.

Hence, these people say that what distinguishes a prophet is his ability to evoke images in the imagination, and that the prophets outwardly expressed the contrary of what they inwardly held for the benefit of the common people. Through their words, they imparted not knowledge but imaginative representations that benefited the common people. They regard this as one of the finest things, praising and venerating the prophets for it.

For life, knowledge, power, speech, and the like are attributes of perfection, and the Lord Most High is more entitled to every perfection. It is therefore impossible for a created being to possess any perfection without the Creator being more entitled to it, just as it is impossible for a created being to be free of any deficiency without the Creator being more entitled to freedom from it. How could it be otherwise, when He creates perfection in those endowed with it?

“Furthermore,” anything that does not possess the attributes of perfection—life, knowledge, hearing, sight, power, speech, and so forth—must either be capable of possessing them but lack them, or be incapable of possessing them.

If it is capable of possessing them but lacks them, then, by the agreement of all rational people, it is characterized by attributes of deficiency, such as death, ignorance, blindness, deafness, incapacity, and muteness. For they agree that whatever is capable of either of two opposing attributes must possess one when it lacks the other. If, however, it is said to be incapable of possessing these attributes, then it is more deficient than something capable of possessing them but lacking them. Thus, a living creature that can sometimes hear and sometimes be deaf, sometimes see and sometimes be blind, sometimes speak and sometimes be mute, is more perfect than an inanimate thing incapable of either condition.

translated_text:
possessing the attributes of perfection is more deficient than one who is capable of them and can possess them. For it originated from Him—not, as the Sabians and those Jahmiyyah who agree with them claim, from the Prophet’s own soul, the “Active Intellect,” or the “air.” Rather, it is a revelation from One who is All-Wise, Praiseworthy. And to Him it will return when it is taken away by night from the written copies and people’s hearts.

Imam Ahmad became a guiding authority for those of Ahl al-Sunnah who came after him, across all their groups. They all agree with his main teachings and the fundamental principles of his doctrine, because he preserved for the Muslim community its inherited faith and prophetic foundations against those who sought to distort and alter them. He did not institute a religion that Allah had not authorized. What he taught is what the other eminent imams taught; indeed, his very statements are explicitly reported from their leading figures. However, he brought together their scattered teachings, strove against those who opposed them, and demonstrated how the Quran and Sunnah supported them. His statements concerning the Jahmiyyah, and those of the imams before and after him, are numerous and well known.

The Jahmiyyah are those who deny Allah’s attributes and follow the misguided Sabians. Offshoots of Jahmism began to circulate in many people’s minds. Some who were known for adhering to the Sunnah and hadith said: “We say neither that it is created nor that it is uncreated; rather, we withhold judgment.” Inwardly, most of them held it to be created, but in their hearts they feared the believers more than they feared Allah.

And “another group” said: “We say that Allah’s speech which He has not sent down is uncreated. As for the Quran which He sent down to His Messenger, and which Gabriel, Muhammad, and the believers recited, it is created.” These are the “Lafziyyah.”

The Muslim community therefore turned to its imam at that time for help, and Ahmad would tell them: “The Jahmiyyah have split into ‘three groups’: one says, ‘The Quran is created’; another says, ‘It is Allah’s speech,’ and says nothing further; and another says, ‘Our utterances and our recitation of the Quran are created.’”

What this last group’s position really entails is that the Quran which Gabriel brought down upon the heart of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is a created Quran which Allah did not speak. Their specious argument rested on the fact that our actions and voices are created, and that we recite it only through our movements and voices. Some of them might even say: “All we have are our utterances and our recitation. There is no Quran on earth other than this, and this is created.”

They were opposed by people who intended to uphold the Sunnah but fell into innovation. They answered falsehood with falsehood and countered one unsound position with another, saying: “Our recitation of the Quran is uncreated, and our utterances of it are uncreated, because this is the Quran, and the Quran is uncreated.” They failed to distinguish between what an unqualified designation denotes and what a qualified designation denotes, or between the referent considered on its own and that referent when coupled with something else and qualified.

Imam Ahmad therefore also condemned those who said that people’s recitation, reading, utterances, and voices were uncreated. He ordered that they be shunned, just as he had declared the former group to be Jahmiyyah and innovators. And reports from him

Abū Tālib went out, met a group of hadith scholars, and told them that Abū ʿAbd Allāh had forbidden him to say, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.”

Despite this, each of the “two groups”—those who say, “Our utterance of the Quran is uncreated,” and those who say, “Our utterance and recitation are created”—claims allegiance to Abū ʿAbd Allāh, attributes its own position to him, and maintains that he held its view. This is because he is an imam accepted by all, and because Ahmad affirms whatever truth each group holds and rejects whatever falsehood each group condemns in the other.

Thus Muhammad ibn Dāwūd al-Missīsī—one of the hadith scholars and one of Abū Dāwūd’s teachers—and a number of his contemporaries, such as Abū Hātim al-Rāzī and others, would say, “Our utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” A group followed them in this, including Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hāmid, Abū Nasr al-Sijzī, Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mandah, Shaykh al-Islam Abū Ismāʿīl al-Ansārī, Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Hamdānī, Abū al-Faraj al-Maqdisī, and others. They say, “Our utterances of the Quran are uncreated,” and report this from Ahmad, claiming that he subsequently adopted this position, as Abū Nasr mentioned in his book al-Ibānah (The Clarification).

These, however, are weak reports with unknown chains of transmission. They cannot stand against what has been mass-transmitted from him through his closest companions, his household, and trustworthy scholars—especially since it is known that, during his lifetime, he declared Abū Tālib mistaken in what he reported from him, until Ahmad made him retract it, and became intensely angry with him.

I have seen some of these people challenge those firmly established reports from him, while others have altered their wording. As for distorting their meanings, various groups have done so.

Those who accepted the reports from him as authentic and agreed with his rejection of both positions include the majority of the people of the Sunnah, as well as speculative theologians who affiliated themselves with them, such as Abū al-Hasan al-Ash'arī and others like him. In “The Doctrines of the People of the Sunnah and Hadith,” al-Ash'arī states that they condemn both those who say, “My utterance of the Quran is created,” and those who say, “My utterance of it is uncreated,” and that he himself holds this position.

Some of these people, however, interpreted the statements of Ahmad and others on this matter as prohibiting the assertion that the Quran is uttered. This interpretation was advanced by al-Ash'arī, Ibn al-Bāqillānī, Judge Abū Ya'lā, and the latter’s followers, such as Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī and others like him.

Among those who interpreted his statements in this way, some affirmed the very meaning that Ahmad had condemned in those who said, “My utterance of the Quran is created.” This was the position taken by al-Ash'arī and his followers. Others instead affirmed the meaning that Ahmad had condemned in those who said, “My utterance of it is uncreated.” This was the position taken by the judge, Ibn al-Zāghūnī, and others like them.

For Ahmad and all the other imams reject the claim that any part of Allah’s speech—whether its letters or its meanings—is created; that the meaning of the Torah is the same as the meaning of the Quran; or that Allah’s speech is the Quran when expressed in Arabic and the Torah when expressed in Hebrew. They also reject the claim that the revealed Quran is not itself Allah’s speech, or that it be asserted without qualification

translated_text:
that what is Allah’s speech is created. Ahmad and the other imams also reject the claim that any human actions or voices are uncreated, let alone eternal. Ahmad’s statements on the questions of recitation, faith, and the Quran follow a consistent pattern: he prohibited declaring without qualification that these are created, because this entails saying that some of Allah’s attributes are created and opens the door to that assertion. He likewise prohibited declaring without qualification that they are uncreated, because of the innovation and misguidance this involves.

Since Ahmad had become the imam of the Sunnah, those who came after him and affiliated themselves with the Sunnah acknowledged him as their imam. Al-Ash‘arī mentions this in his book al-Ibāna and elsewhere, saying:

“If someone says, ‘You have rejected the positions of the Jahmiyyah, the Mu‘tazilah, the Khawārij, the Rāfidah, and the Murji’ah. Tell us, then, the position you uphold and the religion you profess,’ he is told: ‘The position we uphold and the religion we profess consist in adhering to the Book of our Lord, the Sunnah of our Prophet, and what has been transmitted from the Companions and the Successors. We affirm what Abū ‘Abd Allāh Ahmad ibn Hanbal affirmed, and shun whatever contradicts his teachings. For he is the consummate imam and eminent leader through whom Allah made the truth manifest, clarified the path, and suppressed the innovations of the innovators, the deviations of those who stray, and the doubts of the doubters.’”

He then mentioned a number of doctrinal points.

translated_text:
For this reason, those who came after him disagreed on this issue. The group who say, “Our utterance and recitation are uncreated,” identify themselves with him and claim that this was the later of his two positions. Alternatively, they challenge reports from him that contradict this, or interpret his words in ways he did not intend.

The group who say that recitation is created, that the revealed Quran brought down by Gabriel is created, and that Allah did not speak the letters of the Quran, claim that this is Ahmad’s position and that they agree with him. Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī did this in what he reported from Ahmad, how he interpreted his words, and his declaration that he agreed with him. Likewise, Judge Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī sought to clear his fellow adherents of contradicting the Sunnah and its imams, such as Imam Ahmad. Abū Nu‘aym al-Asbahānī did the same in his well-known book on this subject, as did Abū Dharr al-Harawī and Judge ‘Abd al-Wahhāb al-Mālikī.

(Abū Bakr al-Bayhaqī also did this in al-I‘tiqād, in his discussion of Imam Ahmad’s virtues. It was related from Ahmad that he said, “My utterance of the Quran is created.” Al-Bayhaqī interpreted Ahmad’s widely reported condemnation of anyone who said, “My utterance of the Quran is [not] created,” as meaning that he intended the outright Jahmī who claims that the Quran which was not sent down is created) (*).

Similarly, some people falsely alleged that al-Bukhārī, the imam and compiler of the Sahīh, used to say, “My utterance of the Quran is created.” They classed him among the “Lafziyyah,” until a dispute arose between him and his fellow scholars, such as Muhammad ibn Yahyā al-Dhuhlī
translated_footnote:
(*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd stated (p. 108):
The word ghayr (not), placed in square brackets, was added by the compiler, may Allah have mercy on him. The correct wording omits it, because the shaykh mentioned that al-Bayhaqī related from Ahmad that he said, “My utterance of the Quran is created.” Ahmad’s condemnation of this very statement is established by mass transmission n, and al-Bayhaqī offered an interpretation of that condemnation n. Thus, the preceding and following context indicates that the intended wording is “My utterance of the Quran is created.” And Allah knows best.

{مَا يَأْتِيهِمْ مِنْ ذِكْرٍ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ مُحْدَثٍ}

translated_text:
and Abū Zur‘ah, Abū Hātim, and others over this matter. Personal inclinations and suspicions played a part in the affair, until he composed The Creation of Acts. In it, he included his report from Abū Qudāmah, from Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd al-Qattān, who said: “I have always heard our companions say, ‘The acts of Allah’s servants are created.’”

He also stated therein what accords with what he mentioned at the end of his Sahīh: that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated, and that Allah speaks with a voice and calls out with a voice. He presented authentic hadiths and reports on this subject which this is not the place to discuss at length. He explained the distinction between the voice with which Allah calls out and the voices heard from His servants, and that the voice with which Allah spoke is not the voice heard from the reciter. He set out the evidence for this, explaining that the acts and voices of Allah’s servants are created, whereas Allah Most High, His action, and His speech are uncreated.

Concerning His words,

“No reminder comes to them anew from their Lord,”

he said that its newness is unlike that of created beings. He also cited the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah introduces whatever commands He wills, and among what He has introduced is that you must not speak during prayer.”

He related from the scholars of the early generations that the Lord’s act of creating the world is not the created thing itself; rather, His action, which subsists in Him, is uncreated. It was also related from Nu‘aym ibn Hammād al-Khuzā‘ī that action is inseparable from life, and that whoever is living must be active. He mentioned other points of this kind, demonstrating his knowledge and that of the early generations of the truth that accords with authentic transmitted reports and clear reason.

He also mentioned that each of the two factions of the Lafziyyah—those who affirm and those who deny—claims allegiance to Abū ‘Abd Allāh; that much of what is transmitted from Ahmad ibn Hanbal is falsely attributed to him; that they failed to understand some of his statements because of their subtlety and obscurity; and that what he himself and Imam Ahmad said is the position of the imams and scholars, supported by the Quran and Sunnah.

I saw the following in the handwriting of Judge Abū Ya‘lā—may Allah have mercy on him—on the back of his handwritten copy of The Book of al-‘Uddah:

> I copied from the end of al-Bukhārī’s Book of the Epistle, concerning the distinction between reciting and what is recited. He said:
>
> “Reports from Ahmad ibn Hanbal have reached me in twenty-two versions, all contradicting one another. What I consider authentic is that he said: ‘I have never heard a scholar say: My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.’”
>
> He said: “Ahmad ibn Hanbal’s followers split into some fifty groups.”
>
> Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Bukhārī said: “Ibn Hanbal said: ‘A Lafzī is someone who says: The Quran as uttered by us is created.’”

Toward the end of Abū ‘Abd Allāh’s lifetime, there had also emerged members of the Kullābiyyah and similar groups—the followers of Abū Muhammad ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb al-Basrī, who composed works refuting the Jahmiyyah, the Mu‘tazilah, and others. He was one of the speculative theologians who affirmed the divine attributes, and his approach inclined toward the position of the people of hadith and Sunnah. Nevertheless, it contained an element of innovation, because he affirmed that the attributes subsist in Allah’s essence but did not affirm that matters dependent on His will subsist in His essence. Yet, in refuting the Jahmiyyah—those who deny the divine attributes and Allah’s exaltedness—he presented such evidence, arguments, and extensive discussion as demonstrated his distinction

translated_text:
in this field and his refutation of the doctrines of those who deny the attributes through various forms of proof and argument. What he presented became an aid and support for many people of understanding, delivering them from those specious arguments. He thus became an exemplar and leader for those who came after him who affirmed the attributes and refuted those who denied them. Nevertheless, they shared some of the deniers’ unsound foundational principles, which rendered some of their statements rationally unsound and contrary to the Messenger’s Sunnah.

Among his followers were al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī and Abū al-‘Abbās al-Qalānisī, followed by Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī, Abū al-Hasan ibn Mahdī al-Tabarī, Abū al-‘Abbās al-Duba‘ī, Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī, Abū Hātim al-Bustī, and others who affirmed the attributes, affiliated themselves with the Sunnah and hadith, and bore the title “the speculative theologians of the people of hadith.”

Many later followers of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad adopted Ibn Kullāb’s approach of distinguishing between “inherent attributes,” such as life, and “attributes dependent on His will,” holding that the former, but not the latter, subsist in the Lord. These included members of the Tamīmī family: Abū al-Hasan al-Tamīmī, his son Abū al-Fadl al-Tamīmī, and his grandson Rizq Allāh al-Tamīmī. In discussing Ahmad’s beliefs as part of his account of Ahmad’s virtues, Abū Bakr al-Bayhaqī relied on al-Fadl’s creed, which al-Fadl stated was Ahmad’s creed. Likewise, this approach of Ibn Kullāb was adopted by Abū al-Hasan ibn Sālim and his followers

This was also the approach of Abū al-Ma‘ālī al-Juwaynī, Abū al-Walīd al-Bājī, Judge Abū Bakr ibn al-‘Arabī, and others. Although they shared the distinction established by Ibn Kullāb, they divided into two positions concerning the Quran and certain other questions. Their views have been discussed at length elsewhere.

Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and other imams of the Sunnah warned against this principle introduced by Ibn Kullāb and against his followers. This was why Imam Ahmad warned against al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī and other Kullābīs like him.

When these people emerged, there also appeared among those who professed to affirm the divine attributes some who said, “Allah has not spoken with a voice.” Ahmad rejected this and declared those who said it to be Jahmīs. He said, “These heretics seek nothing but the negation of the divine attributes.” He transmitted reports establishing that Allah speaks with a voice. He likewise condemned those who said that the letters were created.

‘Abd Allāh ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal said in the Book of the Sunnah:

“I said to my father, ‘There are people here who say that Allah does not speak with a voice.’ He replied, ‘My son, these people are Jahmīs and heretics. They seek nothing but the negation of the divine attributes.’ He then cited reports contradicting their claim.”
