At the end of the Sahīh and in The Creation of Actions, al-Bukhārī transmitted the reports concerning this matter and explained the distinction between Allah’s voice with which He speaks and the voices of His servants reciting the Quran. In agreement with Imam Ahmad and the other imams, he explained that Allah speaks with a voice, as the reports establish, and that this is not the voice of the servant reciting; that voice, rather, is the servant’s own. He expressly stated all of this in several places.

The imams of the Sunnah and hadith generally affirm this and uphold this distinction. They do not agree with those who claim that divine speech contains neither letters nor sound, nor with those who claim that the voices heard from reciters and their utterances are beginningless. Nor do they say that the Quran consists of nothing but letters and sounds.

I have recorded Imam Ahmad’s statements and explicit pronouncements, along with the statements of the imams before and after him, elsewhere, since the answer to this question does not allow for extensive elaboration. Neither Imam Ahmad nor the other imams stated that the voice with which Allah spoke was beginningless. Rather, they say, “Allah has always been One who speaks.” They may also say, “Allah has always been One who speaks whenever He wills, saying whatever He wills,” as Imam Ahmad, Ibn al-Mubārak, and others have said.

Likewise, in their time and afterward, their followers and others disputed the meaning of the Quran’s being uncreated: whether what is meant is that speech itself is beginningless

and eternal, like His knowledge, or that Allah has always possessed the attribute of speaking whenever He wills. There are two views on this. Al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī reported both views from the adherents of the Sunnah, as did Abū Bakr ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz from the followers of Imam Ahmad in his book al-Shāfī. Abū ʿAbd Allāh Ibn Hāmid also mentioned them in his book Usūl al-Dīn (The Foundations of Religion).

This dispute exists among the various groups adhering to the Sunnah and hadith. It rests on the underlying question of “attributes pertaining to voluntary acts.” This question is disputed among all the groups devoted to hadith, the Sunnah, jurisprudence, and Sufism, including those adherents of the four legal schools who joined them, as well as among the other sects—even among the philosophers. I have examined this thoroughly elsewhere.

This is the source of disagreement among those who agreed with the early generations that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated. They differed over whether the Lord speaks by His will and power, holding two views.

Those who agreed with Ibn Kullāb said that He does not speak by His will and power; rather, His speech is inseparable from His essence, like His life. Some among them recognized that individual letters and sounds cannot be beginningless. They therefore could not say that what is beginningless consists of letters and sounds, because these can only occur in succession, and a sound does not persist for two moments, let alone be beginningless.

They therefore said that what is beginningless is a single meaning, since an infinity of meanings is impossible, as is singling out one number rather than another. Thus, they said that it is a single meaning. They also said that Allah does not speak in Arabic or Hebrew, and that the meaning of the Torah, the Gospel, the Quran, and all of Allah’s other speech is one and the same

and that the Verse of the Throne and the Verse of Debt have one and the same meaning, along with other implications that most rational people regard as self-evidently false.

Some of these people recognized that Allah spoke the Arabic Quran and the Hebrew Torah, that He called out to Moses with a voice and calls out to His servants with a voice, and that the Quran—both its letters and its meanings—is Allah’s speech. Yet they also believed that it is beginningless in its particular existence and that Allah did not speak by His will and power.

They therefore committed themselves to the view that it consists of letters and sounds whose individual existence is beginningless: they have always existed and always will. They said that the letter bā did not precede the sīn, nor did the sīn precede the mīm, and that all the letters coexist in a beginningless conjunction that has always existed and always will. They said, “They are ordered in their reality and essence, but not in their existence.”

Many of them also said that, despite this, they are one thing, along with other “implications” that most rational people regard as self-evidently false.

Some of these people say, “It is beginningless,” without understanding what “beginningless” means. When asked about this, they say, “They are beginningless in divine knowledge,” not realizing that created things, such as heaven and earth, are likewise so, despite being created. Others call it “ancient,” meaning that it precedes other things, without realizing that those who say it is created do not dispute its being ancient in this sense. Still others say, “By saying that it is beginningless, we mean that it is uncreated,” without understanding that, on this view, it is also eternal and has always existed. These people heard

The second position is that Allah speaks by His will and power, while His speech is uncreated. This is the position of the great majority of the people of Sunnah and rational inquiry, and of the leading authorities in Sunnah and hadith. Some of them, however, believed that Allah could not have spoken by His will in beginningless eternity, just as, in their view, He could not have done anything in beginningless eternity. They therefore committed themselves to saying that He spoke by His will after not having spoken, just as He acted after not having acted. This is the position of many scholars of speculative theology, hadith, and Sunnah.

As for the early generations and the leading authorities, they said that Allah speaks by His will and power, while His speech is nevertheless beginningless in kind—meaning that He has always spoken whenever He wills. Speech is an attribute of perfection: one who speaks is more perfect than one who does not speak; one who speaks by his will and power is more perfect than one who does not speak by his will and power; and one who has always spoken by his will and power is more perfect than one for whom speech becomes possible only after having been impossible—even supposing that this were possible. “So by your Lord, We will surely question them all about what they used to do.”

A group of the early Muslims explained that this refers to saying, “There is no god worthy of worship but Allah.” Another example is the Prophet’s statement (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) in an authentic hadith:

“Envy is warranted only in two cases: a man whom Allah has granted the Quran, who recites it throughout the night and day, whereupon another man says, ‘If I had been given what this man has, I would do as he does.’”

For this reason, Ahmad’s followers differed over whether someone who swore not to perform any action that day would break his oath by speaking. There are two opinions, both mentioned by al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā and others.

The “Lafziyyah who affirmed createdness” did not deny that the Quran—its letters and meanings—is Allah’s speech, or that Allah speaks with a voice. Indeed, they might say that the entire Quran, its letters and meanings, is Allah’s speech, for Allah speaks with a voice, as Ahmad, al-Bukhārī, and other leading authorities explicitly affirmed, and as the transmitted reports attest. Yet they say that the letters and meanings sent down to earth are not the very speech of Allah, which is uncreated. They may instead call them a reproduction of Allah’s speech, as Ibn Kullāb does, or an expression of Allah’s speech, as al-Ashʿarī does. They may also call them Allah’s speech, since the intended meaning is understood among them.

But when Abū Muhammad ibn Kullāb emerged and debated the Muʿtazilah using a method of logical inference, he conceded premises that they themselves had devised: that Allah Most High cannot speak in letters, and that “volitional attributes”—actions, speech, and other things connected to His will and power—cannot subsist in His essence. Their reasoning was that this would entail that He had not been free of originated events, and whatever is not free of originated events is itself originated. These concessions compelled him to say that Allah’s speech is nothing but meaning alone, and that letters are not part of Allah’s speech.

Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī followed him in this, although they disagreed over whether the Lord had been commanding and prohibiting from eternity or came to command and prohibit after not having done so. They also disagreed over whether “speech” is one attribute, as al-Ashʿarī maintained, or five attributes, as Ibn Kullāb maintained.

These men thus differed from the leading authorities of the Sunnah and hadith in two respects. (The first is that, in their view, half of the Quran is Allah’s speech, while the other half is not Allah’s speech. Rather, Allah created it in the air or in the Preserved Tablet, or Gabriel or Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—brought it into being.

By holding that half of the Quran is created, these men agree with those who maintain that it is created. Yet these say that this created half is Allah’s speech, while those say that it is created, separate from Allah, and is His speech. Those, however, do not affirm that Allah has any speech connected to Him and subsisting in His own being—neither meanings nor letters. These, on the other hand, say that Allah has speech subsisting in Him

and connected to Him, consisting of meaning. Thus, the former are more extreme in their innovation in denying that Allah truly speaks and in declaring His speech created.

The latter are more extreme in their innovation in excluding from Allah’s speech what actually belongs to it. In this they agree with part, though not all, of what al-Wahīd said, namely, in their claim: “Half of the Quran is not Allah’s speech, but human speech.”

Some of them may argue that, since it is attributed to the Messenger, he must have brought its letters into being. Yet anyone making this argument has failed to reflect and recognize that Allah attributes it on one occasion to a messenger who is Gabriel, and on another to a messenger who is Muhammad. In the first passage, He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger,
possessed of power and securely established with the Lord of the Throne,
obeyed there and trustworthy.”

This is Gabriel. In the other passage, He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.
It is not the word of a poet—little do you believe!
Nor is it the word of a soothsayer—little do you take heed!”

This is Muhammad. If its attribution to the Messenger meant that he originated its letters and brought them into being, it could not properly be attributed to both of them, since it is impossible for each of them to have brought its letters into being.

Furthermore, He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a messenger.”

This is a statement about the Quran—a designation more properly applied to its meaning, both in their view and in that of the people of the Sunnah. Had the Messenger originated it, the Quran would have come from him, not from Allah. Allah attributed it to the Messenger only because he conveyed it, delivered it, and brought it from Allah. Hence He said:

“The word of a messenger,”

rather than “the word of an angel” or “a prophet.” Instead, He used the designation “messenger” to make clear

Some believed that the Quran, and speech generally, consists of nothing but letters and sounds, whereas the other group says that speech is nothing but the meaning subsisting within the self.

Both these newly introduced denials contradict the position of the imams, such as Imam Ahmad, and other imams and leading scholars of the various groups. In their usage, speech denotes both letters and meanings, just as “the human being,” endowed with speech, denotes both body and soul. Whoever says that the human being is nothing but this visible physical whole is like someone who says that speech is nothing but articulated sounds. Whoever says that the human being is nothing but a subtle entity beyond this body is like someone who says that speech is nothing but a meaning beyond these letters and sounds. Both positions deny part of the realities designated by these terms and reject the bounds of what Allah has revealed to His Messenger.

Similarly, the former group’s unqualified assertion that the Quran has no reality other than letters and sounds, their failure to distinguish between Allah’s voice heard from Him and the reciter’s voice, and their assertion that the Quran is eternal led the ignorant among them, and those who lied about them, to report that they held that people’s voices and the ink in the written copy of the Quran are eternal, and that the letters constituting Allah’s speech are the ink itself. Yet they did not say this; rather, they rejected it, just as Allah distinguished words from ink in His saying:

“Say, ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought its like as a supplement.’”

These people made “two errors”: an error concerning their own doctrine and an error concerning the revealed law. As for the error in their “representation of their doctrine,” they should have said that the Quran is in the written copy just as knowledge and meanings are on paper. Just as one says, “Knowledge is in this book,” one says, “Speech is in this book.” For, in their view, speech is the meaning subsisting in the essence. Its analogue should therefore be knowledge subsisting in the essence, not the essence itself.

As for the error concerning “the revealed law,” they should be told: The Quran is in written copies just as Allah’s name is in written copies. For the Quran is speech: it is preserved in hearts just as speech is preserved in hearts, and it is mentioned by tongues just as mention is made of

speech by tongues. It is written in copies of the Quran and on sheets, just as speech is written in copies of the Quran and on sheets. Speech, understood as verbal expression, corresponds to meaning and signifies it, while meaning corresponds to existing realities.

Whoever says, “The Quran is preserved just as Allah is known; it is recited just as Allah is mentioned; and it is written just as the Messenger is written,” has erred by two levels in his analogy and comparison. For he has equated the existence of entities that subsist in themselves with the existence of an expression signifying a meaning that corresponds to those entities. Muslims know the difference between His saying, exalted is He:

“Indeed, it is a noble Quran, in a protected Book,”

and His saying, exalted is He:

“And indeed, it is in the scriptures of the former peoples.”

The Quran was not sent down to anyone before Muhammad—neither its wording nor the entirety of its meanings. Rather, Allah sent down mention of it and information about it, just as He sent down mention of Muhammad and information about him. Thus, the Quran is mentioned in the scriptures of the former peoples just as Muhammad is mentioned in those scriptures, and he is written about in the Torah and the Gospel they possess.

Allah and His Messenger are known in hearts, mentioned by tongues, and written about in the written copy of the Quran, just as the Quran was known to those before us, mentioned to them, and written about in their scriptures. That was only mention of it and information about it. As for us, the Quran itself has been sent down to us, and the Quran itself is written in our copies, just as the Quran itself is in the protected Book and in the purified scriptures.

For this reason, a distinction must be made between His saying, exalted is He:

“And everything they have done is in the records”

and His saying, exalted is He:

“By a Book inscribed on parchment unrolled.”

For deeds are in the records just as the Messenger and the Quran are in the scriptures of the former peoples. As for “the Book inscribed on parchment unrolled,” this is like speech itself being written on a sheet. How different the two are!

This is because everything has “four levels” of existence: existence in external reality, existence in minds, existence in speech, and existence in writing—that is, concrete, cognitive, verbal, and written existence.

For this reason, the first words Allah revealed of the Quran were:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created.”

In this passage, He mentioned that He, glorified is He, bestows both forms of existence. He said:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created—created man from a clinging clot.”

This is existence in external reality. Then He said:

“Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen—taught man what he did not know.”

Thus, He mentioned that He bestowed cognitive, mental existence. He mentioned teaching by the pen because it necessarily entails teaching words and expression, and teaching words and expression necessarily entails teaching meaning. By mentioning the last level, He thus indicated the first. Had He mentioned the first level alone, or spoken simply of teaching, that would not have indicated universality and comprehensiveness.

Since this is so, the Quran is speech, and speech occupies “the third level”; there is no other level intervening between it and the paper. Rather, speech itself is recorded in the book, as Allah, exalted is He, said:

“Indeed, it is a noble Quran, in a Book

well-protected.” And He, exalted is He, said:

“Rather, it is a glorious Quran, in a Preserved Tablet.”

And He said:

“Reciting purified pages containing upright writings.”

And He said:

“No indeed! It is a reminder—so whoever wills may take heed of it—in honored pages, exalted and purified.”

And He said:

“Even if We had sent down to you a book on a sheet of paper.”

It may be said that it is written in them, just as one may say without qualification that it is in them, as He, exalted is He, said:

“By the Mount, and a Book inscribed on parchment unrolled.”

As for the Lord, glorified is He, His Messenger, or any other entity, only the name appears in the scriptures, and that name is speech. Hence He said:

“Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written of in the Torah and the Gospel in their possession.”

What is in the Torah is merely the written record of him, his mention, description, and name. This is the “fourth level” of his existence. How, then, can the Quran or speech being in scriptures or on paper be likened to Allah, His Messenger, the sky, or the earth being in scriptures or on paper? If someone were to say, “Allah or His Messenger is in the scriptures or on paper,” that would be rejected unless accompanied by contextual indications clarifying the intended meaning, as in His saying:

“Everything they did is in the records.”

And His saying:

“Indeed, it is in the scriptures of the former peoples.”

What is meant is its mention and written record. Zubur is the plural of zabūr. Zabūr follows the pattern faʿūl with the meaning of mafʿūl—that is, mazbūr, meaning “written.” Thus, the word zabūr denotes writing. “It originated from Him and came forth from Him.”

This means that He is the One who spoke it; it did not come forth from anyone else. It does not imply that it separated from Him and moved away from Him. For He, glorified be He, said concerning created beings:

“Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths; they speak nothing but a lie.”

It is well known that a created being’s speech does not separate from the one in whom it subsists. Everyone knows that transferring and passing on speech means conveying it, as He said:

“Convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord.”

And He, exalted be He, said:

“Those who convey Allah’s messages and fear Him.”

And He, exalted be He, said:

“So that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“May Allah brighten the face of a person who hears a hadith from us and conveys it to someone who has not heard it. Many a bearer of religious knowledge lacks understanding, and many a bearer of religious knowledge conveys it to someone with greater understanding than his own.”

He also said:

“Convey from me, even if only a single verse.”

translated_text:
and an accident in a substance, so as to become an attribute of it. Nor is it present there as a body is present in the space to which it has moved from another space. Nor is it present there merely as a sign, like the world, which is a sign of the Maker. Rather, it belongs to another category, intelligible in its own right. Not everything that exists must have a counterpart matching it in every respect. By their innate disposition, people understand what it means for a speaker’s speech to be on a sheet of paper. They know that the speech subsisting in him has not separated from his being and come to dwell in something else. They also know that what is on the sheet is not merely a sign pointing directly to a meaning in his mind. Rather, what is on the sheet corresponds to his utterance, his utterance corresponds to his meaning, and his meaning corresponds to external reality.

What is in his mind may also be known through natural signs and voluntary movements that he did not intend to convey anything. Yet no one calls these the speaker’s speech in the same way as the speech heard from him. If speech were so called merely because it signifies something, every sign would share that designation. We shall discuss this, Allah willing.

If what is in a written copy of the Quran required reverence merely because it signifies something, every sign would require reverence. Indeed, that which points to the Maker and His attributes is greater than that which points to His speech, yet it does not possess the sanctity of a written copy of the Quran. As for indications of the meaning within a person’s mind, that meaning may sometimes become known without his choosing. It may become known through natural sounds, such as weeping; through movements not intended to convey anything; through movements intended to convey meaning, such as gestures; or through utterances intended to convey meaning.

Thus, when these people—who declared the doctrine of the “Lafziyyah” erroneous yet added much evil to it—say that “reading” is distinct from what is read, “recitation” from what is recited, and “writing” from what is written, they mean by reading only the readers’ voices, and by “writing” the writers’ ink. They mean that these are distinct from the meaning subsisting in His essence, which is Allah’s speech, and are merely an indication of it and an expression of it. In their view, there is nothing but reading and what is read. Thus, nothing remains except sound, ink, and a meaning subsisting in His essence; there is no Quran beyond these.

They have excluded the letters of Allah’s speech that He spoke, and the reality of the Quran’s meanings in Allah Himself, exalted is He. They have also excluded the Quran’s meanings in the souls of its readers and listeners. For there is no doubt that the Quran we read contains letters and meanings—letters that are spoken and written. If, in their view, there is nothing but the servant’s voice and the ink in the written copy of the Quran, where are the meanings? And where are the letters of the Quran that Allah sent down, even if they regard them as created?

For these people say that the meanings of all Allah’s speech are a single meaning. Thus, the meaning of “May the hands of Abū Lahab perish” is the meaning of “Say: He is Allah, One,” and the meaning of the Torah is the meaning of the Quran and the Gospel. They may then reduce all the meanings of speech to assertion, and may identify the meaning of assertion with knowledge, while treating knowledge of one thing as distinct from knowledge of another.

For this reason, most rational people say that the falsity of this is self-evident. They say that command, prohibition, and assertion are relational attributes of speech, not its types and divisions. Allah’s speech is far greater than the speech of created beings. The speech contained in the written copy of the Quran belongs to this last category, not the preceding categories. How much more so, then, when that wording possesses such distinctive qualities that it is said of it:

“Say: If mankind and jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce its like, even if they helped one another.”

However, some things signify something else intentionally, while others signify something else without any intention on their part to do so, such as inanimate things: they serve purposes other than signifying the Creator. Other things are intended solely to signify, such that mentioning them for their intended purpose amounts to mentioning their referents—as with a name and that which it names. What is intended by a name is the thing named; hence, when the name is mentioned, the thing named is intended. The same applies to “wording” in relation to the meaning it signifies, and to “writing” in relation to wording. Thus, what is intended by writing

They lead those who disagree with them to believe that the very sound heard from the servant is the very sound with which Allah spoke. Whoever reflects on Imam Ahmad’s statements on this subject will find them among the soundest and clearest explanations. He will also find that each group claiming adherence to the Sunnah has held fast to certain statements among them. Yet something of the Sunnah elsewhere may remain hidden from one group while becoming clear to another, and so the former denies it.

The disputes among people throughout the world and the immense, almost unmanageable confusion concerning this subject stem from “two fundamental issues”: the question of Allah’s speaking the Quran and the rest of His speech, and the question of His servants’ uttering Allah’s speech.

The reason for this is that speaking and addressing others have various levels and degrees. Likewise, conveying another’s speech takes different forms and has different characteristics. Some people grasp only certain degrees and characteristics, perhaps grasping only the lowest and then denying the highest. Thus they come to believe in part of the message and disbelieve in another part. Each of the two groups affirms what it has grasped while denying the truth held by the other.

Allah has explained this in His Book and in the Sunnah of His Messenger. He, the Exalted, says:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills.”

For in this verse He encompasses all the degrees of speaking, as the early generations explained. We have received a report in al-Ibānah by Abū Nasr al-Sijzī, in the book of al-Bayhaqī, and in other works, from Uqbah, who said: Ibn Shihāb was asked about this verse:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills. Indeed, He is Most High, All-Wise.”

Ibn Shihāb said: “This verse was revealed to encompass all human beings to whom Allah has given revelation. The speech with which Allah addressed Moses was from behind a veil. Revelation is what Allah communicates to one of His prophets—peace be upon them—so that whatever He, Mighty and Majestic, wills of His revelation may be firmly established in the prophet’s heart and written down. It is Allah’s speech and His revelation. Some of it is between Allah and His messengers. Some of it the prophets convey verbally without writing it down for anyone or commanding that it be written. Rather, they relate it to people and explain it to them, because Allah has commanded them to explain it to people and convey it to them. Some revelation Allah sends through whomever He wills from among His chosen angels, who speak it to His prophets among humankind. Some revelation Allah sends through whomever He wills among the angels, so that it is imparted by revelation into the heart of whomever He wills among His messengers.”

I say: The first is revelation, which is swift, hidden communication: either while awake

or in sleep, for the dreams of prophets are revelation, and the dreams of believers are one of the forty-six parts of prophethood, as is authentically reported from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in the authentic hadith collections. Ubādah ibn al-Sāmit said—and this is also narrated as a statement traced back to the Prophet:

“The believer’s dream is speech by which the Lord addresses His servant in sleep.”

The same applies “while awake.” It is authentically reported from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that he said:

“Among the nations before you were men who received inspiration. If there is any such man in my nation, it is Umar.”

Another version in the authentic collection reads, “men who were spoken to.” Allah Most High says:

“And when I inspired the disciples to believe in Me and My Messenger.”

And He Most High says:

“And We inspired the mother of Moses: ‘Nurse him.’”

Indeed, He Most High also says:

“And He ordained in each heaven its command.”

And He Most High says:

“And your Lord inspired the bee.”

Thus, this kind of revelation may come to those who are not prophets, whether awake or asleep. It may take the form of a voice calling, with the sound occurring within the person rather than outside him, whether awake or asleep, just as the light he sees may also be within him.

This “degree” of revelation, which occurs within a person without his hearing an angel’s voice, occupies the lowest and last rank, though it is the first for someone advancing along the path. The sound a person hears may also originate outside his own soul, coming from the True One, exalted is He, through the tongue of one of His angels or someone other than an angel. This is what the Jahmiyyah among the Muʿtazilah and others have recognized, believing that Allah has no way of speaking other than this. It falls within the category of revelation, which is one of the forms of divine speech, or a category parallel to speech through a messenger. This is “the second category,” as the Exalted says:

“Or He sends a messenger who reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills.”

This is revelation conveyed by the messenger. It differs from the first kind of revelation from Allah, which is one of the forms of divine speech in its broader sense. Revelation conveyed by the messenger also takes various forms. In the two Sahīh collections, ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, reported that al-Hārith ibn Hishām asked the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, “How does revelation come to you?”

He replied: “Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, and this is the hardest form for me. Then it ceases, and I have grasped what was said. At other times, the angel appears to me in the form of a man and speaks to me, and I grasp what he says.”

ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: “I have indeed seen him

receive revelation on a bitterly cold day; when it ceased, his forehead would be streaming with sweat.”

He, peace and blessings be upon him, thus explained that the angel’s descent upon him sometimes takes place inwardly, with a sound like the ringing of a bell, and sometimes with the angel appearing in the form of a man who speaks to him. Thus Gabriel would come in the form of Dihyah al-Kalbī, just as he appeared to Mary as a man of perfect form, and just as the angels came to Abraham and Lot in human form, as Allah has related in several places. Allah has called both these forms of the angel’s conveying his message and speaking “revelation,” because of the concealment involved: when the recipient sees him, he needs to know that he is an angel; and when he comes with something like the ringing of a bell, the recipient needs to understand what the sound conveys.

It has become clear that He spoke to Moses in a specific, full sense, as indicated by His words:

“Among them were those to whom Allah spoke.”

This is understood alongside the knowledge that He revealed to all of them and spoke to them in the general sense. It is also established by His distinguishing His speaking from His revelation to the prophets; by the verbal noun emphasizing His speaking; by His making speaking from behind a veil a category distinct from His revelation; and by the reports transmitted through numerous independent channels from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions concerning His speaking specifically to Moses, directly from Him to Moses. It is established that He spoke to him with a voice that Moses heard, as related in reports from the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars, in accordance with what the Book and the Sunnah indicate.

Here, “the third group,” the Kullābiyyah, erred. They believed that He merely revealed to Moses, peace be upon him, a meaning without sound. They disagreed over whether it could be heard. Some said that Moses heard that meaning through a subtle faculty He created within him. They maintained that hearing, sight, smell, taste, and touch are attributes that can have anything that exists as their object, as al-Ashʿarī and a group of others held.

Others said that Moses did not hear Allah’s speech, since, in their view, it is a meaning, and a meaning cannot be heard. This was the position of al-Qādī Abū Bakr and a group of others.

What they have affirmed falls within the general category of revelation which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, distinguished

translated_text:
al-Junayd:

“Affirming Allah’s oneness” is the heart’s utterance, and “reliance on Allah” is the heart’s action.

They thus attributed speech and power to the heart, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, attributed inner speech to the soul when he said:

“Allah has pardoned my community for what they say to themselves”—then he added—“so long as they neither speak of it nor act upon it.”

It is therefore clear that “speech,” without qualification, consists of letters corresponding to meaning, although, when qualified, the term may apply to other things. Indeed, they may call any intentional communication or indication an utterance, whether conveyed through words, gestures, or finger positions—bending the fingers.

They may also call an indication an utterance even when it is unintentional, as with the indications given by inanimate objects. Thus, they say:

“It said: ‘The breadth of his belly.’”

And:

“The cistern filled and said, ‘Enough, enough!
Gently now—you have filled my belly.’”

And:

“His two eyes said to him, ‘We hear and obey.’”

This is called “the language of circumstance” or “indication through circumstance.” An example is their saying:

“Ask the earth: Who made your rivers gush forth, watered your fruits, and planted your trees? If it does not answer you in words, it answers you through reflection.”

Another example is their saying:

“The eyes tell me what the heart conceals;
There is no good in bashfulness and sidelong glances.”

Another example is their saying:

“I asked the dwelling to tell me
What had become of my loved ones.
It said to me, ‘The people camped
For some days, then departed.’”

This may also be called testimony. Some have claimed that the glorification of Allah by created things mentioned in the Quran belongs to this category: their pointing to the Creator, Most High. The correct view, however, is that there is another glorification beyond their pointing to Him, as explained elsewhere. Yet all these usages require qualification and contextual indication.

Thus, speech and utterance can rightly be denied of these things, as Allah Most High says:

“Did they not see that it could neither speak to them nor guide them to any way?”

And He says:

“Do they not see that it returns no word to them and has no power to harm or benefit them?”

And Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, peace be upon him, said:

“So ask them, if they can speak.”

And Allah Most High says:

“This is a Day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted to offer excuses.”

And He says:

“They will not speak, except those whom the Most Merciful permits and who say what is right.”

And He says:

“They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command.”

It is known self-evidently and through mass transmission that utterance and speech may be denied of a living being who is silent or unable to speak—how much more so of inanimate things! It is also known that Allah Most High possesses the attributes of perfection to the highest degree, and that the messengers affirmed that He speaks with speech that is complete and perfect to the highest degree. translated_text:

This is why Imam Ahmad, when Abū Tālib recited to him, “Say, ‘He is Allah, One,’” told him, “This is uncreated.” Abū Tālib then reported that Ahmad had said, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” Ahmad asked him, “Did I tell you, ‘My utterance is uncreated’?” He replied, “No. But I recited to you, ‘Say, “He is Allah, One,”’ and you said, ‘This is uncreated.’”

Ahmad thus clarified the difference between saying, “This speech is uncreated,” and saying, “This speaker’s utterance is uncreated.” The expression “my utterance” is ambiguous: it encompasses both the speaker’s action and his voice. Thus, saying, “My utterance, recitation, or reading is uncreated,” or, “It is the very thing recited,” suggests that the servant’s action and voice are eternal, and that the meaning and sound subsisting in him are identical to the meaning and sound subsisting in Allah.

Conversely, saying, “My utterance of the Quran, my recitation of the Quran, the utterance of the Quran, or its recitation is created,” or, “The recitation is other than what is recited,” or, “The reading is other than what is read,” implies that the letters of the Quran are in no respect part of Allah’s speech, and that half of the Quran is Allah’s speech while the other half is someone else’s speech. It also implies that Allah’s reading of the Quran is separate from what He reads, and His recitation of the Quran is separate from what He recites; likewise, that the servant’s reading of the Quran is separate from what he reads, and his recitation of it is separate from what he recites.

It further implies that what has been sent down to us is not Allah’s speech. For what is read and recited is Allah’s speech, and, according to these people, difference entails separation. Whatever is separate from His speech cannot be speech of His; thus, what He has sent down would not be His speech.

translated_text:
Since speech occurs only through movement and action that give rise to letters and meanings, it sometimes falls within the terms “action” and “deed,” when considered as movement and action, and sometimes falls outside them, when considered as letters and meanings. Thus, in the Quran and Sunnah, speech is sometimes treated as a kind of action, as in the Most High’s words:

“There is no private conversation among three but He is their fourth, nor among five but He is their sixth, nor fewer than that nor more but He is with them wherever they may be. Then, on the Day of Resurrection, He will inform them of what they did.”

At other times, it is treated as a category distinct from action, as in the Most High’s words:

“To Him ascends good speech, and righteous deeds raise it.”

For this reason, scholars disagreed over whether someone who swears not to perform any action in a particular place breaks his oath by speaking there, when neither his intention nor the circumstances of the oath clarify its scope. There are two views on this within the school of Imam Ahmad and elsewhere; both are reported from Ahmad.

For this reason, Abū Muhammad ibn Qutayba stated, in the book he wrote to explain “utterance,” that recitation is both Quran and action, neither of which can be separated from the other. Whoever says that it is Quran speaks truthfully, and whoever swears that it is an action is truthful in his oath. Whoever declared without qualification that recitation is created was mistaken, as was whoever claimed that it is uncreated. He charged both parties with limited knowledge and inadequate understanding, for the subtlety of this issue had prevented either party from grasping it. One party found that recitation is called Quran and therefore denied that it is created; the other found that recitation is an action for which the reciter is rewarded and therefore affirmed that it comes into being.

Error concerning this principle lies at two extremes, just as it does concerning the first principle. Regarding the first principle, some say that He has no speech subsisting in Him, while others say that His speech is nothing but an abstract meaning or nothing but sound.

Regarding this principle, some say that no one else utters His speech, or that it cannot be heard from anyone else. Others say that when someone else conveys and delivers His speech, its condition is the same as when it is heard from Him and recited. Rather, His messengers and servants utter His speech, speak it, recite it and read it. It remains His speech however it is conveyed, wherever it is recited and wherever it is written. Nevertheless, its condition when His servants recite and write it is not the same as when Allah recites it and they hear it from Him. Nor is someone who hears it from a reciter in the same position as Moses son of ʿImrān, who heard the speech of the Lord of the worlds from Him. As stated in the hadith:

“When creation hears the Quran from Allah on the Day of Resurrection, it will be as though they had never heard it before.”

Indeed, even the Messenger’s recitation and hearing it from him are not like another person’s recitation and hearing it from that person. Nor is one person’s recitation and hearing it from him like another person’s recitation and hearing it from him. In all its conditions, it is the speech of Allah Most High, which is uncreated, even though its conditions differ.

When they say, “This is that very thing,” they do not mean merely that the two are of the same kind, as when someone says, “This blackness is the same as that blackness.” For they use this expression of two utterances, two instances of knowledge, two powers or two individuals that happen to match. In such cases they say, “One thought coincides with another as one hoofprint coincides with another.” In reality, however, one is merely like the other, as Allah Most High says:

“Likewise, those before them said the like of what they say.”

They say, “This is that very thing,” when the two agree in their attributes, and may even do so when there are differences between them that are irrelevant to the point intended. Similarly, they say of a single entity whose attributes have changed, “This is the very same thing.”

Nor is this like adopting someone else’s words, whether verse or prose—for example, when a man adopts another’s saying and thus speaks those words himself, following the example of the original speaker. This is like our saying something that someone else has said, agreeing with that speaker that the statement is true.

As for someone who utters another person’s speech intending to convey and deliver it, or to speak it while believing that he intends only to utter that other person’s speech—the person whose commands and statements these are, and who originally spoke its letters and meanings—then the speech is unquestionably that of the first speaker. It is not the second speaker’s speech in any respect; it has merely reached people through him.

Speech has no counterpart resembling it in every respect to which it can be assimilated. Rather, it is intelligible in its own right. For example, even if Zayd, a created being, has ceased to exist, and the attribute that subsisted in him has also ceased to exist, when another narrator relates his speech and we say:

“This is Zayd’s speech,”

we are referring to the reality that Zayd originated and that was an attribute of his. This is that very same reality—I mean the formal reality, not the matter. For sound as such, in relation to distinct articulated letters, stands in the relation of matter to form. It was not the first speaker’s speech because of sound as such, which is shared by the sounds of human beings, speechless animals, and inanimate objects. Rather, it was his speech because of the form that Zayd composed, together with his composition of its meanings. When people say, “This is Labīd’s poetry,” they refer to both its wording and its meaning. Yet if someone were to say, “I originated the wording of this poetry,” or “This wording is my own composition,” or “My utterance of this poetry is my own creation,” everyone would declare him a liar and say to him:

“Rather, you transmitted it and recited it. But to claim that you originated its wording, that it came into being last night through your uttering it, or that your utterance of it came into being last night—that is false. The wording of this poetry has existed for a very long time, even though you have delivered it through your movements and your voice. Movement and sound are natural phenomena that you share with living beings, both speaking and speechless. You therefore have no share in it insofar as it is speech, nor insofar as it is that poet’s speech; for its being speech, or the speech of a particular speaker, belongs exclusively to that speaker. You have merely delivered it by means of an instrument that you share with speechless animals and inanimate objects.

“Yet praise belongs to Allah, who has granted you reason and discernment by which you find your way and direct your tongue, while He has not granted this to speechless animals. He has thus made your actions and qualities help you understand speech and speak it, without making the actions and qualities of speechless animals do likewise.”

If this holds for a created being conveying the speech of another created being like himself, then what of the speech of the Creator—exalted is His majesty—whose superiority over all other speech is like Allah’s superiority over His creation?

 فَإِنَّ هَذَا جَوَابُ فُتْيَا لَا يَلِيقُ بِهِ إلَّا التَّنْبِيهُ عَلَى جُمَلِ الْأُمُورِ وَإِثْبَاتُ وُجُوبِ نِسْبَةِ الْكَلَامِ إلَى مَنْ بَدَأَ مِنْهُ لَفْظُهُ وَمَعْنَاهُ دُونَ مَنْ بَلَّغَهُ عَنْهُ وَأَدَّاهُ وَأَنَّهُ كَلَامُ الْمُتَّصِفِ بِهِ مُبْتَدِئًا حَقِيقَةً سَوَاءً سُمِعَ مِنْهُ أَوْ سُمِعَ مِمَّنْ بَلَّغَهُ وَأَدَّاهُ بِفِعْلِهِ وَصَوْتِهِ مَعَ الْعِلْمِ بِأَنَّ أَفْعَالَ الْعِبَادِ وَصِفَاتِهِمْ مَخْلُوقَةٌ وَأَنَّ قَوْلَ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ وَالْمُؤْمِنِينَ:
 هَذَا كَلَامُ اللَّهِ وَمَا بَيْنَ اللَّوْحَيْنِ كَلَامُ اللَّهِ حَقِيقَةً لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ وَأَنَّ 
" الْقُرْآنَ "
 الَّذِي يَقْرَؤُهُ الْمُسْلِمُونَ وَيَكْتُبُونَهُ وَيَحْفَظُونَهُ هُوَ كَلَامُ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى وَكَلَامُ اللَّهِ حَيْثُ تَصَرَّفَ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقٍ. وَأَمَّا مَا اقْتَرَنَ بِتَبْلِيغِهِ وَقِرَاءَتِهِ مِنْ أَفْعَالِ الْعِبَادِ وَصِفَاتِهِمْ فَإِنَّهُ مَخْلُوقٌ. لَكِنْ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعُ فِيهِ اشْتِبَاهٌ وَإِشْكَالٌ لَا تَحْتَمِلُ تَحْرِيرَهُ وَبَسْطَهُ هَذِهِ الْفَتْوَى؛ لِأَنَّ صَاحِبَهَا مُسْتَوْفِزٌ عَجْلَانُ يُرِيدُ أَخْذَهَا؛ وَلِأَنَّ فِي
translated_text:
For it has a unique character of its own: conveying it cannot be likened to conveying any other speech, just as it is itself unlike any other speech. No created being can produce its like, whereas the human speech that people convey can be matched. Thus, this speech that is heard—the Quran—may in no way be attributed to anyone other than Allah, except in the sense of conveying it, as in His statement, exalted is He:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.”

Allah, glorified is He, has addressed us through it by means of the Messenger, as explained above. I have discussed these matters at length in their appropriate place: matters that bewilder minds and over which people have fallen into confusion. This, however, is an answer to a request for a fatwa, so it is appropriate here only to indicate the broad principles and establish that speech must be attributed to the one from whom its wording and meaning originated, not to the one who transmitted and delivered it on his behalf. It truly is the speech of the one who originally spoke it and whose attribute it is, whether it is heard from him or from someone conveying and delivering it through his own actions and voice. At the same time, it must be understood that people’s actions and attributes are created, and that the statement of Allah, His Messenger, and the believers—“This is Allah’s speech, and what lies between the two covers is Allah’s speech”—is literally true, beyond doubt. The “Quran” that Muslims recite, write, and memorize is the speech of Allah Most High; and Allah’s speech, however conveyed, is uncreated. As for the human actions and attributes accompanying its transmission and recitation, these are created.

Yet this matter involves ambiguities and difficulties whose precise clarification and detailed explanation lie beyond the scope of this fatwa. The person requesting it is ready to leave and in a hurry to take it, and because in

translated_text:
this matter there are subtleties and obscurities that require citing the relevant texts, explaining their meanings, and giving examples to clarify the reality of the matter. This is not the place for that. What is known “in general,” however, is that Imam Ahmad and the great imams who are widely held in high esteem throughout the Muslim community did not disagree on anything in this subject. Rather, some had greater knowledge of it and were more diligent in fulfilling its obligations than others. Groups of even the most eminent figures have erred in some of these matters. Imam Ahmad, together with the other imams, refuted most of the innovations concerning this subject.

The Jahmiyyah first introduced the doctrines that “the Quran is created” and that “the divine attributes are to be denied.” Those of the Successors who were alive at that time rejected these doctrines, as did the generation following the Successors and the imams after them. They declared those who professed them to be unbelievers.

Then some scholars of hadith and scholastic theology who debated the Jahmiyyah introduced the doctrine that the revealed Quran is created, that it is not Allah’s speech, or that it is neither in the written copies of the Quran nor in people’s hearts. Some of them denied that the letters of the Quran are Allah’s speech or that Allah spoke with a voice. Imam Ahmad and the imams of his time rejected this.

In opposition to them, another group of scholars of scholastic theology and hadith claimed that people’s utterances and voices are uncreated, or maintained that some human actions or attributes are uncreated, or that the Quran heard from people is like what is heard

Their denunciations and refutations of all these innovations are recorded in reliably transmitted works, such as The Book of the Sunnah by al-Khallāl, al-Ibānah (The Elucidation) by Ibn Battah, the books on the ordeal transmitted by Hanbal and Sālih, The Book of the Sunnah by ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ahmad, The Sunnah by al-Lālakā’ī, The Sunnah by Ibn Abī Hātim, and numerous other works.

As for refuting the Jahmiyyah, who deny the divine attributes and maintain that the Quran is created, much concerning this is found in the statements of the Successors, those who followed them, and the renowned imams. There are very many transmitted reports concerning the question of the Quran.

Among these is what Ibn Abī Hātim, Ibn Shāhīn, al-Lālakā’ī, and others narrated through several chains of transmission from ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib—may Allah be pleased with him—that he was told on the day of Siffīn, “You appointed two men as arbitrators.” He replied, “I did not appoint a created being as arbitrator; I appointed only the Quran.”

‘Ikrimah reported: Ibn ‘Abbās was attending a funeral. When he had placed the deceased in the burial niche, a man stood up and said, “O Allah, Lord of the Quran, forgive him.” Ibn ‘Abbās sprang towards him and said, “Stop! The Quran is from Him.”

Another version reads: “The Quran is Allah’s speech and is not subject to lordship. From Him it came forth, and to Him it will return.”

‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd said: “Whoever swears by the Quran owes an expiation for every verse. Whoever disbelieves in a single letter of it has disbelieved in it all.”

translated_text:
Among the widely transmitted reports is that narrated by Sufyān ibn ‘Uyaynah from ‘Amr ibn Dīnār—though some transmitters attribute it only to Sufyān, the former being the well-known version—who said:

“For seventy years, I have known our shaykhs and the people to say: ‘The Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated. From Him it came forth, and to Him it will return.’”

‘Amr’s shaykhs were the Companions and Successors whom he met.

It is also reported from ‘Alī ibn al-Husayn Zayn al-‘Ābidīn and his son Ja‘far ibn Muhammad:

And among the well-known statements in Muhammad ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī’s The Clear Exposition of the Sunnah—transmitted from him through numerous independent chains—is the following. After discussing the various topics of the Sunnah, he said:

“As for people’s utterances of the Quran, we know of no report concerning this from any Companion who passed away or any Successor who followed, except from one whose words offer healing and abundance, whose example brings sound direction and guidance, and whom we regard as holding the standing of the earliest imams: Abū ‘Abd Allāh Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Hanbal. Abū Ismā‘īl al-Tirmidhī related to me that he heard Abū ‘Abd Allāh Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Hanbal say: ‘The Lafziyyah are Jahmiyyah. Allah says, “until he hears the words of Allah.” From whom does he hear them?’”

Ibn Jarīr said:

“I also heard a number of our companions—whose names I do not recall—report that he used to say: ‘Whoever says, “My utterance of the Quran is created,” is a Jahmī; and whoever says, “It is uncreated,” is an innovator.’”

Ibn Jarīr said:

“We consider no statement on this matter permissible for us to make other than his, since we have no imam to follow in it besides him. His position is sufficient and convincing, and he is the imam to be followed.”

Abū al-Fadl Sālih ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal said in The Book of the Ordeal:

“Word reached me that Abū Tālib had reported my father as saying, ‘My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.’ I informed my father of this, and he asked, ‘Who told you?’ I replied, ‘So-and-so.’ He said, ‘Send for Abū Tālib.’ So I sent for him, and he came; Fawrān also came. My father said to him, ‘Did I tell you that my utterance of the Quran is uncreated?’ And he became angry

 مِثْلُ قَوْلِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{زَيِّنُوا الْقُرْآنَ بِأَصْوَاتِكُمْ}
 
" وَقَوْلِهِ: 
{لَلَّهُ أَشَدُّ أَذْنًا إلَى الرَّجُلِ الْحَسَنِ الصَّوْتِ بِالْقُرْآنِ مِنْ صَاحِبِ الْقَيْنَةِ إلَى قَيْنَتِهِ}
 "
 فَذَكَرَ الْخَلَّالُ فِي (كِتَابِ الْقُرْآنِ عَنْ إسْحَاقَ بْنِ إبْرَاهِيمَ قَالَ قَالَ لِي أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ يَوْمًا - وَكُنْت سَأَلْته عَنْهُ -: تَدْرِي مَا مَعْنَى مَنْ لَمْ يَتَغَنَّ بِالْقُرْآنِ؟
 قُلْت:
 لَا.
 قَالَ:
 هُوَ الرَّجُلُ يَرْفَعُ صَوْتَهُ فَهَذَا مَعْنَاهُ إذَا رَفَعَ صَوْتَهُ فَقَدْ تَغَنَّى بِهِ وَعَنْ مَنْصُورِ بْنِ صَالِحٍ أَنَّهُ قَالَ لِأَبِيهِ: يَرْفَعُ صَوْتَهُ بِالْقُرْآنِ بِاللَّيْلِ؟
 قَالَ:
 نَعَمْ إنْ شَاءَ رَفَعَهُ 
" ثُمَّ ذَكَرَ حَدِيثَ أُمِّ هَانِئٍ: 
{كُنْت أَسْمَعُ قِرَاءَةَ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَأَنَا عَلَى عَرِيشٍ مِنْ اللَّيْلِ}
 "
 وَعَنْ صَالِحِ بْنِ أَحْمَد أَنَّهُ قَالَ لِأَبِيهِ: 
" 
{زَيِّنُوا الْقُرْآنَ بِأَصْوَاتِكُمْ}
 "
 فَقَالَ: 
" التَّزْيِينُ "
 أَنْ تُحَسِّنَهُ.
 وَعَنْ الْفَضْلِ بْنِ زِيَادٍ قَالَ سَمِعْت أَبَا عَبْدِ اللَّهِ يُسْأَلُ عَنْ الْقِرَاءَةِ:
 فَقَالَ يُحَسِّنُهُ بِصَوْتِهِ مِنْ غَيْرِ تَكَلُّفٍ وَقَالَ أَبُو بَكْرٍ الْأَثْرَمُ سَأَلْت أَبَا عَبْدِ اللَّهِ عَنْ الْقِرَاءَةِ بِالْأَلْحَانِ؟
 فَقَالَ:
 كُلُّ شَيْءٍ مُحْدَثٌ؛ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يُعْجِبُنِي إلَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ صَوْتُ الرَّجُلِ لَا يَتَكَلَّفُهُ قَالَ الْقَاضِي أَبُو يَعْلَى فِيمَا عَلَّقَهُ بِخَطِّهِ عَلَى 
" جَامِعِ الْخَلَّالِ "
: هَذَا يَدُلُّ مِنْ كَلَامِهِ عَلَى أَنَّ صَوْتَ الْقَارِئِ لَيْسَ هُوَ الصَّوْتَ الْقَدِيمَ؛ لِأَنَّهُ أَضَافَهُ إلَى الْقَارِئِ الَّذِي هُوَ طَبْعُهُ مِنْ غَيْرِ أَنْ يَتَعَلَّمَ الْأَلْحَانَ.
translated_text:
the servant as he recites the Quran to the servant himself, there is much that would take too long to recount. This is also expressed in prophetic hadiths, such as the Prophet’s saying (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Beautify the Quran with your voices.”

And his saying:

“Allah listens more attentively to a man reciting the Quran with a beautiful voice than the owner of a singing girl listens to her.”

Al-Khallāl related in his Book of the Quran that Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm said: “One day Abū ‘Abd Allāh said to me—I had asked him about this—‘Do you know what is meant by “whoever does not recite the Quran melodiously”?’ I replied, ‘No.’ He said, ‘It means a man raising his voice. That is its meaning: when he raises his voice, he has recited it melodiously.’”

He also related that Mansūr ibn Sālih asked his father, “May a man raise his voice when reciting the Quran at night?” He replied, “Yes, he may raise it if he wishes.” Then he mentioned the hadith of Umm Hāni’: “I used to hear the Prophet’s recitation (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) at night while I was on a bed.”

He also related that Sālih ibn Ahmad quoted to his father, “Beautify the Quran with your voices.” His father replied, “‘Beautifying’ means making it beautiful.”

Al-Fadl ibn Ziyād said: “I heard Abū ‘Abd Allāh being asked about recitation. He replied, ‘He should beautify it with his voice, without affectation.’”

Abū Bakr al-Athram said: “I asked Abū ‘Abd Allāh about reciting to melodies. He replied, ‘I dislike anything newly introduced, unless it is simply a man’s own voice, without affectation.’”

Judge Abū Ya‘lā said in his handwritten annotations on al-Khallāl’s Compendium: “His words indicate that the reciter’s voice is not the eternal voice, because he attributed it to the reciter as his natural voice, without his having learned melodies.”

 فَالْجَوَابُ أَنَّ اعْتِصَامَنَا فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ بِظَاهِرِ الشَّرْعِ
translated_text:
As for Ahmad’s and the imams’ denunciation of those who say, “This Quran is created,” and “Recitation is created”; their regarding as grave the assertion, “There is no Quran in people’s hearts or in the written copies”; and the allegation made by some that whoever says this has adopted the position of the Christians and the proponents of divine indwelling—Ahmad’s and others’ denunciations of these views are numerous, widely known, and recorded in many books. This fatwa did not require establishing this principle, so there was no need to discuss it in detail, unlike the other principle. Elsewhere, we have mentioned as much of this as Allah enabled us to mention.

Were I to recount the statements of Ahmad, the leading scholars among his followers, and others refuting those who say that the servant’s utterance or voice is uncreated, or that the voice heard from the reciter is eternal, the discussion would be lengthy.

Consider Abū Nasr al-Sijzī, who wrote the well-known al-Ibānah (The Clarification). He was among the strongest proponents of the view that recitation is what is recited, that uttering the Quran is the Quran itself, and that it is uncreated. He rejected reports attributing any other view to Ahmad. Nevertheless, he said:

“If our opponents object, saying, ‘Although you say that recitation is the Quran and the speech of Allah, you do not declare that the voice heard from the reciter is Allah’s voice. Rather, you attribute it to the reciter. Since you cannot make that declaration, this indicates that it is something other than the Quran.’”

Abū Nasr said: “The answer is that, in this matter, we adhere to the apparent meaning of revelation

translated_text:
and our position concerning recitation and voice is consistent. When a reciter recites the Quran, one does not say, ‘This is Allah’s recitation,’ nor permit such a statement in any way. Rather, one attributes the recitation to the reciter by extension, because it is he who effects the change. One says only that the reciter’s recitation is Quran. This is established in revelation, as everyone agrees.

“For al-Ashʿarī, despite his disagreement with us, says, ‘What is heard from the reciter is Quran.’ We have explained that distinguishing between recitation and the Quran on the point at issue between us is impossible. Likewise, he says that the voice heard from someone reciting the Quran is both recitation and Quran. Revelation requires the position we have stated, and I know of no disagreement among Muslims concerning this.”

Section

As for Imam Ahmad’s explicit statements that “human speech is created” and that “the acts of servants are created,” these occur in many places, just as the other imams explicitly affirmed this. There is no disagreement among Ahl al-Sunnah on this matter.

Thus Yahyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qattān, Imam Ahmad’s teacher, said, “I have always heard our companions say, ‘The acts of servants are created.’” Imam Ahmad was asked, “Are the acts of servants created?” He replied, “Yes.” He explicitly affirmed this concerning human speech in the report transmitted by Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Tirmidhī, as will be discussed, and in his work refuting “the heretics and the Jahmiyyah,” which is

transmitted through his son ʿAbd Allāh from a written text he found (1). Al-Khallāl also included it in his Kitāb al-Sunnah, and Judge Abū Yaʿlā and others quoted from it. Several scholars have reported universal consensus on this, including Abū Nasr al-Sijzī in al-Ibānah, despite his being among the strongest critics of anyone who says that people’s utterances of the Quran are created, or that what is heard from the reciter is not the Quran.

Abū Nasr said:
“As for attributing voices to reciters—as we have done in this chapter and elsewhere in this book—and attributing recitation to them, although those who deviate may rejoice at this, it provides them with no proof. For we have never disagreed about attributing a voice to a person, or about his voice being created when he shouts, speaks human speech, or calls out to someone.”

He said:
“There is no ambiguity about this. The disagreement concerns only what a person listening to a reciter of the Quran actually hears.”

He continued the discussion to its conclusion. Elsewhere, he also mentioned consensus on this.

Section

translated_text:
and dispute in this area, including the question of “faith”—whether it is created or uncreated—and the questions of the “light of faith,” “guidance,” and similar matters over which the scholars of hadith and the Sunnah frequently disagree. Each group clings to part of the truth, until they become like those who were given a portion of the Scripture yet differed over it, each resembling someone who believes in part and disbelieves in part. Most of them are beset by ignorance and injustice: ignorance of the true nature of faith and truth, and injustice toward others. These disputes lead members of the Muslim community to declare one another unbelievers and curse one another, delighting Satan and angering the Most Merciful. Those who do this fall into the division and disagreement Allah has forbidden, departing from the unity and harmony He has commanded.

The root of this is the close connection between what Allah Most High has sent down of the Quran and faith—which pertains to His attributes—and the actions and attributes of His servants. Because distinguishing between them is difficult, some people incline toward excessive affirmation, while others incline toward excessive negation.

For this reason, the position of Imam Ahmad and the great imams was to prohibit blanket affirmation and blanket negation. Rather, one may refrain from both—which is more appropriate for people at large and constitutes the broad outlines of belief. Precise, well-founded distinctions, however, are for believers who possess knowledge, just as the former approach is for believers generally.

This question rests on two foundational principles:

translated_text:
The first is that “the actions of Allah’s servants are created.” This was explicitly affirmed by the imams—Ahmad and others—and by all the imams of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah who opposed the Qadariyya. The Muslim community has unanimously agreed that people’s actions are brought into being.

The second principle concerns the question of “reciting the Quran, reading it, and uttering it”: should this be described as created or uncreated? Imam Ahmad explicitly rejected both statements, as did all the earlier and later imams of the Sunnah. His rejection of the “negationist Lafziyya,” however, was more frequent, more widely known, and more forceful, for two reasons.

The first is that their position leads to further denial of Allah’s attributes and further negation; the tendency toward negation is always worse than the tendency toward affirmation. The messengers brought detailed affirmation of Allah’s attributes and negation in general terms. They described Him as possessing knowledge, mercy, power, wisdom, speech, highness, and other attributes. As for negation:

“There is nothing like Him.”

“And there is none comparable to Him.”

By contrast, those who depart from the true substance of the messengers’ teachings—Sabians, philosophers, polytheists, and others, including those among the prophets’ followers who adopted Jahmī doctrines—follow the method of “detailed negation”: He is not this, He is not that. Their affirmation, however, remains general. Hence the saying: “The denier of Allah’s attributes is blind, while the one who likens Him to His creation is dim-sighted.” Thus, despite their misguidance, those who liken Allah to His creation are better than those who deny His attributes.

The second reason is that Ahmad was specifically tried by the Jahmiyya who denied Allah’s attributes, for they were his opponents,

At that time and place, no one was advocating excessive affirmation, whereas advocates of excessive negation had emerged. Refutation is undertaken as the need arises. When al-Bukhārī was tried by the “affirmationist Lafziyya,” his denunciation of them became evident, as seen in the chapter headings near the end of his Sahīh and in The Creation of Actions. Yet he denounced as a liar anyone, from any region, who reported that he had said, “My utterance of the Quran is created.” I believe he swore an oath to that effect, and he was truthful and righteous.

Section

Ahmad explicitly addressed this very “question” on several occasions. Abū al-Qāsim al-Lālakā’ī related in Foundations of the Sunnah:

Al-Hasan ibn ʿUthmān informed us, saying: ʿAmr ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Tirmidhī narrated to us, saying:

I said to Ahmad ibn Hanbal, “People have become embroiled in controversy over the Quran. What should I say?”

He said, “Are you not created?”

I said, “Yes.”

He said, “Then your speech is from you and is created?”

I said, “Yes.”

He said, “Is the Quran not part of Allah’s speech?”

I said, “Yes.”

He said, “And Allah’s speech is from Allah?”

I said, “Yes.”

He said, “Could anything from Allah, then, be created?”

Ahmad explained to the questioner that speech comes from the speaker and subsists in him. Speech cannot be detached from the speaker or fail to subsist in him, as is evident from the fact that your speech, O created being, comes from you, not from anyone else. Since you are created, your speech must also be created. Since Allah Most High is uncreated, whatever comes from Him and subsists in Him cannot be created.

His purpose was to refute the Jahmiyya, who claim that Allah’s speech neither comes from Allah nor is connected to Him. He thus explained that this conception of speech does not convey what it means for a speaker to speak, nor does it reflect the reality of speaking. Nor is it what the messengers and believers mean when they report that Allah spoke and speaks, uttered the Quran, called out, spoke privately, and summoned, and other such things that His messengers have reported about Him and that believers in Him from every nation have agreed upon.

Hence Allah Most High says:

“But the word from Me has come into effect.”

And He says:

“The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, you receive the Quran from One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Alif Lām Rā. A Book whose verses have been perfected, then set out in detail, from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware.”

The Quran is not a self-subsisting entity such that one could say that this is like His statement:

“And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth—all from Him.”

Thus, when life, knowledge, and power subsist in a subject, the names “living,” “knowing,” and “powerful” must be derived from them for that subject. These names cannot be applied to anyone other than the one in whom knowledge and power subsist. Likewise, when utterance, speech, love, hatred, pleasure, mercy, anger, will, and volition subsist in a subject, the corresponding name and verb must be derived from them for that subject. Thus, one says: He is the Truthful, the Witness, the Wise, the Loving, the Merciful, and the One who commands. No name derived from these attributes can be applied to anyone else.

If Allah, glorified and exalted, were not Himself the One saying:

“I am Allah; there is no deity except Me,”

but instead brought these words into being in something else, He would not be the One issuing these commands or conveying this statement. Rather, the subject in which these words subsisted would be the one issuing this command and conveying this statement. That subject would be either the air or something else. Thus, that created subject would be the one saying to Moses:

“Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me.”

For this reason, the early generations used to say concerning this verse and others like it: “Whoever says that it is created has disbelieved.” They regarded the assertion that this verse and others like it were created as even graver than the same assertion concerning other verses. They considered it an enormity for anyone other than Allah Most High to claim divinity and lordship.

According to them, the Essence is in the same state whether it creates and provides or neither creates nor provides.

On this basis, the Muʿtazila challenged the consistency of their opponents among the Ashʿarī affirmers of the attributes and others like them. Hence He, glorified and exalted, says:

“Is He who creates like one who does not create?”

The distinction between one who creates and one who does not create is like the distinction between one who has power and one who does not. The opposing view maintains that He is described only by power, which encompasses both what He creates and what He does not create, and that He is in Himself the same whether He creates or does not create. On this view, His being Creator entails no “positive attribute”—neither an attribute of perfection nor even any existential attribute—as His being powerful does.

The texts of the Quran and Sunnah require that His names denoting His acts belong to His most beautiful names, for which He deserves praise, commendation, and glorification. translated_text:
Imam Ahmad became a byword for enduring trials and remaining steadfast upon the truth, undeterred by anyone’s blame in the cause of Allah. Indeed, the title “Imam” became inseparable from his name on everyone’s lips: “Imam Ahmad said”; “This is the position of Imam Ahmad.” This accords with the words of Allah Most High:

“And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient and had certainty in Our signs.”

He was granted such patience and certainty as entitled him to leadership in religion. “Three caliphs,” whose power extended from east to west, successively subjected him to persecution. They were supported by scholars of speculative theology, judges, ministers, informers, commanders, and governors whose numbers Allah alone could reckon. Some imprisoned him; others subjected him to dire threats of death and other punishments, inducements of authority and wealth to whatever extent Allah willed, and beatings; still others drove him from his home and banished him. Throughout this, people at large abandoned him—even his own companions among the scholars, the righteous, and the devout. Yet he did not concede a single word of what they demanded. He neither abandoned what the Quran and Sunnah taught, nor concealed knowledge, nor resorted to concealing his beliefs for his own protection.

Rather, he made known the Sunnah of Allah’s Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and the reports concerning him, and repelled innovations contrary to them, to a degree unmatched by any of his peers and fellow scholars, earlier or later. Thus, one of the shaykhs of Syria said: “No one has made known what the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—brought as Ahmad ibn Hanbal did.” How, then, could anyone suppose that he feared for himself over this statement, which was of no consequence?

“A letter is one and the same, and the letters of the alphabet are uncreated wherever they are used, because they are part of Allah’s speech. The essential nature of a letter is one and does not vary.”

It has been reported that Imam Ahmad—may Allah be pleased with him—rebuked those who said that letters were created. When he was told that someone had said, “When Allah created the letters, they prostrated before Him, except for the alif,” Imam Ahmad said, “This is disbelief.” Other imams are also reported to have condemned this. Those holding the former view do not dispute this, for they too condemn anyone who says, “Letters are created,” since such a statement includes the letters of Allah Most High’s speech, whether in the Quran or elsewhere. They confine their discussion to the letters occurring in the speech of created beings, excluding those occurring in Allah’s speech. They say:

“Even if the essential nature of the letters and the name is the same, this is comparable to words that occur in the Quran and have also been spoken by created beings. A speaker sometimes intends to utter another’s words, even if, from our perspective, his wording matches them. This is possible only with a small amount of speech—less than a short surah—for Allah has challenged creation to produce a surah like it and has declared that they will never do so.”

Those holding the former view said:

“Thus, the wording of one utterance matching that of another does not entail that

one is treated like the other in its attribution to a created speaker, so that one utterance is attributed to the speaker of the other. How, then, could this be so when the attribution is to the Creator?

Indeed, when Musaylimah wrote to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘From Musaylimah, the Messenger of Allah, to Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah,’ the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, replied, ‘From Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, to Musaylimah the Liar.’ The expression ‘Messenger of Allah’ was identical in both speakers’ words, yet from one it was true—indeed, among the greatest truths—and from the other it was a lie—indeed, among the vilest lies.

Allah has also recorded in His Book evil statements made by the disbelievers, such as their saying:

‘Allah has taken a son.’

‘They have no knowledge of this, nor did their forefathers. Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths; they speak nothing but lies.’

And their statements:

‘Ezra is the son of Allah,’

and

‘The Messiah is the son of Allah,’

along with other false statements that Allah has quoted from them. When we utter what Allah has quoted from them, we are uttering Allah’s speech. But if we were to quote those statements directly from them, we would be quoting their false and blameworthy speech.

For this reason, the jurists have said that whoever remembers Allah or supplicates to Him may do so while in a state of major ritual impurity, even if the wording matches the Quran, provided that he does not intend recitation.

They have also said that if someone uses Quranic wording during prayer solely to address another person, his prayer is invalid, because this constitutes human speech, and no human speech is permissible during prayer. The reason is that meaning is included in what the term “speech” denotes; it does not denote wording alone. Meaning may be performative or informative, and performative speech includes commands and prohibitions. Clearly, Zayd’s command is not ʿAmr’s command, nor does it have the same status, even when the wording is identical. Likewise, Zayd’s choice is not ʿAmr’s choice, nor does it have the same status, even when the wording is identical.

When a wise person whose commands are obeyed issues a command, it has a different status from the same command issued by someone ignorant and powerless, even if their wording is identical. Likewise, when a knowledgeable, truthful witness reports something, his report has a different status from the same report given by someone ignorant and untruthful, even if their wording is identical.

Accordingly, if someone incorporates into his speech wording that another person has incorporated into his own speech, this does not entail that this wording belongs to that other speaker’s speech, even though the two expressions resemble each other. This is like someone writing letters resembling those in a copy of the Quran but using them to write something else: that does not make them letters of the Quranic text.

The second point:

Even if no one had uttered these letters except by learning them from Allah’s speech, when someone uses them to compose speech of his own, without intending to recite Allah’s speech, they are not, in that instance, part of Allah’s speech. The same applies when someone does this with complete sentences—and applies all the more clearly here. The rulings of Islamic law support this.

The other group—those who maintain that the letters of the alphabet are uncreated without qualification—said: “We have two views concerning names found outside the Quran.” Some of them hold that all names are uncreated, just as they maintain concerning letters. Others do not hold this view. Ibn Hāmid and others have reported both views from those affiliated with the school of Imam Ahmad and from others who maintain that the letters of the alphabet are uncreated. Those who extend this position to all names cite the words of Allah Most High:
