Some held that languages originated through divine instruction. This is the view of Abū Bakr ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Shaykh Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī, and various groups among the followers of Imam Ahmad. It is also the view of al-Ashʿarī, Ibn Fūrak, and others.

Others held that they originated partly through divine instruction and partly through human convention. Various groups held this view, including Ibn ʿAqīl and others.

Still others held that either origin is possible and that we cannot affirm either conclusively. This is the view of Judge Abū Yaʿlā, Judge Abū Bakr ibn al-Bāqillānī, and others.

Only certain groups among the Muʿtazilah and their followers maintained that languages originated entirely through human convention. The leading proponent of this view was Abū Hāshim ibn al-Jubbāʾī. Those who held that languages were “divinely taught” disagreed over whether this instruction took place through speech, through the imparting of direct, non-inferential knowledge, or through both.

For those who maintain that languages originated through divine instruction and that this instruction took place through speech, it follows that they should be described as uncreated, since they are all part of the speech of Allah Most High. Yet we know with certainty that some proper names were newly coined by people themselves, so the uncertainty concerns common nouns.

Moreover, Allah’s teaching Adam through speech does not entail that those names continued unchanged in their wording among his descendants. Rather, it is related that when the people aboard Noah’s Ark disembarked, each group was given a language, and their tongues became confused.

The person who said that a letter is one and the same, and that the letters of the alphabet are uncreated, meant only that they form part of Allah’s speech, are drawn from Allah’s speech, and constitute the elements of its wording, which is uncreated. There is no dispute about this.

An isolated letter, however, exists neither in the Quran nor elsewhere. A letter is pronounced only within combinations forming nouns, verbs, or particles. As for letters pronounced individually, such as alif, lām, mīm, and the like, these are actually the names of letters. They are called letters after what they designate, just as daraba (“he struck”) is called a past-tense verb by reference to what it designates. Thus, when al-Khalīl asked his companions, “How do you pronounce the z in Zayd?” they replied, “We say ‘zā.’” He said, “You have given its name; rather, one says ‘zah.’”

Only half of the alphabet’s letter-names occur in the Quran: fourteen letters. These represent half of the various classes of letters: those pronounced with the breath restrained, those pronounced with the breath flowing, those articulated with the tongue raised, emphatic letters, stops, continuants, and the other classes of letters. This is the nobler of the two halves. The other half occurs in the Quran only within nouns, verbs, or particles—which are neither nouns nor verbs. We must therefore not suppose that all the letters of the alphabet occur by name in the Quran; rather, the letters of the alphabet themselves, which

What he utters may be something he has taken from the wording of Allah Most High’s speech, if that was his starting point, or it may not actually be so.

It is said: A letter, considered in itself, is a single thing. Its absolute reality, involving no combination, exists neither in the speech of Allah Most High nor in the speech of His servants. What exists is only a letter forming part of an expression, or its name when a letter occurs on its own. Yet this universal—even in the case of entities that exist independently in external reality, such as human beings—does not exist among concrete entities apart from its particular instances. It exists apart from particular instances only in the mind, not in external reality. How much more, then, does this apply to a letter, which exists externally only in combination! Even supposing that it existed externally without combination, in multiple individual instances, as human beings do, its absolute reality, considered in itself, would exist only in minds, not in concrete entities.

It thus becomes clear that we must affirm what the leading scholars, such as Ahmad and others, affirmed:

“Human speech is entirely created, both its letters and its meanings, whereas the Quran is uncreated, both its letters and its meanings.”

It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah says: ‘I am al-Rahmān (the Most Merciful). I created the bond of kinship and derived its name from Mine. Whoever maintains it, I will maintain ties with him; and whoever severs it, I will cut him off.’”

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas reported that the Messiah said:

“How astonishing that they disbelieve in Him while enjoying His blessings and uttering His names!”

He also mentioned, concerning most of the letters of the alphabet, that they are the building blocks of Allah’s most beautiful names and His Books sent down from heaven. This is among the arguments advanced by those who say that letters are uncreated. Yet it is no proof: Allah’s names are part of His speech, and His speech is uncreated. Whatever He Himself derives from His names and utters, His utterance of it is uncreated. But when people derive a name and bring it into being, it is they who have brought that name into being. The fact that the source from which something is derived is uncreated does not mean that the derivative is likewise uncreated.

As for what is reported from the Messiah, its authenticity is not established. Even supposing it were authentic, if He has inspired His servants to utter the letters

“In short”: whoever considers that the unvarying essence of a letter exists in Allah’s speech, and that Allah’s speech is uncreated, says that it is created, referring to the essence of the letter itself—not to the particular component of an utterance pronounced by disbelievers and polytheists. For that letter, which is a sound of determinate measure, or a determination of sound, subsisting in a disbeliever or polytheist, cannot reasonably be said to be uncreated. It is not attributed to Allah in any respect. What is attributed to Allah is only that which shares its designation and relates to the meaning attributed to Allah.

This is unlike the letters in Allah’s speech: those remain Allah’s speech whatever forms they take. Since Allah has made His speech easy upon our tongues, we are able to utter His speech, but through our own organs of speech and with our own voices. Yet our uttering it and its being heard from us are not like Allah’s uttering it and its being heard from Him, as indicated earlier. Just as nothing is like Allah, so too with everything else attributed to Him.

However, since Allah enables us to speak through our own organs, movements, and voices, a certain resemblance exists between some aspects of our uttering His speech and our uttering other speech. When we utter other speech, it resembles, in some respects, our utterance and vocal recitation of the Quran; it does not resemble Allah’s speaking it and His reciting it. Thus, if the occurrence of these letters in human speech is not on a par with Allah’s speaking the Quran, but only resembles, in some respects, our speaking it

It merely resembles and approximates it: they are the same in type, but not the same individual instance. This is unlike the letters of Allah’s speech—the Quran—for they remain Allah’s speech whatever forms they take. This involves a subtlety and a source of confusion which we have indicated in this response and explained in its proper place.

Whoever says, “The letters are two distinct letters,” means that they are two distinct individual instances; this is true. Whoever says, “The letter is one and the same,” means that its nature as a type is the same in both cases; this too is true. Whoever says that the letters of the alphabet occurring in human speech are uncreated speaks truly with respect to their nature as a type. Whoever says that they are created with respect to their individual instances also speaks truly.

Many parallels to this occur in the affirmations and negations found in the discourse of scholars and the people of the Sunnah: the dispute concerns two different meanings and is merely verbal, arising from different perspectives. One learned person said, “Most disagreements among rational people arise from using the same terms for different meanings.”

Yet the occurrence of such shared usage and ambiguity leads many people astray, just as many people are guided through it. This is the cause of the misguidance of those ignorant people about whom the question was asked. Their argument is that Allah taught Adam all the names and taught him articulate speech. the view that “languages are divinely imparted,” as held by many jurists of our school and others, such as Abū Bakr ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī. This is also the position of al-Ashʿarī, Ibn Fūrak, and others. But does “divine imparting” mean speaking, making known, or both? This too is disputed, as explained earlier.

Those who say that languages are uncreated maintain that they are “divinely imparted” and that teaching takes place through direct speech. Thus, Allah would have spoken all the names, and Allah’s speech is uncreated.

These ignorant, misguided people said: “Human speech consists only of combinations of letters and names, which are uncreated. Therefore, it too is uncreated.”

They thus based their position on the premises that the letters of the alphabet are uncreated and that the names composed of these letters are uncreated. They also believed that human speech consists only of combinations of names and letters, which are uncreated. Hence they said: “Human speech is uncreated because its constituent elements are uncreated.”

When pressed, they may say that the arrangement and combination are created, whereas the material itself that is arranged and combined is beginningless. They then suppose that the materials so arranged and combined are more integral to what is called speech than the combination and arrangement themselves, just as the parts of a house are more integral to what the word denotes than their assembly, even though the word “house” denotes both the parts and their assembly.

evil found among them is more abundant among others; for it is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“You will surely follow the ways of those before you, as precisely as one arrow-feather matches another, until, even if they entered a lizard’s hole, you would enter it.” They asked, “The Jews and Christians?” He replied, “Who else?”

He also said:

“You will surely adopt the ways of the nations before you, handspan by handspan and cubit by cubit.” They asked, “The Persians and Romans?” He replied, “Who else among the peoples could it be?”

Dispelling these people’s misconception requires discussing whether “letters and names” are created or uncreated, although we have already touched upon this. Rather, we shall proceed on the assumption that they are uncreated, and nevertheless say: it must be affirmed unequivocally that human speech is created. This statement is made without qualification and requires no distinction such as saying, “Its ordering and composition are created, but its letters and names are uncreated,” or, “Its construction is created, but its individual elements are uncreated.” Such distinctions are unnecessary.

This is because a speaker’s speech comprises both his words and their meanings, as we have explained previously. “Speech” does not designate words alone or meanings alone. Generally, wherever the terms “speech” and “saying,” or expressions such as “This is so-and-so’s speech” or “so-and-so’s speech,” occur in the Quran, the Sunnah, and the statements of the early generations and leading scholars—indeed, among all other peoples, Arab and non-Arab—their unqualified use encompasses both wording and meaning together

because it encompasses both. It does not literally denote wording alone, as some maintain, nor meaning alone, as others maintain. Nor is it an equivocal term denoting either separately, as some maintain. Nor is it equivocal when applied to human speech but literal in denoting meaning when applied to Allah’s speech, as some maintain.

Examples include the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah has pardoned my community for what they say within themselves, so long as they neither voice it nor act upon it.”

And Mu‘ādh’s question to him, “Will we really be held accountable for what we say?” He replied:

“May your mother be bereaved of you, Mu‘ādh! What casts people into the Fire upon their noses except the harvests of their tongues?”

And his saying:

“Two phrases are heavy in the balance, light upon the tongue, and beloved to the Most Merciful: ‘Glory and praise be to Allah; glory be to Allah, the Magnificent.’”

And his saying:

“The truest words ever spoken by a poet are the words of Labīd: ‘Indeed, everything apart from Allah is vain.’”

And his saying:

“I know a saying which no one utters at the time of death without his soul finding comfort in it. Whoever’s last words are ‘There is no deity worthy of worship but Allah’ will enter Paradise.”

There are also passages in the Quran, such as His saying:

“To Him good words ascend, and righteous deeds raise them.”

And His saying:

“When you speak, be just, even if it concerns a close relative.”

All such terms for saying and speech, and other similar expressions, encompass both wording and meaning when used without qualification.

Sībawayh, the sage of the Arabic language, mentions this in his chapter on quoting with “to say,” where he explains that “to say” is used to quote what constitutes speech, but not what is merely an utterance. Only complete, meaningful sentences are quoted with “to say.” Thus, it is clear that these constitute speech in the Arabic language.

When jurists apply the term “speech” to two or more letters in their discussions of prayer, they are concerned only with what invalidates prayer, whether or not it conveys a complete meaning and whether its expressions have an assigned meaning or none. Even producing a prolonged vocal sound and intoning melodies used in singing invalidates prayer, although this is not speech in the linguistic sense.

When someone swears that he will not speak, or that he will certainly speak, however, they make the fulfilment or breach of his oath depend only on what constitutes speech according to his customary usage, even if this is narrower than the speech that invalidates prayer. Thus, if someone swears without qualification that he will not speak, he breaks his oath by uttering the speech of created beings. But does he break it by speaking the words of the Quran?

Some scholars say that he does not break it under any circumstances. Others say that he does not break it by reciting it during prayer. Still others withhold judgment, because an oath is interpreted according to the oath-taker’s customary usage. Thus, the breadth or narrowness of the term “speech,” as these jurists use it, depends on the rulings attached to it.

Those engaged in the study of the principles of jurisprudence may define speech as what consists of two or more letters, or what is composed of “letters”—that is, distinct sounds established by convention. They also hold two views on whether a single letter combined with others may itself be called speech. Similarly, most of their speculative theologians say that a body is a composite, and that the smallest composite consists of two substances. They likewise hold two views on whether a single substance forming part of a composite may itself be called a body. This, however, is terminology peculiar to them.

Likewise, grammarians have conventionally agreed to call a single expression, such as a noun or a particle, a “word,” although in the language of the pure Arabs, “word” is found only as a designation for a complete sentence—unless there is an instance that does not come to mind at present.

Since people agree that speech belongs to the one who composes its wording and meanings, even if he learned its vocabulary from someone else, every doubt concerning this issue is dispelled. It must therefore be stated without qualification that human speech is created, just as one states without qualification that this poetry is the speech of so-and-so, and that this discourse is the speech of so-and-so—not the speech of those who previously used those words and their constituent letters. Human speech belongs to those who originated and first produced it, composing its wording and meanings, even though they may have learned its words and letters from one another, and even if they had heard those words from Allah Most High.

He also said:

“Allah listens far more attentively to a man with a beautiful voice reciting the Quran than the owner of a singing girl listens to her.”

People of all nations agree on this. When they hear someone recite a poem such as “Halt, you two, and let us weep” or “Have the poets left,” a “sermon” such as the sermons of ‘Alī and Ziyād, a “letter” such as a letter by ‘Abd al-Hamīd and others like him, rhymed prose from the soothsayers, or a fabricated Quran such as the Quran of Musaylima the Liar, they say: “This is the poetry of Imru’ al-Qays, the speech of ‘Alī, the speech of ‘Abd al-Hamīd, and the Quran of Musaylima; it is his speech.” They do not regard it as the speech of the intermediary who conveys and delivers it, even though he conveys it through his own actions and voice.

When a man composes a poem, a sermon, a letter, or rhymed prose, or speaks in ordinary prose, giving an order or conveying information, they say: “This is so-and-so’s speech and utterance,” even though he learned its individual words from others and was taught them by someone else.

Whoever says that speech belongs to the person from whom its individual words were learned is further removed from reason and religion than someone who says that speech belongs to the person who conveys and delivers it. Rather, speech belongs only to the one to whom it pertains and of whom it is an attribute, who composed and originated it, and who makes its assertions, issues its commands, and pronounces its prohibitions.

As for the questioner’s inquiry, “Is the ruler obliged to rebuke and restrain them?”—yes, he must do so with these people and anyone who openly advances a doctrine contrary to the Quran and Sunnah. This is among the “wrong” that Allah has commanded be forbidden, as He, Most High, says:

“Let there be among you a group who call to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong.”

It is also among the “sin” of which Allah says:

“Why do their religious scholars and rabbis not forbid them from sinful speech and consuming unlawful gain?”

Anyone among those who deny Allah’s attributes or liken Him to His creation who affirms of Allah what He has denied of Himself, or denies of Allah what He has affirmed of Himself, has spoken untruth about Allah. This is something Allah has forbidden in His words to the Christians:

“O People of the Scripture, do not go to extremes in your religion, and say nothing about Allah except the truth.”

And in His words:

“Say, ‘O People of the Scripture, do not go to extremes in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the desires of people who went astray before, led many others astray, and strayed from the right path.’”

He says of Satan:

“He only commands you to commit evil and indecency, and to say about Allah what you do not know.”

And He says:

“Say, ‘My Lord has only forbidden shameful deeds, whether committed openly or in secret, sin, and unjust aggression

and associating with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and saying about Allah what you do not know.’”

Whoever speaks untruth has said about Allah what he does not know. Falsehood can be known only as falsehood; believing it to be the truth is ignorance, not knowledge. Thus, whoever asserts it has said what he does not know. Likewise, anyone who follows his forefathers and predecessors in these or other matters of religion without holding fast to the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus is among those whom Allah condemns in His Book, as in His words:

“When they are told, ‘Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger,’ they say, ‘What we found our forefathers following is enough for us.’ Even though their forefathers knew nothing and were not guided?”

And His words:

“On the Day their faces are turned about in the Fire, they will say, ‘If only we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!’”

“And they will say, ‘Our Lord, we obeyed our leaders and our great men, and they led us astray from the path.’”

“‘Our Lord, give them double the punishment and curse them with a mighty curse.’”

Likewise, whoever follows conjectures and desires, believing them to be “rational truths” and “experiential insights,” is among those of whom Allah says:

“They follow nothing but conjecture and what their souls desire, although guidance has already come to them from their Lord.”

Only the Book sent down from heaven and the Messenger supported by divine tidings can settle people’s disputes, as He, Most High, says:

“Bring me a scripture predating this one, or some remnant of knowledge, if you are truthful.”

He, Most High, also says:

“Mankind was one community; then Allah sent the prophets

translated_text:
as bearers of glad tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Scripture in truth to judge between people concerning their differences.”

He, Most High, also says:

“If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and best in outcome.”

He, Most High, also says:

“Whatever you differ about, its judgment rests with Allah.”

Rather, people must adhere to the comprehensive, universal principles upon which the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars agreed: they must believe in what Allah has described Himself with and what His Messenger has described Him with, without distortion or denial, and without specifying how His attributes are or likening them to those of creation. No one may declare any Muslim a disbeliever, even if he is mistaken and in error, until the proof has been established against him and the clear path has been explained to him. Whoever’s Islam is established with certainty does not cease to be a Muslim on the basis of doubt; that can occur only after the proof has been established and the doubt dispelled.

Section

As for declaring the person who makes this statement a disbeliever, this rests upon a principle to which attention must be drawn. Failure to understand it precisely has caused great confusion within the Muslim community over declaring the followers of innovation and whims to be disbelievers, just as they have been confused, in earlier and later times, over denying faith to the immoral and those who commit major sins. Many followers of innovation—such as the Khawārij, the Rāfidah, the Qadariyyah, the Jahmiyyah, and those who liken Allah to His creation—have come to hold a misguided belief

which they regard as the truth, and they consider those who disagree with them on it to be disbelievers. They thus come to share, to a marked degree, the traits of the People of the Book in their rejection of the truth and their injustice toward others. Perhaps most of those who declare others disbelievers do so on account of a “statement” whose true meaning is not understood and whose proof is not known.

At the opposite extreme from those who falsely declare others disbelievers are people who do not properly understand the beliefs of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah, or who know some of them but are ignorant of others. What they do know, they may fail to explain to people, concealing it instead. They neither forbid innovations that contradict the Quran and Sunnah nor condemn and punish those who follow innovations. Indeed, they may condemn all discussion of the Sunnah and the fundamentals of religion without distinguishing between what the Quran, Sunnah, and scholarly consensus establish and what the adherents of innovation and division say. Or they allow everyone to retain their differing doctrines, just as scholars are allowed their differing views in matters of independent scholarly judgment where disagreement is permissible.

This approach may predominate among many of the Murjiʾah and some students of jurisprudence, Sufis, and philosophers, just as the first approach predominates among many who follow whims and engage in speculative theology. Both approaches are deviant and depart from the Quran and Sunnah.

Rather, what is required is to explain that with which Allah sent His messengers and revealed His scriptures, to convey what the messengers brought from Allah, and to fulfill the covenant Allah took from the scholars. One must therefore know what the messengers brought, believe in it, convey it, and call others to it

With this established, know that “questions of declaring people disbelievers or sinners” belong to the questions of “religious designations and rulings.” These concern the promise of reward and the threat of punishment in the Hereafter, as well as allegiance and enmity, killing and inviolability, and other matters in this worldly life.

For Allah, glorified is He, has guaranteed Paradise to the believers and forbidden it to the disbelievers. This is among the universal rulings that apply at every time and in every place. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, those who believe, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians—whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds—will have their reward with their Lord. No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.”

And the Most High says, after mentioning the claim of the Jews and Christians:

“None will enter Paradise unless they are Jews or Christians.” Such are their wishful hopes. Say, “Produce your proof, if you are truthful.”

He thus commanded him to demand their proof for this sweeping denial and the false affirmation it entails. Then He said:

“Yes, whoever submits himself to Allah while doing good will have his reward with his Lord. No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.”

He, glorified is He, thus declared concerning those Jews, Christians, and Sabians of earlier times who adhered to a true religion, and concerning the believers after Muhammad was sent—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—that whoever combines the “three qualities” encompassing all righteousness will receive his reward and be spared punishment. These qualities are belief in creation and resurrection—in the beginning and the return—namely, faith in Allah and the Last Day, together with righteous deeds, which consist in fulfilling what is commanded and refraining from what is forbidden. His reward is with his Lord; he will have no fear of what lies ahead and will not grieve over what lies behind.

For this reason, He said:

“Yes, whoever submits himself to Allah while doing good.”

This means devoting one’s religion sincerely to Allah: worshipping Him alone, without partner. This is the true meaning of His words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

He is also “doing good.” Thus, the “first”—submitting oneself to Allah—is the intention, while this “second”—doing good—is the deed. What He has mentioned in these two verses is faith in its universal sense and Islam in its universal sense, which Allah has enjoined upon all His servants, from the earliest to the latest generations.

and it is “Allah’s universal religion,” besides which He accepts no other religion from anyone, and with which He sent all the messengers. As He, Most High, said:

“We certainly sent a messenger to every nation, saying, ‘Worship Allah and shun false gods.’”

He, Most High, also said:

“We never sent a messenger before you without revealing to him: ‘There is no deity worthy of worship except Me, so worship Me.’”

And He, Most High, said:

“Ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you: Have We appointed gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?”

And He, Most High, said:

“He has ordained for you the same religion He enjoined upon Noah, and that which We have revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: uphold the religion and do not divide within it.”

He, Most High, said to all the children of Adam:

“When guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer misery.”

“But whoever turns away from My remembrance will have a life of hardship, and We will raise him blind on the Day of Resurrection.”

In the other passage, He said:

“Whoever follows My guidance will have no fear, nor will they grieve.”

“But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs will be the inhabitants of the Fire, remaining there forever.”

Among the earliest innovations and divisions to arise within this community was “the innovation of the Khawārij,” who declared people unbelievers on account of sin. They discussed the status of the sinful member of the Muslim community. The Khawārij and the Muʿtazilah claimed that major sins—and, according to some of them, minor sins as well—can never coexist with faith. Rather, they contradict and invalidate it, just as eating and drinking invalidate fasting. They argued: “Faith consists in fulfilling what is commanded and refraining from what is forbidden. Whenever any part of it is invalidated, the whole is invalidated, as with all other composite wholes.”

Thus, they declared these two caliphs and the majority of the Muslim community unbelievers. The Muʿtazilah upheld an intermediate position between the two states: the sinner leaves faith but does not enter unbelief.

Opposing them were the Murjiʾah, the Jahmiyyah, and those among the Ashʿariyyah and Karrāmiyyah who followed them. They said: “Performing obligatory deeds and refraining from prohibited bodily acts are not part of faith. Faith does not admit of increase or decrease; rather, it is a single entity in which all believers are equal: angels, prophets, those brought near to Allah, those who follow a middle course, and those who wrong themselves.”

The jurists among the Murjiʾah said: “Faith is affirmation in the heart and by the tongue.” Most of their speculative theologians said: “It is affirmation in the heart,” while some said: “It is affirmation by the tongue.” They argued: “If practical obligations were included in faith, anyone who failed to fulfil them would fall outside it, just as the Khawārij maintain.” At the root of all these views is their mistaken assumption that whoever abandons part of faith has abandoned it entirely.

This is the wording used by the early generations, including the Companions and others, although in some contexts “faith” may denote something distinct from deeds. Nevertheless, all righteous deeds fall within the meaning of religion and faith. Speech includes the speech of the heart and the tongue, while deeds include the actions of the heart and the limbs.

Those who expounded their doctrine explained that faith has foundations and branches, comprising pillars, obligations that are not pillars, and recommended acts. The same applies to what is denoted by Hajj, prayer, and other acts of worship. The term “Hajj” encompasses every prescribed action and abstention within it, such as entering the state of consecration, refraining from what is prohibited in that state, staying at ‘Arafah, Muzdalifah, and Minā, circling Allah’s Sacred House, and passing between the two hills flanking it, namely al-Safā and al-Marwah. Yet Hajj comprises pillars whose omission renders it invalid, such as being present at ‘Arafah.

It also requires abstaining from a prohibited act whose commission invalidates Hajj, namely sexual intercourse. It further comprises obligations involving actions and abstentions: deliberately neglecting these is sinful, and neglecting them—whether for an excuse or otherwise—requires compensation through a sacrificial offering. Examples include entering the state of consecration at the designated geographical boundaries, being present at ‘Arafah by both day and night, casting pebbles at the pillars, and similar acts; as well as refraining from ordinary clothing, perfume, hunting, and other such things.

It also comprises recommended actions and abstentions that perfect Hajj. Omitting them incurs neither sin nor a sacrificial offering. Examples include raising one’s voice in the pilgrimage invocation, repeating it frequently, leading the sacrificial animals, and remembering Allah,

Whoever performs what is obligatory and avoids what is forbidden has completed Hajj and ‘Umrah for Allah. In this deed, he follows a moderate course and is among the people of the right. But whoever also performs what is recommended is more perfect in his observance and more complete in his Hajj; he is among the foremost, brought near to Allah. Whoever neglects what is commanded and does what is forbidden, yet fulfills the essential pillar of Hajj and avoids what invalidates it, has performed a deficient Hajj. Whoever fails to fulfill an essential pillar of Hajj or commits an act that invalidates it has performed an invalid Hajj that does not discharge the obligation; rather, he must repeat it. There may nevertheless be disagreement over whether he is rewarded for what he has performed, even though it does not discharge the obligation. The more likely correct view is that he is rewarded for it.

Thus, “Hajj falls into three categories”: perfect through the performance of recommended acts; complete through the performance of obligatory acts alone; and deficient through falling short of what is obligatory. The jurists likewise divide ablution and the full ritual bath into perfect and sufficient forms. By “perfect,” however, they mean performing both the obligatory and recommended elements; by “sufficient,” they mean restricting oneself to the obligatory elements.

The faith of the foremost, those brought near to Allah, involves fulfilling both obligatory and recommended duties, whether these entail acting or refraining. The faith of those who follow a moderate course, the people of the right, involves fulfilling obligatory duties, whether these entail acting or refraining. The faith of the wrongdoers involves neglecting some obligations or committing some prohibited acts.

For this reason, the scholars of the Sunnah, when describing “the creed of the people of the Sunnah and the community,” state that they do not declare anyone who prays toward the qiblah an unbeliever on account of a sin. This alludes to the innovation of the Kharijites, who declare people unbelievers for sins as such.

As for the foundation of faith—acknowledging what the messengers brought from Allah, believing it to be true and submitting to it—anyone who lacks this foundation is not a believer. Thus, it is established through mass-transmitted hadiths:

“Bring out of the Fire anyone whose heart contains an atom’s weight of faith.”

“A grain’s weight of faith.”

An authentic narration also has:

“A grain’s weight of goodness.”

“An atom’s weight of goodness.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith narrated from Abū Hurayrah and reported by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“Faith has sixty-odd—or sixty-odd, or seventy-odd—branches. The highest is saying, ‘There is no god but Allah,’ and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road. Modesty is a branch of faith.”

the Sunnah: that faith does not admit of division into parts, but is a single whole—either all of it is present or none of it is.

Related to this is the need to understand that faith is one of the terms used in the revealed scriptures, the Quran, and the prophetic teachings, and belongs to religion and revealed law. What it denotes therefore varies in extent and character with the different divine scriptures. Some of it is shared by all believers, earlier and later, and by all divine scriptures: acknowledging Allah and the Last Day, worshipping Allah alone without any partner, truthfulness, and justice.

Know that most of the Meccan surahs, which Allah revealed in Mecca, concern this general faith shared by all prophets and all believers. This shared foundation is broader and more fully developed in some religious dispensations. What Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought concerning Allah’s names and attributes and the description of the Last Day is more complete than what the other prophets brought.

Other aspects vary between revealed laws and prescribed ways, such as the direction of prayer, rites of worship, the prescribed amounts, times, and forms of worship, established practices, rulings, and other matters. Thus, what faith and religion denoted at the beginning of Islam is not what they denoted at the end of the prophetic period; rather, what they denoted at the end was more complete. As Allah Most High said:

“Today I have perfected your religion for you.”

And He said in the same surah:

“Whoever rejects faith, his deeds have come to nothing.”

For this reason, Imam Ahmad said: “At the beginning of Islam, faith was incomplete, and then it gradually became complete.” Likewise,

Thus, believers among earlier and later generations—among the Jews, Christians, Sabians, and believers of Muhammad’s community, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—share faith in Allah and the Last Day, and righteous deeds, as the Quran indicates.

Yet the Jews were required to acknowledge matters that we are not required to acknowledge, such as the obligations and prohibitions of the Torah concerning the Sabbath and the fat surrounding the entrails and kidneys. They were not required to believe in detail in matters concerning Allah’s names and attributes and the descriptions of the Last Day that had not been revealed to them. We, however, are required to believe in matters of this kind that were not obligatory for them. We are also required to acknowledge the five daily prayers, obligatory zakat, pilgrimage to the House, and other matters that form part of our faith but did not form part of theirs. Acknowledging these matters is part of faith by the consensus of the Muslim community. Likewise, acknowledging particular prophets formed part of the faith of those before us, whereas our faith includes acknowledging them only in general.

Others say that it retains its original meaning of assent while also including deeds, for deeds themselves form part of assent: a believer confirms his words through his deeds. As al-Hasan al-Basrī said, “Faith is neither wishful thinking nor outward adornment; rather, it is what takes firm root in the heart and is confirmed by deeds.” Another example is the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The private parts confirm that or belie it.”

Others say that faith, linguistically, does not mean assent but acknowledgment; in revealed law it likewise means acknowledgment, and acknowledgment encompasses both speech and action. This is not the place to elaborate on this, as I have discussed it at length elsewhere.

Once what faith encompasses is understood, then when deserving Paradise, salvation from the Fire, censure of those who abandon some part of faith, and similar matters are mentioned, what is meant is obligatory faith. Such is His saying:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them”—and the rest of the verse.

“Prepared for those who believe in Allah and His messengers.”

And the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“No adulterer commits adultery while he is a believer; no thief steals while he is a believer; and no one drinks wine while he is a believer.”

What is denied of such a person is the obligatory faith by which he deserves Paradise. This does not entail denying the foundation of faith or all its other parts and branches.

This is what they mean when they say, “The completeness of faith is denied, not its reality.” That is, they mean obligatory completeness, not the recommended completeness meant when jurists describe a ritual bath as either complete or sufficient.

Another example is the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Whoever cheats us is not one of us.”

This does not mean that he is a disbeliever, as the Khawārij have interpreted it, nor that he is not among the best of us, as the Murjiʾah have interpreted it. Rather, the pronoun corresponds to its explicit referent: the believers who deserve reward and are safe from punishment. The person who cheats is not one of us because he exposes himself to Allah’s wrath and punishment.

Once this is clear, whoever omits some obligatory aspect of faith because he is unable to fulfil it—whether because he has no means of acquiring the knowledge, as when the message does not reach him, or because he is unable to act—is not commanded to do what he cannot do, and that is not part of the faith

The people of the Sunnah and the united community, together with all who follow them, agree that many people will experience both, as established by the mass-transmitted reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Furthermore, the people of the Sunnah and the united community do not hold that everyone who commits a major sin must be punished, nor do they testify that any particular Muslim will enter the Fire because of a single major sin he has committed. Rather, they consider it possible that Allah will admit a major sinner into Paradise without punishment: because of good deeds, his own or those of others, that erase his major sin; because of afflictions that have expiated it; because of an answered supplication made by him or by someone else on his behalf; or for some other reason.

The advocates of the inevitable fulfilment of threats of punishment among the Khawārij and Muʿtazilah hold that those who commit major sins must be punished, since the texts threatening punishment encompass them. An example is His saying:

“Indeed, those who unjustly consume the property of orphans consume nothing but fire into their bellies, and they will burn in a blazing Fire.”

The Muʿtazilah make the fulfilment of threats of punishment one of the “five principles,” declaring anyone who opposes them an unbeliever. They differ from the people of the Sunnah and the united community by holding that the threatened punishment must be carried out upon those who commit major sins and that they must remain in the Fire forever. For this reason, the Khawārij and Muʿtazilah deny that our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, will intercede for those who commit major sins—that is, to have them brought out of the Fire.

This is refuted by the mass-transmitted reports from him concerning this matter, such as his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

The purpose here is not to examine these principles in detail, but merely to draw attention to them. What led them into this error was that they heard the texts threatening punishment, understood them to be universal in scope, and said:

“They must apply to everyone they encompass. This is a statement of fact, and Allah’s statements are true. If He failed to carry out His threat, it would be like His failing to fulfil His promise, and it is impossible for Allah to lie.”

The extremists among the Murji’ah countered them with the texts promising reward, since these may encompass many who commit major sins. Each group thus reverted to its own unsound principle.

The former said: “The texts promising reward encompass only believers, and these people are not believers.”

The latter said: “The texts threatening punishment encompass only unbelievers.”

Both positions are mistaken. Texts such as His saying:

“Indeed, those who unjustly consume the property of orphans”

do not stipulate unbelief as a condition; rather, they concern those who profess Islam.

Likewise, his saying:

“Whoever’s last words are ‘There is no god but Allah’ will enter Paradise”

does not stipulate the fulfilment of religious obligations as a condition. Indeed, it is established in the authentic hadith collections:

“Even if he has committed unlawful sexual intercourse, even if he has stolen, and even if he has drunk wine.”

Those who took a middle course said:

“Rather, universal scope is valid, and these expressions do convey universality; nevertheless, a general statement may have its scope restricted. This is the position of everyone, from the earliest generations to the latest, except this small faction.”

They said: “Anyone who is pardoned is thus excepted from the general scope.”

Others said:

“Rather, failing to carry out a threat does not constitute lying. The Arabs do not regard it as shameful or disgraceful for a man to threaten harm and then not carry it out, as they do when he promises good and then fails to fulfil it.”

This is the position of various groups among both earlier and later scholars. They cited as evidence the words of Ka‘b ibn Zuhayr, addressing the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“I have been told that Allah’s Messenger has threatened me,
yet pardon from Allah’s Messenger is hoped for.”

They said: “This was a threat directed at a particular individual, yet he expressed hope for pardon while addressing the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It is therefore clear that pardoning someone who has been threatened is permissible, even when this does not involve restricting the scope of a general statement.”

Just as the texts promising reward for righteous deeds are conditional upon the absence of disbelief that nullifies those deeds—for the Quran indicates that whoever apostatizes has rendered his deeds worthless—so too the texts threatening punishment for disbelievers and sinners are conditional upon the absence of repentance. For the Quran indicates that Allah forgives all sins for whoever repents, and this is agreed upon among Muslims. The same principle therefore applies to matters of dispute.

Through well-known texts, Allah has made clear that good deeds erase evil deeds; that whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it; that He answers the supplicant’s prayer when he calls upon Him; that worldly afflictions expiate sins; that He accepts the intercession of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for those who have committed major sins; and that He does not forgive associating partners with Him, but forgives anything less than that for whomever He wills. Likewise, He has made clear that charity is nullified by reminders of generosity and hurtful conduct, that usury nullifies deeds, and that Allah accepts only from those who fear Him—that is, in the deed in question—and other such matters.

Thus, He has established things that remove the punishment for evil deeds, just as He has established things that may nullify the reward for good deeds. Yet nothing effaces all evil deeds except repentance, just as nothing nullifies all good deeds except apostasy.

We do not, however, testify that a particular individual is in the Fire, because we do not know whether the threatened punishment will apply to that individual. Its application to a particular individual depends upon certain conditions being fulfilled and impediments being absent, and we do not know whether those conditions are fulfilled and those impediments absent in his case. The purpose of the threat is to explain that this sin is a cause that warrants this punishment; yet a cause may take effect only when its conditions are fulfilled and its impediments absent.

This is illustrated by the established report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“cursed wine, the one who presses it, the one who has it pressed, the one who carries it, the one to whom it is carried, the one who drinks it, the one who serves it, the one who sells it, the one who buys it, and the one who consumes its proceeds.”

It is also established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī, on the authority of ʿUmar, that:

“A man used to drink wine frequently, and another man cursed him. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Do not curse him, for he loves Allah and His Messenger.’”

Thus, he prohibited cursing this particular individual, despite his habitual drinking, because he loved Allah and His Messenger, although wine drinkers had been cursed in general terms.

We shall begin with the position of the imams of the Sunnah on this question before drawing attention to the evidence. We say:

The well-known position of Imam Ahmad and the general body of the imams of the Sunnah is that the Jahmiyyah are disbelievers. They are those who negate the attributes of the Most Merciful. Their doctrine explicitly contradicts the Scripture brought by the messengers, and its true substance is a denial of the Creator. It thus entails denying the Lord and denying what He has revealed about Himself through His messengers.

For this reason, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak said:

“We can recount the statements of the Jews and Christians, but we cannot bring ourselves to recount the statements of the Jahmiyyah.”

More than one imam stated that they were more deeply steeped in disbelief than the Jews and Christians, meaning in this particular respect. For this reason, they declared to be disbelievers those who say that the Quran is created; that Allah will not be seen in the Hereafter; that Allah is not above the Throne; or that Allah has no knowledge, power, mercy, anger, or other such attributes.

As for the “Murjiʾah,” his recorded statements consistently indicate that he did not declare them to be disbelievers. Their innovation is of the same kind as the jurists’ disagreements over subsidiary matters, and the dispute over much of what they say comes down to a dispute over words and designations. translated_text:
religion; hence, anyone who disputed it was deemed an innovator. Likewise, his position concerning the “Shia” who give Ali precedence over Abū Bakr is consistent: they are not to be declared disbelievers, since this is also the view of a group of jurists, although they are deemed innovators.

As for the “Qadariyyah” who affirm Allah’s knowledge, the “Rāfidah” who are not extremists, the Jahmiyyah, and the Khawārij, two positions are reported from him concerning whether they are to be declared disbelievers. This is the actual purport of his general statements, although his predominant stance was to refrain from declaring the Qadariyyah who affirm Allah’s knowledge and the Khawārij disbelievers, despite his statement: “I know of no people worse than the Khawārij.”

Some of his followers, however, report two positions from him concerning the declaration of adherents of innovation as disbelievers generally, even including the Murji’ah in this. Yet that is not the case. Two positions are also reported from him concerning whether someone who does not declare them disbelievers is himself a disbeliever; the sounder position is that he is not. Some of his followers may present this disagreement concerning someone who does not declare others disbelievers as applying without qualification. This is an outright error.

According to many of the early scholars—such as Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Yūsuf ibn Asbāt, and a group of Imam Ahmad’s followers and others—the Jahmiyyah are not among the seventy-two sects into which this community divided. Rather, in their view, the main groups from which these sects arose are the Khawārij, the Shia, the Murji’ah, and the Qadariyyah. This is what is transmitted

translated_text:
from Ahmad. It is also reported from the imams of the Sunnah and hadith generally that they used to say: “Whoever says that the Quran is created is a disbeliever,” and “Whoever says that Allah will not be seen in the Hereafter is a disbeliever,” and similar statements.

Abū Nasr al-Sijzī then related two positions from them on this matter. The first is that this constitutes disbelief that takes a person outside Islam. He said: “This is the position of the majority.” The second is that it constitutes disbelief that does not take a person outside Islam. Accordingly, al-Khattābī said that they made these statements as a stern warning.

Likewise, the later scholars of our school disagreed over whether those among these groups who are declared disbelievers will remain eternally in Hell. Most affirmed their eternal punishment without qualification, as is also reported from a number of the earlier hadith scholars, such as Abū Hātim (?), Abū Zurʿah, and others. Some, however, refrained from affirming eternal punishment.

The reason for this disagreement is the apparent conflict between the evidence. They see evidence requiring that the rulings pertaining to disbelief be applied to these people. Yet they also see particular individuals who have voiced these views possessing such faith as precludes their being disbelievers. Thus, the two bodies of evidence appear to them to conflict.

In reality, they have encountered the same difficulty with the general wording of the imams’ statements that earlier people encountered with the general wording of the revealed texts. Whenever they saw the imams saying, “Whoever says such-and-such is a disbeliever,” the listener assumed that this wording encompassed everyone who said it. They did not consider that declaring someone a disbeliever involves conditions and impediments that may not apply in a particular individual’s case, and that a general declaration of disbelief does not entail declaring a particular individual a disbeliever

unless the conditions are met and the impediments are absent. This is illustrated by the fact that Imam Ahmad and the imams generally who made these sweeping statements did not declare most of those who uttered these very words to be disbelievers as individuals.

Imam Ahmad, for example, dealt directly with the “Jahmiyyah,” who called upon him to affirm that the Quran was created and to deny the divine attributes. They subjected him and the other scholars of his time to an inquisition. They persecuted believing men and women who did not agree with their Jahmī doctrines by beating, imprisoning and killing them, dismissing them from office, cutting off their stipends, rejecting their testimony, and failing to secure their release from enemy captivity.

Indeed, many of those in authority at that time—governors, judges and others—were Jahmīs. They declared anyone who was not a Jahmī and did not agree with their denial of the divine attributes, such as the assertion that the Quran was created, to be a disbeliever. They applied to him the rulings they applied to a disbeliever: they would not appoint him to office, ransom him from the enemy, give him anything from the public treasury, or accept his testimony, legal opinions or transmitted reports. They tested people when appointing them to office, accepting their testimony, ransoming them from captivity, and in other circumstances. Whoever affirmed that the Quran was created, they judged to be a believer; whoever did not affirm it, they did not accord the rulings applicable to believers. Anyone who called people to doctrines other than those of the Jahmiyyah, they killed, or beat and imprisoned.

It is well known that this is among the most extreme forms of Jahmī doctrine, for calling people to a doctrine is more serious than

{رَبَّنَا لَا تُؤَاخِذْنَا إنْ نَسِينَا أَوْ أَخْطَأْنَا}

translated_text:
professing it. Rewarding those who profess it and punishing those who reject it are more serious than merely calling people to it; and punishing someone who professes it by execution is more serious than punishing him by beating.

Yet Imam Ahmad prayed for the caliph and others who had beaten and imprisoned him. He sought forgiveness for them and pardoned them for their mistreatment of him and their advocacy of a doctrine that constitutes disbelief. Had they been apostates from Islam, seeking forgiveness for them would not have been permissible, for seeking forgiveness for disbelievers is forbidden by the Quran, the Sunnah and scholarly consensus.

These statements and actions of his, and those of other imams, clearly show that they did not declare the individual Jahmīs who said that the Quran was created and that Allah would not be seen in the Hereafter to be disbelievers. Reports from Ahmad also indicate that he declared certain specific people disbelievers on this account. To attribute two different positions to him on this issue, however, is open to question. Alternatively, the matter should be understood by drawing the necessary distinctions:

Those whom he declared disbelievers individually were those for whom evidence established that the conditions for declaring disbelief were met and the impediments were absent. Those whom he did not declare disbelievers individually were those for whom this was not established. All this was despite his pronouncing disbelief in general, unrestricted terms.

The evidence for this principle is the Quran, the Sunnah, scholarly consensus and reasoned consideration.

As for the Quran, Allah, glorified and exalted, says:

“There is no blame upon you for what you do by mistake.”

And He, exalted is He, says:

“Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake.”

and that “he would not recite a single letter of them without being granted it.”

Since the Quran, as explained by the Sunnah, establishes that Allah has pardoned this community for mistakes and forgetfulness, this is a general ruling whose full scope remains intact. Nothing in the scriptural evidence entails that Allah punishes anyone in this community for an error, even if He punishes someone outside this community who errs.

It is also established in the Sahīh, in a hadith narrated by Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

translated_text:
This hadith is mass-transmitted from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Scholars of hadith and chains of transmission have narrated it from Abū Sa‘īd, Hudhayfah, ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Amr, and others, from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, through numerous routes. Hadith scholars know that these routes yield certain knowledge for them, even if such certainty is not attained by others who do not share their means of acquiring knowledge.

This man had fallen into doubt and ignorance concerning Allah Most High’s power to restore a human being after he had been burned and scattered, and concerning the fact that He would bring the dead person back to life and gather him for judgment after this had been done to him. These are two fundamental matters:

The first concerns Allah Most High: belief that He has power over all things.

The second concerns the Last Day: belief that Allah will bring this dead person back to life and recompense him for his deeds.

Nevertheless, he believed in Allah in a general sense and believed in the Last Day in a general sense—that Allah rewards and punishes after death. He had also performed a righteous deed: his fear that Allah would punish him for his sins. Allah therefore forgave him on account of the faith he possessed in Allah and the Last Day, and his righteous deed.

Furthermore, it is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah will bring out of the Fire whoever has a dinar’s weight of faith in his heart.”

translated_text:
and in another narration:

“a dinar’s weight of goodness. Then He will bring out of the Fire whoever has a mustard seed’s weight of faith in his heart.”

Another narration reads “goodness.”

“And He will bring out of the Fire whoever has an atom’s weight of faith or goodness in his heart.”

These and similar reports, widely transmitted from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, show that whoever possesses any faith and goodness, however little, will not remain in the Fire forever, and that faith is divisible and consists of parts. It is known with certainty that many of those who make these errors possess some measure of faith in Allah and His Messenger, for our discussion concerns precisely such people.

Moreover, many of the early generations erred concerning many of these matters, yet they agreed that such errors did not warrant declaring a person an unbeliever. For example, some Companions denied that the dead could hear the calls of the living; some denied that the Ascension occurred while the Prophet was awake; and some denied that Muhammad saw his Lord. Some also expressed well-known views concerning the caliphate and relative merit. Likewise, some made well-known statements concerning fighting others, cursing others, and declaring others unbelievers.

The judge Shurayh rejected the recitation:

“Rather, you marvel,”

saying, “Allah does not marvel.” When this reached Ibrāhīm al-Nakha‘ī, he said, “Shurayh is merely a poet, impressed with his own knowledge. ‘Abd Allāh had greater understanding than he did, and he used to recite:

‘Rather, you marvel.’”

Thus, he rejected an established recitation and denied an attribute indicated by the Quran and Sunnah. Nevertheless, the Muslim community agreed that he was one of its leading scholars. Likewise, some of the early generations denied

certain Quranic readings. For example, one of them rejected His words:

“Have those who believe not yet realized,”

and said, “The wording is actually: ‘Has it not become clear to those who believe?’” Another rejected the reading of His words:

“Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him,”

and said, “The wording is actually: ‘Your Lord has enjoined.’” One of them had omitted the two surahs of seeking refuge, while another would write down the surah of supplication. These are errors established as such by consensus and mass transmission. Nevertheless, because these matters had not reached them through mass transmission, they were not declared unbelievers, even though someone against whom proof had been established through mass transmission would fall into unbelief by doing the same.

Furthermore, the Quran and Sunnah indicate that Allah does not punish anyone until the message has been conveyed to them. Whoever has not received the message at all will not be punished at all. Whoever has received it in general, but not some of its details, will be punished only for denying those matters concerning which the proof conveyed by the messengers has been established against them. This is indicated by the words of the Most High:

“So that people would have no argument against Allah after the messengers.”

And His words:

“O company of jinn and mankind, did messengers not come to you from among yourselves, relating My verses to you?”

And the rest of the verse.

And His words:

“Did We not grant you lives long enough for anyone who would take heed to do so? And the warner came to you.”

And His words:

“And its keepers said to them, ‘Did messengers not come to you from among yourselves, reciting to you the verses of your Lord?’”

And the rest of the verse.

And His words:

“We never punish until We have sent a messenger.”

And His words:

“Your Lord would never destroy the towns until He had sent to their principal town a messenger reciting Our verses to them.”

And His words:

“Whenever a group is cast into it, they will be asked

by its keepers, ‘Did no warner come to you?’”

“They will say, ‘Yes, a warner did come to us, but we denied him and said, “Allah has not sent down anything.”’”

And His words:

“Had We destroyed them with a punishment before him, they would have said, ‘Our Lord, why did You not send us a messenger so that we could have followed Your verses before we were humiliated and disgraced?’”

And His words:

“Were it not that a calamity might befall them because of what their own hands have sent forth, and they would say, ‘Our Lord, why did You not send us a messenger so that we could have followed Your verses and been among the believers?’”

There are many similar passages in the Quran. If someone believes in Allah and His Messenger but is unaware of some of what the Messenger brought, and therefore does not believe in those particulars—whether because he has not heard them, has heard them through a channel that does not require him to accept them as true, or has understood them differently through an excusable interpretation—then he has been granted faith in Allah and His Messenger that warrants Allah’s rewarding him for it. As for what he has not believed in, the proof whose rejection constitutes unbelief has not been established against him concerning it.

Furthermore, the Quran, the Sunnah, and consensus establish that certain errors in religion do not render the person who makes them an unbeliever, or even a transgressor; indeed, he incurs no sin at all. Such is the case with errors in subsidiary matters of practice. Although some scholastic theologians and jurists believe that whoever errs in these matters incurs sin, while others believe that everyone exercising independent scholarly judgment in them is correct, both views are anomalous. Even so, no one has declared the scholars who exercise independent judgment and disagree over these matters to be unbelievers. Yet, in some of these questions, the error of the dissenting party has been established

by the scriptural texts and the early consensus—for example, some among the early and later generations regarded certain forms of usury as lawful, others regarded certain kinds of intoxicating drinks as lawful, and still others regarded fighting during civil strife as lawful.

The adherents of the Sunnah and the community agree that none of those known for their virtue—including the well-known Companions and others who fought on either side at the Battles of the Camel and Siffīn—is to be judged a transgressor, much less declared an unbeliever. Some jurists even extended this principle to all rebels: although they held that fighting them was obligatory, they prohibited judging them to be transgressors because they acted on an interpretation. These imams likewise state:

“Someone who drinks the disputed beverage nabīdh on the basis of an interpretation is neither flogged nor deemed a transgressor.”

Allah Most High says:

“And remember David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field into which a people’s sheep had strayed by night; We were witness to their judgment.”

“We gave Solomon understanding of the case, and to each We gave judgment and knowledge.”

And He Most High says:

“Whatever palm trees you cut down or left standing on their roots, it was by Allah’s permission.”

It is established in the authentic hadith collections, through the reports of ‘Amr ibn al-‘Ās and Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When a judge exercises independent judgment and reaches the correct decision, he has two rewards; when he exercises independent judgment and errs, he has one reward.”

It is also established in the authentic collection, on the authority of Buraydah ibn al-Husayb, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When you besiege the people of a fortress and they ask you to let them surrender subject to Allah’s judgment, do not let them surrender subject to Allah’s judgment. Rather, let them surrender subject to your judgment and that of your companions, for you do not know what Allah’s judgment concerning them is.”

The proofs of this principle are numerous and belong in another discussion. It is established by the Quran, the Sunnah and consensus that anyone whom the Prophet’s message has reached, yet who does not believe in him, is an unbeliever. His appeal to independent judgment is not accepted as an excuse, because the proofs of the message and the signs of prophethood are clear.

This is also because being excused for error is a ruling of the revealed law. Just as sins are divided into major and minor sins, and obligations into essential pillars and obligations that are not pillars, so too errors are divided into those that are forgiven and those that are not. The scriptural texts establish exemption from accountability for error specifically for this community.

That being so, someone who errs concerning some of these matters must be classed either with the unbelievers among the polytheists and the People of the Book, despite differing from them on most of the foundations of faith, or with those who err concerning matters of obligation and prohibition, even though these too belong to the foundations of faith. Indeed, believing that the clear obligations established by mass transmission are obligatory, and that the clear prohibitions established by mass transmission are forbidden, is among the greatest foundations of faith and principles of religion. Whoever denies them is an unbeliever by consensus. Yet someone who exercises independent judgment concerning some of them is, by consensus, not an unbeliever despite his error.

Since he must be classed with one of these two groups, it is evident that he more closely resembles those believers in Allah and His Messenger who err than he does the polytheists and the People of the Book

The second fundamental principle is that declarations of unbelief in general terms—like general threats of punishment—must be affirmed in their unrestricted, general sense.

As for judging a particular individual to be an unbeliever, or affirming that he is destined for the Fire, this requires evidence specific to that individual. Such a judgment depends on establishing that its conditions are fulfilled and that no impediments to it exist.

It should be understood here that the Sharia may command us to impose a prescribed punishment upon someone in this world—whether execution, flogging, or otherwise—although he will not be punished in the Hereafter. Examples include fighting rebels and those acting on an interpretation, even though they retain their moral probity; and imposing the prescribed punishment upon someone who sincerely repents after being apprehended. We nevertheless impose the prescribed punishment upon him, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, imposed it upon Māʿiz ibn Mālik and the Ghāmidī woman, despite saying:

“She has repented with such repentance that, had a collector of unlawful levies repented in the same way, he would have been forgiven.”

Another example is imposing the prescribed punishment upon someone who drinks nabīdh (a fruit-based drink) whose permissibility is disputed, relying on an interpretation, despite knowing that he retains his moral probity. This differs from the case of someone who has no such interpretive basis. For when some of the Companions drank wine

and believed it to be lawful for a select few, interpreting His words:

“There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have consumed, provided they fear Allah, believe, and do righteous deeds, then fear Allah and believe, then fear Allah and do good.”

The Companions, including ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib, and others, agreed that if they acknowledged its prohibition, they were to be flogged; but if they persisted in declaring it lawful, they were to be executed. Likewise, we know that many people are not punished in this world although they are unbelievers in the Hereafter, such as non-Muslims under Muslim protection who agree to pay the jizya (poll tax) while remaining in unbelief.

Another example is the hypocrites who outwardly profess Islam: the rulings of Islam apply to them, although they are unbelievers in the Hereafter, as the Quran indicates in numerous verses, including His words:

“Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire, and you will never find anyone to help them”—and so on.

And His words:

“On the Day when the hypocrite men and women say to the believers, ‘Wait for us, so that we may take some of your light,’ they will be told, ‘Go back and seek a light.’ Then a wall with a gate will be placed between them: within it is mercy, and outside it is punishment.”

“They will call out to them, ‘Were we not with you?’ They will reply, ‘Yes, but you led yourselves into temptation, waited, doubted, and were deluded by false hopes until Allah’s decree came, and the deceiver deceived you concerning Allah.’”

“So today no ransom will be accepted from you, nor from those who disbelieved”—and so on.

This is because true recompense is only in the Hereafter, which is the abode of reward and punishment. As for this world, only such punishment is prescribed as serves to ward off

Since this is so, punishment in this world does not necessarily entail punishment in the Hereafter, nor does the reverse hold true.

For this reason, most of the early scholars call for the execution of an advocate of religious innovation who leads people astray, because of the corruption he causes in religion, whether they consider him an unbeliever or not.

Once this is understood, declaring a “particular individual” among these ignorant people and others like them an unbeliever—judging him to be one of the unbelievers—is not permissible until the proof conveyed by the messengers has been established against him, making it clear that they are opposing the messengers, even though there is no doubt that this statement constitutes unbelief. The same applies to declaring any “particular individuals” unbelievers, although some forms of this

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about a man who said:

“Allah did not truly speak to Moses; rather, He created speech and sound in the tree, and Moses, peace be upon him, heard from the tree, not from Allah. Nor did Allah, Mighty and Majestic, speak the Quran to Gabriel; rather, Gabriel took it from the Preserved Tablet.” Is he correct or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. This man is not correct. Rather, he is misguided, a fabricator and a liar, according to the agreement of the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars. Indeed, he is an unbeliever who must be called upon to repent and, unless he repents, be put to death.

If he says, “I do not deny the wording of the Quran”—namely, Allah’s statement,

“And Allah spoke to Moses directly”

—“Rather, I acknowledge that this wording is true, but I deny its meaning and reality,” then such people are the Jahmiyyah, whom the early generations and leading scholars unanimously regarded as among the worst adherents of deviant beliefs and innovations. Many leading scholars even excluded them from the seventy-two sects. The first person in Islam to express this doctrine was a man called al-Ja‘d ibn Dirham

translated_text:
and Khālid ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Qasrī slaughtered him as a sacrifice on Eid al-Adha. He addressed the people, saying in his sermon:

“Offer your sacrifices, O people; may Allah accept your sacrifices. I shall offer al-Ja‘d ibn Dirham as a sacrifice, for he claimed that Allah did not take Abraham as a close friend and did not speak to Moses directly. Exalted is Allah far above what al-Ja‘d says!”

Then he stepped down and slaughtered him. This occurred during the time of the Successors, who commended the act. Jahm ibn Safwān adopted this doctrine from him, and Salamah ibn Ahwaz killed Jahm in Khurasan. This doctrine was named after Jahm and is called “the doctrine of the Jahmiyyah.” It consists in denying the attributes of Allah Most High. They say that Allah will not be seen in the Hereafter, that He does not speak to His servants, and that He has no knowledge, life, power, or other such attributes. They also say, “The Quran is created.”

The Mu‘tazilah, the followers of ‘Amr ibn ‘Ubayd, agreed with Jahm on this and added other innovations concerning divine decree and other matters. However, the Mu‘tazilah say that Allah truly spoke to Moses and truly uttered speech. Yet, according to them, this means that He created speech in something other than Himself—whether in a tree, in the air, or in something else—without speech, knowledge, power, mercy, will, life, or any other attribute subsisting in Allah Himself.

The Jahmiyyah sometimes openly declare the true substance of their doctrine, saying, “Allah did not speak to Moses directly, nor does He speak.” At other times, they do not openly use this wording because it is so abhorrent and contrary to Islam and the religions of the Jews and Christians, so they affirm the wording

but couple it with the claim that He created speech in something other than Himself.

All the imams of the religion agree upon what the Quran and Sunnah teach and what the early generations of the Muslim community unanimously affirmed: that Allah spoke directly to Moses; that the Quran is the speech of Allah, uncreated; that the believers will see their Lord in the Hereafter, as affirmed in the mass-transmitted hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; and that Allah possesses knowledge, power, and other such attributes.

The imams’ statements on these matters are widely known and abundantly transmitted. Indeed, when the hadith scholar Abū al-Qāsim al-Tabarī recorded the statements of the early generations and the imams concerning the fundamentals of religion in his book, Sharh Usūl al-Sunnah (Explanation of the Foundations of the Sunnah), he listed those who said, “The Quran is the speech of Allah, uncreated.” He said:

“These are five hundred and fifty people or more from among the Successors and the recognized imams, apart from the Companions, spanning different eras and successive years. They include about a hundred imams whose opinions people accepted and whose teachings they followed in their religious practice.

“Had I undertaken to transmit the statements of the scholars of hadith, their names would have numbered in the thousands. Instead, I have kept this brief, transmitting the statements of these individuals, generation after generation, without anyone objecting to them. Whoever rejected their position, they called upon him to repent, or ordered that he be killed, banished, or crucified.”

He said: “There is no disagreement within the Muslim community that the first to say that the Quran was created was Ja‘d ibn Dirham, in the 120s AH, followed by Jahm ibn Safwān. As for Ja‘d, Khālid ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Qasrī killed him. As for Jahm, he was killed in Merv during the caliphate of Hishām ibn ‘Abd al-Malik.”
