 مَنْ حَلَفَ بِالْقُرْآنِ فَعَلَيْهِ بِكُلِّ آيَةٍ يَمِينٌ.
 وَهَذَا ثَابِتٌ عَنْ ابْنِ مَسْعُودٍ وَعَنْ سُفْيَانَ بْنِ عُيَيْنَة قَالَ:
 سَمِعْت عَمْرَو بْنَ دِينَارٍ يَقُولُ: أَدْرَكْت مَشَايِخَنَا وَالنَّاسَ مُنْذُ سَبْعِينَ سَنَةً يَقُولُونَ: الْقُرْآنُ كَلَامُ اللَّهِ مِنْهُ بَدَأَ وَإِلَيْهِ يَعُودُ وَفِي لَفْظٍ يَقُولُونَ: الْقُرْآنُ كَلَامُ اللَّهِ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقٍ وَقَالَ حَرْبٌ الكرماني ثنا إسْحَاقُ بْنُ إبْرَاهِيمَ يَعْنِي ابْنَ رَاهَوَيْه عَنْ سُفْيَانَ بْنِ عُيَيْنَة عَنْ عَمْرِو بْنِ دِينَارٍ قَالَ: أَدْرَكْت النَّاسَ مُنْذُ سَبْعِينَ سَنَةً أَدْرَكْت أَصْحَابَ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَمَنْ دُونَهُمْ يَقُولُونَ: اللَّهُ الْخَالِقُ وَمَا سِوَاهُ مَخْلُوقٌ إلَّا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ كَلَامُ اللَّهِ مِنْهُ خَرَجَ وَإِلَيْهِ يَعُودُ. وَهَذَا قَدْ رَوَاهُ عَنْ ابْنِ عُيَيْنَة إسْحَاقُ وَإِسْحَاقُ إمَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ سَمِعَهُ مِنْهُ أَوْ مِنْ بَعْضِ أَصْحَابِهِ عَنْهُ وَعَنْ جَعْفَرِ بْنِ مُحَمَّدٍ الصَّادِقِ - وَهُوَ مَشْهُورٌ عَنْهُ - أَنَّهُمْ سَأَلُوهُ عَنْ الْقُرْآنِ أَخَالِقٌ هُوَ أَمْ مَخْلُوقٌ؟
 فَقَالَ:
 لَيْسَ بِخَالِقِ وَلَا مَخْلُوقٍ وَلَكِنَّهُ كَلَامُ اللَّهِ. وَهَكَذَا رُوِيَ عَنْ الْحَسَنِ الْبَصْرِيِّ وَأَيُّوبَ السختياني وَسُلَيْمَانَ
translated_text:
He also related, through two chains of transmission, from ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, that they said to him on the day of Siffīn, “You appointed two men as arbiters?” He replied, “I appointed no created thing as arbiter; I appointed only the Quran.”

He also related from ‘Ikrimah, who said: “Ibn ‘Abbās was attending a funeral. When the deceased was placed in the burial niche, a man stood up and said, ‘O Allah, Lord of the Quran, forgive him.’ Ibn ‘Abbās rushed over to him and said, ‘Stop! The Quran is from Him.’”

It is also related from ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd that he said, “Whoever swears by the Quran is bound by an oath for every verse.” This is established from Ibn Mas‘ūd.

Sufyān ibn ‘Uyaynah said: “I heard ‘Amr ibn Dīnār say, ‘For seventy years I have known our teachers and the people to say: The Quran is the speech of Allah; from Him it originated, and to Him it will return.’” In another wording, they say, “The Quran is the speech of Allah, uncreated.”

Harb al-Kirmānī said: “Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm—that is, Ibn Rāhawayh—narrated to us from Sufyān ibn ‘Uyaynah, from ‘Amr ibn Dīnār, who said: ‘I have known the people for seventy years. I met the Companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and those who came after them, saying: Allah is the Creator, and everything besides Him is created, except the Quran, for it is the speech of Allah; from Him it came forth, and to Him it will return.’”

Ishāq related this from Ibn ‘Uyaynah. Either Ishāq heard it from him directly, or he heard it from one of his companions who related it from him.

It is also related from Ja‘far ibn Muhammad al-Sādiq—and this is well known from him—that they asked him about the Quran: “Is it a creator or is it created?” He replied, “It is neither a creator nor created; rather, it is the speech of Allah.” The same was related from al-Hasan al-Basrī, Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī, and Sulaymān

التيمي وَخَلْقٍ مِنْ التَّابِعِينَ.
 وَعَنْ مَالِكِ بْنِ أَنَسٍ وَاللَّيْثِ بْنِ سَعْدٍ وَسُفْيَانَ الثَّوْرِيِّ وَابْنِ أَبِي لَيْلَى وَأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد بْنِ حَنْبَلٍ وَإِسْحَاقَ بْنِ رَاهَوَيْه وَأَمْثَالِ هَؤُلَاءِ مِنْ الْأَئِمَّةِ وَكَلَامُ هَؤُلَاءِ الْأَئِمَّةِ وَأَتْبَاعِهِمْ فِي ذَلِكَ كَثِيرٌ مَشْهُورٌ بَلْ اشْتَهَرَ عَنْ أَئِمَّةِ السَّلَفِ تَكْفِيرُ مَنْ قَالَ:
 الْقُرْآنُ مَخْلُوقٌ وَأَنَّهُ يُسْتَتَابُ فَإِنْ تَابَ وَإِلَّا قُتِلَ كَمَا ذَكَرُوا ذَلِكَ عَنْ مَالِكِ بْنِ أَنَسٍ وَغَيْرِهِ؟ وَلِذَلِكَ قَالَ الشَّافِعِيُّ لِحَفْصِ الْفَرْدِ -
 وَكَانَ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ ضِرَارِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو مِمَّنْ يَقُولُ:
 الْقُرْآنُ مَخْلُوقٌ فَلَمَّا نَاظَرَ الشَّافِعِيَّ وَقَالَ لَهُ: الْقُرْآنُ مَخْلُوقٌ قَالَ لَهُ الشَّافِعِيُّ -
 كَفَرْت بِاَللَّهِ الْعَظِيمِ:
 ذَكَرَهُ ابْنُ أَبِي حَاتِمٍ فِي الرَّدِّ عَلَى الْجَهْمِيَّة قَالَ: كَانَ فِي كِتَابِي عَنْ الرَّبِيعِ بْنِ سُلَيْمَانَ قَالَ: حَضَرْت الشَّافِعِيَّ أَوْ حَدَّثَنِي أَبُو شُعَيْبٍ إلَّا أَنِّي أَعْلَمُ أَنَّهُ حَضَرَ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ عَبْدِ الْحَكَمِ وَيُوسُفُ بْنُ عَمْرِو بْنِ يَزِيدَ فَسَأَلَ حَفْصٌ عَبْدَ اللَّهِ قَالَ: مَا تَقُولُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ؟ فَأَبَى أَنْ يُجِيبَهُ فَسَأَلَ يُوسُفَ بْنَ عَمْرٍو فَلَمْ يُجِبْهُ وَكِلَاهُمَا أَشَارَ إلَى الشَّافِعِيِّ فَسَأَلَ الشَّافِعِيَّ فَاحْتَجَّ عَلَيْهِ وَطَالَتْ فِيهِ الْمُنَاظَرَةُ فَقَامَ الشَّافِعِيُّ بِالْحُجَّةِ بِأَنَّ الْقُرْآنَ كَلَامُ اللَّهِ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقٍ وَكَفَّرَ حَفْصًا الْفَرْدَ.
 قَالَ الرَّبِيعُ:
 فَلَقِيت حَفْصًا فِي الْمَسْجِدِ بَعْدَ هَذَا فَقَالَ: أَرَادَ الشَّافِعِيُّ قَتْلِي. وَأَمَّا مَالِكُ بْنُ أَنَسٍ فَنُقِلَ عَنْهُ مِنْ غَيْرِ وَجْهٍ الرَّدُّ عَلَى مَنْ يَقُولُ الْقُرْآنَ مَخْلُوقٌ وَاسْتِتَابَتُهُ وَهَذَا الْمَشْهُورُ عَنْهُ مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِ بَيْنَ أَصْحَابِهِ.
translated_text:
al-Taymī and many of the Successors.

It was also related from Mālik ibn Anas, al-Layth ibn Sa‘d, Sufyān al-Thawrī, Ibn Abī Laylā, Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, and other imams like them. The statements of these imams and their followers on this subject are numerous and well known. Indeed, the imams of the early generations were widely reported to have declared anyone who said, “The Quran is created,” an unbeliever, and to have held that he should be called upon to repent and, if he did not, be executed. This was related from Mālik ibn Anas and others.

Thus, when Hafs al-Fard—a follower of Dirār ibn ‘Amr who held that the Quran was created—debated al-Shāfi‘ī and said to him, “The Quran is created,” al-Shāfi‘ī told him, “You have disbelieved in Allah the Almighty.”

Ibn Abī Hātim mentioned this in his Refutation of the Jahmiyyah, saying: “My written record contained a report from al-Rabī‘ ibn Sulaymān, who said: ‘I was present with al-Shāfi‘ī—or Abū Shu‘ayb related it to me—but I know that ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Abd al-Hakam and Yūsuf ibn ‘Amr ibn Yazīd were present. Hafs asked ‘Abd Allāh, “What do you say about the Quran?” He refused to answer him. He then asked Yūsuf ibn ‘Amr, who did not answer him either. Both directed him to al-Shāfi‘ī. He therefore asked al-Shāfi‘ī, who presented his arguments against him, and the debate continued at length. Al-Shāfi‘ī established the proof that the Quran is the speech of Allah, uncreated, and declared Hafs al-Fard an unbeliever.’”

Al-Rabī‘ said: “After this, I met Hafs in the mosque, and he said, ‘Al-Shāfi‘ī wanted to have me killed.’”

As for Mālik ibn Anas, reports through several chains relate his refutation of those who say that the Quran is created and his requirement that they be called upon to repent. This is the well-known position transmitted from him, and his followers agree upon it.

translated_text:
As for Abū Hanīfah and his followers, Abū Ja‘far al-Tahāwī stated in the creed that he introduced with the words, “An exposition of the creed of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah according to the jurists of the faith”—Abū Hanīfah al-Nu‘mān ibn Thābit al-Kūfī, Abū Yūsuf Ya‘qūb ibn Ibrāhīm al-Ansārī, and Abū ‘Abd Allāh Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybānī:

“The Quran is the speech of Allah. It originated from Him as speech, without specifying how, and He sent it down to His Prophet as revelation. The believers accepted this as truth and affirmed that it is truly the speech of Allah Most High, not created like the speech of His creatures. Whoever hears it and claims that it is human speech has disbelieved. Allah has condemned and censured him, threatened him with His punishment, and warned him when He said:

‘I will cast him into Saqar.’

Since Allah threatened with Saqar whoever said:

‘This is nothing but human speech,’

we know that it is the speech of the Creator of humankind and does not resemble human speech.”

As for Ahmad ibn Hanbal, his statements on such matters are well known and transmitted through numerous independent reports. He became renowned for the ordeal inflicted upon him by these Jahmiyyah. They openly proclaimed their denial of Allah Most High’s attributes and the realities signified by His names, and their assertion that the Quran was created, so that the true import of their position amounted to negating the Creator, glorified and exalted is He. They called people to this and punished those who would not comply, whether by execution, cutting off their livelihood, dismissal from office, imprisonment, or beating. They declared those who opposed them unbelievers.

But Allah Most High kept Imam Ahmad steadfast until, through him, Allah extinguished their falsehood and granted the people of faith and the Sunnah victory over them. He humbled them after their ascendancy and consigned them to obscurity after their prominence. translated_text:
Allah and is uncreated, and the unqualified declaration that whoever says it is created has disbelieved likewise became widespread.

As for declaring that Allah did not speak to Moses, this contradicts the explicit text of the Quran and is therefore graver than saying that the Quran is created. Such a person must undoubtedly be called upon to repent; if he repents, well and good; otherwise, he is to be put to death, for he has denied the explicit text of the Quran. This is the ruling issued by the imams and the early generations concerning such a person. Whoever says that the Quran is created agrees with him in substance; this is why the early generations declared him an unbeliever.

Al-Bukhārī said in The Creation of Acts: “Sufyān al-Thawrī said: ‘Whoever says that the Quran is created is an unbeliever.’”

He also reported that ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak said: “Whoever says that ‘Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity but Me’ is created is an unbeliever. It is not fitting for any created being to say this.”

He also reported that Ibn al-Mubārak said: “We do not say, as the Jahmiyyah do, that He is here on earth. Rather, He rose over the Throne.” He was asked, “How are we to know our Lord?” He replied, “Above His heavens, over His Throne, distinct from His creation.”

He also said: “Whoever says that ‘There is no deity but Allah’ is created is an unbeliever. We can recount the words of the Jews and Christians, but we cannot recount the words of the Jahmiyyah.”

He also reported that ‘Alī ibn ‘Āsim said: “Those who say that Allah has a child are no greater in disbelief than those who say that Allah does not speak.”

Al-Bukhārī said: “Ismā‘īl ibn Abī Idrīs used to call them the heretics of Iraq.”

He was also asked, “Have you heard anyone say that the Quran is created?” He replied, “These heretics do.”

Al-Bukhārī said: “Abū al-Walīd said: ‘I heard Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd, when it was mentioned to him that some people were saying that the Quran is created, say: “How do they account for ‘Say, He is Allah, One’? How do they account for His words, ‘Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity but Me’?”’”

He said: “Abū ‘Ubayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām said: ‘I have examined what the Jews and Magians say, yet I have seen no people more astray in their disbelief than these. Indeed, I consider anyone who does not declare them unbelievers to be ignorant, except someone who is unaware of their disbelief.’”

He said: “Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd al-Hāshimī said: ‘Whoever says that the Quran is created is an unbeliever. If the Quran were created, as they claim, why should Pharaoh be more deserving of remaining in the Fire forever for saying, “I am your lord, the Most High”? They claim that he is created, yet the one who said, “Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity but Me, so worship Me,” has also made the same claim as Pharaoh. Why, then, should Pharaoh be more deserving of remaining in the Fire forever than this one, when, in such a person’s view, both are created?’ Abū ‘Ubayd was informed of this and approved of it and admired it.”

What these early scholars—may Allah be pleased with them—meant is that whoever says that Allah’s speech is created, and that He created it in the tree or elsewhere—as this Jahmī Mu‘tazilī about whom the question was asked has said—is in fact saying that it was the tree that said to Moses:

“Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity but Me, so worship Me.”

Whoever maintains that it was a created being who said this regards that created being as being like Pharaoh, who said:

“I am your lord, the Most High.”

Both are created beings, and both made that claim. Thus, if Pharaoh’s statement constitutes disbelief, then the statement of these people also constitutes disbelief.

There is no doubt that their position ultimately amounts to Pharaoh’s, even if they do not understand this. Pharaoh denied what Moses told him: that his Lord is the Most High and that He had spoken to him. As Allah Most High says:

“Pharaoh said, ‘O Hāmān, build me a tower so that I may reach the ways—the ways into the heavens—and look upon the God of Moses, though I certainly think he is a liar.’”

Thus, he denied that Allah had spoken to Moses.

These people, however, say that if Allah creates speech in something other than Himself, He thereby becomes the one speaking it. This is falsehood and error for many reasons.

First, Allah, glorified be He, has caused all things to speak, both in ordinary and extraordinary ways. Allah Most High says:

“Today We shall seal their mouths, and their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn.”

And He says:

“When they reach it, their hearing, their sight, and their skins will testify against them concerning what they used to do. They will say to their skins, ‘Why did you testify against us?’ They will reply, ‘Allah, who causes all things to speak, has caused us to speak.’”

And He says:

“On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do.”

He also says:

“We subjected the mountains to glorify Us with him in the evening and at sunrise.”

Furthermore, “it has been established that pebbles used to glorify Allah in the hand of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and that a stone used to greet him.” There are other similar instances of inanimate things being made to speak. If creating speech in something other than Himself made Him the one speaking it, then all of this would be the speech of Allah Most High, and He would have spoken to whoever heard it just as He spoke to Moses son of ‘Imrān. Thus, if Allah creates motion, taste, color or odor in a body, it is that body which moves, has the color, bears the odor or possesses the taste. If He creates life, knowledge, power, will or speech in a subject, it is that subject which lives, knows, has power, wills or speaks.

If He were to create speech in a tree or any other body, it would be that body which spoke those words, just as it would possess will, life or knowledge if He created these in it. Allah would not be the one speaking those words. Likewise, if He creates life, power, hearing or sight in a subject, it is that subject which lives, has power, hears or sees by virtue of those attributes.

He, glorified be He, cannot be characterized by the attributes He creates, whether they presuppose life or not. Thus, He is not the one moving by virtue of the movements He creates in something other than Himself, nor the one producing sound by virtue of the sounds He creates in something other than Himself. Nor are His hearing, sight and power the hearing, sight and power He creates in something other than Himself. Likewise, His speech is not the speech He creates in something other than Himself, nor does He speak by virtue of that speech.

Moreover, these terms derived from verbal nouns apply only to subjects in which the meanings denoted by those verbal nouns inhere. Thus, only a subject in which life inheres is called living; only one in which motion inheres is called moving; only one in which knowledge inheres is called knowing; and only one in which power inheres is called powerful. A subject in which the meaning denoted by the verbal noun does not inhere cannot be described by the corresponding active participle or similar descriptive forms. This is evident from examining all analogous cases. For the active participle and similar derived forms have a composite meaning, denoting both the subject and its attribute; a composite cannot be realized unless its constituent elements are realized.

Just as this holds for derived nouns, it also holds for verbs, such as “spoke,” “addressed,” “speaks,” “addresses,” “knew,” “knows,” “heard,” “hears,” “saw,” “sees,” and the like. Whether one holds that the verb is derived from the verbal noun or that the verbal noun is derived from the verb, everyone agrees that the subject of the verb is the agent of the action denoted by the verbal noun. Thus, when one says “addressed,” “knew,” “spoke,” or “learned,” the agents of addressing and teaching are the one who addresses and the one who teaches, respectively. The same applies to learning and speaking. The agent is the subject in which the meaning of the verbal noun—addressing, teaching, speaking, or learning—inheres. Thus, when one says, “So-and-so spoke,” or “So-and-so addressed another person,” it is that person who speaks and addresses.

“Those messengers—We favored some over others. Among them were those to whom Allah spoke, and He raised some in rank,”

and His words:

“When Moses came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him,”

entail that Allah Himself is the one who speaks. Just as it is impossible to say that He is a speaker by virtue of speech inhering in another, it is impossible to say that He spoke by means of speech inhering in another.

These, then, are five arguments:

First, the Jahmiyyah’s position necessarily entails that every instance of speech Allah creates is His speech. For, according to them, calling the Quran Allah’s speech means nothing more than that He created it; whoever produces speech, even in another, is, in their view, the one who speaks it. For them, speech denotes nothing inhering in the essence of the Lord Most High. If the meaning of “inhering” indicates His having created a sound in a subject—and a proof must apply consistently—then every sound He creates must likewise be His speech. They allow created sound to have any qualities whatsoever. Thus, on their account, no distinction remains between sound that is the speech of Allah Most High and sound that is not speech.

Second, when an attribute—such as knowledge, power, speech, or motion—inheres in a subject, its corresponding description applies to that subject, not to another.

Third, from it are derived the verbal noun, the active participle, and the assimilated adjective

and the like; such derivatives are not used to describe anything other than that subject. All this is clear and evident. It explains the statement of the early generations and the imams that whoever says Allah created speech in something other than Himself must concede that it is that subject, not Allah, that is described as speaking.

Fourth, Allah emphasized His speaking to Moses by using the verbal noun, saying: taklīman (“directly”). Several scholars have stated that emphasis through the verbal noun rules out a figurative meaning, lest it be supposed that He sent Moses a messenger or wrote him a letter. Rather, He Himself spoke directly to him.

Fifth, by speaking to Moses, Allah favored him over those to whom He did not speak. He said:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger,”

to the end of the verse. Thus, Allah spoke to Moses from behind the veil. He also said:

“O Moses, I have chosen you above the people through My messages and My speaking to you.”

And He said:

“Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him,”

up to His words:

“And Allah spoke to Moses directly.”

Revelation is what Allah sends down upon the hearts of the prophets without an intermediary. If His speaking to Moses were merely a sound He created in the air, the revelation received by the prophets would have been superior to it: those prophets understood the intended meaning without an intermediary, whereas Moses understood it only through an intermediary. For this reason, the extremist Jahmiyyah among the Ittihādiyyah and their like claim that the inspiration they receive is superior to what Moses son of ʿImrān received. This is one of the gravest forms of disbelief, by the consensus of the Muslims.

The early generations understood the true nature of these people’s doctrine and that it nullifies the prophetic mission, for the messengers were sent only to convey Allah’s speech. Indeed, it nullifies monotheism itself, for one who neither speaks nor possesses knowledge or life is like lifeless matter. Rather, one who possesses no attributes is sheer nonexistence, since an essence without attributes can only be conceived in the mind, not exist in external reality—just like conceiving an absolute existence that is neither individuated nor specified. Their position thus resembled that of the “eternalist philosophers,” who regard the Lord’s existence as an absolute existence, stipulated to be absolute, without any attributes. Yet it is known that what is absolute on condition of remaining absolute exists only in the mind.

These eternalists also deny that He truly spoke to Moses. They say that it was merely an emanation flowing upon him from the active intellect, and they say the same about revelation to all the prophets. Their position amounts to saying that the Quran is human speech, though it proceeded from a pure and noble soul.

Wakīʿ ibn al-Jarrāh said:

“Whoever claims that the Quran is created has claimed that something of Allah is created.”

He was asked, “On what basis do you say this?” He replied, “Because Allah says:

‘But the word from Me will come into effect.’

And nothing of Allah can be created.” A number of the early generations stated the same.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said, “Allah’s speech is from Allah and is not separate from Him.” This is the meaning of the statement of the early generations: “The Quran is Allah’s speech; from Him it originated, from Him it came forth, and to Him it will return.” Likewise, in the hadith reported by Ahmad and others from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, he said that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“You will never return to Allah with anything better than that which came forth from Him.”

He meant the Quran. It has also been reported from Abū Umāmah as a saying attributed to the Prophet.

When Abū Bakr al-Siddīq heard Musaylimah’s Quran, he said to the followers of Musaylimah the Liar, “Woe to you! Where have your minds gone? This is speech that has not come forth from a god”—that is, from a Lord.

When the early generations and the imams said, “From Him it came forth, and from Him it originated,” they did not mean that it separated from His essence and came to reside in another. For when a created being speaks, his speech does not leave him

translated_text:
and come to reside in another—so how could Allah’s speech do so? Allah Most High says:

“Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths; they speak nothing but a lie.”

He thus states that the word comes out of their mouths, yet it has not become separate from them. Moreover, an attribute does not become separate from that which it describes and come to reside in another, whether it is an attribute of the Creator or of a created being. When people hear the speech of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and then convey it from him, the speech they convey remains the speech of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, although they convey it through their own movements and voices. This applies all the more to the Quran: the speech is the Creator’s speech, while the voice is the reciter’s voice. Allah Most High says:

“If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection so that he may hear Allah’s speech.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Beautify the Quran with your voices.”

Rather, the early generations intended to refute these Jahmiyyah, who claimed that Allah created the Quran in something other than Himself. On their account, it would therefore have originated and come forth from the place in which it was created, not from Allah—just as they say that His speech to Moses came forth from the tree. The early generations and the imams therefore made clear that the Quran originated and came forth from Allah. They cited His words:

“But the word from Me will come into effect.”

He thus states that the word is from Him, not from any of His creatures. The preposition “min” (“from”) indicates the point of origin. If the noun governed by it denotes an entity subsisting in its own right, it is not

an attribute of Allah, as in His words:

“He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth—all from Him.”

And His words concerning the Messiah:

“And a spirit from Him.”

The same applies to what subsists in entities, as in His words:

“Whatever blessing you have is from Allah.”

But when the noun governed by this preposition denotes an attribute, and no locus is mentioned for it, it is an attribute of Allah, as in His words:

“But the word from Me will come into effect.”

Likewise, He has stated in several places in the Quran that the Quran was sent down from Him and that Gabriel brought it down from Him, refuting this innovator and fabricator and others like him who say that it did not come down from Him. Allah Most High says:

“Shall I seek a judge other than Allah, when it is He who has sent down to you the Book explained in detail? Those to whom We gave the Scripture know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth.”

The Holy Spirit is Gabriel, as He says in another verse:

“The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart.”

And He says:

“Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel—it is he who has brought it down upon your heart by Allah’s permission.”

Here He says:

“The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord.”

He thus makes clear that Gabriel brought it down from Allah, not from air, a tablet, or anything else. The same applies to the other verses of the Quran, such as His words:

“The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

And His words:

“Hā Mīm. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Knowing.”

And His words:

“Hā Mīm. A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.”

And His words:

“Alif Lām Mīm. The revelation of the Book, in which there is no doubt, is from the Lord of all worlds.”

And His words:

“O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord.”

Thus He has made clear in several places that it was sent down from Allah. Whoever says that it was sent down from some created thing, such as the Tablet or the air, fabricates lies against Allah, denies the Book of Allah, and follows a path other than that of the believers.

Do you not see that Allah distinguishes between what came down from Him and what He sent down from created things, such as rain, by saying:

“He sent down water from the sky”?

He mentions rain in several places and states that He sent it down from the sky, whereas He states that the Quran was sent down from Him. He also speaks of sending down without specifying its source, as in His words:

“And We sent down iron.”

This is because iron is brought down from the mountaintops; it does not descend from the sky. The same applies to animals, for the male discharges seminal fluid into the females. Thus, He did not say “from the sky” in this case.

If Gabriel had taken the Quran from the Preserved Tablet, the Jews would have been more honoured by Allah than the nation of Muhammad. For it is established through authentic transmission that Allah wrote the Torah for Moses with His own Hand and sent it down in written form. The Children of Israel would therefore have read the tablets that Allah had written, whereas the Muslims received the Quran from Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; Muhammad received it from Gabriel; and Gabriel received it from the Tablet. The Children of Israel would thus have occupied Gabriel’s position, and their rank would have been higher than that of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, according to the position of these Jahmiyyah.

Yet Allah, glorified be He, made it one of the distinctions of the nation of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, that He sent down to them a Book that water cannot wash away, and that He sent it down to them as recitation, not as writing. For this reason, He sent it down to them in portions. He said:

“And We have divided the Quran into parts so that you may recite it to the people at intervals, and We have sent it down progressively.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Those who disbelieve say, ‘Why was the Quran not sent down to him all at once?’ Thus We have sent it down to strengthen your heart with it, and We have recited it in a measured recitation.”

Moreover, if Gabriel did not hear it from Allah but merely found it written, its wording would be Gabriel’s, and the Quran would be Gabriel’s speech, rendered by him on Allah’s behalf—just as one interprets for a mute person who has written something but cannot utter it. This is contrary to the religion of the Muslims.

If someone appeals to His words:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, endowed with strength and held in honour with the Lord of the Throne,”

he should be told that Allah also says in another passage:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger. It is not the word of a poet—little do you believe! Nor is it the word of a soothsayer—little do you take heed!”

The messenger in the latter passage is Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, whereas the messenger in the former is Gabriel. If this meant that the messenger originated its wording, the two statements would contradict one another.

It is therefore clear that He attributed it to the messenger as its transmitter, not its originator. This is why He said:

“The word of a messenger,”

rather than “an angel” or “a prophet.” There is no doubt that the messenger conveyed it, as Allah Most High says:

“O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would present himself to people during the pilgrimage season and say: “Is there any man who will take me to his people so that I may convey the speech of my Lord? Quraysh have prevented me from conveying the speech of my Lord.”

When Allah sent down:

“Alif Lām Mīm. The Romans have been defeated,”

Abū Bakr al-Siddīq went out and recited it to the people. They asked, “Is this your speech or your companion’s speech?”

He replied, “It is neither my speech nor my companion’s speech; rather, it is the speech of Allah.”

If someone appeals to His words:

“No new reminder comes to them from their Lord,”

he should be told:

This verse is evidence against you, for when He says:

“No new reminder comes to them from their Lord,”

it is understood that some reminders are new and others are not. When an indefinite noun is qualified, the qualification distinguishes what possesses that attribute from what does not. This is like saying, “No Muslim man comes to me without my honouring him,” or “I eat only lawful food,” and similar expressions.

It is also clear that “new” in this verse does not mean “created,” as the Jahmī claims. Rather, it means newly revealed. Allah sent down the Quran portion by portion, so what was revealed first is old relative to what was revealed later. Everything that precedes something else is called “old” in Arabic, as He says:

“Like an old date stalk.”

And He says:

“By Allah, you are indeed in your old error.”

And He says:

“Since they have not been guided by it, they will say, ‘This is an old falsehood.’”

And He says:

“Have you considered what you have been worshipping—you and your forefathers of old?”

The same applies to His words:

“We have made it an Arabic Quran.”

He did not merely say, “We have made it,” which might be understood to mean, “We have created it.” Rather, He said:

“We have made it an Arabic Quran,”

meaning that He made it Arabic. He had the power to send it down in a non-Arabic language; when He sent it down in Arabic, He thereby made it Arabic rather than non-Arabic.

This matter is one of the foundational principles of the people of faith and the Sunnah, by which they distinguish themselves from the Jahmiyyah among the Mu'tazilah, the philosophers, and others like them. It is discussed at length elsewhere. And Allah knows best.

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about someone who said, “Allah did not truly speak to Moses.” Another person replied, “Rather, He did truly speak to him.” The first then said, “If you say that He spoke to him, speech can only consist of letters and sound, and letters and sound are brought into being. Whoever says that Allah spoke to Moses with letters and sound is an unbeliever.” Is the matter as he says, or not?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah.

As for someone who says that Allah did not truly speak to Moses, if he has not heard the Quran, he is to be informed that this is explicitly stated in the Quran. If he denies it after that, he is to be asked to repent; if he repents, so be it, otherwise he is to be put to death. His statement is not accepted if it follows his denial of the explicit text of the Quran. Indeed, even if he were to say, “What I mean is that He created a sound in the air and caused Moses to hear it,” his statement would still constitute disbelief. This is the position of the Jahmiyyah, whom the early generations declared unbelievers, saying, “They are to be asked to repent; if they repent, so be it, otherwise they are to be put to death.”

However, someone who believes in Allah and His Messenger in general, but has not received the knowledge that would make the truth clear to him, is not to be judged an unbeliever until the proof has been established against him, opposition to which constitutes disbelief. For many people

As for the leaders who were instructed to put such people to death—those who deny that Allah will be seen in the Hereafter and say that the Quran is created, and the like—it has been said that they were instructed to execute them because of their disbelief. It has also been said that this was because, if they called people to their innovation, they would lead them astray; thus they were put to death for spreading corruption in the land and to safeguard people’s religion against their misguidance. In short, the early generations of this community and its leading scholars agreed that the Jahmiyyah are among the worst groups of religious innovators, to the extent that many excluded them from the seventy-two sects.

Among the Jahmiyyah are the adherents of philosophy and the Muʿtazilah, who say that Allah’s speech is created; that Allah spoke to Moses only through created speech which He created in the air; that He will not be seen in the Hereafter; and that He is not separate from His creation. It is well known that someone who denies what the Book and Sunnah expressly state is more deserving of being judged an unbeliever than someone who affirms what the Book and Sunnah teach. If someone who denies the explicit texts of the Book and Sunnah claims that reason supports him, the one who adheres to those texts replies: ‘Rather, reason supports me and agrees with the Book and Sunnah.’ The latter thus claims the support of both revelation and reason, whereas the former supports his position only with what he claims to be rational evidence, whose unsoundness his opponent demonstrates.

Even supposing that reason were on his side, ‘disbelief’ is a judgment determined by Islamic law. Not everyone who contradicts something established through rational inquiry is an unbeliever. Even if someone were to deny some self-evident rational truths, he would not be judged an unbeliever unless his statement constituted disbelief according to Islamic law. As for someone who contradicts what is known to have been brought by the Messenger, he is an unbeliever without dispute.

Neither the Book and Sunnah nor the statements of any of this community’s early generations and leading scholars describe Allah as spatially located or as not spatially located. Nor do the Book and Sunnah state that whoever makes either assertion becomes an unbeliever. This is an innovated expression, and disbelief is not determined merely by innovated terms that have no basis in the Book and Sunnah. Likewise, when he says, ‘He is not spatially located,’ if he means that creation does not contain the Creator, he is correct. But if he says that the Creator is not distinct or separate from creation, he is mistaken.

Once this is understood, those who respond to his untenable argument—namely, ‘If I were to say that He spoke to him, speech can only consist of letters and sounds, and letters and sounds are temporally originated’—fall into three groups. One group rejects his first premise; another rejects his second premise; and a third rejects neither premise, but asks him to clarify his meaning and explains that this does not preclude Allah’s having truly spoken to Moses.

The first group comprises Abū Muhammad Abd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb, Abū al-Hasan ‘Alī ibn Ismā‘īl al-Ash‘arī, and their followers. They said: ‘We do not concede that speech can only consist of letters and sounds. Rather, speech is a meaning subsisting in the speaker’s essence, and letters and sounds express it.’ That meaning subsisting in Allah’s essence encompasses the command to do everything He has commanded and the information concerning everything He has communicated. If expressed in Syriac, it is the Gospel. They said that the term ‘speech’ applies to it literally. Thus, the term ‘speech’ would either have distinct literal senses, or be figurative when applied to the Creator’s speech and literal when applied to a creature’s speech.

They conceded that speech can only consist of letters and sounds, but rejected the second premise: that letters and sounds can only be temporally originated.

One group said that what is brought into being is the same as what is temporally originated, whether it subsists independently or in something else, and that He speaks with speech that is not eternal and consists of letters and sounds. These people said concerning letters and sounds much the same as their predecessors said concerning meanings.

They said: “Speech without letters or sounds is inconceivable, and a single meaning that constitutes a command, a prohibition, and a statement is impossible according to sound reason. Excluding letters from what the term ‘speech’ denotes is self-evidently erroneous in every language. If it is permissible to say that letters and sounds created in something else are literally Allah’s speech, then it would be possible for Him to have spoken to Moses with speech created in something other than Himself.”

" صِنْفَانِ "

translated_text:
and that He has created an explanatory expression … (1), then if you say that this expression is literally His speech, your argument against the Muʿtazilah collapses. For your strongest argument against them is your assertion that He cannot speak with speech that He creates in something other than Himself, just as He cannot know through knowledge subsisting in another, exercise power through power subsisting in another, or will through a will subsisting in another. If, however, you say that it is speech figuratively, it follows that ‘speech’ applies literally to meaning but figuratively to wording. The falsity of this is self-evident in every language.”

As for “the third group,” they did not reject either premise, but asked their opponents to clarify what they meant and explained that this does not establish the truth of their position. Rather, they said: “If you say that letters and sounds are temporally originated, meaning that they must be created by Him and separate from Him, this demonstrates the falsity and inconsistency of your position; this assertion is not conceded. If you mean that they are not eternal, that is conceded, but this terminology is newly introduced.”

These fall into “two groups.” One group said: “What is temporally originated is what is created and separate from Him. Thus, when we say that letters and sounds can only be temporally originated, this is equivalent to saying that they can only be created. In that case, this Muʿtazilite would have refuted his own position

by his own statement: he claimed that He speaks with created letters and sounds, then argued for this on grounds implying that He speaks, but not with created speech. This involves obfuscation. We do not say that He spoke to Moses with eternal speech or with created speech. Rather, glorified is He, He speaks when He wills and remains silent when He wills, just as He, glorified and exalted, created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne; turned to the heaven while it was smoke; and comes in canopies of clouds, together with the angels. As He said:

‘And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank.’

And He said:

‘Are they waiting for anything but that the angels should come to them, or your Lord should come, or some of your Lord’s signs should come?’

And He, exalted is He, said:

‘His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, “Be,” and it is.’

And He, exalted is He, said:

‘And say, “Do deeds; Allah will see your deeds, as will His Messenger and the believers.”’

There are many similar passages in the Quran and hadith. Allah, glorified is He, makes clear that, when He wills, He does what He has described concerning His speaking and His acts that subsist in Him. What subsists in Him is His speech, not the speech of another. Nothing created subsists in the Creator, nor is the Lord a locus for created things. Rather, whatever He wills of His words and acts subsists in Him, glorified is He, and none of this is created. Only that which is separate from Him is created.

Allah’s speech is from Allah; it is not separate from Him. Hence the early generations said:

‘The Quran is the speech of Allah, uncreated; from Him it originated

translated_text:
and to Him it will return.’ They explained that ‘from Him it originated’ means that He is the One who spoke it, not that He created it in some created bodies. This ‘answer’ is that of the leading scholars of hadith, Sufism, and jurisprudence, as well as leading figures among certain groups of speculative theologians, including the Hishāmiyya, the Karrāmiyya, and others.

Among the followers of the four imams—Abū Hanīfa, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad—some choose the answer of the first category. These accept Ibn Kullāb’s position on the Quran and include groups of later followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and Abū Hanīfa. Others choose the answer of the second category. These reject Ibn Kullāb’s position and say that the Quran is eternal; they include the Sālimiyya and groups among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and Abū Hanīfa.

Still others choose the answer of the third group. These reject the positions of the two preceding groups, the Kullābiyya and the Sālimiyya. Among these, some adopt the position of the Karrāmiyya—who affiliate themselves with Abū Hanīfa—while others also reject the Karrāmiyya’s position because it contains a further contradiction. Rather, they adopt the position of the leading hadith scholars, such as al-Bukhārī, ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd al-Dārimī, and Muhammad ibn Ishāq ibn Khuzayma, and their predecessors among the early generations:

translated_text:
such as Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn al-Hārith ibn Hishām, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī, al-Zuhrī, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, as well as what has been transmitted on this matter from the Companions and the Successors. There are many well-known reports concerning this in the collections of Sunnah and early traditions, too numerous to include in this brief account.

The disputes and subtle distinctions among these three categories are likewise beyond the scope of this brief account. We have discussed them at length elsewhere, explaining the true nature of each position and identifying the correct position in light of clear rational evidence and authentic transmitted reports. Yet all these groups agree that those who say that Allah’s speech is created are misguided.

The Muslim community agrees that anyone who says that Allah’s speech is created and that He did not truly speak to Moses must be called upon to repent. If he repents, well and good; otherwise, he is to be put to death.

All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds. May Allah bestow blessings and abundant peace upon our master Muhammad and his family.

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked about someone who said:

“Allah spoke directly to Moses. Moses heard His speech with his own ears and comprehended it in his heart. Allah wrote the Torah with His own hand and handed it to Moses, from His hand to his.”

Another person said: “He spoke to him only through an intermediary.”

He answered:

The person who said that Allah spoke directly to Moses—as He has stated in His Book—is correct. As for the person who said that Allah spoke to Moses through an intermediary, he is misguided and mistaken. Indeed, the imams have explicitly stated that anyone who says this must be called upon to repent. If he repents, well and good; otherwise, he is to be put to death. This statement denies what is necessarily known in the religion of Islam and what is established by the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus.

Allah Most High says:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation or from behind a veil,”

and the verse continues. He thus distinguishes between His speaking from behind a veil—as He spoke to Moses—and His speaking through the intermediary of a messenger, as He revealed to prophets other than Moses. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him,”

up to His words:

“And Allah spoke directly to Moses.”

translated_text:
There are many hadiths to this effect in the two Sahīh collections and the Sunan collections. Among the reliably transmitted reports from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is the following:

“Adam and Moses met. Adam said: ‘You are Moses, to whom Allah spoke directly, without placing between you and Himself any messenger from His creation.’”

The early generations of the Muslim community and its imams declared the Jahmiyyah disbelievers for saying that Allah created speech in certain physical bodies, which Moses then heard, and interpreting His speaking to Moses in this way.

As for his statement, “Allah wrote the Torah with His own hand,” this has been narrated in the two Sahīh collections. Whoever denies it is mistaken and misguided. If he denies it after learning of the authentic hadith, he deserves punishment.

As for his statement, “He handed it from His hand to his,” this is reported from a number of the Successors, and this is also how it is related among the People of the Book. However, I know of no wording other than this transmitted from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Thus, if the person using this expression intends something contrary to that, he is mistaken. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
What do the honoured and eminent scholars, the imams of the religion—may Allah be pleased with them all—say concerning the following:

Is this Quran that we recite, which subsists in us during recitation, the speech of Allah that subsisted in Him when He spoke it and was an attribute of His, or not? If it is His speech, then when we recite it and it subsists in us, is it to be called Allah’s speech and His attribute, or Allah’s speech but not His attribute? Or are there distinctions here that must be explained?

When it subsists in us, has it transferred from Allah after having subsisted in Him? Or does it subsist in both us and Him at the same time? Or is what subsists in us an expression of Allah’s speech or a representation of it, such that calling it Allah’s speech is figurative? Is it a newly originated attribute of ours, subsisting in a newly originated being, since the eternal cannot subsist in a newly originated being, and what is newly originated cannot be eternal? And is “recitation” identical to what is recited, or not? Give us your ruling; may you be rewarded.

translated_text:
this question rests upon a “preliminary point”: one must understand what it means when someone says of words conveyed to him from another person, “These are that person’s words.”

When a hadith narrator relates from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—his saying:

“Actions are judged only by intentions, and each person will have only what he intended,”

or his saying:

“The lawful is clear, and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters of which many people have no knowledge,”

or his saying:

“Whoever performs an act that does not conform to our command will have it rejected,”

or other such sayings, it is well known that these are the words of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He spoke them, both their wording and their meaning: he communicated their meaning, arranged their letters, and uttered them in his own voice. The person conveying them from him then conveyed his words, as the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“May Allah grant radiance to a person who hears a hadith from us and conveys it just as he heard it. For a bearer of knowledge may lack understanding, and a bearer of knowledge may convey it to someone with greater understanding than himself.”

He thus prayed for radiance for anyone who heard a hadith from him and conveyed it just as he heard it. He thereby made clear that the hadith heard from him is the very hadith conveyed from him, although it is known that the transmitter conveys it through his own actions and voice, and that the voice heard from the transmitter is his own, not the voice of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Although the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—spoke that hadith in his own distinctive voice, what is conveyed from him is the hadith heard from him, whereas the voice that is heard is not his voice.

Thus, if someone asks:

“Is this hadith which the narrator has read out, and which subsists in him

during the reading, the speech of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—which subsisted in him when he spoke it and was an attribute of his, or not?”

He should be told:

“If you mean that the hadith itself, considered as such, is the speech of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—which subsisted in him when he spoke it and was an attribute of his, then yes: this hadith, considered as such, is the speech of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. But if you mean that the movements and vocal sounds particular to the reader are what subsisted in the Messenger, that is not so. Likewise, if you mean that the very movements, vocal sounds, and attributes that subsisted in the Messenger himself passed from him and came to subsist in the reader, that is not so.”

Statements such as “This is that,” “It is not that,” “This is the very same as that,” and “It is not the very same as that” are ambiguous. Someone who transmits another person’s words just as he heard them and writes them in a book may say: “These are the very words of so-and-so; these are his words themselves; these are his selfsame words.” He means that the very words that person spoke are what he has conveyed from him and what is written in the book, without any addition or omission.

Thus, if someone says of what he hears from the reciter, “This is the very speech of Allah,” or “This is Allah’s selfsame speech,” or “This is Allah’s speech itself,” or says of what lies between the two covers of the Quran, “This is Allah’s selfsame speech; this is the very speech of Allah,” he is speaking truthfully.

 لَكِنْ لَمَّا كَانَ النَّاسُ فِي زَمَانِنَا يَعْلَمُونَ أَنَّ أَحَدًا لَا يَسْمَعُ كَلَامَ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مِنْهُ:
 لَمْ يَسْبِقْ هَذَا الْمَعْنَى إلَى ذِهْنِ أَحَدٍ بَلْ كُلُّ أَحَدٍ يَعْلَمُ أَنَّا إذَا قُلْنَا سَمِعْنَا كَلَامَ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَهَذَا كَلَامُ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِعَيْنِهِ وَهَذَا عَيْنُ كَلَامِهِ فَإِنَّمَا الْمُرَادُ
translated_text:
and anyone who denies this in this sense necessarily implies that additions and omissions have been made to the Quran. Thus, people have unanimously agreed that what lies between the two covers is Allah’s speech, and have condemned those who deny this.

Of a speaker’s words heard directly from him, one may also say, “This is Zayd’s selfsame speech,” “This is the very speech of Zayd,” or “This is Zayd’s speech itself,” meaning that it is heard from him without an intermediary, so that one hears the attribute peculiar to that speaker. As Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī said: “Al-Hasan would utter words that came out like pearls. Then others uttered those same words after him, and they came out like dung.”

A human speaker has a voice and tone peculiar to him, just as he has his own distinctive disposition. As Allah Most High says:

“and the diversity of your languages and your colors”

If his speech is a command, a prohibition, or a statement, he also has a state, quality, and manner peculiar to him. Thus, if his speech is heard with the attribute peculiar to him, and someone says, “This is his selfsame speech,” “This is his very speech,” or “This is his speech itself,” including that distinctive attribute in what is meant by “selfsame” and “itself,” this would not be true of his speech when transmitted by someone else.

Yet, since people in our time know that no one hears the speech of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—directly from him, this meaning does not occur to anyone. Rather, everyone knows that when we say, “We have heard the speech of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace,” “This is the selfsame speech of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace,” or “This is his very speech,” the sole intended meaning is

the first meaning: that it is heard from someone conveying it on his behalf, not that it is heard directly from him, nor that his own act of speaking those words has occurred. If this is so with the speech of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—then it applies all the more to the speech of Allah, glorified be He. People know that none of them has heard it from Allah as Moses heard Allah’s speech from Him. Rather, they know that Allah’s speech has been heard only from those who convey it, as Allah Most High says:

“O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord. If you do not, then you have not conveyed His message.”

And Allah Most High says:

“So that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord.”

And Noah said:

“But I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds.”

“I convey to you the messages of my Lord.”

In Sunan Abī Dāwūd, Jābir relates that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—used to say at the gathering:

“Will no man take me to his people so that I may convey the speech of my Lord? Quraysh have prevented me from conveying the speech of my Lord.”

Since this understanding was firmly established in the listeners’ hearts, they knew that Allah Most High’s words,

“And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of Allah,”

refer only to hearing it from those who convey it, not to hearing it directly from Him. Such hearing is not like Moses hearing Allah’s speech from Allah, for Moses heard it from Him without an intermediary. When we hear the speech of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—from the Companions, our hearing is not like that of the Companions

translated_text:
who heard it from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—even though they convey his words just as they heard them. It is understood that they did not reproduce the Prophet’s voice—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Their voices are neither his voice nor like his voice, although they conveyed his words just as they heard them. Thus, it is all the more appropriate to say of the Quran that Gabriel conveyed it just as he heard it, that the Messenger conveyed it just as he heard it, and that the community conveyed it just as it heard it; that what it conveyed is what it heard; and that it is the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic, in both cases.

This is so even though the Messenger is a human being like other human beings, whereas Allah Most High says:

“There is nothing like Him.”

The difference between the attributes of the Creator and those of created beings is greater than the difference between the lowest and highest created beings. If the Successors’ hearing the Prophet’s speech—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—from the Companions is not like the Companions’ hearing it from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—then hearing Allah’s speech from Allah is still further removed from resembling any instance of one created being hearing another.

When someone says of what he hears from a person conveying the Messenger’s words, “This is the Messenger’s speech,” or “These words are correct,” or “true,” or “sound,” or “This is the hadith of Allah’s Messenger, conveyed just as he heard it,” or “This is the very speech of the Messenger,” or “his exact words,” he means only the speech itself: that which is present when it is heard from either the transmitter or the one whose words he transmits. He is not referring to anything peculiar to either of them. He is thus referring neither to the transmitter’s voice alone, nor to the voice of the one whose words he transmits alone, nor to the movement of either of them. Rather, there is something that is the same in both cases

and another that differs, each of them having what is peculiar to him. Thus, when someone says, “This is his speech,” he is referring to what is identical and common to both. When he says, “This is his voice,” he is referring to what is distinct and peculiar to each. Hence one may say, “This is a deep voice,” or “a thin voice,” or “a beautiful voice,” or “one that is not beautiful.” This is illustrated by the hadith in Sunan Ibn Mājah, in which the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Allah listens more attentively to a man reciting the Quran with a beautiful voice than the owner of a singing slave woman listens to her.”

And in the well-known hadith:

“Beautify the Quran with your voices.”

Ahmad said, “He should beautify it with his voice as much as he can.” Imam Ahmad thus made clear that the voice belongs to the reciter, while the speech belongs to the Creator. Just as this is understood when conveying the speech of Allah and His Messenger, so it is when conveying anyone’s speech. When people hear someone reciting:

“Indeed, everything apart from Allah is vain,”

they say, “This is Labīd’s poetry, in both wording and meaning,” and “This is Labīd’s speech.” As the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“The truest words ever spoken by a poet are Labīd’s words: ‘Indeed, everything apart from Allah is vain.’”

If the reciter were to say, “This is my poetry,” or “my speech,” people would call him a liar, just as they would if he said, “This is Labīd’s voice.” But if he said, “This is Labīd’s wording,” in the familiar sense—that these spoken words are Labīd’s speech, with its arrangement and composition—they would affirm that he spoke the truth.

translated_text:
But if he says, “This is his utterance,” meaning that it is being uttered by him, people would call him a liar. For “utterance” may denote either the act of uttering or the words uttered. Likewise, “recitation” and “reading” may denote either the act itself or the actual speech being read and recited.

The basis of this is to understand what hearing speech from its speaker has in common with hearing it from someone conveying it on the speaker’s behalf, and what distinguishes the two. In both cases, it is the original speaker’s speech. In one case, however, it is heard from him in an unqualified sense, without an intermediary; in the other, it is heard from him in a qualified sense, through the intermediary who conveys it. Similarly, sometimes you see the sun, moon, and stars directly, without needing an intermediary, and sometimes you see them in water, a mirror, or the like, through that transparent body. In both instances, they are what you intend to see. In one case, however, you see them themselves directly, in an unqualified sense; in the other, you see them in a qualified sense, through an intermediary.

If you say of what someone conveys from another person, “This is a hikāyah (reproduction) of that person’s speech,” such unqualified language is mistaken. For the term hikāyah, when used without qualification, means that someone has produced speech resembling the other person’s speech, as when one says, “This imitates that,” or, “This has imitated that.” Yet one may say, “So-and-so has related these words from so-and-so,” just as one says that he narrated, conveyed, transmitted, or reported them from him. Hence the wording found in hadith: “From the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in what he narrates from his Lord.” Thus, whatever the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, conveyed from Allah, he related and narrated from Him.

If someone says of a reciter, “He is reproducing Allah’s speech,” or, “He is reproducing the Quran,” this may be understood to mean that he produces speech that imitates Allah’s speech, and this is disbelief. If, however, he means that the reciter conveys and recites it, the meaning is correct. Nevertheless, he should express this in words that do not suggest a false meaning, saying instead, “He reads it, recites it, conveys it, and delivers it.”

For this reason, there is no objection to saying, “He relates the seven Quranic readings, narrates them, and transmits them,” because this is understood only to mean that he conveys them, not that he produces their like.

Section

With this established, we say: This Quran, which we recite, convey, and hear, is the speech of Allah, which He spoke and which the Holy Spirit brought down from Him. As Allah Most High says:

“When you recite the Quran, seek refuge in Allah from Satan, the accursed.”

“He has no authority over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord.”

“His authority extends only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate partners with Allah.”

“When We replace one verse with another—and Allah knows best what He sends down—they say, ‘You are nothing but a fabricator.’ But most of them do not know.”

“Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth, to strengthen those who believe, and as guidance and good tidings for the Muslims.”

“We certainly know that they say, ‘It is only a human being who teaches him.’ The tongue of the person they point to is foreign, whereas this is clear Arabic speech.”

This passage concerns the Quran, of which they said, “It is only a human being who teaches it to him.” Allah refuted this by saying:

“The tongue of the person they point to is foreign, whereas this is clear Arabic speech.”

This shows that what is meant is the Arabic Quran itself, which could not have been taught to him by the non-Arabic speaker they pointed to. It has been said that this was a man in Mecca who was a client of Ibn al-Hadramī. Abstract meanings, however, can be learned from a non-Arabic speaker, unlike this Arabic Quran. This therefore shows that this Quran was brought down by the Holy Spirit from Allah, Blessed and Most High.

translated_text:
Likewise, Allah Most High says in another verse:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth.”

This speech is an attribute of Allah Most High. As for what subsists exclusively in us—our movements, voices, understanding, and other attributes—none of it subsists in Allah’s Essence, glorified is He. Likewise, whatever subsists exclusively in the Lord Most High does not pass from Him or subsist in anyone else, nor does anything like it.

When one created being hears another’s speech and conveys it on his behalf, what he conveys is the latter’s speech, as in the previously cited saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“May Allah make radiant the face of one who hears a hadith from us and conveys it as he heard it.”

Yet what subsisted in the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—inwardly, his knowledge, will, and so forth, and outwardly, his movements, voice, and so forth—did not pass from him or subsist in anyone else. Indeed, none of the attributes of created beings leaves their beings and passes from them. How, then, can it be said that an attribute of the Creator has left His Essence and passed from Him?

When a student acquires his teacher’s knowledge and transmits it from him, that knowledge does not leave the first person’s being and pass into the second. Rather, the same reality of knowledge comes to be present in him as in his teacher—or it is not identical to it, but resembles it. This is why knowledge is likened to the light of a lamp: everyone draws light from it, yet it remains undiminished. It is well known that when someone lights his lamp from another’s, no part of the substance of that flame, nor any of the attributes subsisting in it, passes into his lamp. Rather, through contact with the flame, Allah makes it a flame like the first.

original_footnote:
قال الشيخ ناصر بن حمد الفهد (ص ١١٠):
وقوله هنا (إن أريد بذلك أن الشعر من حيث هو هو إن أريد أن نفس ما قام بذاته فارق ذاته وانتقل إلينا، فليس كذلك) فيه سقط ظاهر، فإن قوله (إن أريد بذلك. . .) جملة شرطية لا جواب لها.
وقد ذكر الشيخ قبل هذه الصفحة بصفحات قلائل ما يشبه هذه الجمل الشرطية، فقال (١٢/ ٥٣٥، ٥٣٦) (فإذا قال القائل: هل هذا الحديث الذي قرأه المحدث القائم به حين القراءة هو كلام النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، الذي قام به حين تكلم به وكان صفة له أم لا؟ قيل له: إن كنت تريد: أن نفس الحديث من حيث هو هو كلام النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، الذي قام به حين تكلم به كان صفة له، فنعم. هذا الحديث من حيث هو هو كلام النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، وإن كنت تريد: أن ما اختص بالقارئ من حركاته وأصواته هو القائم بالرسول، فليس كذلك).
فمن هذا النص يكون صواب العبارة السابقة والله أعلم:
(إن أريد بذلك أن الشعر من حيث هو هو [شعر لبيد الذي قام به حين تكلم به كان صفة له فنعم، و] إن أريد أن نفس ما قام بذاته فارق ذاته وانتقل إلينا، فليس كذلك. .).
translated_text:
Thus, the reality of fire is present, even though this particular flame is not that one. Yet fire and knowledge are not like speech conveyed on another’s behalf. Rather, their case resembles that of someone who hears another’s speech or poetry and then produces something of the same kind, saying something similar to what the other person said. As the saying goes:

“One thought may coincide with another, just as one hoofprint may fall upon another.”

This has nothing to do with conveying or transmitting another’s words.

(For the words someone utters:

“Indeed, everything apart from Allah is vain,”

are Labīd’s words, however people recite or write them. The poetry someone recites here is Labīd’s very own poetry.

If it is said, “The poetry that subsists in us is the same as that which subsisted in Labīd,” the reply is: “If what is meant by this is that the poetry, considered in itself… If what is meant is that the very thing that subsisted in his being left his being and passed into us, that is not so. Likewise, if what is meant is that the very attribute peculiar to that person, such as his movement and voice, is identical to the attribute peculiar to us, such as our movement and voice, that is not so.”) (*).

Your statement, “This is the same as that,” is therefore an expression whose ambiguity is clarified by its context. If you say, “This speech is the same as that,” or “This poetry is the same as that,” you are speaking truthfully. But if you say, “This voice is the same as that,” the statement is false.

When people say, “This is Labīd’s poetry,” they mean only what is common to both
translated_footnote:
Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd said (p. 110):
His statement here, “If what is meant by this is that poetry, considered in itself, if what is meant is that the very thing that subsisted in his being departed from his being and passed into us, that is not so,” contains an obvious omission, since “If what is meant by this…” is a conditional clause without a consequent.

A few pages earlier, the Shaykh used similar conditional clauses, saying (12:535–536): “If someone asks, ‘Is this hadith, which the hadith scholar has recited and which subsists in him during the recitation, the speech of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, which subsisted in him when he uttered it and was an attribute of his, or not?’ he is told: ‘If you mean that the hadith, considered in itself, is the speech of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, which subsisted in him when he uttered it and was an attribute of his, then yes. This hadith, considered in itself, is the speech of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. But if you mean that what is peculiar to the reciter—his movements and sounds—is what subsisted in the Messenger, that is not so.’”

On the basis of this passage, the correct wording of the earlier statement would be—and Allah knows best:

“If what is meant by this is that poetry, considered in itself, [is Labīd’s poetry, which subsisted in him when he uttered it and was an attribute of his, then yes; and] if what is meant is that the very thing that subsisted in his being departed from his being and passed into us, that is not so…”

translated_text:
—namely, the reality considered in itself, disregarding what is peculiar to either.

If it is said, “What is common to both is an unrestricted universal, and universals exist only in minds, not in concrete entities,” the reply is:

“Raising this point here is mistaken. It would apply only if a man had uttered Labīd’s poetry without knowing his poetry. We would then say: these are two things that share a universal kind, each distinguished from the other by what is peculiar to it. A universal exists as a universal only in the mind, not in the external world.

“Here, however, Labīd’s poetry itself had an existence in the external world. What is meant by the reality of the speech—disregarding Zayd’s voice and ʿAmr’s voice—existed when Labīd uttered it and exists when someone other than Labīd recites it. That same reality exists in both instances. This is not like the existence of humanity in Zayd, ʿAmr and Khālid: Zayd’s humanity is not ʿAmr’s humanity, but is like it, and what they have in common does not exist in the external world.

“Here, the person reciting Labīd’s words utters the very speech that Labīd uttered. We do not say that he composed something like it, or that he recited something like it. Rather, we say that he recited Labīd’s very own poetry. Poetry, however, is an accident, and an accident can subsist only in something else. It must therefore subsist either in Labīd or in someone else. Even if what subsists in him is not like what subsists in someone else, what is intended by both is one and the same. Thus, likeness and difference pertain to the means, while identity pertains to the intended reality. That reality is Labīd’s composition, not anyone else’s. And rational people

translated_text:
know that the sound heard from Labīd is not the same sound heard from the reciter. Yet what the sound is intended to convey is the speech itself, for sound is a means of conveying it. Thus, whatever merits praise or blame in the voice belongs to the person conveying the speech, while whatever merits praise or blame in the speech—in its wording, composition and meaning—belongs to the speaker whose words are being conveyed.

Once this is understood, someone may ask: “Is this Quran which we recite, and which subsists in us during recitation, the speech of Allah that subsisted in Him when He spoke it and was an attribute of His, or not?”

He should be told:

“As for the speech, it is Allah’s speech, not ours or anyone else’s. It is heard from the person conveying it, not from Allah—as explained earlier. It is heard through an intermediary, constituting hearing in a qualified sense, not unqualified hearing from Allah—as explained earlier. Nothing that subsists in His Essence has departed from Him and passed to us, nor does anything peculiar to our own beings—such as our movements and voices, which proceed from us—subsist in Him.”

As for his question, “Is this Quran which we recite, and which subsists in us during recitation, the speech of Allah that subsisted in Him when He spoke it?”, the term “subsisting” is ambiguous here. If he means that the Lord’s own attribute becomes an attribute of someone else, or that the servant’s attribute becomes an attribute of the Lord, that is not so. If he means that what is uncreated has itself become created, or that what is created has become uncreated, that is not so. If he means that someone else shares with the Lord that which subsists exclusively in Him, that is not so. And if

translated_text:
he means that the speech itself is His speech, not anyone else’s, in both cases—as established earlier—then that is so. It is known that hearing it from Allah is not the same as hearing it from His creation. This distinguishes the two situations, even though the speech is one and the same. If this distinction holds for a created being’s speech, whether heard directly from him or conveyed on his behalf, it holds all the more for Allah’s speech. Nothing is like Allah in His Essence, His attributes or His acts. As for his words:

“Or is that which subsists in us an expression of Allah’s speech or a hikāya (reproduction or narration) of it, so that calling it Allah’s speech is figurative?”

The answer is:

Giving expression to hidden speech refers to the case where someone has a meaning within himself which another person then expresses, just as someone who understands the intent of a person unable to speak expresses what is within him. Those who said, “The Quran is an expression of Allah’s speech,” intended this meaning. This is false. Rather, Allah spoke the Arabic Quran, and Gabriel conveyed it from Him.

As for “hikāya,” it can mean something that resembles another thing, as when one says, “This person imitates so-and-so,” if he produces words or deeds like his. This is impossible in the case of the Quran, for Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce its like’”—to the end of the verse.

The term may also be used to say that someone related another person’s words, meaning that he conveyed and transmitted them from him. Thus, hadith reports contain the wording, “The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, relating from his Lord…” It is also said, “The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, narrated from his Lord and related from his Lord.”

Therefore, if it is said that he related from Allah, meaning that he conveyed from Allah, this is correct.

As for the question:

“Is calling it Allah’s speech figurative?”

The answer is:

The hallmark of figurative usage is that it can truthfully be denied. Yet we know beyond doubt that if someone were to say in the Messenger’s presence, “This is not Allah’s speech,” he would not, in the Messenger’s judgment, be speaking in accordance with the literal linguistic meaning.

Furthermore, this applies to everyone who conveys another’s words: they are called the words of the one from whom they are conveyed, not the words of the one conveying them. And Allah knows best.

What do the esteemed imams of the religion say concerning two men, one of whom said, “The Quran that is heard is Allah’s speech,” while the other said, “It is Gabriel’s speech, as Allah Most High says: ‘Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger’”?
