Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah sanctify his soul—answered:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. Rather, the Quran is the speech of Allah Most High, not the speech of Gabriel or of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is agreed upon by the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, and the imams of the Muslims and their followers whose opinions form the basis of fatwas in Islam, such as Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others.

Gabriel heard it from Allah, and Muhammad heard it from Gabriel, as Allah Most High says:

“Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth.”

The Holy Spirit is Gabriel. Allah Most High also says:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth.”

And He Most High says:

“The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

And He Most High says:

“Hā Mīm. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Knowing.”

Thus, it is sent down from Allah, as He says:

Most High:

“The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart, so that you may be one of the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue.”

As for His words, “Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger,” He attributed it to the messenger because he conveyed and delivered it, not because he produced or originated any of it. For He, glorified be He, says in one of the two passages:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger. It is not the word of a poet—little do you believe! Nor is it the word of a soothsayer—little do you take heed! It is a revelation from the Lord of all worlds.”

The messenger here is Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. In the other passage, He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, endowed with power and held in high esteem by the Lord of the Throne, obeyed there and trustworthy.”

The messenger here is Gabriel. Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind. If its attribution to either of them meant that he had composed its Arabic wording or otherwise originated any part of it, these statements would contradict one another. For if one of them had composed it, the other would not have composed it.

Moreover, He said, “the word of a messenger”; He did not say “the word of an angel” or “of a prophet.” The term “messenger” indicates that he conveys it from the One who sent him, not that he originated any of it himself.

Furthermore, in His words, “Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger,” the pronoun refers to the Quran.

and the Quran encompasses both its meanings and its wording. Taken together, these are not the speech of anyone other than Allah, by the unanimous agreement of the Muslims. To state without qualification that the Quran is the speech of Gabriel, Muhammad, or any other created being is disbelief; none of the leading scholars of the Muslims has said this.

Indeed, Allah sternly condemned anyone who says that it is the word of a mortal. He, Most High, said:

“Leave Me with the one I created alone,”

up to His words:

“He thought and deliberated.
May he be destroyed—how he deliberated!
Again, may he be destroyed—how he deliberated!
Then he looked,
then he frowned and scowled,
then he turned away and was arrogant,
and said, ‘This is nothing but magic handed down;
this is nothing but the word of a mortal.’
I will cast him into Saqar.
And what will make you know what Saqar is?”

Whoever says that the Quran is the word of a mortal has disbelieved, as has anyone who says that it is the word of an angel.

Only one of two kinds of men says that it is Gabriel’s word: either a man from among the heretics and philosophers who say that it is an emanation flowing into the Prophet’s soul from the Active Intellect, which they identify as Gabriel. They also say that Gabriel is the imagined form that takes shape within the soul of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They say that he received it as abstract meanings, which then took the form of letters within his soul, just as forms arise within the soul of a sleeper. This is what Ibn ʿArabī, the author of al-Fusūs, and other heretics say.

For this reason, he claims that he draws from the same source from which the angel who conveys it as revelation to the Messenger draws. For, according to him, the “source” is the intellect, and the “angel” is the imagined form within his soul. In their view, the Prophet receives from this imagined form.

 الَّتِي هِيَ الْمَصْدَرُ غَيْرَ الْمَقْرُوءِ كَمَا يُجْعَلُ التَّكَلُّمُ الَّذِي هُوَ فِعْلُهُ غَيْرَ الْكَلَامِ الَّذِي هُوَ يَقُولُهُ وَأَرَادَ بِالْغَيْرِ أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ هُوَ إيَّاهُ فَقَدْ صَدَقَ فَإِنَّ الْكَلَامَ الَّذِي يَتَكَلَّمُ بِهِ الْإِنْسَانُ يَتَضَمَّنُ فِعْلًا كَالْحَرَكَةِ وَيَتَضَمَّنُ مَا يَقْتَرِنُ بِالْفِعْلِ مِنْ الْحُرُوفِ وَالْمَعَانِي؛ وَلِهَذَا يُجْعَلُ الْقَوْلُ قَسِيمًا لِلْفِعْلِ تَارَةً وَقِسْمًا مِنْهُ أُخْرَى.
 فَالْأَوَّلُ كَمَا يَقُولُ:
 الْإِيمَانُ قَوْلٌ وَعَمَلٌ. وَمِنْهُ قَوْلُهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{إنَّ اللَّهَ تَجَاوَزَ لِأُمَّتِي مَا حَدَّثَتْ بِهِ أَنْفُسَهَا مَا لَمْ تَتَكَلَّمْ أَوْ تَعْمَلْ بِهِ}
 
" وَمِنْهُ قَوْله تَعَالَى 
{إلَيْهِ يَصْعَدُ الْكَلِمُ الطَّيِّبُ وَالْعَمَلُ الصَّالِحُ يَرْفَعُهُ}
 "
. وَمِنْهُ قَوْله تَعَالَى 
{وَمَا تَكُونُ فِي شَأْنٍ وَمَا تَتْلُو مِنْهُ مِنْ قُرْآنٍ وَلَا تَعْمَلُونَ مِنْ عَمَلٍ}
 وَأَمْثَالِ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا يُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ الْقَوْلِ وَالْعَمَلِ. وَأَمَّا دُخُولُ الْقَوْلِ فِي الْعَمَلِ فَفِي مِثْلِ قَوْله تَعَالَى 
{فَوَرَبِّكَ لَنَسْأَلَنَّهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ}
 
{عَمَّا كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ}
 . أَجْمَعِينَ عَمَّا كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ وَقَدْ فَسَّرُوهُ بِقَوْلِ لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ وَلَمَّا
translated_text:
Allah has, as its recited content, something other than the Quran that He spoke; his error is plain. Likewise, anyone who says that the Quran recited by Muslims is other than what Muslims recite is mistaken.

If, however, by “Quran” he means the verbal noun of qara'a, yaqra'u (“to recite”)—whose forms are qirā'ah and qur'ān (“recitation”)—and says, “I meant that recitation is other than what is recited,” then the word “recitation” is ambiguous. It may mean the Quran itself, or it may mean the act of reciting. Whoever distinguishes “recitation,” understood as the act denoted by the verbal noun, from what is recited—just as one distinguishes speaking, which is one's act, from the speech one utters—and means by “other” that the two are not identical, is correct. For the speech a person utters involves an act, such as movement, as well as the letters and meanings accompanying that act. This is why speech is sometimes contrasted with action and sometimes included within it.

An example of the former is the statement, “Faith is speech and action.” Another is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah has pardoned my community for their inward thoughts, so long as they neither utter them nor act upon them.”

Another is the saying of the Most High:

“To Him ascends good speech, and righteous deeds raise it.”

And His saying:

“You are not engaged in any matter, nor do you recite any of the Quran, nor do you do any deed.”

There are other similar passages that distinguish speech from action. As for speech being included within action, an example is the saying of the Most High:

“So, by your Lord, We will surely question them all about what they used to do.”

All of them, about what they used to do. They have explained this as referring to saying, “There is no god but Allah.” And when

he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked, “Which deed is best?” he replied, “Faith in Allah.” He also said:

“Faith has seventy-odd branches, the highest of which is saying, ‘There is no god but Allah,’ and the lowest is removing harmful things from the road.”

There are many similar examples. On this basis, scholars have disagreed over whether someone who swears not to perform any act breaks his oath by speaking, as in recitation and the like. There are two views on this within the school of Ahmad and among others.

Thus, unless the meanings of these ambiguous and potentially confusing expressions are distinguished, dispute and confusion arise. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, knows best.

He was asked:

“Is the physical copy the Quran itself, or its written form? And is what is in the hearts of the reciters the Quran itself, or their memorization of it?”

He answered:

One must use the expressions used in the Book and the Sunnah, as in the words of Allah Most High:

“Rather, it is a glorious Quran, in a Preserved Tablet.”

And His words:

“Indeed, it is a noble Quran, in a protected Book, which none touch except the purified.”

And His words:

“By the Mount, and by a Book inscribed on parchment spread open.”

And His words:

“Reciting purified pages containing upright writings.”

And the words of Allah Most High:

“No indeed! It is a reminder—so whoever wills may heed it—in honored pages, exalted and purified, in the hands of scribes, noble and righteous.”

Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The Quran must not be taken on a journey into enemy territory.”

And he said:

“Keep refreshing your memory of the Quran, for it escapes from people’s hearts more readily than camels escape their tethers.”

Both reports are in the two Sahih collections. He also said:

“A heart containing nothing of the Quran is like a ruined house.”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “An authentic hadith.”

original_text:
فَمَنْ قَالَ:
 الْقُرْآنُ فِي الْمَصَاحِفِ وَالصُّدُورِ فَقَدْ صَدَقَ وَمَنْ قَالَ: فِيهَا حِفْظُهُ وَكِتَابَتُهُ فَقَدْ صَدَقَ وَمَنْ قَالَ: الْقُرْآنُ مَكْتُوبٌ فِي الْمَصَاحِفِ مَحْفُوظٌ فِي الصُّدُورِ فَقَدْ صَدَقَ وَمَنْ قَالَ: إنَّ الْمِدَادَ أَوْ الْوَرَقَ أَوْ صِفَةَ الْعَبْدِ أَوْ فِعْلَهُ أَوْ حِفْظَهُ وَصَوْتَهُ قَدِيمٌ أَوْ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقٍ فَهُوَ مُخْطِئٌ ضَالٌّ وَمَنْ قَالَ: إنَّ مَا فِي الْمُصْحَفِ لَيْسَ هُوَ كَلَامَ اللَّهِ أَوْ مَا فِي صُدُورِ الْقُرَّاءِ لَيْسَ هُوَ كَلَامَ اللَّهِ أَوْ قَالَ: إنَّ الْقُرْآنَ الْعَزِيزَ لَمْ يَتَكَلَّمْ بِهِ اللَّهُ وَلَكِنْ هُوَ مَخْلُوقٌ أَوْ صَنَّفَهُ جِبْرِيلُ أَوْ مُحَمَّدٌ وَقَالَ: إنَّ الْقُرْآنَ فِي الْمَصَاحِفِ كَمَا أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا فِي التَّوْرَاةِ وَالْإِنْجِيلِ فَهُوَ أَيْضًا مُخْطِئٌ ضَالٌّ. فَإِنَّ الْقُرْآنَ كَلَامٌ وَالْكَلَامُ نَفْسُهُ يُكْتَبُ فِي الْمُصْحَفِ. بِخِلَافِ الْأَعْيَانِ فَإِنَّهُ إنَّمَا يُكْتَبُ اسْمُهَا وَذِكْرُهَا فَالرَّسُولُ مَكْتُوبٌ فِي التَّوْرَاةِ وَالْإِنْجِيلِ ذِكْرُهُ وَنَعْتُهُ كَمَا أَنَّ الْقُرْآنَ فِي زُبُرِ الْأَوَّلِينَ وَكَمَا أَنَّ أَعْمَالَنَا فِي الزُّبُرِ.
 قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{وَإِنَّهُ لَفِي زُبُرِ الْأَوَّلِينَ}
 وَقَالَ تَعَالَى: 
{وَكُلُّ شَيْءٍ فَعَلُوهُ فِي الزُّبُرِ}
 وَمُحَمَّدٌ مَكْتُوبٌ فِي التَّوْرَاةِ وَالْإِنْجِيلِ كَمَا أَنَّ الْقُرْآنَ فِي تِلْكَ الْكُتُبِ وَكَمَا أَنَّ أَعْمَالَنَا فِي الْكُتُبِ وَأَمَّا الْقُرْآنُ فَهُوَ نَفْسُهُ مَكْتُوبٌ فِي الْمَصَاحِفِ لَيْسَ الْمَكْتُوبُ ذِكْرُهُ وَالْخَبَرُ عَنْهُ كَمَا يُكْتَبُ اسْمُ اللَّهِ فِي الْوَرَقِ وَمَنْ لَمْ يُفَرِّقْ بَيْنَ كِتَابَةِ الْأَسْمَاءِ وَالْكَلَامِ وَكِتَابَةِ الْمُسَمَّيَاتِ وَالْأَعْيَانِ - كَمَا جَرَى لِطَائِفَةٍ مِنْ النَّاسِ - فَقَدْ غَلِطَ غَلَطًا سَوَّى فِيهِ بَيْنَ الْحَقَائِقِ الْمُخْتَلِفَةِ كَمَا قَدْ
translated_text:
Thus, whoever says, “The Quran is in physical copies and in people’s hearts,” speaks the truth. Whoever says, “They contain its memorization and its written form,” speaks the truth. Whoever says, “The Quran is written in physical copies and preserved in people’s hearts,” speaks the truth. But whoever says that the ink, paper, a servant’s attribute or action, or his memorization and voice are eternal or uncreated is mistaken and astray.

Likewise, whoever says that what is in the physical copy is not Allah’s speech, or that what is in the reciters’ hearts is not Allah’s speech; or says that Allah did not speak the glorious Quran, but that it is created or was composed by Gabriel or Muhammad, and says, “The Quran is in physical copies just as Muhammad is in the Torah and the Gospel”—such a person is also mistaken and astray.

For the Quran is speech, and speech itself is written in the physical copy. This differs from concrete entities, of which only the names and references to them are written. Thus, what is written of the Messenger in the Torah and the Gospel is his mention and description, just as the Quran is in the scriptures of earlier peoples, and our deeds are in the records.

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, it is in the scriptures of earlier peoples.”

And He says:

“And everything they have done is in the records.”

Muhammad is recorded in the Torah and the Gospel just as the Quran is in those scriptures and our deeds are in the records. As for the Quran, it is itself written in physical copies: what is written is not a mention of it or an account of it, as when Allah’s name is written on paper.

Whoever fails to distinguish between the writing of names and speech and the recording of the things named and concrete entities—as has happened to a group of people—has made an error that equates distinct realities, just as

original_text:
يَجْعَلُ مِثْلُ هَؤُلَاءِ الْحَقَائِقَ الْمُخْتَلِفَةَ شَيْئًا وَاحِدًا كَمَا قَدْ جَعَلُوا جَمِيعَ أَنْوَاعِ الْكَلَامِ مَعْنًى وَاحِدًا. وَكَلَامُ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ يُسْمَعُ تَارَةً مِنْهُ وَتَارَةً مِنْ الْمُبَلِّغِ.
 فَالنَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَمَّا قَالَ:

 فَهَذَا الْكَلَامُ قَالَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِلَفْظِهِ وَمَعْنَاهُ؛ فَلَفْظُهُ لَفْظُ الرَّسُولِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَمَعْنَاهُ مَعْنَى الرَّسُولِ. فَإِذَا بَلَّغَهُ الْمُبَلِّغُ عَنْهُ بَلَّغَ كَلَامَ الرَّسُولِ بِلَفْظِهِ وَمَعْنَاهُ؛ وَلَكِنَّ صَوْتَ الصَّحَابِيِّ الْمُبَلِّغِ لَيْسَ هُوَ صَوْتَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ. فَالْقُرْآنُ كَلَامُ اللَّهِ لَفْظُهُ وَمَعْنَاهُ سَمِعَهُ مِنْهُ جِبْرِيلُ وَبَلَّغَهُ عَنْ اللَّهِ إلَى مُحَمَّدٍ؛
 وَمُحَمَّدٌ سَمِعَهُ مِنْ جِبْرِيلَ وَبَلَّغَهُ إلَى أُمَّتِهِ فَهُوَ كَلَامُ اللَّه حَيْثُ سُمِعَ وَكُتِبَ وَقُرِئَ كَمَا قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{وَإِنْ أَحَدٌ مِنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ اسْتَجَارَكَ فَأَجِرْهُ حَتَّى يَسْمَعَ كَلَامَ اللَّهِ ثُمَّ أَبْلِغْهُ مَأْمَنَهُ}
 . وَكَلَامُ اللَّهِ تَكَلَّمَ اللَّهُ بِهِ بِنَفْسِهِ تَكَلَّمَ بِهِ بِاخْتِيَارِهِ وَقُدْرَتِهِ لَيْسَ مَخْلُوقًا بَائِنًا عَنْهُ. بَلْ هُوَ قَائِمٌ بِذَاتِهِ مَعَ أَنَّهُ تَكَلَّمَ بِهِ بِقُدْرَتِهِ وَمَشِيئَتِهِ لَيْسَ قَائِمًا بِدُونِ قُدْرَتِهِ وَمَشِيئَتِهِ.
translated_text:
such people sometimes treat distinct realities as a single thing, just as they have treated all kinds of speech as a single meaning. A speaker’s words may be heard directly from him or from someone conveying them.

Thus, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Actions are only according to intentions, and each person shall have only what he intended. Whoever’s migration is to Allah and His Messenger, his migration is to Allah and His Messenger. But whoever’s migration is for worldly gain he seeks to obtain or a woman he wishes to marry, his migration is to that for which he migrated,”

these words were spoken by the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in both their wording and their meaning. Their wording is the Messenger’s wording, and their meaning is the Messenger’s meaning. When someone conveys them on his behalf, he conveys the Messenger’s speech in its wording and meaning. Yet the voice of the Companion conveying it is not the voice of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Likewise, the Quran is Allah’s speech in both its wording and its meaning. Gabriel heard it from Him and conveyed it from Allah to Muhammad. Muhammad heard it from Gabriel and conveyed it to his community. It remains Allah’s speech wherever it is heard, written or recited, as Allah Most High says:

“If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection until he hears the speech of Allah, then escort him to a place of safety.”

Allah Himself spoke His speech, speaking it by His choice and power. It is not something created and separate from Him. Rather, it subsists in His essence, while He spoke it by His power and will; it does not subsist independently of His power and will.

وَالسَّلَفُ قَالُوا:

 وَكَانُوا يَقُولُونَ:
 الْقُرْآنُ كَلَامُ اللَّهِ مُنَزَّلٌ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقٍ مِنْهُ بَدَأَ وَإِلَيْهِ يَعُودُ.
 وَلَمْ يَقُلْ أَحَدٌ مِنْهُمْ إنَّ الْقُرْآنَ قَدِيمٌ وَلَا قَالُوا:
 إنَّ كَلَامَهُ مَعْنًى وَاحِدٌ قَائِمٌ بِذَاتِهِ وَلَا قَالُوا: إنَّ حُرُوفَ الْقُرْآنِ أَوْ حُرُوفَهُ وَأَصْوَاتَهُ قَدِيمَةٌ أَزَلِيَّةٌ قَائِمَةٌ بِذَاتِ اللَّهِ وَإِنْ كَانَ جِنْسُ الْحُرُوفِ لَمْ يَزَلْ اللَّهُ مُتَكَلِّمًا بِهَا إذَا شَاءَ؛
 بَلْ قَالُوا:
 إنَّ حُرُوفَ الْقُرْآنِ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقَةٍ وَأَنْكَرُوا عَلَى مَنْ قَالَ: إنَّ اللَّهَ خَلَقَ الْحُرُوفَ.
 وَكَانَ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرُهُ مِنْ السَّلَفِ يُنْكِرُونَ عَلَى مَنْ يَقُولُ:

translated_text:
And the early generations said:

“Allah Most High has always spoken whenever He wills.”

If someone says, “Allah’s speech is eternal,” meaning that He did not become a speaker after not having been a speaker, that His speech is neither created nor a single eternal meaning subsisting in His essence, but that He has always spoken whenever He wills, then this is correct. None of the early generations said that any particular instance of speech was itself eternal.

They used to say:

“The Quran is Allah’s speech, sent down and uncreated. From Him it began, and to Him it returns.”

None of them said that the Quran was eternal, nor did they say that His speech was a single meaning subsisting in His essence. Nor did they say that the letters of the Quran—or its letters and sounds—were eternal and beginningless, subsisting in Allah’s essence, although, with respect to letters as a kind, Allah has always spoken with them whenever He wills. Rather, they said that the letters of the Quran were uncreated, and they condemned anyone who said that Allah created the letters.

Ahmad and others among the early generations condemned anyone who said:

“My utterance of the Quran is created,” or “uncreated.”

They would say:

“Whoever says it is created is a Jahmī, and whoever says it is uncreated is an innovator.”

For “utterance” may refer to the act of uttering—the verbal noun of “to utter”—or it may refer to what is uttered, namely the actual letters spoken. As for people’s voices and the ink in copies of the Quran, none of the early generations hesitated to affirm that these were created. Ahmad explicitly stated that the reciter’s voice is the servant’s voice, as did other leading scholars besides Ahmad.

translated_text:
says, ‘My utterance of the Quran is created,’ meaning the Quran itself, is a Jahmī.”

The human being and all his attributes are created. His movements, actions, and sounds are created, and all his attributes are created. Whoever says that any of the servant’s attributes are uncreated or eternal is mistaken and astray. Whoever says that any of Allah’s speech or attributes is created is likewise mistaken and astray.

As for people’s voices when reciting the Quran and the ink in copies of the Quran, none of the early generations hesitated on this matter. Rather, they all agreed that people’s voices are created, that all ink is created, and that Allah’s speech, which is written with ink, is uncreated. Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought its like as a supplement.’”

These matters have been discussed at length elsewhere, where people’s views and their inconsistencies concerning them have also been set out.

He also said—may Allah sanctify his soul:

Section

The Quran contained between the two covers of the codex is established by mass transmission. The Companions agreed upon these written copies and transmitted them as the Quran from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They have been transmitted by mass transmission since the time of the Companions, and we know with self-evident certainty that they have not been altered.

Any reading transmitted from the early generations and conforming to the codex may be used in recitation, without disagreement among the imams. The imams make no distinction between the readings of Abū Ja'far, Ya'qūb and Khalaf and those of Hamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Abū 'Amr and Nu'aym. None of the early generations or imams of this ummah said that recitation was restricted to the seven reciters.

It was only after three hundred years had elapsed since the Hijrah that Abū Bakr ibn Mujāhid collected the readings of these seven, and people followed his lead. His intention was to select the readings of seven reciters from the various cities. Neither he nor any of the imams said that any reading outside these seven was invalid, or that the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“The Quran was revealed in seven modes,”

referred to the readings of these seven. However,

And Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

As for “the letters,” are they created or uncreated? Disagreement over this is well known among the later generations. As for the early generations, none of them is reported to have said that the letters, wording, or recitation of the Quran are created, or anything implying this.

Indeed, it is established that several of them refuted anyone who said, “Our utterances of the Quran are created.” They said, “He is a Jahmite,” and some declared him an unbeliever. Some used the expression “the recitation of the Quran,” while others used “the letters.”

Among those from whom this is reliably established are Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abū al-Walīd al-Jārūdī, an associate of al-Shāfi‘ī, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, al-Humaydī, Muhammad ibn Aslam al-Tūsī, Hishām ibn ‘Ammār, and Ahmad ibn Sālih al-Misrī. Whoever wishes to consult their exact statements should examine the works compiled on the Sunnah, such as Refutation of the Jahmites by Imam ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Abī Hātim, The Sacred Law by al-Ājurrī, The Elucidation by Ibn Battah, The Sunnah by al-Lālakā’ī, and The Sunnah by al-Tabarānī,

Yet it is established through a reliable chain of transmission that he said:

“Whoever claims that I said, ‘My utterance of the Quran is created,’ has lied.”

The chapter headings towards the end of his Sahīh make this clear.

There are three matters here:

First: The letters of the Quran, which constitute its wording, before Gabriel brought them down and after he brought them down. Whoever says that these are created has contradicted the consensus of the early generations. In their time, no one said this except those who said that the Quran was created. Those people held that its words—the words of the Quran—were created. As for anything beyond that, they do not acknowledge its existence, whether created or uncreated.

More than one leading scholar of dialectical theology has acknowledged this. Among them was ‘Abd al-Karīm al-Shahrastānī, with his extensive knowledge of religions and sects. He stated that the early generations, without qualification, held that the letters of the Quran are uncreated. He said, “The emergence of the view that the Quran originated in time was a later development.” He also expounded the position of the early generations in his book entitled Nihāyat al-Kalām (The Culmination of Dialectical Theology).

Third: The recitation that proceeds audibly from a person following the movement of the verse. Some describe this as created. The first to say this—as far as we have learned—were Husayn al-Karābīsī, his pupil Dāwūd al-Asbahānī, and a group of others. The scholars of the Sunnah at that time rejected their position and spoke very sternly against them. Most of them—those whom the early generations called the Lafziyyah—say, “Our utterance of the Quran is created,” or, “The Quran as uttered by us is created,” and similar statements.

Many scholars of hadith and the Sunnah opposed them, saying, “Our utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” The settled position expressed in the statements of Imam Ahmad and the scholars of his generation was that whoever says, “My utterance of the Quran is created,” is a Jahmī, while whoever says it is uncreated is an innovator. The correct position, according to the overwhelming majority of the people of the Sunnah, is that neither statement should be made without qualification. This was the position of Imam Ahmad and the majority of the early generations, because either unqualified statement can convey an erroneous meaning.

People’s voices unquestionably originate in time, although some who defended the Sunnah denied that the sound heard from a person reciting the Quran was created—the sound corresponding to the amount of the Quran being conveyed. and other leading scholars of guidance. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Adorn the Quran with your voices.”

As for the recited text itself—the letters and words of the Quran—it is uncreated. A servant merely recites Allah’s speech with his own voice. Likewise, when he says, “The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said, ‘Actions are judged only by intentions,’” these words, in both wording and meaning, are the speech of Allah’s Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him; the person has merely conveyed them through his movements and voice. Similarly, the Quran, in both wording and meaning, is the speech of Allah Most High. The creature merely conveys and recites it in his own voice.

No discerning person can fail to recognize the distinction between the recited text itself—before created beings utter it and after they utter it—and the servant’s own acts and deeds in reciting the Quran. Some supporters and opponents alike erred by treating these two distinct matters as one. They sought to prove that the Quran’s letters themselves originated in time by citing evidence that the actions of servants, and what arises from those actions, originate in time. This is among the gravest errors. Neither rational nor scriptural arguments provide evidence that the Quran’s letters themselves originated in time, except arguments of the same kind as those used to argue that its meanings originated in time. The response to the one set of arguments is like the response to the other, for anyone who seeks Allah’s guidance and is guided by Him.

As for the Quranic verses and hadiths concerning the divine attributes which they mentioned, the way of the early generations of this community—the Companions, the Successors, and all the other imams followed as authorities—is to affirm them and accept them as transmitted. It was stated by

Abū Sulaymān al-Khattābī and Abū Bakr al-Khatīb:

“The way of the early generations concerning the Quranic verses and hadiths on the divine attributes is to accept them according to their apparent meaning, without specifying their modality or likening them to creation.”

They also said concerning this:

“Discussion of the attributes follows from discussion of the essence and proceeds along the same lines. Since affirming His essence means affirming its existence, not specifying its modality, affirming His attributes likewise means affirming their existence, not specifying their modality. Thus, we do not say that ‘hand’ means power or that ‘hearing’ means knowledge.”

These are their words.

One of them said:

“If a Jahmī asks you, ‘How does He descend to the lowest heaven?’ ask him, ‘What is the modality of His own essence?’ If he says, ‘We do not know the modality of His essence,’ reply, ‘Nor do we know the modality of His attributes. How could we know the modality of an attribute when we do not know the modality of the One who possesses it?’”

Whoever understands Allah’s attributes as implying origination in time and as being of the same kind as created attributes, then seeks to deny this of Allah, has both likened Him to creation and negated His attributes. Rather, we must describe Allah only as He has described Himself or as His Messenger has described Him, without going beyond the Quran and hadith. We must also know that nothing is like Allah Most High—in His essence, His attributes, or His actions—and that the minds of created beings cannot fully comprehend Him, nor can their tongues adequately describe Him.

“Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they ascribe!
And peace be upon the messengers.
And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.”

May Allah send blessings and peace upon Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

 وَيُرْوَى عَنْ أَبِي بَكْرٍ وَعُمَرَ أَنَّهُمَا قَالَا:
 
" إعْرَابُ الْقُرْآنِ أَحَبُّ إلَيْنَا مِنْ حِفْظِ بَعْضِ حُرُوفِهِ "
 فَإِذَا قَرَأَ الْقَارِئُ 
{الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ}
 كَانَتْ الضَّمَّةُ وَالْفَتْحَةُ وَالْكَسْرَةُ مِنْ تَمَامِ لَفْظِ الْقُرْآنِ. وَإِذَا كَانَ كَذَلِكَ فَالْمِدَادُ الَّذِي يُكْتَبُ بِهِ الشَّكْلُ وَالنَّقْطُ كَالْمِدَادِ الَّذِي
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“What of someone who says that vowel marks and dots are part of the speech of Allah, Blessed and Exalted? Is this true or false? What is the ruling concerning the letters: are they the speech of Allah or not? Explain this to us; may you be rewarded.”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds. In the copies of the Quran written by the Companions, they neither added vowel marks to the letters nor dotted them, for they were Arabs who made no grammatical errors. Later, toward the end of the Companions’ era, when grammatical errors began to appear, people began adding dots and vowel marks to copies of the Quran. Most scholars consider this permissible, and this is one of the two positions reported from Ahmad. Some scholars considered it disliked, but the correct view is that it is not disliked, because there is a need for it.

There is no disagreement among scholars that vowel marks and dots have the same status as the written letters. The dots distinguish the letters from one another, while the vowel marks clarify the grammatical inflections, since these form an integral part of the utterance.

It is reported that Abū Bakr and ‘Umar said:

“Reciting the Quran with correct grammatical inflections is dearer to us than memorizing some of its wording.”

Thus, when a reciter recites:

“Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds,”

the u, a, and i vowel sounds are an integral part of the Quran’s wording as pronounced. Since this is so, the ink used to write the vowel marks and dots is like the ink with which

the letters are written. All the ink is created; none of it is uncreated. The voice with which people recite the Quran is the voice of Allah’s servants, but the speech is the speech of Allah Most High. He says:

“If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of Allah.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Beautify the Quran with your voices.”

Thus, the speech is the Creator’s speech, while the voice is the reciter’s voice. This is not the voice with which Allah calls His servants and which Moses and others hear, as established by the Quran and the Sunnah.

According to the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars, Allah’s speech is uncreated. They also hold that He speaks by His will and power: He has always spoken whenever He wills, and His speech is therefore eternal in kind. As for the particular “call” with which He called Moses, and other such instances, He issued that call to him at that particular time. As He Most High says:

“When he came to it, he was called: ‘O Moses!’”

The same applies to similar instances. Thus, the early generations distinguished between speech as a kind and a particular utterance. He Most High says:

“Say, ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought as much again to replenish it.’”

Allah’s speech, including His calling and all else that falls within His speech, is not a created thing separate from Him; rather, it is from Him. Gabriel heard the Quran from Allah and brought it down to Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He Most High says:

“Say, ‘The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth.’”

He Most High also says:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth.”

And He Most High says:

“The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

There are other similar passages.

" الْمَسَائِلُ "
 مَبْسُوطَةٌ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْجَوَابِ. وَلَكِنْ هَذَا قَدْرُ مَا وَسِعَتْهُ هَذِهِ الْوَرَقَةُ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, conveyed it to the Muslim community, and Muslims hear it from one another. This is not like Moses hearing Allah’s speech, for he heard it without an intermediary. What Muslims recite and write in their copies of the Quran is Allah’s speech, not the speech of anyone else. They recite it with their own voices and write it with their own ink on their own paper. Their actions, voices, and ink are created.

The Quran they recite and write is the uncreated speech of Allah Most High, whether or not they are rewarded for their recitation, and whether they write it with vowel marks and consonant dots or without them. This does not alter the fact that what is written is the Quran—the speech of Allah which He sent down to Muhammad. What is between the two covers is Allah’s speech, whether it has vowel marks and consonant dots or not. Allah’s speech is sent down and uncreated, while the voices of His servants and the ink are created.

The Arabic Quran is Allah’s speech, which He Himself spoke. It is not that part of it is Allah’s speech and part of it is not. Neither Gabriel nor Muhammad had any role in it other than conveying it; neither of them originated any of its letters. Rather, all of it is the speech of Allah, Blessed and Most High.

These “questions” are discussed at length elsewhere, beyond this answer. This, however, is as much as this sheet could accommodate. And Allah knows best.

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

Section

The debate about the “Quran” and “speech”—whether it consists of letters and sound or not—is a later development. It arose around the third century AH and became widespread in the fourth.

When Abū Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb, followed by Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī and others like them, debated the Mu‘tazilah in affirmation of Allah’s attributes and of the Quran being uncreated, they considered that this could only be established if the Quran were eternal, without beginning. They held that it could only be eternal if it were a meaning subsisting in Allah Himself, like His knowledge. They further asserted that Allah does not speak with sound or in any language, whether eternal or otherwise, because they considered it impossible for anything newly occurring to subsist in Him.

In this they differed from the majority of Muslims among the scholars of hadith, jurisprudence, speculative theology, and Sufism, despite their differing grounds. The transmitted reports testify that Allah speaks with sound. For this reason, Imam Ahmad and others declared those who denied this to be Jahmīs.

‘Abdullāh ibn Ahmad said:

“I said to my father: ‘Some people say that Allah does not speak with sound.’

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about two men who debated. One said, “The Quran is letters and sound,” while the other said, “It is neither letters nor sound.” One of them also said, “The dots and vowel marks in the written copy of the Quran are part of the Quran,” while the other said, “They are not part of the Quran.” What is correct concerning this?

He—may Allah be pleased with him—replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. Many people dispute this “question” and mix truth with falsehood concerning it. If the person who says that the Quran is letters and sound means that this Quran which Muslims recite is Allah’s speech, which the Trustworthy Spirit brought down to Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—the last of the prophets and messengers; that Gabriel heard it from Allah, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—heard it from Gabriel, and the Muslims heard it from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—as Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth.’”

And He says:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth.”

Then he is correct in this, for this is the position of the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars. The evidence for it from the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus is abundant.

If anyone says that Allah did not speak the Arabic Quran, but that it is merely the speech of Gabriel or someone else, used to express the meaning subsisting in Allah’s essence—as Ibn Kullāb, al-Ashʿarī, and those who agree with them maintain—then this assertion is false in many respects.

For they say that it is a single meaning subsisting in His essence; that the meaning of the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran is one and the same; and that it is neither multiple nor divisible. They say that if it is expressed in Arabic, it is the Quran; in Hebrew, it is the Torah; and in Syriac, it is the Gospel. Thus, they make the meaning of the Verse of the Throne, the Verse of Debt, “Say, ‘He is Allah, One,’” “May the hands of Abū Lahab perish,” the Torah, the Gospel, and other scriptures all one and the same. This position is invalid according to both reason and revelation. It was introduced by Ibn Kullāb; none of the early generations had preceded him in it.

If, however, the one who speaks of letters and sound means that the voices heard from the reciters and the ink in the written copies of the Quran are eternal and beginningless, then he has erred, introduced an innovation, and said something contrary to reason and revelation. For the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Beautify the Quran with your voices.”

He thus made clear that the voice is the reciter’s voice, while the speech is the Creator’s speech. As Allah Most High says:

“If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of Allah.”

The Quran that Muslims recite is therefore Allah’s speech, not the speech of anyone else, just as Allah has stated. Allah spoke the Quran, with its letters and meanings, in His own voice, and He called to Moses in His own voice, as established by the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations. The imams of Islam—Ahmad and the imams before him—explicitly affirmed what the Book and the Sunnah declare: that Allah calls with a voice; that the Quran is His speech, which He spoke with letters and sound, no part of it being the speech of anyone else, whether Gabriel or another; and that His servants recite it with their own voices and through their own actions. and that He calls His servants in His own voice. They also agree that the voices heard from reciters are the voices of the servants, and that neither the servants’ voices nor the ink in copies of the Quran is beginningless. Rather, the Quran is written in Muslims’ copies, recited by their tongues, and preserved in their hearts, and it is all Allah’s speech.

When the Companions wrote copies of the Quran, they wrote them without vowel marks or dots, because they were Arabs who made no grammatical errors. When such errors arose, people added dots and vowel marks to the copies. Writing them without vowel marks or dots is permissible; writing them with dots and vowel marks is also permissible and is not disliked according to the stronger of the scholars’ two opinions. This is also one of the two positions reported from Ahmad.

“Dots and vowel marks” have the same ruling as the letters: vowel marks indicate the Quran’s grammatical inflections, just as dots distinguish its letters. The ink used to write the letters, vowel marks, and dots is created. But Allah’s Arabic speech, which He revealed and which is written in copies of the Quran, with or without vowel marks and dots, is not created. Grammatical inflections have the same ruling as the letters, but they do not stand independently; rather, they depend on the written letters. There is therefore no need to isolate the two and discuss them separately. Rather, the Quran that Muslims recite is Allah’s speech—its meanings, letters, and grammatical inflections. Allah spoke the Arabic Quran that He revealed to Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and people recite it through their own actions and voices.

What is written in Muslims’ copies of the Quran is Allah’s speech. It is the Arabic Quran that He revealed to His Prophet, whether it is written

with vowel marks and dots or without them. The ink with which the Quran is written is not beginningless; rather, it is created. But the Quran written in the copy with that ink is Allah’s speech, revealed and uncreated. Copies of the Quran must be treated with respect by the consensus of Muslims, because Allah’s speech is written in them. When a copy includes dots and vowel marks, these must be respected just as its letters are, by the consensus of Muslim scholars. Likewise, the Quran’s grammatical inflections have the same sanctity as its dotted letters, by the consensus of Muslims. Hence Abū Bakr and ʿUmar—may Allah be pleased with them both—said: “Preserving the Quran’s grammatical inflections is dearer to us than preserving some of its letters.”

Allah spoke the Quran, its letters and its meanings; all of it is therefore Allah’s speech. It must not be said that some of it is Allah’s speech and some of it is not. He, glorified be He, called to Moses in a voice that Moses heard. He has stated in several places in the Quran that He called to Moses, as in His words, Most High:

“Has the story of Moses reached you?”

“When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwā.”

By the agreement of scholars of the Arabic language, a call can only be made with a voice. The Most High also says:

“Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Tribes, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron and Solomon; and to David We gave the Psalms.”

“And messengers whose stories We have told you before, and messengers whose stories We have not told you. And Allah spoke directly to Moses.”

Thus Allah distinguished between His revelation to the prophets and His speaking to Moses.

Thus, whoever says, “Moses did not hear a voice; rather, its meaning was conveyed to him by inspiration,” has failed to distinguish between Moses and others. Allah Most High says:

“Of those messengers, We favored some over others. Among them were those to whom Allah spoke, and He raised some of them in rank.”

He also says:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills.”

He thus distinguished between revelation and speaking from behind a veil, as Allah spoke to Moses. Whoever equates the two is astray.

Imam Ahmad—may Allah be pleased with him—and other imams said: “Allah has always spoken whenever He wills.” He speaks by His will and power, saying one thing after another, as the Most High says:

“When he came to it, he was called: ‘O Moses!’”

He called to him when he came to it, and did not call to him before that. The Most High also says:

“When they tasted the tree, their nakedness became apparent to them, and they began covering themselves with leaves from Paradise. Their Lord called to them: ‘Did I not forbid you that tree and tell you that Satan is your clear enemy?’”

He, glorified be He, called to them when they ate from it, and did not call to them before that. Likewise, the Most High says:

“We created you, then fashioned you, then said to the angels: ‘Prostrate before Adam.’”

This was after He had created and fashioned Adam; He had not commanded them before that. Likewise, He says:

“Indeed, the likeness of Jesus in Allah’s sight is that of Adam: He created him from dust, then said to him, ‘Be,’ and he is.”

He thus states that He said to him, “Be,” and he is, after He had created him from dust. There are many such accounts in the Quran: He states that He spoke at a particular time and called at a particular time. It has also

is created, insofar as the underlying premise of their doctrine is concerned. For their fundamental premise is that nothing involving choice subsists in the Lord. Thus, neither speech nor action subsists in Him by His choice and will. They said:

“These are occurrences that begin in time, and no such occurrences subsist in the Lord.”

They thereby contradicted authentic revelation and clear reason. They believed that by this they were refuting the philosophers and establishing that the world came into existence. But they were mistaken: they neither defended Islam nor defeated the philosophers. They claimed that, in eternity past, the Lord had no power to utter speech or perform an act, and that He became able after having been unable, without anything new occurring. Or they change their wording and say, “He has always had power.” Yet they say:

“What was within His power was impossible, and acting became possible for Him after it had become impossible for Him, without anything new arising.”

They sometimes express this by saying:

“In eternity past, He had power over what would be possible in the unending future, not over what was impossible in eternity past.”

They thus combine two contradictory claims, affirming that He had power while maintaining that what He had power over was impossible. They failed to distinguish between speech and action as kinds and particular instances of them, just as the philosophers failed to distinguish between the two. Rather, the philosophers claimed that a particular thing He produced was coeternal with Him. In this they went astray and contradicted clear reason and authentic revelation. For the evidence does not establish the eternity of any particular thing in the world. that are conclusive. Clear reason and the general agreement of rational people establish that nothing produced by an agent acting by his will is necessarily inseparable from his essence. Indeed, this holds for every agent: none of his effects is necessarily inseparable from his essence, nor is it conceivable that a particular effect should be simultaneous with him—even supposing that he acts without will. How much more, then, does this apply to an agent who acts by will!

The claim that an effect is simultaneous with its cause is valid only for causes that function as conditions. A condition need not precede what depends upon it; rather, it may accompany it, just as life accompanies knowledge. An agent, however—whether called a cause or not—must precede the particular act, and none of the effects of that particular act can be simultaneous with it. Rational people have never known an agent from whom a particular effect is necessarily inseparable. The statement, “I moved my hand, so the ring moved,” concerns a condition, not an agent.

Furthermore, if the world were eternal, its agent would necessarily produce its effect by virtue of his very essence from eternity, and what he necessitated and entailed would not come after him. Were that so, no event could ever come into being. This contradicts what is observed—even if He, glory be to Him, has always had the power to speak and act; indeed, has always spoken whenever He wills, done whatever He wills, and possessed the attributes of perfection and the qualities of majesty and honor.

translated_text:
events that demonstrate the power of the Lord Most High, even though the Lord is intrinsically worthy of the attributes of perfection. He is worthy of every perfection whose existence is possible and which entails no deficiency, and He is free of every deficiency. He, glory be to Him, has no equal in any respect. He is therefore described in detail by the attributes of perfection, without being likened or equated to others in them, and He is absolutely free of deficiencies. Indeed, attributing deficiencies to Him is among the greatest falsehoods. His perfection is inseparable from His holy essence; He does not acquire it from another. Rather, He bestows His favors upon His creation by bringing them into existence and endowing them with the attributes of living beings. The Creator of the attributes of perfection is all the more worthy of them, and He has no equal in them.

The root of people’s confusion over “the question of Allah’s speech” is that, when the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah debated the philosophers over “the question of the world’s having a beginning,” they believed that anything in which successive attributes and acts subsist must itself have come into being, on the premise that the infinite cannot exist. They consequently accepted that, in pre-eternity, the Lord was incapable of acting and speaking; indeed, that both were impossible for Him, and that He was inactive in both respects.

They sometimes express this by saying that, in pre-eternity, He had the power to act in the everlasting future, although acting in pre-eternity was impossible for Him. Thus, they combine two contradictories, ascribing power to Him while what that power concerns is intrinsically impossible. For an act necessarily entails having a beginning, whereas pre-eternity has no beginning; affirming and denying a beginning at the same time is to combine two contradictories.

translated_text:
They failed to distinguish between what necessarily entails a beginning and coming into existence—namely, a particular act and its particular effect—and what does not, namely, acting and speaking as such. The latter can be perpetual even though each individual instance comes into being, just as they can continue perpetually into the future even though each individual instance passes away. This is unlike a creator whose particular creation is perpetually inseparable from him: that is false according to clear reason and authentic revelation. Hence, the natural dispositions of rational people concur in rejecting it. Only a handful of philosophers disputed this, such as Avicenna and his like, who claimed that a contingent thing produced by an agent could be beginningless and necessarily existent through another. In this they opposed the vast majority of rational people, as well as their predecessors, Aristotle and his followers. The latter did not maintain this, although they held the celestial spheres to be beginningless.

Aristotle was the first of the Peripatetic philosophers to maintain that the spheres were beginningless, basing this on the affirmation of a final cause for the celestial sphere’s motion, which the sphere moves to imitate. They did not affirm an originating agent for it, nor did they affirm anything contingent that was beginningless and necessarily existent through another. Although they were more ignorant of Allah and more deeply steeped in unbelief than their later followers, they conceded to the majority of rational people that whatever is contingent in itself must have come into being after not existing.

They were therefore compelled to say: “His speech is created and separate from Him.”

Another group agreed with them that the existence of an infinity is impossible, but held that acts of choice subsist in Him. They therefore said that in pre-eternity He did not speak, and indeed speech was not even within His power; then He began to speak, with speech subsisting in Him, without any new occurrence. This is the position of the Hāshimiyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, and others.

{وَقُلِ اعْمَلُوا فَسَيَرَى اللَّهُ عَمَلَكُمْ وَرَسُولُهُ وَالْمُؤْمِنُونَ}
 وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ: إنَّهُ لَا يَرَاهَا إذَا وُجِدَتْ؛ بَلْ إمَّا أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَزَلْ رَائِيًا لَهَا وَإِمَّا أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَتَجَدَّدْ شَيْءٌ مَوْجُودٌ بَلْ تَعَلُّقٌ مَعْدُومٌ إلَى أَمْثَالِ هَذِهِ الْمَقَالَاتِ الَّتِي خَالَفُوا فِيهَا نُصُوصَ الْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ مَعَ مُخَالَفَةِ صَرِيحِ الْعَقْلِ.
 وَاَلَّذِي أَلْجَأَهُمْ لِذَلِكَ مُوَافَقَتُهُمْ للجهمية عَلَى أَصْلِ قَوْلِهِمْ فِي أَنَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ لَا يَقْدِرُ فِي الْأَزَلِ عَلَى الْفِعْلِ وَالْكَلَامِ وَخَالَفُوا السَّلَفَ وَالْأَئِمَّةَ فِي قَوْلِهِمْ:
 لَمْ يَزَلْ اللَّهُ مُتَكَلِّمًا إذَا شَاءَ ثُمَّ افْتَرَقُوا أَحْزَابًا أَرْبَعَةً كَمَا تَقَدَّمَ: الخلقية والحدوثية والاتحادية والِاقْتِرَانِيَّةُ.
translated_text:
Another group maintained that if the Quran is uncreated, it must be beginningless as a particular entity and inseparable from the Lord’s essence, so that He does not speak by His will and power. Some of them then said: “It is a single, beginningless meaning.” They thus made the Verse of the Throne, the Verse of Debt, all the other verses of the Quran, the Torah, the Gospel, and every utterance Allah speaks a single meaning admitting neither multiplicity nor division. Others said that it consists of letters and sounds existing simultaneously and inseparable from His essence.

These, too, agreed with the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah on their fundamental claim that He speaks with speech that does not subsist in Him by His will and power, and that no acts of choice subsist in Him. They also held that He did not rise over His Throne after creating the heavens and the earth; that He will not come on the Day of Resurrection; that He did not call Moses when He called him; and that sins do not anger Him, acts of obedience do not please Him, and the repentance of those who repent does not bring Him joy.

Concerning His words:

“Say, ‘Do deeds! Allah will see your deeds, and so will His Messenger and the believers,’”

and similar passages, they said that He does not see those deeds when they come into existence. Rather, either He has always seen them, or nothing existent has newly arisen, but only a nonexistent relation. They made other such statements in which they contradicted the explicit texts of the Book and the Sunnah, as well as clear reason.

What drove them to this was their agreement with the Jahmiyyah’s fundamental claim that He, glorified be He, had no power in pre-eternity to act or speak. They opposed the early generations and the leading scholars, who said: “Allah has always spoken whenever He wills.” They then divided into four factions, as mentioned above: the Khalqiyyah, the Hudūthiyyah, the Ittihādiyyah, and the Iqtirāniyyah.

translated_text:
Worse than these are the Sabians and the philosophers who say that Allah has never spoken—neither with speech subsisting in His essence nor with speech He utters by His will and power: neither speech beginningless in kind nor speech beginningless as a particular entity, neither originated nor created. Rather, His speech, in their view, is what emanates into the souls of the prophets. They say that He spoke to Moses from the heaven of his intellect. They may also say that He, exalted be He, knows universals but not particulars, for He knows them only in a universal manner. Yet they also say that He knows Himself and knows what He does.

Their statement that He knows Himself and what He has brought into existence is true, as He, exalted be He, says:

“Does He who created not know, when He is the Most Subtle, the All-Aware?”

But their further claim that He does not know particular individual entities is ignorance and contradiction. His holy Self is a particular entity, the celestial spheres are particular entities, and everything that exists is a particular entity. If He did not know particulars, He would know nothing that exists, since universals exist as universals only in minds, not in external reality. Thus, whoever knows only universals knows nothing that exists. Exalted is Allah, far above what the wrongdoers say!

What drove them to this deviation was their attempt to avoid affirming the occurrence of new states in the Creator, exalted be He. Yet these same people say that temporal events subsist in that which is beginningless and that temporal events have no beginning. They denied this of the Creator, however, because they believed that He has no attributes, but is instead absolute existence. They said that knowledge is identical with the knower, that power is identical with the one who possesses it, that knowledge and the knower are one and the same, and that the one who wills and the will

translated_text:
are one and the same. Thus they identified each attribute with the others and identified the attributes with the One described by them. Some go further, saying that knowledge is the entirety of what is known, as al-Tūsī, author of Sharh al-Ishārāt (Commentary on the Pointers), maintains. He criticized Ibn Sīnā for affirming that He knows Himself and what proceeds from Himself. Ibn Sīnā was closer to the truth, yet he nevertheless contradicted himself by denying that attributes subsist in Him, identifying the attribute with the One described by it, and identifying every attribute with every other.

Thus these thinkers went further in monism and heresy than those who say that the meanings of speech are one and the same. Yet they argued that their position necessarily followed from the latter’s view, saying: “If multiple meanings can be one and the same, then knowledge can be identical with power, and power with will.” The most astute among the latter acknowledged that there was no answer to this argument.

They then said: “And if one attribute can be identical with another, then the attribute can be identical with the One described by it.” Then came Ibn ʿArabī, Ibn Sabʿīn, al-Qūnawī, and other heretics like them, who said: “If one attribute can be identical with another, and the attribute with the One described by it, then the necessarily existent, beginningless Creator can be identical with the contingently existent, originated creature.” They therefore said that the existence of every creature is identical with the existence of the Creator, and said: “Existence is one.” They did not distinguish between being one in kind and being one

 مَحَلُّ الْمِدَادِ قَدِيمٌ أَزَلِيٌّ.

 الْمِدَادُ قَدِيمٌ أَزَلِيٌّ وَأَكْثَرُهُمْ يَتَكَلَّمُونَ بِلَفْظِ الْقَدِيمِ وَلَا يَفْهَمُونَ مَعْنَاهُ؛ بَلْ مِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَظُنُّ أَنَّ مَعْنَاهُ أَنَّهُ قَدِيمٌ فِي عِلْمِهِ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَظُنُّ أَنَّ مَعْنَاهُ مُتَقَدِّمٌ عَلَى غَيْرِهِ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَظُنُّ أَنَّ مَعْنَى اللَّفْظِ أَنَّهُ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقٍ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ لَا يُمَيِّزُ بَيْنَ مَا يَقُولُ فَصَارَ هَؤُلَاءِ حُلُولِيَّةً اتِّحَادِيَّةً فِي الصِّفَاتِ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَقُولُ بِالْحُلُولِ وَالِاتِّحَادِ فِي
translated_text:
and the same entity, just as those others failed to distinguish between one individual instance of speech and speech of a single kind.

Those who deviated concerning speech ultimately arrived at this negation of the divine attributes, unbelief, and union professed by the proponents of monism, indwelling, and union between the Creator and created beings. Likewise, those who failed to distinguish between speech as a kind and its individual instances, and said that He speaks with beginningless letters and sound, initially maintained that He does not speak by His will and power, and that the letter bā does not precede the letter sīn. Rather, when He called to Moses and said:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me.”

“Indeed, I am Allah, Lord of the worlds.”

the hamza, the nūn, and everything between them had existed together from all eternity, each simultaneous with the others, inseparable from the essence of Allah Most High, without beginning or end.

Then a group among them said that this beginningless speech is identical with the sounds heard from the reciters. Others said, rather, that two sounds are heard: one beginningless and the other originated. Some said that the shapes traced in ink are beginningless and eternal. Others said that the material bearing the ink is beginningless and eternal. It is also related that some of them said that the ink itself is beginningless and eternal.

Most of them use the term qadīm (beginningless) without understanding its meaning. Some think it means that it is beginningless in His knowledge; others think it means that it precedes something else; and others think that the word means uncreated. Still others make no distinctions in what they say. Thus these people became proponents of indwelling and union with respect to the attributes, and some of them affirm indwelling and union in

translated_text:
the essence and the attributes. Both groups ultimately arrived at negation.

The correct position on this matter and others is that of the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars:

He, glorified be He, has always spoken whenever He wills, and He speaks by His will and power. His words have no end. He called to Moses with a voice that Moses heard, and He called to him only when he came, not before that. The Lord’s voice does not resemble the voices of His servants, just as His knowledge does not resemble their knowledge and His power does not resemble their power.

He, glorified be He, is distinct from His creatures in His essence and attributes. Nothing of His essence or of His attributes that subsist in His essence is within His creatures, nor is anything of His creatures within His essence. The views of the proponents of negation and union, who deny the divine essence, attributes, speech, or acts, are false. Likewise, the views of the proponents of indwelling, who affirm indwelling with respect to the essence or the attributes, are false.

These matters are discussed at length elsewhere, and we have expounded them in al-Wājib al-kabīr. Allah knows best what is correct.

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“What should be done with an old copy of the Quran if it becomes torn? If someone writes something from the Quran and then washes it off with water or burns it, does it retain its sanctity or not?”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. An old copy of the Quran, or one that has become so torn that it can no longer be used for reading, should be buried somewhere it will be protected, just as a believer’s body is honoured by being buried somewhere it will be protected.

If something from the Quran or words of remembrance is written in a vessel or on a tablet, then washed off with water or something else, there is no harm in drinking the resulting liquid. Ahmad and others explicitly stated this. They also reported that Ibn ‘Abbās—may Allah be pleased with him and his father—used to write words from the Quran and words of remembrance and instruct that the resulting liquid be given to someone suffering from an illness to drink. This implies that it contains a blessing.

The water used by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for ablution was likewise blessed water. Some of it was poured over Jābir when he was ill, and the Companions used to seek blessings through it. Nevertheless, the Prophet would perform ablution over the earth and elsewhere. No prohibition against pouring such water onto the earth or similar places has reached me, nor do I know of any prohibition concerning this. have the same sanctity as it does while the Quran and words of remembrance remain inscribed. Likewise, if silver, gold or copper were fashioned into the shapes of letters spelling out the Quran or words of remembrance, or a stone were engraved in that form, and the metalwork and stone were subsequently altered, the material would no longer be entitled to the sanctity it had while bearing the writing.

Al-‘Abbās ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib used to say concerning Zamzam water:

“I do not permit its use for bathing, but it is freely lawful for anyone to drink.”

It is also reported that he said:

“For a drinker and one performing ablution.”

For this reason, scholars differed over whether bathing and performing ablution with Zamzam water are disliked, mentioning two views reported from Ahmad. Al-Shāfi‘ī cited the report from al-‘Abbās as evidence, while those who permitted it cited a hadith stating that:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed ablution with Zamzam water.”

The Companions also performed ablution with the water that flowed from between his fingers, despite its blessed nature; however, that was a time of need.

The correct view is that al-‘Abbās’s prohibition concerned bathing alone, not ablution. The distinction between bathing and ablution rests on this consideration: bathing resembles the removal of physical impurity. Thus, whatever must be washed to remove physical impurity must also be washed when purifying oneself from major ritual impurity. Accordingly, there are grounds for protecting these blessed waters from physical impurities, unlike protecting them from earth and other pure substances. And Allah knows best.
